questions.stem: Which of the following has got the highest value of specific speed?
questions.solution:
**Kaplan.**

**The specific speed ranges, which are the whole answer:**

| Turbine | Flow | Energy transfer | Head | Specific speed (metric, rpm) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **PELTON, single jet** | **TANGENTIAL** | **IMPULSE** | **HIGH (300 m and above)** | **LOW: 0-30** |
| **Pelton, multi-jet (3 jets)** | Tangential | Impulse | High | **30-50 — higher than single jet** |
| **FRANCIS** | **RADIAL / mixed** | **REACTION** | **MEDIUM (30-300 m)** | **MEDIUM: 60-300** |
| **Propeller** | **AXIAL** | **REACTION** | **LOW (below 30 m)** | **300-600** |
| **KAPLAN** | **AXIAL** | **REACTION** | **LOW** | **HIGHEST: 600-1000** ← |

> **The trend to fix: LOW specific speed goes with HIGH head, and HIGH specific speed with LOW head.**

> **Kaplan sits at the low-head end, so it has the highest specific speed.**

**Why the trend runs that way — the reasoning, not the memory:**

> **N_s = N√P / H^{5/4}**, so a **large H drives the specific speed DOWN.**

> **Physically: a high-head machine extracts a great deal of energy from a SMALL FLOW**, so it can be small and comparatively slow-turning for its power.

> **A low-head machine must pass a LARGE FLOW to develop the same power**, so it needs a big flow area and runs fast for its head.

> **So specific speed is really a SHAPE parameter — it tells you how the runner must be proportioned**, and the three turbine families are simply the three shapes that work at the three ends of the range.

**Why a MULTI-JET Pelton has a higher specific speed than a single-jet one — this is what option (c) is testing:**

> **Dividing the flow between several jets lets the RUNNER be SMALLER for the same total power.**

> **A smaller runner at the same head turns faster, so N rises and with it N_s.**

> **That is why multi-jet Peltons (up to six jets) are used to adapt a Pelton to a somewhat LOWER head than a single jet would suit** — the machine is stretched down toward the Francis range.

> **But even six jets do not take a Pelton anywhere near a Kaplan's range**, so option (c) is a real refinement and still the wrong answer.

**The Kaplan's defining feature, since it separates it from the propeller turbine:**

> **A KAPLAN has ADJUSTABLE runner blades; a PROPELLER turbine has fixed ones.** Otherwise they are the same machine.

> **A fixed-blade propeller turbine's efficiency COLLAPSES away from its design flow**, because the blade angle no longer matches the flow angle.

> **A Kaplan adjusts BOTH its guide vanes and its runner blades together — "double regulation" — so the angles match at every discharge.**

| Turbine | Efficiency at part load |
|---|---|
| **Propeller (fixed blades)** | **Falls sharply** |
| **KAPLAN (adjustable)** | **Stays high over a WIDE range — a FLAT efficiency curve** ← |
| Francis | Falls moderately |
| **Pelton, multi-jet** | **Stays high — jets shut off individually** |

> **That flat part-load curve is exactly what a LOW-HEAD RIVER installation needs**, where the discharge varies enormously between seasons and the machine must work well at all of them.

**And the selection logic, which is what the classification is for:**

> **HIGH head, LOW flow → PELTON. LOW head, HIGH flow → KAPLAN. In between → FRANCIS.**

> **Nepal's mountain sites are overwhelmingly high-head and low-flow**, which is why the Pelton dominates the country's small and micro-hydro schemes — **and why Kaplan turbines appear mainly on canal-drop and Terai-edge schemes where the head is small and the flow large.**

examTip.trick: **LOW specific speed goes with HIGH head.** Pelton 0-30, Francis 60-300, propeller 300-600, **Kaplan 600-1000** — the highest, at the low-head end.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) is a real refinement**: a MULTI-JET Pelton does have a higher specific speed than a single-jet one, because dividing the flow lets the runner be smaller and faster. It is still nowhere near a Kaplan.
examTip.mnemonic: **Specific speed is a SHAPE parameter** — a high-head machine takes much energy from little flow, so it is small and slow for its power. And **Kaplan = adjustable blades, propeller = fixed**, which is why the Kaplan's efficiency curve stays flat.

questions.stem: If the free haul distance is 200 m, the cost of borrow (including excavation and hauling) is Rs 4/m³ at station, and the cost of haulage beyond free haul is Rs 0.75/m³-station metre, what is the limit of economical haul distance?
questions.solution:
**360 m.**

**Step 1 — convert the haulage cost to a per-metre basis.**

> **ONE STATION = 30 m** (the standard station length in earthwork estimating).

> **Cost of haulage = Rs 0.75 per m³ per STATION = 0.75/30 = Rs 0.025 per m³ per METRE**

> **That conversion is the step the question is really testing**, and forgetting the 30 m station makes the answer wrong by a factor of thirty.

**Step 2 — the economic HAULAGE distance (the extra distance beyond free haul):**

> **EOD = (cost of borrow per m³) ÷ (cost of haul per m³ per metre)**

> **= 4 / 0.025 = 160 m**

> **The logic: hauling is worth doing only while it is CHEAPER THAN BORROWING.** At 160 m beyond the free-haul limit, the accumulated haulage cost has risen to Rs 4/m³ — exactly the cost of simply borrowing the material instead. **Beyond that point, borrow.**

**Step 3 — the economical haul LIMIT:**

> **Limit of economical haul = FREE HAUL distance + economic overhaul distance**

> **= 200 + 160 = 360 m** ✓

> **Option (d) 400 m is what you get by doubling the 160 or by other slips; option (a) 340 m by using 140.** The clean route is 4 ÷ 0.025 = 160, then add 200.

**The three earthwork distances, which must be kept apart:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **FREE HAUL distance** | **The distance within which haulage is INCLUDED in the excavation rate — no extra payment** |
| **OVERHAUL** | **Haulage BEYOND the free haul distance, paid for separately** |
| **ECONOMIC (limit of) HAUL** | **The distance beyond which it is CHEAPER TO BORROW than to haul** ← |

> **The free haul distance is a CONTRACTUAL quantity — it is whatever the contract says, commonly 150 to 300 m.**

> **The economic haul limit is an ENGINEERING quantity — it follows from the relative costs and cannot be negotiated.**

> **Confusing the two is the conceptual error the question guards against: the first is a matter of the bill of quantities, the second of arithmetic.**

**Why this matters — the MASS HAUL DIAGRAM:**

> **On a road project, earthwork is balanced by plotting the CUMULATIVE VOLUME of cut minus fill against the chainage — the MASS HAUL DIAGRAM.**

| Feature of the diagram | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **A RISING curve** | **Cut exceeds fill — material is accumulating** |
| **A FALLING curve** | **Fill exceeds cut — material is needed** |
| **A MAXIMUM or MINIMUM** | **The curve turns where cut changes to fill — a point of no haul** |
| **A horizontal BALANCING LINE** | **Cuts the curve so that cut and fill balance between its ends** |
| **The AREA between the curve and the balancing line** | **The HAUL, in m³-metres — proportional to the transport cost** ← |

> **The area being the haul is the key insight**: minimising the transport cost is minimising that area, which is a geometric problem on the diagram.

> **And the economic haul limit is what decides where a balancing line should be broken**: if hauling material from one cut to a distant fill would exceed the economic limit, **the fill should be supplied from BORROW and the cut sent to SPOIL instead** — even though that looks wasteful.

> **That is a genuinely counter-intuitive conclusion and it is the practical value of the calculation: it is sometimes cheaper to throw material away and buy more than to carry it.**

**And the terms that complete the vocabulary:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **BORROW** | **Material brought in from OUTSIDE the project to make up a shortfall of fill** |
| **SPOIL (waste)** | **Surplus excavated material DISPOSED of rather than used** |
| **LEAD** | The distance material is moved |
| **LIFT** | The vertical distance it is raised |
| **Shrinkage / bulking** | **Excavated material occupies a different volume when compacted — earth typically SHRINKS about 10 %, rock BULKS about 30 %** |

> **The shrinkage and bulking factors are the ones most often forgotten in a volume balance**, and they matter: **1 m³ of cut in soil does not make 1 m³ of compacted fill**, so a diagram plotted on loose volumes will not balance on the ground.

examTip.trick: **ONE STATION = 30 m**, so Rs 0.75/m³-station = Rs 0.025/m³-metre. Then EOD = 4/0.025 = 160 m, and the limit = 200 + 160 = **360 m.**
examTip.trap: **Forgetting the 30 m station makes the answer wrong by a factor of thirty.** And keep the two distances apart: free haul is CONTRACTUAL, the economic limit is ARITHMETIC.
examTip.mnemonic: **Haul only while it is cheaper than borrowing.** On a mass haul diagram the AREA between the curve and the balancing line IS the haul — so it is sometimes cheaper to SPOIL a cut and BORROW for a fill than to carry material across.

questions.stem: The minimum ductility value for paving bitumen is:
questions.solution:
**75 cm.**

**The test and what it measures:**

> **The DUCTILITY TEST measures the distance, in centimetres, to which a standard briquette of bitumen can be STRETCHED before the thread breaks.**

| Condition | Value |
|---|---|
| **Temperature** | **27 °C** |
| **Rate of pull** | **50 mm per minute** |
| **Specimen** | A briquette moulded to a standard shape |
| **Result** | **The elongation at break, in cm** |
| **Minimum for paving bitumen (BIS)** | **75 cm** ← |

> **The source states it plainly: a minimum ductility value of 75 cm has been specified by the BIS.**

**Why ductility matters — what a brittle binder does:**

> **A pavement is not a static structure. It FLEXES under every wheel, and it expands and contracts with temperature.**

> **A binder must be able to STRETCH with those movements without breaking.**

| Consequence of LOW ductility | Note |
|---|---|
| **CRACKING under repeated flexing** | **The binder cannot follow the pavement's movement, so the film ruptures** ← |
| **Loss of the aggregate-binder bond** | Once cracked, water enters and STRIPS the binder |
| **Ravelling** | Aggregate is lost from the surface |
| **Poor performance at low temperature** | Where the binder is stiffest and least ductile |

> **So ductility is a measure of the binder's ability to accommodate MOVEMENT**, and it is the property that governs the pavement's resistance to cracking rather than to deformation.

> **Which is why it is specified alongside penetration: penetration tells you how STIFF the binder is, and ductility tells you how far it can STRETCH before it fails.** Two different requirements, and a binder can pass one and fail the other.

**How ductility relates to the other properties:**

| Relation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Ductility generally RISES with penetration** | **A softer binder stretches further** |
| **Ductility FALLS as the binder AGES** | **Oxidation and loss of volatiles make it brittle — the principal ageing mechanism** ← |
| **Ductility falls with temperature** | Which is why the test is at a controlled 27 °C |
| Ductility falls with excessive heating during mixing | Overheating ages the binder prematurely |

> **The ageing row is the practically important one.** A bitumen that meets 75 cm when supplied may fall well below it after years in the road — **and that loss of ductility is precisely what produces the AGE-RELATED BLOCK CRACKING seen on old surfaces.**

> **It is also why overheating bitumen in the boiler is a serious site error rather than an inefficiency: heating above about 175 °C ages the binder in hours**, delivering a material that already fails the ductility requirement before it reaches the road.

**The bitumen test family, since they are examined as a set:**

| Test | Measures | Typical requirement |
|---|---|---|
| **PENETRATION** | **Consistency at 25 °C, in units of 0.1 mm** | **The grading test — e.g. 80/100** |
| **DUCTILITY** | **Elongation at break at 27 °C** | **Minimum 75 cm** ← |
| **SOFTENING POINT (ring and ball)** | **Temperature at which it flows** | **35-70 °C** |
| **VISCOSITY** | Resistance to flow | Basis of VG grading |
| **FLASH and FIRE POINT** | **Safe heating temperature** | **Flash point above ~175 °C — a SAFETY test** |
| **Specific gravity** | Density | 0.97-1.02 |
| **Loss on heating** | Volatile content | A durability indicator |
| **Stripping value** | **Adhesion to aggregate in the presence of WATER** | **Maximum 25 %** |

> **Note that penetration and softening point move in OPPOSITE directions** — a high-penetration (soft) bitumen has a LOW softening point — **so either can be inferred from the other.**

> **And the FLASH POINT is a safety requirement rather than a performance one**: it is the temperature at which the vapour above heated bitumen will ignite, and it sets the absolute ceiling on boiler temperature. **The 175 °C figure is not advice; it is a limit.**

**Why the distractors are wrong:** **50, 60 and 100 cm are plausible-looking round figures with no standing in the specification.** The question tests a recalled BIS value, and **the anchor to fix is 75 cm at 27 °C, pulled at 50 mm per minute.**

examTip.trick: **75 cm minimum, at 27 °C, pulled at 50 mm/min.** Ductility measures how far the binder STRETCHES before breaking — its ability to follow the pavement's movement.
examTip.trap: **Penetration and ductility are different requirements**: penetration says how STIFF the binder is, ductility how far it can STRETCH. A binder can pass one and fail the other.
examTip.mnemonic: **Ductility FALLS as bitumen ages** — which is what produces age-related BLOCK CRACKING. And overheating above ~175 °C ages it in hours, so the flash point is a limit, not advice.

questions.stem: The critical path is:
questions.solution:
**Always the longest path.**

**The definition, and the apparent paradox it contains:**

> **The CRITICAL PATH is the LONGEST path through the network, measured in TIME.**

> **And its length is the SHORTEST POSSIBLE PROJECT DURATION.**

> **Those two statements sound contradictory and are not, which is the whole content of the question.**

**Why the longest path sets the shortest duration:**

> **Every path through the network must be completed for the project to finish.**

> **So the project cannot finish before the SLOWEST path is done.**

> **The longest path is therefore the binding constraint — it is what the project duration is** — and no amount of accelerating the other paths will shorten it.

> **The source's own explanation puts it exactly: the critical path is the longest path requiring the maximum amount of time, but it represents the MINIMUM duration required to complete the project.**

> **The resolution is that "longest" describes the PATH and "shortest" describes the PROJECT.** They are statements about different things.

**The equivalent definition, which is often more useful:**

> **The critical path is the chain of activities with ZERO TOTAL FLOAT.**

> **Those two descriptions are exactly equivalent, and holding both makes most network questions immediate:**

| Question | Which definition to use |
|---|---|
| **What is the project duration?** | **The LENGTH of the longest path** |
| **Which activities are critical?** | **Those with zero total float** |
| **Can this activity be delayed?** | Its total float |
| **How do I shorten the project?** | **Shorten an activity ON the critical path** ← |

> **The last row is the practical payoff of the whole technique: accelerating an activity NOT on the critical path achieves nothing at all.** It merely increases that activity's float.

> **Which is why identifying the critical path is the first step of any acceleration exercise, and why "working harder on everything" is a demonstrably wasteful response to a late project.**

**Why options (c) and (d) are wrong — the words "maybe" and "always":**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Always the shortest path** | **Exactly inverted** |
| **Always the longest path** | ✓ |
| **Maybe the shortest path** | **It is never the shortest, unless every path has the same length** |
| **Maybe the longest path** | **Too weak — it is ALWAYS the longest, by definition** ← |

> **Option (d) is the designed near-miss and rewards care: it states a true-but-insufficient claim.**

> **"Maybe the longest" is not wrong as a matter of fact; it is wrong as a definition**, because the critical path is the longest path by construction rather than by coincidence. **A question asking what something IS wants the definition, not a probability.**

> **That is a reading skill worth naming: when one option states a fact weakly and another states it as a rule, and the thing genuinely is a rule, the rule is the answer.**

**A qualification worth knowing, since it is where the concept gets interesting:**

> **A network can have MORE THAN ONE critical path.** If two paths have the same length, both are critical and both have zero float.

> **And the critical path can CHANGE during a project**, for two reasons:

| Cause | Effect |
|---|---|
| **An activity overruns** | **A previously non-critical path can become the longest** |
| **The critical path is CRASHED (shortened)** | **Once it is shortened past the second-longest path, THAT path becomes critical** ← |

> **The second is the crucial one for anyone accelerating a project: crashing the critical path only helps until another path takes over.**

> **So acceleration is iterative — shorten the critical path, re-identify it, shorten again** — and the cost per day saved RISES at each step, because eventually several paths must be shortened together.

> **That rising cost is what makes the TIME-COST TRADE-OFF analysis necessary, and it is why there is an optimum project duration rather than simply "as fast as possible".**

**And the vocabulary that accompanies it:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Forward pass** | **EF = ES + D; gives the earliest times** |
| **Backward pass** | **LS = LF − D; gives the latest times** |
| **TOTAL float** | **LF − EF; delay possible without delaying the PROJECT** |
| **FREE float** | Delay possible without delaying any successor |
| **CRASHING** | **Deliberately shortening an activity at extra cost** |
| **Dummy activity** | Shows dependence without consuming time or resource |

> **Note that a critical activity has zero total float and therefore zero free float too** — since free float can never exceed total float. **So every critical activity delays both the project and its successors if it slips.**

examTip.trick: **The LONGEST path sets the SHORTEST project duration** — no contradiction, because "longest" describes the PATH and "shortest" the PROJECT. Every path must finish, so the slowest binds.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) "maybe the longest" is true-but-insufficient.** The critical path is the longest BY DEFINITION, not by coincidence — and a question asking what something IS wants the rule.
examTip.mnemonic: **Accelerating an activity NOT on the critical path achieves nothing.** And crashing only helps until the SECOND-longest path takes over — which is why acceleration is iterative and its cost per day RISES.

questions.stem: The function of a surge tank is to:
options: relieve water hammer pressures in the penstock pipe
questions.solution:
**To relieve water hammer pressures in the penstock pipe.**

**What water hammer is and why it must be relieved:**

> **When the turbine's gates CLOSE SUDDENLY — on load rejection or a machine trip — the moving column of water in the conduit is decelerated abruptly.**

> **A column of water in motion has momentum and cannot stop instantly, so the pressure at the closed valve rises sharply and a pressure wave travels back up the conduit.**

> **That is WATER HAMMER, and the magnitude is startling:**

> **Joukowsky's equation for instantaneous closure: Δh = (a/g) × V**, with the wave speed a = 900-1200 m/s in a steel penstock.

> **For V = 4 m/s and a = 1000 m/s: Δh = (1000/9.81) × 4 ≈ 408 m of head.**

> **A pressure rise of four hundred metres from a four-metre-per-second flow** — comparable with or greater than the static head on many plants. **A conduit designed for static head alone would burst on the first load rejection.**

> **The surge tank gives the water somewhere to go: it rises up the open shaft, converting the excess pressure into a rise in level.**

**The second function, which the option list does not mention but which matters equally:**

> **On LOAD ACCEPTANCE — gates opening suddenly — the turbine demands water faster than the long tunnel can accelerate it.**

> **The pressure at the penstock inlet DROPS, risking column separation.**

> **The tank SUPPLIES water immediately from its own volume until the tunnel flow catches up.**

> **So the tank both absorbs and supplies — it is a hydraulic FLYWHEEL** — and without the supplying function a sudden demand would draw a negative pressure whose subsequent rejoining produces worse hammer than the original event.

**Why option (a) is the substantive distractor:**

> **"Supply water at constant pressure" is close to something true — the tank does stabilise the pressure at the penstock inlet — but it misdescribes the mechanism.**

> **The tank does not MAINTAIN a constant pressure; it LIMITS the EXCURSIONS from the steady value.** Its level oscillates, and the oscillation is precisely what absorbs the surge.

> **A device that held the pressure genuinely constant would have to be infinitely large.** The tank works by moving, not by being rigid.

> **And option (c) inverts the purpose entirely: the tank ABSORBS surges rather than producing them.** It is worth noting that a badly designed surge tank CAN produce sustained oscillations — but that is a failure, not a function.

**Where the tank must be placed, and why:**

> **AS CLOSE TO THE POWERHOUSE AS THE TOPOGRAPHY ALLOWS** — where a long, low-pressure headrace tunnel meets the steep penstock.

> **The pressure rise depends on the LENGTH of the column being decelerated.**

> **The tank cuts the effective column length to the PENSTOCK ALONE, leaving the long tunnel to see only slow, gentle surges.**

> **That division of duty is the design idea: the TUNNEL is protected by the tank, and the PENSTOCK is designed to take the hammer.**

> **Which is why a surge tank is needed only where the conduit is LONG** — a plant whose penstock runs straight from the intake needs none, and many small run-of-river schemes on steep ground have none.

**The types, and the trade-off between them:**

| Type | Feature |
|---|---|
| **SIMPLE** | **A plain vertical shaft — largest oscillations, slowest damping** |
| **RESTRICTED ORIFICE (throttled)** | **An orifice at the base dissipates energy — smaller oscillations, but a HIGHER initial pressure rise** |
| **DIFFERENTIAL (Johnson)** | **A riser inside the tank — fast response AND good damping; the most effective** |
| Expansion chamber | Widened at top and bottom |
| Inclined | Follows the hillside; more effective surface area |

> **The throttled type shows a genuine trade-off: the orifice damps faster but transmits a higher initial spike**, because the water cannot enter the tank freely. **Quick damping or a low peak — not both, unless the tank is differential.**

> **The DIFFERENTIAL type resolves it with two elements: a narrow riser that reacts instantly to pressure, and a wide chamber that absorbs volume.**

**And the discrimination examiners most often want here:**

| | **FOREBAY** | **SURGE TANK** |
|---|---|---|
| **Located on** | **An open CANAL system** | **A closed TUNNEL system** |
| **Purpose** | **STORE water for load fluctuations; settle silt; house the trashrack** | **Absorb PRESSURE surges** |
| **Sized by** | Volume of storage needed | **Amplitude of the surge** |

> **Forebay for a canal, surge tank for a tunnel.** Both are open to atmosphere and both hold water, which is why they are confused — **the difference is what they are sized for.**

examTip.trick: **Joukowsky: Δh = aV/g.** At a = 1000 m/s and V = 4 m/s that is 400 m of head — often more than the static head. The tank gives the water somewhere to go.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) misdescribes the mechanism.** The tank does not HOLD the pressure constant; it LIMITS the excursions, by moving. A device that held it truly constant would have to be infinitely large.
examTip.mnemonic: **It works BOTH ways** — absorbing on load rejection and SUPPLYING on load acceptance, a hydraulic flywheel. Place it near the powerhouse so it cuts the decelerating column to the PENSTOCK alone.

questions.stem: The surface overflow rate (SOR) of a plain sedimentation tank is:
questions.solution:
**12,000 to 18,000 litres per day per square metre.**

**What the surface overflow rate is:**

> **SOR = (rate of flow) ÷ (SURFACE AREA of the tank)**

> **It has the units of a VELOCITY — volume per unit area per unit time — and that is the key to the whole concept.**

> **Converting: 12,000-18,000 l/day/m² = 500-750 litres per hour per m² = 0.5-0.75 m³/h/m² = about 0.14-0.21 mm/s.**

> **The source gives the hourly form directly: plain sedimentation 500-750 l/hr/m².**

**The values with and without coagulation:**

| Tank | SOR |
|---|---|
| **PLAIN sedimentation** | **12,000-18,000 l/day/m² (500-750 l/hr/m²)** ← |
| **Sedimentation WITH COAGULATION (clariflocculator)** | **24,000-30,000 l/day/m² (1000-1250 l/hr/m²)** |

> **Coagulation roughly DOUBLES the permissible overflow rate**, and the reason is direct: **coagulation and flocculation combine fine particles into much larger FLOC, and larger particles settle faster.**

> **So a coagulated tank can be run at twice the rate — or, equivalently, can be half the size for the same flow.** That is the economic case for coagulation, quite apart from its effect on water quality.

> **Options (c) and (d) lie in the coagulated range and above, which is what makes them plausible distractors: they are real numbers for a different tank.**

**Why SOR is THE design parameter — and this is the important idea:**

> **Because SOR has the dimensions of a velocity, it can be compared directly with a particle's SETTLING VELOCITY.**

| Comparison | Result |
|---|---|
| **Settling velocity ≥ SOR** | **100 % of those particles are REMOVED** |
| **Settling velocity < SOR** | **Removal = (Vs / Vo) × 100 %** |

> **The source gives exactly this table, and it is the whole theory of ideal settling.**

> **The consequence is remarkable and worth stating plainly: for an ideal settling tank, REMOVAL EFFICIENCY DEPENDS ONLY ON THE SURFACE AREA — not on the depth, and not on the detention time.**

> **The reason is geometric: a particle settling at Vs falls the tank's depth H in time H/Vs, and it is carried the tank's length in the detention time. Working the geometry through, the depth cancels.**

> **So doubling the depth of a settling tank does NOT improve its performance**, while doubling its area does. **That is genuinely counter-intuitive and it is the single most useful result in the topic.**

**Why tanks nonetheless have a specified depth:**

| Reason for depth | Note |
|---|---|
| **SLUDGE STORAGE at the bottom** | The settled solids must go somewhere between removals |
| **Avoiding SCOUR of settled sludge** | A shallow tank has higher horizontal velocity for the same flow |
| **Inlet and outlet turbulence** | Needs depth to dissipate |
| **Wind-induced currents** | Disturb a shallow tank more |
| Structural and practical | — |

> **So the ideal theory says depth is irrelevant and practice requires it anyway — for reasons the ideal theory does not model.** Typical depths are 3 to 4.5 m.

**The other design parameters, since SOR alone does not size a tank:**

| Parameter | Typical value |
|---|---|
| **DETENTION TIME** | **2-6 hours (plain); 2-4 hours (with coagulation)** |
| **SURFACE OVERFLOW RATE** | **12,000-18,000 l/day/m²** ← |
| **HORIZONTAL VELOCITY** | **0.15-0.9 m/min — must be low enough not to SCOUR settled sludge** |
| **WEIR LOADING rate** | 150-300 m³/day per metre of weir |
| **Depth** | 3-4.5 m |
| **Length : width** | 3:1 to 5:1 |
| **Removal achieved** | **60-70 % of suspended solids; 30-40 % of BOD (for sewage)** |

> **The length-to-width ratio matters because SHORT-CIRCUITING is the practical enemy of a settling tank**: if water finds a fast route from inlet to outlet, part of the tank does no work and the effective SOR is much higher than the nominal one.

> **A long narrow tank, with well-designed inlet baffles to spread the flow, is what prevents it** — and it is why a tank's measured performance is usually worse than the ideal theory predicts.

**And the classification of settling, since the ideal theory covers only the first kind:**

| Type | Description | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Type I — DISCRETE (free) settling** | **Particles settle independently at constant velocity** | **Plain sedimentation; grit chambers — the ideal theory applies** |
| **Type II — FLOCCULENT settling** | **Particles coalesce as they fall, so they ACCELERATE** | Coagulated tanks; primary sedimentation |
| **Type III — ZONE (hindered) settling** | **The whole mass settles as a blanket with a distinct interface** | **Secondary clarifiers in activated sludge** |
| **Type IV — COMPRESSION** | The sludge layer consolidates under its own weight | Sludge thickeners |

> **Type I is the only one the surface-overflow-rate theory strictly describes**, which is why coagulated and secondary tanks are designed against SOLIDS LOADING as well — the settled sludge's own behaviour becomes the constraint.

examTip.trick: **12,000-18,000 l/day/m² plain; 24,000-30,000 with COAGULATION** — roughly double, because floc is larger and settles faster. Options (c) and (d) are the coagulated range.
examTip.trap: **SOR has the dimensions of a VELOCITY**, so it compares directly with a particle's settling velocity. Which gives the counter-intuitive result: **removal depends only on SURFACE AREA, not on depth or detention time.**
examTip.mnemonic: **Doubling the depth does NOT improve performance; doubling the area does.** Depth is provided for SLUDGE STORAGE and to avoid scour — reasons the ideal theory does not model. And short-circuiting is the practical enemy.

questions.stem: Which of the following methods of contouring is most suitable for a hilly terrain?
questions.solution:
**The tachometric method.**

**Why tachometry suits hills — the reason is the number of instrument set-ups:**

> **A TACHEOMETER measures DISTANCE and ELEVATION together, by observing the staff intercept — so both are obtained from one angular observation.**

> **Because it measures distance optically rather than by tape, it can command points FAR from the instrument and OVER BROKEN GROUND.**

> **The source states the argument exactly: the number of stations that can be commanded by a tachometer is far more than by a level, so the number of instrument settings is considerably reduced.**

> **That is the decisive advantage in hills.** Chaining and levelling across steep, broken ground requires a set-up every few tens of metres — **and each set-up costs time and introduces error.**

**The methods compared:**

| Method | How it works | Suits | Speed |
|---|---|---|---|
| **DIRECT (radial / cross-section)** | **Points ON the contour are located and staked in the field, then joined** | **Small areas needing high accuracy** | **Very SLOW and tedious** |
| **SQUARE (grid) method** | **A grid is laid out and the RL of every grid point taken; contours interpolated** | **PLAIN, open ground of small extent** | Moderate |
| **CROSS-SECTIONS method** | **Sections taken at right angles to a centre line; RLs plotted and interpolated** | **ROUTE surveys — roads, railways, canals** | Moderate |
| **TACHOMETRIC method** | **Distance and elevation from one angular observation; contours interpolated** | **HILLY and broken terrain** | **FAST — fewest set-ups** ← |

> **The DIRECT method is the accurate one and the slow one: it locates points that actually lie on each contour, so no interpolation is needed** — but finding those points by trial in the field is laborious, and in hills it is impractical.

> **All the others are INDIRECT: they take spot levels at convenient points and INTERPOLATE the contours afterwards.** That is why they are quicker and slightly less accurate.

**The distinction that organises the whole topic:**

| | **DIRECT contouring** | **INDIRECT contouring** |
|---|---|---|
| **What is located** | **Points ON the contours themselves** | **Spot heights at convenient points** |
| **Contours obtained by** | **Joining the located points** | **INTERPOLATION between spot heights** |
| **Accuracy** | **Higher** | Adequate |
| **Speed** | **Slow** | **Fast** |
| **Methods** | Radial lines, cross-sections along a line | **Square/grid, cross-sections, TACHOMETRIC** |

> **Note that "cross-sections" appears in both columns in some texts**, depending on whether contour points are staked out or merely levelled — which is a genuine ambiguity in the terminology and worth knowing when reading different books.

**Contour interval, since it is the companion decision:**

| Factor | Effect on the interval |
|---|---|
| **Scale of the map** | **Larger scale → SMALLER interval** |
| **Nature of the ground** | **FLAT ground → small interval; STEEP ground → large interval** ← |
| **Purpose of the survey** | Detailed design needs a small interval |
| **Time and funds available** | A small interval costs more |

> **The steep-ground row is the one to reason about: on steep ground a small contour interval crowds the lines together until the map is unreadable**, so a larger interval is used.

| Terrain and purpose | Typical contour interval |
|---|---|
| **Building site, flat ground** | **0.2-0.5 m** |
| **Town planning, gentle slopes** | **0.5-2 m** |
| **Reservoir and dam surveys** | 2-3 m |
| **HILLY terrain, small-scale maps** | **5-25 m** |

**The properties of contours, since they are examined alongside:**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **Contours CLOSE together** | **STEEP slope** |
| **Contours WIDE apart** | Gentle slope |
| **EQUALLY spaced contours** | **UNIFORM slope** |
| **Contours NEVER cross** | **Except at an overhanging cliff** |
| **A contour closing on itself** | **A HILL or a DEPRESSION — distinguished by the direction the values increase** |
| **Contours cross a RIDGE or VALLEY at right angles** | **A V pointing UPHILL is a VALLEY; pointing DOWNHILL is a RIDGE** ← |
| Contours are perpendicular to the steepest slope | By definition |

> **The V-shape rule is the most useful one for reading a map: the V of a contour crossing a stream points UPSTREAM, that is, uphill.** A ridge's contours point downhill.

> **Getting that backwards inverts the whole landscape**, and it is the commonest error in interpreting a contour map — **so it is worth checking against a known watercourse whenever a map is read.**

examTip.trick: **A tachometer gets distance AND elevation from one observation and commands distant points over broken ground** — so it needs far fewer set-ups, which is what matters in hills.
examTip.trap: **The DIRECT method is the ACCURATE one and the SLOW one** — it locates points actually on the contours, needing no interpolation. In hills that is impractical, which is why an indirect method wins.
examTip.mnemonic: **Steep ground needs a LARGER contour interval**, or the lines crowd unreadably. And reading a map: **a contour V pointing UPHILL is a VALLEY, downhill is a RIDGE** — get it backwards and the whole landscape inverts.

questions.stem: For the Benkelman beam deflection test, the deflection measurement point for a single lane is:
questions.solution:
**0.6 m from the edge.**

**The rule, which depends on the lane width:**

| Lane width | Measurement point |
|---|---|
| **3.5 m OR LESS (single lane)** | **0.6 m from the pavement EDGE** ← |
| **MORE than 3.5 m** | **0.9 m from the edge** |

> **The source states it exactly: for lane width 3.5 m or less it is measured 0.6 m from the edge; for more than 3.5 m, at 0.9 m from the edge.**

> **Note that BOTH figures are measured from the EDGE, not from the centre** — which is what disposes of options (c) and (d) at once.

**Why measure from the edge, and why at that particular offset:**

> **The measurement point must represent the position where the WHEEL PATH actually falls**, because deflection is what a wheel load causes and the wheel does not run down the centre line.

> **On a narrow lane, vehicles run closer to the edge; on a wide one, further from it.** Hence the two offsets.

> **And the EDGE is the correct datum because it is the fixed, identifiable feature** — the centre line of a single-lane road is not marked and the road may not be symmetrical about it.

> **There is a second and more important reason: the pavement EDGE is its WEAKEST part.**

| Why the edge is weakest | Note |
|---|---|
| **Less LATERAL CONFINEMENT** | **A granular layer derives its strength from confinement, and at the edge there is soil or shoulder on one side only** ← |
| **Poorer compaction at the edge** | The roller cannot work as effectively at a free edge |
| **Drainage water concentrates there** | The camber sheds water to the edge |
| **Shoulder may be weaker or unsealed** | Little support |

> **So measuring near the edge is measuring near the critical location**, which is what a strengthening design should be based on. **A deflection taken at the centre line would flatter the pavement.**

> **And it explains the characteristic failure of a road with poor shoulders: EDGE FAILURE, the pavement crumbling inward from its boundary.**

**The rest of the test, since this is one detail of it:**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Axle load** | **8170 kg (80 kN)** |
| **Tyre pressure** | **5.6 kg/cm²** |
| **Beam total length** | **3.66 m** |
| **Pivot to probe** | **2.44 m** |
| **Pivot to dial gauge** | **1.22 m** |
| **Lever ratio** | **2 : 1 — every dial reading is DOUBLED** |
| **Readings** | **Initial (Do), intermediate at 2.7 m (Di), final at 9 m (Df)** |

> **It measures REBOUND — the elastic recovery as the truck moves away — not the deflection under load.**

**The corrections, which are where the marks are:**

> **True deflection D = 2(Do − Df).**

> **LEG CORRECTION, if (Di − Df) > 0.025 mm:  D = 2[(Do − Df) + 2.91(Di − Df)]** — applied because the beam's own legs were sitting on deflected pavement.

> **TEMPERATURE correction to 35 °C**: bitumen is stiffer when cold, so a cold-weather deflection UNDERSTATES the true value.

> **SEASONAL correction**: the subgrade is weakest just after the monsoon, so a dry-season test must be factored UP.

> **Both corrections matter more than they look. A deflection measured in a cold, dry January and used untreated makes a weak pavement look adequate — and the overlay designed from it fails in the first monsoon.**

**What the result is used for:**

> **CHARACTERISTIC DEFLECTION = mean + 2 standard deviations** (mean + 1 SD for lesser roads), over at least ten points on a homogeneous section.

> **That figure, entered in the IRC 81 chart with the design traffic, gives the required OVERLAY THICKNESS.**

> **So the whole purpose is STRENGTHENING design of an existing pavement — it answers "how much overlay?" without excavating anything.**

> **The statistical treatment matters: an overlay designed for the AVERAGE deflection would be inadequate over the weakest half of the road.** Taking mean + 2SD designs for roughly the worst 2.5 per cent, which is a deliberate decision about how much of the road may fail early.

> **And it is why at least ten points are required — a standard deviation from three readings is meaningless.**

examTip.trick: **0.6 m from the edge for lanes 3.5 m or less; 0.9 m for wider.** Both are from the EDGE, which disposes of the two "from center" options at once.
examTip.trap: **The offsets represent where the WHEEL PATH actually falls** — closer to the edge on a narrow lane. And the edge is the pavement's WEAKEST part, from lack of lateral confinement, so measuring there is measuring the critical location.
examTip.mnemonic: **Correct to 35 °C and for season, then take mean + 2SD over at least ten points** → IRC 81 gives the overlay. An uncorrected cold, dry-season reading makes a weak pavement look adequate.

questions.stem: A bitumen with a penetration of 8.3 mm falls under which grade?
questions.solution:
**80/100.**

**The reasoning:**

> **The penetration grade is named after the RANGE of penetration, expressed in units of ONE TENTH OF A MILLIMETRE.**

> **Grade 80/100 therefore means a penetration between 8.0 mm and 10.0 mm.**

> **8.3 mm lies inside that band, so the bitumen is grade 80/100.** ✓

> **The source states it directly: grade 80/100 means penetration 8 to 10 mm, so 8.3 falls between those values.**

**Why the other options fail:**

| Option | Range implied | Does 8.3 mm fall in it? |
|---|---|---|
| **85/90** | **8.5 to 9.0 mm** | **NO — 8.3 is BELOW 8.5** ← the closest miss |
| **85** | **A single value, 8.5 mm** | **NO — and a grade is a RANGE, not a value** |
| **80/100** | **8.0 to 10.0 mm** | **YES** ✓ |
| **85/100** | **8.5 to 10.0 mm** | **NO — again below the lower bound** |

> **Options (a) and (d) are the well-made distractors, and both fail for the same reason: 8.3 is BELOW their lower limit of 8.5.**

> **So the question is entirely about checking the LOWER bound**, and a candidate who checks only that 8.3 is below 10 will find three options that appear to qualify.

> **That is the discipline the question rewards: a range has TWO limits, and both must be checked.**

> **Option (b) "85" also fails on a structural ground: a penetration grade is always a BAND, written as two numbers, because bitumen's consistency varies from batch to batch and no refinery can deliver a single exact value.**

**A note on the stem's wording, which is loose:**

> **The stem asks for a "viscosity grade", and 80/100 is a PENETRATION grade, not a viscosity grade.**

> **The two systems are different:**

| System | Grades | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| **PENETRATION grading** | **30/40, 60/70, 80/100, 180/200** | **Penetration at 25 °C, in 0.1 mm** ← 80/100 belongs here |
| **VISCOSITY grading (IS 73:2013)** | **VG-10, VG-20, VG-30, VG-40** | **Absolute viscosity at 60 °C, in poise** |

> **The move to VISCOSITY grading was made for a good reason: viscosity is measured at 60 °C, close to the temperature the pavement actually reaches, whereas penetration is measured at 25 °C, which is neither the mixing nor the service temperature.**

> **So the modern system grades the binder at a temperature that matters.**

> **The rough correspondence: VG-10 ≈ 80/100, VG-30 ≈ 60/70, VG-40 ≈ 30/40** — and it is only rough, because the two systems measure different properties.

> **Penetration grades nonetheless remain in wide use and in every examination**, so both systems are worth knowing.

**The grades and where each belongs:**

| Grade | Penetration | Consistency | Suits |
|---|---|---|---|
| **30/40** | **3-4 mm** | **HARDEST of the paving grades** | **HOT climates; heavy traffic** |
| **60/70** | 6-7 mm | Medium | Moderate climates |
| **80/100** | **8-10 mm** | **SOFTER** | **COLD climates; lighter traffic** ← |
| 180/200 | 18-20 mm | Very soft | Surface dressing; cold regions |

> **The rule to reason from: a HIGHER penetration number means a SOFTER bitumen.**

> **HOT climate → HARD bitumen (low number), or a soft binder bleeds and ruts.**

> **COLD climate → SOFT bitumen (high number), or a hard binder becomes brittle and cracks.**

**Nepal's particular difficulty, since it is a real design problem:**

> **The country runs from the Terai (over 40 °C in summer) to high mountain roads (well below freezing in winter), sometimes within a hundred kilometres.**

> **No single grade suits the whole country**, and a road climbing from the Terai to the hills passes through both regimes on one alignment.

> **Hence grade selection by ALTITUDE BAND, and the increasing use of POLYMER-MODIFIED BITUMEN**, which widens the temperature range over which the binder behaves acceptably rather than optimising for one end of it.

verification.notes: Stem wording adjusted. The source asked which "viscosity grade" 8.3 mm penetration falls under, but 80/100 is a PENETRATION grade; viscosity grades are VG-10 to VG-40, measured at 60 degrees C. The stem now says "grade", which is what the options are, and the solution sets out the difference between the two grading systems explicitly. The keyed answer (c) is unchanged.

examTip.trick: **The unit is 0.1 mm, so 80/100 means 8.0 to 10.0 mm — and 8.3 falls inside it.**
examTip.trap: **Options (a) 85/90 and (d) 85/100 both fail on their LOWER bound: 8.3 is below 8.5.** A range has TWO limits, and checking only that 8.3 < 10 leaves three options apparently qualifying.
examTip.mnemonic: **80/100 is a PENETRATION grade (at 25 °C); VG-10 to VG-40 are VISCOSITY grades (at 60 °C).** The move to viscosity grading was made because 60 °C is a temperature the pavement actually reaches.

questions.stem: What is the percentage content of asphalt in cut-back asphalt?
questions.solution:
**80 per cent (the usual range being 80 to 85 per cent).**

**What cut-back bitumen is:**

> **CUT-BACK asphalt is bitumen whose viscosity has been reduced by BLENDING IT WITH A VOLATILE PETROLEUM SOLVENT** — a "cutter" such as naphtha, kerosene or diesel.

> **The source states the composition: cutbacks containing 80-85 per cent asphalt are used like emulsion, because they reduce the asphalt viscosity for lower-temperature application.**

> **So the remaining 15 to 20 per cent is the solvent**, and the point of the material is that it can be applied WITHOUT heating the bitumen to normal mixing temperatures.

> **After application the solvent EVAPORATES, leaving the bitumen behind to do its work.** That evaporation is called **CURING**.

**The three grades, classified by how fast the solvent evaporates:**

| Grade | Solvent used | Curing speed | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RC — Rapid Curing** | **NAPHTHA or gasoline (most volatile)** | **Fast** | **Surface dressing, patch repair, tack coat** |
| **MC — Medium Curing** | **KEROSENE** | **Medium** | **PRIME COAT on a granular base; premix** |
| **SC — Slow Curing (road oil)** | **HIGH-BOILING gas oil / diesel** | **Slow** | **Dust laying; low-type surfaces; stabilisation** |

> **The naming is straightforward once the mechanism is understood: the more volatile the cutter, the faster the cure.**

> **And the grade is chosen by the job: a tack coat must set quickly before traffic runs on it (RC), while a prime coat must stay fluid long enough to soak into the base (MC).**

**Why cut-backs exist at all — and why they are being displaced:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Can be applied at LOW temperature** | **No hot boiler needed for light work** |
| **PENETRATES a granular base** | Which is exactly what a prime coat must do |
| **Simple equipment** | Suits small and remote works |

| Disadvantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **The solvent is LOST to the atmosphere** | **A volatile organic compound emission — an environmental and health objection** ← |
| **The solvent is expensive and is thrown away** | It performs no function in the finished road |
| **FIRE HAZARD** | **Naphtha and kerosene cutters have low flash points** |
| **Slow strength gain** | Full strength only after the solvent has gone |

> **The environmental objection is the decisive one and it is why BITUMEN EMULSIONS have largely replaced cut-backs.**

**The comparison with emulsion, which is the substantive contrast:**

| | **CUT-BACK** | **EMULSION** |
|---|---|---|
| **Bitumen is dispersed in** | **A PETROLEUM SOLVENT** | **WATER, with an emulsifying agent** |
| **Bitumen content** | **80-85 %** ← | **40-70 %** |
| **Sets by** | **EVAPORATION of the solvent** | **BREAKING — water separates and evaporates** |
| **Environmental effect** | **VOC emission** | **Water only** |
| **Fire risk** | **Significant** | **None** |
| **Can be used on a DAMP surface?** | **NO** | **YES — a real practical advantage** ← |
| Cost of the carrier | Expensive, lost | Cheap |

> **The damp-surface row is worth emphasising because it is a genuine operational advantage in a monsoon climate: an emulsion can be applied to a surface that is merely damp, while a cut-back cannot.**

> **In Nepal, where the working season is bounded by the monsoon, that difference converts directly into more working days.**

**The emulsion types, since they follow the same logic of setting speed:**

| Type | Sets | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **RS — Rapid Setting** | Fast | Surface dressing, tack coat |
| **MS — Medium Setting** | Medium | Premix with coarse aggregate |
| **SS — Slow Setting** | Slow | Premix with fine aggregate; soil stabilisation |

> **And emulsions are additionally classified by CHARGE — CATIONIC (positively charged) or ANIONIC — which matters because the charge must be opposite to the aggregate's.**

> **CATIONIC emulsions adhere well to SILICEOUS (negatively charged) aggregates such as quartzite and granite**, which are the common aggregates in Nepal — **so cationic emulsions are the usual choice, and using an anionic emulsion on a siliceous aggregate gives poor adhesion for a reason that is electrostatic rather than mechanical.**

examTip.trick: **80-85 % bitumen, the rest a volatile solvent** that evaporates on curing. The point is application WITHOUT heating to normal mixing temperature.
examTip.trap: **Do not confuse the bitumen content of a CUT-BACK (80-85 %) with that of an EMULSION (40-70 %)** — the emulsion's carrier is water, so there is proportionally more of it.
examTip.mnemonic: **RC = naphtha (fast), MC = kerosene (medium), SC = gas oil (slow)** — the more volatile the cutter, the faster the cure. And an EMULSION can be used on a DAMP surface while a cut-back cannot: real working days in a monsoon climate.

questions.stem: If the shear force is constant throughout a section, then the bending moment is:
questions.solution:
**Linear.**

**The relation that settles it in one line:**

> **dM/dx = V**

> **So the bending moment is the INTEGRAL of the shear force.**

> **Integrating a CONSTANT gives a LINEAR function:**

> **V = c  ⟹  M = ∫c dx = cx + constant**

> **The source states it exactly: as SF = constant = c, BM should be cx = linear.** ✓

**The degree ladder, which answers every question of this form:**

| Loading | Shear force | Bending moment |
|---|---|---|
| **No load (between point loads)** | **CONSTANT (degree 0)** | **LINEAR (degree 1)** ← |
| **Uniform load (udl)** | **LINEAR (degree 1)** | **PARABOLIC (degree 2)** |
| **Triangular (linearly varying) load** | **PARABOLIC (degree 2)** | **CUBIC (degree 3)** |
| **Parabolic load** | Cubic | Fourth degree |

> **Each integration raises the degree by ONE**, and the whole table follows from that single rule.

> **Note that every option in this question is one row of the middle or right column** — so the question is a clean test of whether the ladder is known.

**When is the shear force constant? — worth knowing, because it identifies the physical situation:**

> **Shear is constant wherever there is NO DISTRIBUTED LOAD**, since dV/dx = −w and w = 0 gives dV/dx = 0.

| Situation | Where shear is constant |
|---|---|
| **Between two point loads on a beam** | **The whole span between them** |
| **A cantilever with a point load at the tip** | **The ENTIRE cantilever** |
| **A simply supported beam with a central point load** | Each half separately (with a sign change at the load) |
| **The middle region of a beam under two symmetric point loads** | **Shear is ZERO there — a special case of constant** ← |

> **The last row is the interesting one: shear can be constant AND ZERO, and then the moment is constant rather than linear** (since c = 0 makes cx + k = k).

> **That is the region of PURE BENDING between two symmetric point loads, and it is exactly the arrangement used in the FOUR-POINT BENDING TEST for the modulus of rupture** — chosen precisely because it gives a region of uniform moment with no shear to complicate the failure.

> **So option (a) "constant" is not absurd: it is the correct answer for the special case V = 0.** The general answer for a non-zero constant shear is linear, which is what the question asks.

**The three companion relations, which make any diagram checkable:**

> **dV/dx = −w** — the slope of the shear diagram is minus the load intensity.

> **dM/dx = V** — the slope of the moment diagram is the shear force.

> **Therefore M is MAXIMUM where V = 0 or changes sign.**

> **The last is the workhorse: to find the maximum moment, find where the shear crosses zero.** That is faster than differentiating a moment expression, and it works for unsymmetrical loading where guessing the location would fail.

**The standard results, since they are the currency of the subject:**

| Beam and load | Maximum BM | Maximum deflection |
|---|---|---|
| **SSB, central point load W** | **WL/4** | **WL³/48EI** |
| **SSB, udl w** | **wL²/8** | **5wL⁴/384EI** |
| **Cantilever, end point load W** | **WL** | **WL³/3EI** |
| **Cantilever, udl w** | **wL²/2** | **wL⁴/8EI** |
| **Fixed beam, udl w** | **wL²/12 at supports, wL²/24 at centre** | **wL⁴/384EI** |
| Fixed beam, central point load | **WL/8 at supports and centre** | WL³/192EI |

> **Note that the fixed beam's udl deflection is exactly ONE FIFTH of the simply supported value** (wL⁴/384 against 5wL⁴/384) — the end restraint is worth a factor of five in stiffness while cutting the moment only by 1.5.

> **Restraint buys far more stiffness than strength**, which is the general lesson and the reason continuity is worth building into a structure.

**And the design consequence of the shear-moment relation:**

> **Shear is maximum where moment is zero, and moment is maximum where shear is zero** — a direct consequence of dM/dx = V.

> **So SHEAR governs near the SUPPORTS and BENDING near MID-SPAN.**

> **Which is exactly why stirrups are closely spaced near the ends of an RCC beam and widely spaced in the middle**, while the main tension bars are fullest at mid-span and may be curtailed toward the supports.

> **A candidate who sees that connection understands why a beam is detailed as it is, rather than merely remembering the detail.**

examTip.trick: **dM/dx = V, so M is the INTEGRAL of V.** A constant integrates to a linear function. Each integration raises the degree by one: no load → constant shear → linear moment.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) "constant" is right for the special case V = 0** — the pure-bending region between two symmetric point loads, which is why the four-point bending test is arranged that way.
examTip.mnemonic: **M is maximum where V crosses zero** — faster than differentiating. Which is why **shear governs near the SUPPORTS and bending near MID-SPAN**, and why stirrups crowd the ends of an RCC beam.

questions.stem: If the fineness modulus of a sand sample is high (more), then the sand sample will be:
questions.solution:
**Coarse sand.**

**What the fineness modulus is — and the name is misleading:**

> **FINENESS MODULUS (FM) = (sum of the CUMULATIVE PERCENTAGES RETAINED on each standard sieve) ÷ 100**

> **It is an index of the MEAN PARTICLE SIZE.**

> **A COARSE sand retains a lot of material on the upper sieves, so its cumulative retained percentages are large, so its FM is HIGH.**

> **A FINE sand passes through the upper sieves, retaining little, so its FM is LOW.**

> **So a HIGH fineness modulus means COARSE sand** — which is the opposite of what the word "fineness" suggests, and precisely the trap the question sets.

> **The source states it directly: if the mean size is high, it is coarse.**

**The FM ranges:**

| Type of sand | Fineness modulus |
|---|---|
| **FINE sand** | **2.2 - 2.6** |
| **MEDIUM sand** | **2.6 - 2.9** |
| **COARSE sand** | **2.9 - 3.2** ← high FM |

> **Note how NARROW the whole range is: 2.2 to 3.2.** A change of 0.3 in FM moves a sand from one class to the next.

> **That narrowness is why FM is a sensitive quality-control parameter — and why a sand's FM should be checked on delivery rather than assumed from its source.**

> **For reference, coarse aggregate has an FM of about 5.5 to 8.0, and all-in aggregate 3.5 to 6.5.**

**Why the naming is the way it is — worth understanding rather than resenting:**

> **The modulus is computed from the CUMULATIVE PERCENTAGE RETAINED, and "retained" means "did not pass".**

> **A coarse material is retained; a fine material passes.** So the sum is large for coarse material.

> **The word "fineness" describes what the index is ABOUT (the fineness of the grading) rather than the direction in which it increases** — an unfortunate but standard usage.

> **The safe habit: read FM as a SIZE INDEX. Bigger number, bigger particles.**

**How the FM is actually computed, since the definition is easy to misapply:**

> **Sieve the sample through the standard set (4.75, 2.36, 1.18 mm, 600, 300, 150 μm for fine aggregate).**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. Weigh the material retained on each sieve** | — |
| **2. Convert to a PERCENTAGE of the total** | — |
| **3. Compute the CUMULATIVE percentage retained** | **Adding down from the coarsest sieve** ← the step most often got wrong |
| **4. SUM the cumulative percentages** | Across all the standard sieves |
| **5. DIVIDE by 100** | Gives the FM |

> **Step 3 is the one that catches people: it is the CUMULATIVE retained, not the individual retained, that is summed.** Using the individual percentages gives 100/100 = 1 for every sample, which is obviously wrong and is a useful check that the method has been applied correctly.

**Why the FM matters — what it is used for:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **Mix design** | **The FM enters the selection of the fine-to-coarse aggregate ratio** |
| **Quality control of a sand source** | **A CHANGE in FM between deliveries changes the concrete's workability and water demand** ← |
| **Comparing sands** | A single number instead of a whole grading curve |
| **Zoning of fine aggregate (IS 383)** | Grading zones I to IV |

> **The quality-control use is the practical one, and it has a direct consequence: a FINER sand (lower FM) has MORE SURFACE AREA per unit weight, so it needs MORE WATER for the same workability.**

> **And more water means a higher water/cement ratio and lower strength, unless the mix is corrected.**

> **So an unnoticed change in the sand's FM shows up as either a stiffer mix or a weaker one** — which is why the slump test's real value is detecting exactly that kind of change between batches.

**And the limitation of the FM, stated honestly:**

> **The FM is a single number summarising a whole grading curve, so DIFFERENT GRADINGS CAN HAVE THE SAME FM.**

> **A well-graded sand and a gap-graded one — two sizes with nothing between them — can share an FM and behave quite differently in concrete.**

> **So the FM tells you the average size and says NOTHING about the DISTRIBUTION.** It is a useful index and not a substitute for the grading curve, which is why IS 383 specifies grading ZONES with limits on each sieve rather than an FM range alone.

examTip.trick: **HIGH fineness modulus means COARSE sand** — the opposite of what the word suggests. FM is computed from the percentages RETAINED, and coarse material is what gets retained.
examTip.trap: **Sum the CUMULATIVE percentages retained, not the individual ones.** Using the individual figures gives 1 for every sample — a useful check that the method was applied.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fine 2.2-2.6, medium 2.6-2.9, coarse 2.9-3.2** — a very narrow range, so FM is sensitive. A finer sand has more surface area and needs MORE WATER, hence lower strength unless the mix is corrected.

questions.stem: The fine imposed after the violation of copyright for the first time is:
options: NPR 10,000 to NPR 100,000, or six months in prison, or both
up to two lakh rupees or imprisonment for a year, or both
one lakh to two lakh rupees or imprisonment for a year, or both
questions.solution:
**NPR 10,000 to NPR 100,000, or six months in prison, or both.**

**The two-tier penalty under Nepal's copyright law:**

| Offence | Penalty |
|---|---|
| **FIRST offence** | **Fine of NPR 10,000 to NPR 100,000, or up to SIX MONTHS' imprisonment, or both** ← |
| **SECOND offence** | **Fine of up to TWO LAKH rupees, or imprisonment for up to ONE YEAR, or both** |

> **The source states both tiers, and option (b) is the SECOND-offence penalty** — which is what makes it the designed trap.

> **The escalation is the point: a repeated infringement is treated as substantially more serious, roughly doubling the maximum fine and the maximum term.**

> **Option (d) can be dismissed on principle: a statute that imposed no penalty for a first offence would give the right no protection at all**, since every infringer's first act would be free.

**Why copyright matters to a civil engineer — this is not a peripheral topic:**

> **An engineer's principal work products are DOCUMENTS, and documents are what copyright protects.**

| Protected by copyright | Note |
|---|---|
| **DRAWINGS and design documents** | **The original expression, not the underlying engineering** |
| **Specifications and reports** | Written work |
| **Software** | Including spreadsheets and macros the engineer writes |
| **Photographs, maps, models** | — |
| **Databases and compilations** | Where there is originality in the selection |

> **And the two most common ways an engineer infringes are worth naming plainly, because they are routine rather than exotic:**

| Common infringement | Note |
|---|---|
| **USING UNLICENSED SOFTWARE** | **The commonest by far — design and drafting software used on more machines than are licensed** ← |
| **Reusing another firm's drawings** | Copying a detail or a whole drawing from a previous employer or a competitor |
| **Copying specification text without permission** | Standard clauses are often themselves copyright |
| Reproducing figures in a report | Textbook and journal figures need permission |

> **The unlicensed-software case deserves emphasis because it is so widely tolerated and is unambiguously an infringement.** It also carries a professional risk beyond the legal one: **a design produced on unlicensed software is vulnerable to challenge, and an engineer who cannot show a license has a difficulty they did not need.**

**What copyright protects and what it does not — the distinction that matters most:**

> **Copyright protects the EXPRESSION of an idea, not the IDEA itself.**

| Protected | NOT protected |
|---|---|
| **The particular drawing** | **The engineering solution it depicts** |
| **The words of a specification** | **The technical requirement expressed** |
| **A report's text and figures** | **The facts and data reported** |
| The code of a program | The algorithm's mathematical content |

> **So another engineer may study a bridge and design a similar one; they may not photocopy the drawings.**

> **That distinction is why copyright is the WRONG instrument for protecting a technical innovation — a PATENT is.** And in engineering practice most technical content is not protectable at all, which is why the profession relies on standards and shared practice.

**The intellectual property family, since the four are constantly confused:**

| Right | Protects | Typical term |
|---|---|---|
| **COPYRIGHT** | **The EXPRESSION of original work — drawings, text, software** | **Life of the author + 50 years (Nepal)** |
| **PATENT** | **A new, useful and non-obvious INVENTION** | **About 20 years** |
| **TRADEMARK** | **A mark distinguishing goods or services** | **Renewable indefinitely** |
| **DESIGN registration** | The aesthetic appearance of an article | Shorter, renewable |
| Trade secret | Confidential information | As long as it stays secret |

> **Nepal's principal statute is the COPYRIGHT ACT 2059 (2002) with its Regulation 2061**, and Nepal is a member of the World Intellectual Property Organization.

> **Note that copyright arises AUTOMATICALLY on creation — registration is not required for the right to exist**, though registration helps in proving it. **That is a genuine difference from patents and trademarks, which must be granted.**

**And the point of professional practice that follows:**

> **In a consultancy, the question of WHO OWNS the copyright in drawings is a contractual matter and should be settled in the appointment.**

| Common arrangement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Consultant retains copyright; client gets a LICENSE to use** | **The usual professional position** |
| Copyright assigned to the client | Common in public contracts |
| Joint ownership | Rare and awkward |

> **The default in most systems is that the AUTHOR owns the copyright unless it is assigned or created as an employee's work**, so a consultancy that has not addressed the point in its contract may find its client's rights narrower — or broader — than either party assumed.

> **Which is a good general lesson about professional practice: the questions that cause trouble are the ones nobody thought to write down.**

examTip.trick: **First offence: NPR 10,000-100,000 or six months. SECOND offence: up to two lakh or one year.** The escalation is the point, and option (b) is the second-offence penalty.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) fails on principle** — a statute imposing no penalty for a first offence would give the right no protection, since every infringer's first act would be free.
examTip.mnemonic: **Copyright protects the EXPRESSION, not the IDEA** — so another engineer may design a similar bridge but not photocopy the drawings. For a technical innovation the right instrument is a PATENT. And unlicensed software is the commonest infringement in practice.

questions.stem: When was the Master's programme recognised by the Nepal Engineering Council?
questions.solution:
**2076/09/06.**

**The three recognition and amendment dates, which must be held as a set:**

| Event | Date (BS) |
|---|---|
| **BACHELOR'S programme recognition** | **2066/06/23** |
| **MASTER'S programme recognition** | **2076/09/06** ← |
| **First AMENDMENT to the NEC Act** | **2079/05/05** |

> **The source gives all three together, which is why the question's option list contains all of them: it is a matching exercise, and knowing one date is not enough.**

> **Only option (c) 2077/05/26 has no standing in this set.**

**The logic that makes the ordering memorable:**

> **BACHELOR'S recognition came FIRST (2066) and MASTER'S a decade later (2076).**

> **That order is not arbitrary. The Council's primary function is to license engineers to PRACTISE, and the practising qualification is the bachelor's degree** — so bachelor's programmes were the first that had to be recognised.

> **A master's degree is a SPECIALISATION rather than an entry qualification**, so bringing master's programmes into the recognition system was a later refinement — extending the Council's quality assurance upward once the base was established.

> **And the 2079 amendment to the Act came later still, consolidating the arrangements.**

> **So the sequence runs: recognise the practising qualification, then the specialist ones, then amend the statute.** Reasoning that through fixes the order without memorising three numbers in isolation.

**Why recognition matters at all — the consequence for a graduate:**

> **A graduate of an UNRECOGNISED programme CANNOT REGISTER with the Council, and therefore cannot practise as an engineer in Nepal.**

> **That consequence falls on the STUDENT, after four years and considerable expense — not on the institution.**

> **Which is why the Council publishes the list of recognised programmes, and why checking it BEFORE enrolling is genuine practical advice rather than a formality.**

> **And the warning that is regularly ignored: UNIVERSITY AFFILIATION DOES NOT IMPLY COUNCIL RECOGNITION.**

| Approval | Answers the question |
|---|---|
| **University affiliation** | **Can this institution award this university's degree?** |
| **NEC recognition** | **Does that degree qualify its holder to PRACTISE engineering on the public?** |

> **Two separate approvals, answering different questions**, and an institution can hold the first without the second.

**How recognition is maintained — the inspection cycle:**

| Programme | Approval status | Inspection interval |
|---|---|---|
| **Bachelor** | **PERMANENT** | **Every 2 years** |
| **Bachelor** | **TEMPORARY** | **Every 1 year** |
| **Master** | **Temporary** | **Every 1 year** |
| **Master** | **PERMANENT** | **Every 18 months** |

> **The logic is straightforward: TEMPORARY approval means sustained compliance has not yet been demonstrated, so the institution is watched annually.** Permanent approval lengthens the interval.

> **And what an inspection examines is worth knowing, because it is what recognition actually means:**

| Examined | Note |
|---|---|
| **FACULTY — numbers, qualifications, permanence** | **The single most important input** |
| **LABORATORIES and equipment** | Engineering cannot be taught without them |
| **Student intake against sanctioned capacity** | **Over-enrolment dilutes everything else** |
| Library and learning resources | — |
| Curriculum and its delivery | Against the recognised syllabus |

> **Faculty and laboratories are what an inspection is really about, because they are the two things that cannot be produced quickly for a visit and cannot be substituted for.**

**The wider set of regulatory facts, since this corner of the syllabus recurs heavily:**

| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| **NEC Act** | **2055 BS (1998 AD)** |
| **NEC Regulation** | **2057 BS** |
| **Bachelor's recognition** | **2066/06/23** |
| **Master's recognition** | **2076/09/06** ← |
| **First amendment to the Act** | **2079/05/05** |
| **Nature of the Council** | **AUTONOMOUS body** |
| **Who approves its rules** | **Government of Nepal** |
| **Vice chairman** | **B.E. + 10 years** |
| **NEA-elected members** | **5, tenure 4 years** |
| **Members nominated by the Council itself** | **2** |
| **Minimum qualification to register** | **Bachelor's degree** |

> **This is a small, closed body of facts that appears in almost every sitting** — and it is among the cheapest marks in the examination. **Learning the set as a set answers most of what is asked; meeting each fact separately does not.**

examTip.trick: **Bachelor's 2066/06/23, Master's 2076/09/06, Act amendment 2079/05/05.** Three of the four options are from that set, so it is a matching exercise — one date is not enough.
examTip.trap: **Reason out the ORDER rather than memorising numbers**: the practising qualification (bachelor's) had to be recognised FIRST, specialisations later, the statute amended later still.
examTip.mnemonic: **University affiliation does NOT imply Council recognition** — two approvals answering different questions. A graduate of an unrecognised programme cannot register, and that falls on the student, not the institution.

questions.stem: If a section is fixed at both ends, the crippling load is ....... times the section having both ends hinged.
questions.solution:
**4 times.**

**The derivation, which is one substitution:**

> **Euler's crippling load:  P_cr = π²EI / L_e²**, where **L_e is the EFFECTIVE LENGTH.**

| End conditions | Effective length L_e | P_cr relative to hinged-hinged |
|---|---|---|
| **BOTH ENDS FIXED** | **L/2** | **4 ×** ← |
| **Both ends hinged** | **L** | **1 × (the reference)** |
| **One fixed, one hinged** | **L/√2 ≈ 0.7L** | **2 ×** |
| **One fixed, one FREE (cantilever)** | **2L** | **1/4 ×** |

> **Since L_e appears SQUARED, halving it multiplies the load by FOUR:**

> **P_cr = π²EI/(L/2)² = 4π²EI/L²** ✓

> **The source works it through in the equivalent form P_cr ∝ 1/k², with k the effective length factor: (0.5)²/(1)² = 0.25, so P_cr1 = 4 P_cr2.**

**Why the effective length is L/2 — the physical picture:**

> **The effective length is the distance between successive POINTS OF INFLECTION (points of zero moment) in the buckled shape.**

> **A hinged-hinged column buckles into a single half sine wave with zero moment at each end**, so the inflection points ARE the ends and L_e = L.

> **A fixed-fixed column cannot rotate at its ends, so its buckled shape has inflection points at the QUARTER POINTS** — a distance L/2 apart.

> **Between those two inflection points the column behaves exactly like a hinged-hinged column of length L/2**, which is why the substitution works.

> **Visualising that also explains the 0.7L for the fixed-pinned case: one inflection point at the pinned end and the other about 0.3L from the fixed end.**

**The direction check, which needs no recall:**

> **FIXING the ends RESTRAINS the column, so it must carry MORE load.**

> **Any answer less than 1 × the hinged value is wrong for fixed ends** — which immediately eliminates option (a) "equal" and would eliminate a 1/4 option if one were offered.

> **Then options (b) and (d) must be judged on the factor, and L_e = L/2 with the squaring gives 4.**

> **Option (d) 6 times has no basis in any end condition, and option (b) 2 times is the FIXED-HINGED value** — a real number from the same table, which is what makes it the better distractor.

**The assumptions behind Euler's formula, since they bound its use:**

| Assumption | Note |
|---|---|
| **Perfectly STRAIGHT column** | No initial curvature |
| **Perfectly AXIAL load** | No eccentricity |
| **Material HOMOGENEOUS and remaining ELASTIC** | **The critical limitation** ← |
| **LONG and SLENDER — failure by buckling, not crushing** | — |
| Self-weight neglected | — |

> **The elastic assumption fails first, and it fails for SHORT columns.**

> **Euler's formula predicts an INFINITE load as L → 0, which is obviously wrong: a very short column CRUSHES at its yield stress rather than buckling.**

> **So the formula applies only above a certain slenderness:**

> **Critical stress σ_cr = π²E/(L_e/k)²**, where **L_e/k is the SLENDERNESS RATIO** and k the radius of gyration.

| Slenderness ratio L_e/k | Failure mode | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| **< ~30** | **CRUSHING** | **σ = f_y** |
| **30 - 100** | **Combined — the PRACTICAL range** | **RANKINE, or a code curve** |
| **> ~100** | **Elastic BUCKLING** | **EULER** |

> **Most real columns lie in the INTERMEDIATE range**, where neither pure crushing nor pure Euler buckling applies — which is why codes use empirical curves rather than Euler's formula directly.

> **RANKINE'S formula spans the whole range: 1/P = 1/P_crushing + 1/P_Euler**, tending to each limit at the appropriate end. **Its elegance is that it requires no decision about which regime applies.**

**And the practical caution about "fixed" ends:**

> **A truly fixed end is very difficult to achieve.** A real connection has some rotational flexibility, so the actual effective length lies between the theoretical values.

> **Codes therefore give CONSERVATIVE effective length factors — for example 0.65L rather than 0.5L for a nominally fixed-fixed column.**

> **Claiming full fixity for a connection that cannot deliver it is unconservative, and since L_e enters SQUARED, a 30 per cent error in L_e is a 70 per cent error in the buckling load.**

> **Which makes the effective length the assumption a column design most depends on** — more than the material properties, and more than the section's exact dimensions.

examTip.trick: **L_e = L/2 for fixed-fixed, and L_e is SQUARED — so the load is 4×.** The family: fixed-fixed L/2, hinged L, fixed-hinged 0.7L, cantilever 2L.
examTip.trap: **Check the direction first: fixing RESTRAINS, so the load must RISE** — which kills option (a) at once. Option (b) 2 times is the FIXED-HINGED value, a real number from the same table.
examTip.mnemonic: **Effective length is the distance between POINTS OF INFLECTION** — at the quarter points for fixed-fixed, hence L/2. And Euler applies only above slenderness ~100; below ~30 the column CRUSHES.

questions.stem: A foundation is called a deep foundation when:
questions.solution:
**(B/D) < 1 — that is, the depth exceeds the width.**

**Getting the ratio the right way round, which is the whole of this question:**

> **A DEEP foundation is one whose DEPTH is large compared with its WIDTH.**

> **So D > B, and therefore B/D < 1.** ✓

> **Equivalently, D/B > 1 — and on the stricter Terzaghi criterion, D/B > 4 to 5.**

| Foundation | Depth-to-width | Width-to-depth |
|---|---|---|
| **SHALLOW** | **D/B ≤ 1 (loosely), or D/B < 4** | **B/D ≥ 1** |
| **DEEP** | **D/B > 1 (loosely), or D/B > 4** | **B/D < 1, or B/D < 1/4** ← |

> **The criterion is a RATIO, not an absolute depth.** A 3 m wide raft at 3 m depth is SHALLOW (D/B = 1); a 0.5 m diameter pile 10 m long is DEEP (D/B = 20).

> **Which is why a large raft several metres below ground is still classed as shallow — a result that surprises candidates and is worth holding.**

**Testing each option, since three of the four are wrong for different reasons:**

| Option | Means | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **(B/D) < 1** | **D > B — the depth exceeds the width** | **CORRECT — the deep-foundation condition** ✓ |
| **(D/B) < 1** | **B > D — the width exceeds the depth** | **This is the SHALLOW condition, exactly inverted** |
| **(B/D) < 4** | **D > B/4 — satisfied by almost everything, including a wide shallow raft** | **Useless as a criterion — far too weak to distinguish anything** |
| **(B/D) > 4** | **B > 4D — the width exceeds FOUR TIMES the depth** | **A WIDE SHALLOW footing — the opposite of deep** |

> **Option (c) deserves a note because it fails in an instructive way: it is not the wrong direction, it is simply too weak to be a criterion at all.** A 3 m footing at 1 m depth satisfies B/D = 3 < 4 and is plainly shallow.

> **A criterion satisfied by both cases distinguishes neither**, and spotting that is a legitimate way to eliminate an option.

**Why the ratio rather than an absolute depth — the mechanical reason:**

> **The classification exists because the two kinds of foundation TRANSFER LOAD DIFFERENTLY:**

| | **SHALLOW** | **DEEP** |
|---|---|---|
| **Load transfer** | **By BEARING on the soil directly beneath** | **By SKIN FRICTION along the shaft PLUS end bearing at the tip** |
| **The overburden term q·N_q** | Modest | **Large — it grows with depth and comes to dominate** |
| **Settlement** | Larger; mostly immediate plus consolidation | Smaller; mostly elastic shortening plus tip settlement |
| **Suits** | **Competent soil near the surface** | **Weak soil near the surface, competent stratum deeper — or heavy, uplift or lateral loads** |

> **A foundation becomes "deep" in behaviour when the SHAFT contribution becomes significant relative to the base** — and that happens when the depth-to-width ratio is large, whatever the absolute dimensions.

> **So the ratio is the physically meaningful criterion, and any absolute depth would be arbitrary.**

**When a deep foundation becomes necessary:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Weak or compressible soil near the surface** | **The commonest reason — reach a firm stratum below** |
| **Very heavy or concentrated loads** | Bridge piers, tall buildings |
| **UPLIFT or overturning loads** | **A pile can carry TENSION; a footing essentially cannot** ← |
| **Large horizontal loads** | Piles resist by bending along their length |
| **SCOUR-prone sites (bridges in rivers)** | **Must be founded BELOW the maximum scour depth** |
| Expansive or collapsible soil | Bypass the active zone |
