> **The uplift capability is one a shallow foundation simply lacks**, which is why transmission towers, tall chimneys and overturning-critical structures need piles or anchors.

> **And the scour requirement is why bridge foundations in Himalayan rivers are almost always deep: the bed can scour several metres in a single flood, and a foundation resting above that level is founded on ground that will not be there.**

**The two families, for completeness:**

| **SHALLOW foundations** | **DEEP foundations** |
|---|---|
| **Spread / isolated footing** | **PILE foundation** |
| **Combined footing** | **WELL (caisson) foundation** |
| **STRAP (cantilever) footing** | **Pier / drilled shaft** |
| **MAT (raft) foundation** | Caisson (open, box, pneumatic) |
| Strip / continuous footing | Barrette, micropile |

> **Note that the shallow family contains several purpose-made variants — combined, strap, trapezoidal, raft — and all of them remain shallow.** The variation is in PLAN geometry, not in depth.

verification.notes: Answer corrected from (d) to (a). The source keyed (d) B/D > 4 and its own explanation repeats the same inversion ("for deep foundation the ratio of B/D>4 is preferred"). But B/D > 4 means the WIDTH exceeds four times the DEPTH, which describes a wide SHALLOW footing. A deep foundation has the DEPTH greater than the width - D > B, hence B/D < 1, and on the stricter Terzaghi criterion D/B > 4, i.e. B/D < 1/4. No option states D/B > 4, so the only defensible answer among those offered is (a) B/D < 1. Note also that option (c) B/D < 4 is satisfied by almost every foundation including wide shallow rafts, so it distinguishes nothing and cannot be a criterion.

examTip.trick: **Deep means the DEPTH exceeds the WIDTH: D > B, so B/D < 1.** And the criterion is a RATIO, not an absolute depth — a 3 m raft at 3 m depth is SHALLOW.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) B/D > 4 means the width exceeds FOUR TIMES the depth — a wide shallow footing.** And option (c) B/D < 4 is satisfied by nearly everything, so it distinguishes nothing: a criterion true of both cases is no criterion.
examTip.mnemonic: **The ratio matters because the two transfer load differently** — a shallow footing bears on the soil beneath, a deep one adds SKIN FRICTION along its shaft. And **a pile can carry TENSION; a footing cannot.**

questions.stem: Dowel bars are placed along the ........ of a concrete road.
options: along 45° to the direction of traffic
can be placed along any direction
questions.solution:
**Along the longitudinal direction of traffic.**

**What a dowel bar does, and why its direction follows:**

> **A DOWEL BAR is a plain round bar placed across a TRANSVERSE JOINT of a concrete pavement, to TRANSFER LOAD from one slab to the next.**

> **A transverse joint runs ACROSS the road; so a bar crossing it must run ALONG the road — in the direction of traffic.**

> **The source states both points: the purpose is to transfer load between two slabs and keep them at the same height, and the bars are provided in the direction of the traffic (longitudinal).**

> **So the direction is a geometric consequence of the joint it serves.**

**Why load transfer matters — what happens without it:**

> **A wheel approaching a joint loads the edge of the departing slab.**

> **Without a dowel, that slab's edge deflects while the next slab does not — so the wheel drops as it crosses, and the loaded slab edge carries the whole load alone.**

| Consequence of no load transfer | Note |
|---|---|
| **FAULTING (stepping) at the joint** | **One slab settles relative to the next — the classic defect** ← |
| **High edge stress in the loaded slab** | Corner and edge cracking |
| **PUMPING of subgrade fines** | The repeated deflection pumps water and fines out through the joint |
| Rough riding | Each joint becomes a bump |

> **PUMPING is the mechanism that destroys jointed concrete pavements**, and it is progressive: deflection pumps out fines, the loss of support increases the deflection, and the process accelerates. **A dowel bar interrupts it at the start by sharing the load.**

**The critical detail that makes a dowel work — and it is counter-intuitive:**

> **A dowel bar must be PLAIN (not deformed) and must be COATED or GREASED over at least half its length, so that it can SLIDE.**

> **The joint must be free to OPEN AND CLOSE with temperature.** If the dowel gripped the concrete on both sides, it would restrain that movement and the slab would crack instead.

> **So the dowel transfers SHEAR while permitting AXIAL MOVEMENT** — which is exactly why it is a smooth bar and not a deformed one.

> **A deformed bar used as a dowel is a real and serious site error: it locks the joint, and the pavement then cracks somewhere the designer did not choose.**

**The contrast with a TIE BAR, which is the discrimination examiners want:**

| | **DOWEL BAR** | **TIE BAR** |
|---|---|---|
| **Placed across** | **TRANSVERSE joints** | **LONGITUDINAL joints** |
| **Runs in the direction** | **LONGITUDINAL (of traffic)** ← | **TRANSVERSE** |
| **Purpose** | **TRANSFER LOAD between slabs** | **HOLD the slabs together — prevent them separating** |
| **Bar type** | **PLAIN, greased — must SLIDE** | **DEFORMED, anchored — must GRIP** |
| **Is it a load transfer device?** | **YES** | **NO** |
| **Size** | Larger diameter, closer spacing | **Smaller, at wider spacing** |

> **Every row is opposite, which makes the pair easy to confuse and easy to remember once the logic is seen:**

> **A DOWEL must slide (so plain), a TIE must grip (so deformed).** Their purposes demand opposite bond behaviour.

> **The source's own note confirms it: tie bars are NOT load transfer devices but serve to tie two slabs; hence they must be deformed or hooked and anchored into the concrete, and they are smaller than dowel bars and placed at larger intervals.**

**The joints of a concrete pavement, since the bars serve them:**

| Joint | Direction | Purpose | Bar used |
|---|---|---|---|
| **EXPANSION joint** | Transverse | **Allow the slab to EXPAND — a gap with a filler** | **DOWEL** |
| **CONTRACTION joint** | Transverse | **Control where shrinkage cracks form** | **DOWEL** |
| **CONSTRUCTION joint** | Transverse | Where a day's work ends | Dowel |
| **WARPING joint** | Either | Relieve warping stresses | — |
| **LONGITUDINAL joint** | Longitudinal | **Control cracking where the pavement is wider than about 4.5 m; relieve warping and uneven settlement** | **TIE BAR** |

> **The longitudinal joint's threshold of 4.5 m is worth knowing: a pavement wider than that will crack longitudinally whether a joint is provided or not**, so the joint is provided to choose where.

> **Which is the general principle of jointing: concrete WILL crack, and a joint is a crack the engineer decided the location of.** Contraction joints exist for exactly the same reason.

**And the modern alternative, worth a line:**

> **CONTINUOUSLY REINFORCED CONCRETE PAVEMENT (CRCP) eliminates transverse joints altogether**, using heavy continuous longitudinal reinforcement to hold the inevitable fine cracks tightly closed.

> **No joints means no faulting, no pumping and a smoother ride — at the cost of much more steel.** It is the recognition that the joints, not the concrete, were the weak point of the traditional pavement.

examTip.trick: **A dowel crosses a TRANSVERSE joint, and a joint running across the road needs a bar running ALONG it** — so the direction is a geometric consequence of the joint it serves.
examTip.trap: **DOWEL versus TIE bar is opposite in every respect.** Dowel: transverse joint, longitudinal bar, PLAIN and greased, transfers load. Tie: longitudinal joint, transverse bar, DEFORMED and anchored, does NOT transfer load.
examTip.mnemonic: **A dowel must SLIDE (hence plain and greased) so the joint can open and close** — a deformed bar used as a dowel locks the joint and the slab cracks elsewhere. And jointing exists because **concrete will crack; a joint is a crack you chose the location of.**

questions.stem: The correction for Benkelman beam deflection is done as:
options: Reduced 0.01 mm for every degree of temperature more than 35 °C
Increased 0.01 mm for every degree of temperature less than 35 °C
no correction for deflection at 35 °C and temperature less than 20 °C
questions.solution:
**All of the above — the three statements together describe the temperature correction.**

**The correction rule:**

> **35 °C is the STANDARD pavement temperature to which all deflections are corrected.**

| Measured temperature | Correction |
|---|---|
| **ABOVE 35 °C** | **REDUCE the deflection by 0.01 mm per degree** |
| **BELOW 35 °C** | **INCREASE the deflection by 0.01 mm per degree** |
| **AT 35 °C** | **No correction — it is already at the standard** |
| **BELOW 20 °C** | **No correction applied** |

> **The source states all four cases and concludes "All are correct".**

> **Options (a), (b) and (c) are three of those cases, none contradicting the others — so (d) is the honest answer.**

**Why the correction runs in that direction — the physical reason:**

> **Bitumen is a THERMOPLASTIC material: it is STIFFER when COLD and SOFTER when HOT.**

> **A HOT pavement is softer, so it deflects MORE — and the measured deflection overstates the pavement's condition at the standard temperature. Hence REDUCE it.**

> **A COLD pavement is stiffer, so it deflects LESS — and the measured deflection UNDERSTATES the true value. Hence INCREASE it.**

> **The direction follows entirely from that, and it is worth reasoning rather than memorising: correct TOWARD what the pavement would have done at 35 °C.**

> **And the practical consequence is the reason the correction exists: a deflection measured on a cold morning and used untreated makes a WEAK pavement look ADEQUATE — and the overlay designed from it is too thin and fails.**

**Why there is no correction below 20 °C — the honest explanation:**

> **The 0.01 mm per degree rule is a LINEAR approximation, and it was calibrated over a limited temperature range.**

> **Below about 20 °C the bitumen's stiffness no longer changes linearly with temperature — it approaches a glassy state where further cooling changes little.**

> **So extrapolating the linear correction to very low temperatures would OVERCORRECT**, and the code simply stops applying it.

> **That is a good example of a general point about empirical corrections: they are valid only over the range in which they were established**, and applying them beyond it produces confident nonsense.

**The OTHER corrections, since the temperature one is not the only one:**

> **LEG CORRECTION**, applied when the beam's own legs were sitting on deflected pavement:

> **If (Di − Df) > 0.025 mm, then  D = 2[(Do − Df) + 2.91(Di − Df)]**

> **Otherwise simply  D = 2(Do − Df)**, the factor 2 coming from the beam's 2:1 lever ratio.

> **SEASONAL (moisture) CORRECTION**: the subgrade is weakest just after the monsoon, so a dry-season measurement must be factored UP to represent the critical condition.

| Correction | Why |
|---|---|
| **Lever ratio (×2)** | **Geometric — the probe arm is twice the gauge arm** |
| **LEG correction** | The reference frame was itself deflecting |
| **TEMPERATURE to 35 °C** | **Bitumen stiffness varies with temperature** ← |
| **SEASONAL** | **The subgrade is weakest after the monsoon** |

> **All four must be applied, and the seasonal one is the largest and most often omitted.** In Nepal, where the difference between post-monsoon and dry-season subgrade strength is substantial, **a deflection survey timed for convenience rather than for the critical season can be seriously misleading.**

**How the corrected values are then used:**

> **CHARACTERISTIC DEFLECTION = mean + 2 standard deviations** for a major road (mean + 1 SD for lesser roads), computed over at least ten points on a homogeneous section.

> **That figure, with the design traffic, gives the required OVERLAY THICKNESS from the IRC 81 chart.**

> **The statistical treatment is deliberate: an overlay designed for the AVERAGE deflection would be inadequate over the weakest half of the road.** Mean + 2SD designs for roughly the worst 2.5 per cent — **a decision about how much of the road may fail early, not merely a formula.**

> **And it is why at least ten points are required: a standard deviation computed from three readings carries no information.**

**Why "all of the above" is right here, when it usually deserves suspicion:**

> **An all-of-the-above fails if ANY member is false.**

> **Here each option states a different case of one rule, and none contradicts the others.** The correct method is mechanical: **verify each statement independently, then decide.**

> **A candidate who reasons "only one of these can be the rule, so I must choose the best" has imported an assumption the question does not make** — and here the three statements are complementary rather than competing.

examTip.trick: **Correct TOWARD what the pavement would have done at 35 °C.** Hot pavement is softer and deflects more → REDUCE; cold is stiffer and deflects less → INCREASE. The direction follows from the physics.
examTip.trap: **The three options are three cases of ONE rule, not competing claims** — so all-of-the-above is honest here. Verify each independently rather than assuming only one can be right.
examTip.mnemonic: **No correction below 20 °C because the LINEAR rule was calibrated over a limited range** — extrapolating it would overcorrect. And the SEASONAL correction is the largest and most often omitted.

questions.stem: The design speed for a 1st class road in plain terrain is:
questions.solution:
**120 km/h.**

**The design speed table, which is what the question is drawn from:**

| Road class | Plain | Rolling | Mountainous | Steep |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **I** | **120** | **100** | **80** | **60** |
| **II** | **100** | **80** | **60** | **40** |
| **III** | **80** | **60** | **40** | **30** |
| **IV** | **60** | **40** | **30** | **20** |

> **The source reproduces this table exactly, and its structure is what makes it learnable rather than four rows of numbers.**

**The pattern — and it is highly regular:**

> **Reading ACROSS a row, the speed falls as the terrain steepens.**

> **Reading DOWN a column, the speed falls as the road class descends.**

> **And the entries repeat along diagonals: 120, 100, 80, 60 appears as row I; 100, 80, 60, 40 as row II** — each row is the previous one shifted one step down the same sequence.

> **So the whole table is generated by ONE sequence — 120, 100, 80, 60, 40, 30, 20 — read from a different starting point for each class.**

> **Note that every option in this question is a member of that sequence**, and three of them are the other entries in row I. **So the question tests whether the table's structure is known, not whether one number was memorised.**

**Why the terrain matters so much — the four classifications:**

| Terrain | Cross slope of the country |
|---|---|
| **PLAIN** | **0 to 10 %** |
| **ROLLING** | **10 to 25 %** |
| **MOUNTAINOUS** | **25 to 60 %** |
| **STEEP** | **Greater than 60 %** |

> **The terrain is classified by the CROSS SLOPE of the ground, measured perpendicular to the road's general alignment** — not by altitude, and not by the road's own gradient.

> **That is worth knowing because it is counter-intuitive: a road along a valley floor in the high Himalaya may be in PLAIN or ROLLING terrain by this definition**, while a road across a steep hillside at low altitude is MOUNTAINOUS.

> **The classification is about how difficult the ground is to build on, which is what actually limits the achievable geometry.**

**What design speed governs, since it is the master variable of geometric design:**

| Element | Dependence on design speed V |
|---|---|
| **STOPPING SIGHT DISTANCE** | **0.278Vt + V²/(254f) — grows faster than V** |
| **Minimum radius of horizontal curve** | **R = V²/[127(e+f)] — as V²** |
| **Length of summit curve** | **As V², through the SSD** |
| **Length of valley curve** | Similar |
| **Superelevation** | e = V²/(127R) − f |
| **Overtaking sight distance** | Grows steeply with V |
| Extra widening, transition length | Both increase with V |

> **Almost every geometric requirement grows as V² or faster**, which is the single most important consequence of the table above.

> **So raising a road's design speed by 25 per cent raises the required curve radii and sight distances by more than 50 per cent** — and in mountainous terrain that can be the difference between a feasible alignment and an impossible one.

> **That is precisely why the design speed is reduced for difficult terrain: not because vehicles cannot go faster, but because the GEOMETRY a higher speed demands cannot be built at acceptable cost.**

**The distinction that matters in practice:**

| Speed | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **DESIGN speed** | **The speed the GEOMETRY is designed for — the basis of every element above** |
| **Speed LIMIT** | **The legal maximum, set from the 85th percentile of observed speeds** |
| **85th percentile speed** | The speed 85 % of drivers do not exceed |
| **98th percentile speed** | **Sometimes used AS the design speed** |

> **The design speed is generally HIGHER than the speed limit**, which is deliberate: **the geometry must be safe for the fastest realistic vehicle, not merely for the legal maximum.**

> **And a road should be designed to a CONSISTENT speed along its length.** A stretch of generous geometry followed by a sharp curve built to a lower standard is more dangerous than a uniformly modest road, **because drivers calibrate their speed to what the road appears to permit.**

> **That principle — design consistency — is why the design speed is chosen for a whole homogeneous section rather than element by element**, and it is the reason an isolated substandard curve is treated as a serious defect rather than a local economy.

examTip.trick: **One sequence generates the whole table — 120, 100, 80, 60, 40, 30, 20 — read from a different start for each road class.** Class I plain is the top: 120 km/h.
examTip.trap: **All four options are entries in row I** (120, 100, 80, 60 for plain, rolling, mountainous, steep). So the question tests the table's STRUCTURE, not one memorised number.
examTip.mnemonic: **Terrain is classified by the CROSS SLOPE of the ground (plain 0-10 %, rolling 10-25 %, mountainous 25-60 %, steep >60 %)** — not by altitude. And almost every geometric requirement grows as V² or faster, which is why difficult terrain gets a lower design speed.

questions.stem: Find the fire demand for a population of 1 lakh using Kuichling's formula:
questions.solution:
**31,820 litres per minute.**

**Kuichling's formula:**

> **Q = 3182 √P  litres per minute**, where **P is the population in THOUSANDS.**

**The computation:**

> **P = 1 lakh = 100,000 = 100 thousand**

> **Q = 3182 × √100 = 3182 × 10 = 31,820 L/min** ✓

> **The whole difficulty is the unit of P: it must be in THOUSANDS.**

> **Putting P = 100,000 directly gives 3182 × 316 = 1,006,000 L/min — off the option list, which is at least a warning.**

> **And note that option (c) 3182 L/min is the coefficient itself** — what you get with √P = 1, that is, a population of one thousand. **The designed trap for anyone who does not substitute at all.**

**Why the options are so instructive:**

| Option | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| **318.2 L/min** | **The coefficient divided by ten** |
| **31,820 L/min** | ✓ **3182 × 10** |
| **3182 L/min** | **The bare COEFFICIENT — P not substituted** ← |
| **318,200 L/min** | **3182 × 100 — using P = 100 without the square root** ← |

> **Option (d) is the more interesting error: it omits the SQUARE ROOT**, multiplying by 100 instead of by √100 = 10.

> **So the two substantive traps are forgetting the thousands and forgetting the root** — and the option list punishes each separately.

**Why fire demand is proportional to √P rather than to P — this is the concept:**

> **Fire demand grows much more SLOWLY than population, because a fire is a LOCAL event.**

> **A city of a million does not have ten times as many simultaneous fires as a city of a hundred thousand — it has a somewhat larger number of simultaneous fires, and each still needs the same water to fight.**

> **So the demand scales with roughly the square root of the population**, and every empirical fire-demand formula has that form.

| Formula | Expression (Q in L/min, P in thousands) |
|---|---|
| **KUICHLING'S** | **Q = 3182 √P** ← |
| **FREEMAN'S** | **Q = 1136 [(P/5) + 10]** |
| **BUSTON'S** | **Q = 5663 √P** |
| **National Board of Fire Underwriters** | **Q = 4637 √P (1 − 0.01√P)** |
| Ministry of Urban Development (India) | Q = 100 √P (in kL/day) |

> **Several formulae, all giving different answers for the same population** — which is worth noticing rather than glossing over.

> **For P = 100 thousand: Kuichling gives 31,820 L/min while Buston gives 56,630** — a factor of nearly two. **So the choice of formula matters as much as the arithmetic, and a question must state which formula to use.** This one does.

**How fire demand enters the design of a water supply:**

> **Fire demand is not added to the average demand. It is a SEPARATE, SHORT-DURATION, HIGH-RATE requirement that must be met SIMULTANEOUSLY with the maximum daily demand.**

| Design check | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Normal operation** | **The system meets the maximum HOURLY demand** |
| **Fire condition** | **The system meets the maximum DAILY demand PLUS the fire demand** ← |
| Duration | **The fire flow must be sustainable for 4 to 10 hours** |
| Residual pressure during a fire | **A minimum pressure must remain at the hydrant, typically 100-150 kPa** |

> **The combination in the second row is the standard one, and the logic is a probability judgement: a fire is unlikely to coincide with the peak HOURLY demand, but it must be assumed to coincide with a busy DAY.**

> **Note the small per-capita contribution in ordinary terms: fire demand works out to only about 1 to 5 litres per person per day when averaged over the year** — because a fire lasts hours and happens rarely.

> **But the INSTANTANEOUS rate is enormous, and it is the rate that sizes the mains, the pumps and the service reservoir.**

> **So fire demand is a small quantity of water delivered very fast, and that is why it governs pipe DIAMETERS in a distribution network far more than it affects the source.**

**And the practical consequence for small towns:**

> **In a small settlement, the fire demand can EXCEED the entire domestic demand.**

> **For P = 5 thousand: Kuichling gives 3182 × √5 = 7,116 L/min = 10.2 MLD** — while the domestic demand at 135 lpcd is only 0.68 MLD.

> **Fifteen times the domestic demand.** Which means a small town's network sized for full fire flow would be grossly oversized for its everyday use — **oversized pipes run slowly, water stagnates, and the residual chlorine decays.**

> **So in practice small schemes accept a reduced fire-fighting standard**, relying on tankers and on a smaller number of hydrants, rather than building a network the town cannot otherwise use. **That is a defensible engineering compromise and worth being able to explain.**

examTip.trick: **Q = 3182√P with P in THOUSANDS.** For 1 lakh, P = 100, so Q = 3182 × 10 = 31,820 L/min.
examTip.trap: **Two separate traps: option (c) is the bare COEFFICIENT (P not substituted) and option (d) omits the SQUARE ROOT** (multiplying by 100 instead of 10). Putting P = 100,000 directly gives an answer off the list entirely.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fire demand goes as √P because a fire is a LOCAL event** — a city ten times larger does not have ten times the simultaneous fires. Design for maximum DAILY demand PLUS fire demand, and note that in a small town fire demand can exceed all domestic use.

questions.stem: Quartzite is:
questions.solution:
**A siliceous rock.**

**Why — the classification is by CHEMICAL COMPOSITION:**

> **Quartzite is metamorphosed SANDSTONE, and it consists almost entirely of QUARTZ — silicon dioxide, SiO₂.**

> **A rock whose dominant constituent is silica is a SILICEOUS rock.**

> **The source states it plainly: quartzite is a metamorphic siliceous rock.**

**The chemical classification of rocks, which is what the options are drawn from:**

| Class | Dominant constituent | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **SILICEOUS** | **SILICA, SiO₂** | **QUARTZITE, granite, sandstone (silica-cemented), basalt, gneiss** ← |
| **CALCAREOUS** | **LIME, CaCO₃** | **LIMESTONE, marble, dolomite, chalk** |
| **ARGILLACEOUS** | **CLAY (alumina), Al₂O₃** | **Slate, shale, laterite, mudstone** |

> **Three chemical classes, and the question offers only one of the other two (calcareous) as a distractor.**

> **The distinction has real engineering consequence, which is why it exists as a classification rather than as chemistry for its own sake:**

| Class | Engineering behaviour |
|---|---|
| **SILICEOUS** | **HARD, DURABLE, chemically INERT — resists acid attack and weathering. The best aggregates** |
| **CALCAREOUS** | **SOLUBLE in acid — attacked by acidic water and by industrial atmospheres; softer** |
| **ARGILLACEOUS** | **Prone to SOFTENING when wet; splits along cleavage; low durability if clay-rich** |

> **So a siliceous rock is generally the one to want for aggregate**, and quartzite in particular is among the best aggregates there is — hard, tough and inert.

> **That is why quartzite is a major aggregate source in Nepal**, where it occurs abundantly in the Lesser and Higher Himalayan sequences.

**Why options (a) and (c) fail on a category error, not on chemistry:**

> **"ORGANIC rock" and "INORGANIC rock" are a different and much cruder division — by ORIGIN, not by composition.**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **ORGANIC rock** | **Formed from the remains of PLANTS or ANIMALS — coal, some limestones (coral, shell), peat** |
| **INORGANIC rock** | **Everything else — virtually all rocks** |

> **Quartzite IS inorganic, so option (c) is not FALSE — it is merely useless.** It is true of almost every rock, so it identifies nothing.

> **That is the discrimination the question rewards: option (c) is a true statement that answers no question**, and recognising an uninformative option is a legitimate technique.

> **Option (a) organic is simply wrong: quartzite has no biological origin.**

**The GEOLOGICAL classification, since the three schemes are examined together:**

| Class | Formation | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **IGNEOUS** | **Solidified magma** | **Granite (intrusive), basalt and trap (extrusive)** |
| **SEDIMENTARY** | **Deposited and compacted** | **Sandstone, limestone, shale, conglomerate** |
| **METAMORPHIC** | **Altered by heat and pressure** | **QUARTZITE, marble, slate, gneiss, schist** ← |

> **The metamorphic PAIRS are the ones examined, and they are worth learning as pairs:**

| Parent rock | Metamorphoses to |
|---|---|
| **SANDSTONE** | **QUARTZITE** ← |
| **LIMESTONE** | **MARBLE** |
| **SHALE** | **SLATE** (then phyllite, then schist) |
| **GRANITE** | **GNEISS** |
| Coal | Anthracite, then graphite |

> **Note that metamorphism generally makes a rock HARDER, DENSER and LESS POROUS**, because heat and pressure recrystallise it and close its voids.

> **Quartzite is markedly stronger and less porous than the sandstone it came from** — the individual quartz grains have recrystallised into an interlocking mass, so the rock breaks THROUGH the grains rather than around them.

> **That is why quartzite is a good aggregate and many sandstones are not**, even though they are chemically the same material.

**The requirements of a good building stone, since they follow:**

| Property | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Crushing strength** | **Not less than about 100 N/mm² for structural work** |
| **WATER ABSORPTION** | **Below 5 % — the most diagnostic single durability test** ← |
| **Appearance and texture** | Uniform, fine-grained, free of cracks and cavities |
| **Durability, hardness, toughness** | Resists weathering and abrasion |
| **Ease of dressing** | Should work without shattering |

> **Water absorption is the most diagnostic test because almost every mechanism that destroys stone — freezing, salt crystallisation, chemical attack — needs water to get INSIDE it first.**

> **A low-absorption stone is largely immune to all of them at once**, which is why the single cheap test screens so effectively — and why quartzite, with very low porosity, performs so well.

examTip.trick: **Quartzite is almost pure SiO₂, so it is SILICEOUS.** The chemical classes are siliceous (silica), calcareous (lime) and argillaceous (clay) — and the engineering behaviour follows from each.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) "inorganic" is TRUE and useless** — it is true of almost every rock, so it identifies nothing. Recognising an uninformative option is a legitimate technique.
examTip.mnemonic: **Learn the metamorphic PAIRS: sandstone→quartzite, limestone→marble, shale→slate, granite→gneiss.** Metamorphism makes rock harder and less porous, which is why quartzite is an excellent aggregate and many sandstones are not.

questions.stem: A liquid will not wet the surface of a solid if the angle of contact is:
questions.solution:
**Obtuse.**

**The rule, and the physical reason behind it:**

> **The ANGLE OF CONTACT is measured INSIDE the liquid, between the solid surface and the tangent to the liquid surface at the point of contact.**

> **It is set by the competition between two forces:**

| Force | Acts between |
|---|---|
| **ADHESION** | **The LIQUID and the SOLID** |
| **COHESION** | **The liquid and ITSELF** |

> **If ADHESION WINS, the liquid spreads over the solid — it WETS it — and the contact angle is ACUTE.**

> **If COHESION WINS, the liquid pulls itself together and retreats from the solid — it does NOT wet it — and the contact angle is OBTUSE.**

> **So "not wetting" and "obtuse" are two descriptions of the same condition.**

**The four cases the source sets out:**

| Contact angle | Behaviour | Capillary tube |
|---|---|---|
| **ZERO** | **COMPLETE wetting — the liquid spreads entirely** | Maximum rise |
| **ACUTE (< 90°)** | **WETS the surface** | **Level RISES above the outside** |
| **RIGHT ANGLE (90°)** | **Neither wets nor repels** | **Level does NOT change** |
| **OBTUSE (> 90°)** | **Does NOT wet** | **Level FALLS below the outside** ← |

> **The two examples to anchor it:**

> **WATER on GLASS: contact angle about 0-8°, strongly acute. Water wets glass, and rises in a glass capillary.**

> **MERCURY on GLASS: contact angle about 130-140°, strongly obtuse. Mercury does not wet glass, and FALLS in a glass capillary — forming a convex meniscus.**

> **The source gives exactly this pair, and it is the clearest illustration of the principle.**

**Why option (b) "unity" can be dismissed immediately:**

> **An ANGLE is measured in DEGREES or RADIANS. "Unity" is a dimensionless number, not an angle.**

> **So option (b) is a CATEGORY error rather than a wrong value** — it does not name a possible angle at all.

> **Recognising that costs nothing and eliminates an option without any knowledge of surface tension.**

**The capillary rise formula, which quantifies all of this:**

> **h = 4σ cos θ / (ρ g d)**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **σ** | **SURFACE TENSION of the liquid** |
| **θ** | **CONTACT ANGLE** |
| **d** | **Diameter of the tube** |
| **ρ, g** | Density and gravity |

> **The cos θ term carries the whole of the wetting behaviour:**

| θ | cos θ | h |
|---|---|---|
| **0°** | **+1** | **Maximum RISE** |
| **Acute** | **POSITIVE** | **RISE** |
| **90°** | **ZERO** | **NO change** |
| **Obtuse** | **NEGATIVE** | **DEPRESSION (fall)** ← |

> **So the sign of the capillary rise IS the sign of cos θ** — which is a compact way to hold the whole table, and it explains why mercury's depression follows from the same formula as water's rise rather than needing a separate one.

> **Note also that h is INVERSELY proportional to d: capillary effects matter in FINE tubes and are negligible in wide ones.** Which is why a wide manometer tube reads accurately and a narrow one needs a correction.

**Where capillarity matters in civil engineering — this is why it is in the syllabus:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **CAPILLARY RISE in soil** | **Water drawn up above the water table into the CAPILLARY FRINGE — the mechanism behind frost heave and salinity** ← |
| **RISING DAMP in masonry** | **Water climbing through the fine pores of brick and mortar — the reason a DPC exists** |
| **Manometer readings** | A correction is needed in fine tubes |
| **Soil suction and negative pore pressure** | Gives unsaturated soil apparent cohesion |
| Water retention in fine-grained soil | Governs drainage behaviour |

> **The capillary rise in soil is the most consequential, and its magnitude is striking:**

| Soil | Capillary rise |
|---|---|
| **Coarse sand** | **0.03-0.15 m** |
| **Fine sand** | **0.3-2 m** |
| **Silt** | **1.5-10 m** |
| **CLAY** | **10 m or more** ← |

> **Because h goes as 1/d, and clay's pores are minute, the rise in clay can be tens of metres.**

> **That is the mechanism behind SALINITY in irrigated land: capillary action lifts saline groundwater to the surface, evaporation removes the water, and the salt stays.** It is also why a high water table in fine soil affects the ground far above the water table itself.

> **And it is why the capillary fringe must be considered in foundation design: soil that appears above the water table may be saturated by capillarity, with the pore pressures — and therefore the effective stresses — that implies.**

examTip.trick: **Adhesion wins → wets → ACUTE. Cohesion wins → does not wet → OBTUSE.** Water on glass ~0-8° (rises); mercury on glass ~130-140° (falls).
examTip.trap: **Option (b) "unity" is a CATEGORY error** — an angle is measured in degrees, not as a dimensionless number. That eliminates it with no knowledge of surface tension.
examTip.mnemonic: **h = 4σcosθ/(ρgd), so the SIGN of the rise is the sign of cos θ** — positive for acute, negative for obtuse. And h ∝ 1/d, which is why capillary rise in CLAY reaches tens of metres and drives salinity.

questions.stem: If a soil has a liquid limit of 60 % and a plastic limit of 40 %, then the soil falls under:
questions.solution:
**MH — inorganic silt of high compressibility.**

**Step 1 — compute the plasticity index:**

> **I_p = w_L − w_P = 60 − 40 = 20 %**

**Step 2 — locate the point relative to the A-LINE:**

> **The A-line is defined by  I′_p = 0.73 (w_L − 20)**

> **At w_L = 60:  I′_p = 0.73 (60 − 20) = 0.73 × 40 = 29.2 %**

> **The soil's actual I_p = 20, which is LESS than 29.2 — so the point lies BELOW the A-line.**

**Step 3 — read off the group symbol:**

| Position | First letter |
|---|---|
| **ABOVE the A-line** | **C — CLAY** |
| **BELOW the A-line** | **M — SILT (or O — organic)** ← |

| Liquid limit | Second letter |
|---|---|
| **w_L < 35** | **L — LOW plasticity / compressibility** |
| **35 < w_L < 50** | **I — INTERMEDIATE** |
| **w_L > 50** | **H — HIGH** ← w_L = 60 |

> **Below the A-line gives M; w_L = 60 > 50 gives H.**

> **Therefore MH.** ✓

**Why each distractor is wrong — and each fails on a specific step:**

| Option | Why not |
|---|---|
| **MH** | ✓ |
| **CH** | **Would require the point ABOVE the A-line — but I_p = 20 < 29.2, so it is below** ← the main trap |
| **LH** | **NOT A VALID SYMBOL AT ALL.** L is a compressibility letter and belongs SECOND, not first. "LH" has two second-letters and no soil-type letter |
| **ML** | **Right soil type (M) but wrong compressibility: w_L = 60 is HIGH, not low** |

> **Option (c) LH is worth naming as a structural impossibility rather than a wrong answer**: the symbol grammar is (soil type)(plasticity), so the first letter must be one of G, S, M, C, O and the second one of W, P, M, C, L, I, H. **"LH" violates that, and spotting it eliminates the option without any calculation.**

> **Option (b) CH is the substantive trap and it is the one to be careful with: it requires the A-line comparison, which is the only real work in the question.** A candidate who classifies on the liquid limit alone gets the H right and the C wrong.

**Reading the plasticity chart, since that is what the calculation is doing:**

> **The chart plots PLASTICITY INDEX (vertical) against LIQUID LIMIT (horizontal), and two lines divide it:**

| Line | Equation | Separates |
|---|---|---|
| **A-LINE** | **I_p = 0.73(w_L − 20)** | **CLAYS (above) from SILTS and ORGANIC soils (below)** |
| **U-LINE** | **I_p = 0.9(w_L − 8)** | **The upper bound — NO real soil plots above it** |

> **The U-line is a useful check on laboratory work rather than a classification boundary: a result plotting above it is almost certainly a TESTING ERROR**, not a remarkable soil.

> **And the vertical lines at w_L = 35 and 50 give the three compressibility bands, L, I and H.**

**Why the distinction between M and C matters in practice — it is not merely nomenclature:**

| | **SILT (M)** | **CLAY (C)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Plasticity** | **LOW — crumbles, cannot be rolled thin** | **HIGH — rolls into a thread, feels sticky** |
| **PERMEABILITY** | **HIGHER (10⁻⁵ to 10⁻⁷ m/s)** | **LOWER (below 10⁻⁹ m/s)** |
| **Consolidation** | **FASTER** | **Very SLOW** |
| **Dry strength** | **Low — crushes easily between fingers** | **HIGH — hard to break** |
| **Dilatancy (shaking test)** | **QUICK reaction — water appears on the surface** | **NO reaction** |
| **Frost susceptibility** | **HIGH — silt is the worst soil for frost heave** ← | Lower |
| **Volume change on wetting** | Small | **LARGE in expansive clays** |

> **The frost-heave row is a genuinely useful discrimination: SILT is the most frost-susceptible soil there is**, because its pores are fine enough to draw water up by capillarity and coarse enough to let it move quickly. **Clay draws water higher but too slowly to feed an ice lens; sand does not draw it at all.**

> **So a silt subgrade in a cold region is a specific problem that a clay subgrade is not**, which is exactly the kind of conclusion the classification exists to deliver.

> **And the DILATANCY (shaking) test is the field method for telling them apart with no equipment: pat a moist pat of soil in the palm and water appears on the surface of a SILT and not of a CLAY.**

**The full symbol set, for reference:**

| First letter (type) | Second letter |
|---|---|
| **G** — gravel | **W** — well graded |
| **S** — sand | **P** — poorly graded |
| **M** — silt | **M** — with silt |
| **C** — clay | **C** — with clay |
| **O** — organic | **L / I / H** — low / intermediate / high |
| **Pt** — peat | — |

> **So MH, CH, ML, CI, SW, GP and so on are valid; LH, HM and HC are not** — and knowing the grammar is a fast way to eliminate malformed options, which appear in this examination more than once.

examTip.trick: **I_p = 60 − 40 = 20. A-line at w_L = 60 gives 0.73(60−20) = 29.2. Since 20 < 29.2 the point is BELOW the A-line → M; and w_L = 60 > 50 → H.** Hence MH.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) "LH" is not a valid symbol at all** — L is a second-position letter, so LH has two of them and no soil type. Symbol grammar eliminates it with no calculation. And CH requires the A-line comparison, which is the only real work here.
examTip.mnemonic: **SILT is the most FROST-SUSCEPTIBLE soil** — fine enough to draw water by capillarity, coarse enough to move it fast. Clay draws it higher but too slowly; sand not at all. And the field test is DILATANCY: water appears on a shaken silt, not a clay.

questions.stem: The vertical clearance height at a cliff in a hill road is:
questions.solution:
**5 m.**

**What the requirement is:**

> **Where a hill road passes beneath an overhanging cliff or a rock overhang, a MINIMUM VERTICAL CLEARANCE of 5 m must be maintained above the carriageway.**

> **The source states it directly: the vertical clearance should be 5 m.**

**Why 5 m and not less — what the clearance must accommodate:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **The tallest vehicle expected** | **A loaded truck or bus is about 3.8 to 4.2 m; containers taller** |
| **A margin for future RESURFACING** | **Every overlay RAISES the road and REDUCES the clearance** ← |
| **Load overhang and irregular loads** | Timber, machinery, hay |
| **Rockfall protection measures** | Netting or a canopy may be added later |
| **Survey and construction tolerance** | The rock face is irregular |

> **The resurfacing point is the one worth emphasising, because it is a slow trap: each overlay adds 40 to 100 mm, and over decades a road can rise a quarter of a metre.**

> **A clearance set at exactly the vehicle height when built will not be adequate for the life of the road**, which is why the standard includes a margin rather than a measurement.

> **And where a clearance is genuinely tight, the correct response at resurfacing is to MILL OFF the old surface rather than overlay it** — a decision that must be recorded, or it will not be made.

**The related clearances, since they are examined as a set:**

| Situation | Minimum vertical clearance |
|---|---|
| **Under an overhanging CLIFF (hill road)** | **5.0 m** ← |
| **Under a road bridge or overpass** | **5.0 m (commonly 5.5 m allowed for future resurfacing)** |
| **Under a railway overbridge** | 4.75 to 5.0 m |
| **Under a foot overbridge** | 5.5 m |
| **Electrical clearance, low-tension line** | 5.5 m and upward with voltage |
| **Under a subway or tunnel** | 5.0 m minimum |

> **The 5 m figure recurs, which makes it the number to anchor on** — and the exceptions are all UPWARD, for structures whose failure would be more serious or which cannot be milled.

**Why hill roads have their own set of geometric problems, since this is one of them:**

| Constraint | Note |
|---|---|
| **VERTICAL CLEARANCE at overhangs** | **5 m** ← |
| **Ruling gradient** | **5 % in mountainous, 6 % limiting, 7 % exceptional** |
| **Minimum radius at HAIRPIN bends** | **14 m (or 20 m on the inner edge), with a design speed of 20 km/h** |
| **Extra widening at curves** | **Larger than in plain terrain, because radii are small** |
| **Passing places on single-lane roads** | At intervals within sight of each other |
| **Camber and drainage** | **Water must be shed to the HILLSIDE drain, not over the valley edge** |

> **The HAIRPIN BEND is the element unique to hill roads, and the reason for its very low design speed is unavoidable: the bend exists because the alignment must gain height in a limited horizontal distance.**

> **A hairpin's geometry is therefore set by the terrain rather than by the design speed, and a 20 km/h restriction is accepted as the price of gaining the height at all.**

> **Which is why hill roads are designed as a sequence of straights at the general design speed connected by hairpins at a much lower one — and why signing and sight distance at the approach to each hairpin matter so much.**

**And the drainage point, since it is where hill roads most often fail:**

> **The camber on a hill road sheds water toward the HILLSIDE, into a lined side drain, and not over the valley edge.**

> **The reason is that water discharged over the edge erodes the fill slope and, over time, undermines the road from beneath.**

| Element | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Hillside (catch) drain** | **Collects road water AND hillside runoff** |
| **CATCH-WATER DRAIN above the cutting** | **Intercepts hillside runoff BEFORE it reaches the cut slope** ← |
| **Cross drains / culverts at intervals** | Take the collected water across the road to a controlled outfall |
| Chutes and cascades on the fill side | Convey water down the slope without eroding it |

> **The catch-water drain is the cheapest and most effective measure on a hill road, and its omission is the commonest cause of slope failure**: hillside runoff arriving at the top of a cut slope will saturate and destabilise it, and no amount of retaining structure compensates for that.

> **So on a hill road, DRAINAGE is the principal design activity rather than a supporting one** — which is a genuine difference from a road in plain terrain, where the pavement dominates.

examTip.trick: **5 m minimum vertical clearance**, and the same 5 m recurs for bridges and subways — so it is the figure to anchor on. Exceptions are all UPWARD.
examTip.trap: **The margin above vehicle height exists for future RESURFACING** — each overlay adds 40-100 mm, and over decades a road can rise a quarter of a metre. Where clearance is tight, MILL rather than overlay.
examTip.mnemonic: **On a hill road, DRAINAGE is the principal design activity** — camber sheds to the HILLSIDE, and the CATCH-WATER DRAIN above the cutting is the cheapest, most effective and most often omitted measure.

questions.stem: The formula for degree of saturation is:
questions.solution:
**S = V_w / V_v — the volume of water divided by the volume of VOIDS.**

**The definition and why the denominator is the voids:**

> **DEGREE OF SATURATION is the fraction of the VOID SPACE that is filled with water.**

> **Water can only occupy the voids — it cannot occupy the solids** — so the voids are the space available, and the degree of saturation measures how much of that available space is used.

> **S = V_w / V_v**, usually expressed as a percentage.

**The limiting checks, which confirm the formula:**

| Condition | V_w | S |
|---|---|---|
| **Fully SATURATED soil** | **V_w = V_v (water fills all the voids)** | **S = 100 %** ✓ |
| **Completely DRY soil** | **V_w = 0** | **S = 0 %** ✓ |
| Partly saturated | 0 < V_w < V_v | 0 < S < 100 % |

> **The source gives exactly these two checks, and they are the fastest way to verify the formula: any candidate expression must give 100 % when the voids are full and 0 % when they are empty.**

> **Test the distractors that way:**

| Option | At full saturation (V_w = V_v) | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **V_w/V_v** | **1 = 100 %** ✓ | **Correct** |
| **V_v/V_w** | **1 = 100 %** ✓ — but it is INFINITE for dry soil | **Fails the dry check** |
| **V_w/V_s** | **V_v/V_s = the void ratio, NOT 1** | **Fails** |
| **V_s/V_w** | Not 1, and infinite when dry | **Fails** |

> **Option (b) is the designed trap — the INVERTED ratio — and the dry-soil check kills it instantly: V_v/V_w becomes infinite as the soil dries, and a degree of saturation cannot exceed 100 per cent.**

> **That is a general defence against inverted-ratio distractors: find the limiting case where the wrong version misbehaves.**

**The related relation, which is how S is usually computed in practice:**

> **S e = w G**, that is:  **S = wG / e**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **w** | **WATER CONTENT (by weight) — what the laboratory measures** |
| **G** | **Specific gravity of the solids (~2.65-2.70 for most soils)** |
| **e** | **VOID RATIO** |

> **This form is the useful one because the laboratory measures WEIGHTS, not volumes.** The water content w = W_w/W_s is obtained by oven-drying, and the volumes are inferred.

> **The source's own explanation gives it: S = wG/e.**

> **And note the elegance of the relation Se = wG: it links a volumetric quantity (S, e) to a gravimetric one (w) through the specific gravity, which is the bridge between the two systems of measurement in soil mechanics.**

**The full set of phase relationships, since they are used constantly and confused often:**

| Quantity | Definition | Range |
|---|---|---|
| **VOID RATIO e** | **V_v / V_s** | **0 to ∞ — CAN exceed 1** |
| **POROSITY n** | **V_v / V** | **0 to 1 — can NEVER exceed 1** |
| **DEGREE OF SATURATION S** | **V_w / V_v** | **0 to 1** ← |
| **AIR CONTENT a_c** | **V_a / V_v = 1 − S** | 0 to 1 |
| **Water content w** | **W_w / W_s** | **0 to ∞ — CAN exceed 100 %** |
| **Specific gravity G** | γ_s / γ_w | 2.6-2.8 typically |

> **Two facts in that table catch people out, and both are worth stating:**

> **VOID RATIO can exceed 1** (a very loose soil has more void volume than solid volume), **while POROSITY cannot** (the voids are a fraction of the whole). **That is the check that tells the two apart when the formulae e = n/(1−n) and n = e/(1+e) are confused.**

> **WATER CONTENT can exceed 100 per cent**, which sounds impossible until one notices it is a ratio to the SOLIDS' weight, not to the total. **A soft marine clay can have w = 150 per cent, and organic soils far more.**

**And the derived unit weights, since they all follow from the phase diagram:**

| Unit weight | Expression |
|---|---|
| **BULK (moist)** | **γ = (G + Se)γ_w / (1 + e)** |
| **SATURATED (S = 1)** | **γ_sat = (G + e)γ_w / (1 + e)** |
| **DRY (S = 0)** | **γ_d = G γ_w / (1 + e)** |
| **SUBMERGED** | **γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w = (G − 1)γ_w / (1 + e)** |

> **All four come from ONE expression with S set to 1, 0 or left general** — which is worth noticing, because it means the whole family need not be memorised separately.

> **And γ′ = (G−1)γ_w/(1+e) is the one that appears in every effective-stress calculation below the water table.**

examTip.trick: **Water can only occupy the VOIDS, so the voids are the denominator: S = V_w/V_v.** Check it: full voids give 100 %, empty voids give 0 %.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) is the INVERTED ratio, and the DRY check kills it** — V_v/V_w becomes infinite as the soil dries, and a saturation cannot exceed 100 %. Find the limiting case where a wrong version misbehaves.
examTip.mnemonic: **Se = wG links volumes to weights** — the bridge between the two measurement systems. And two facts that catch people: **void ratio CAN exceed 1 (porosity cannot), and water content CAN exceed 100 %** (it is a ratio to the solids).

questions.stem: The water absorption for a first class brick should not be more than:
questions.solution:
**15 per cent.**

**The limits by brick class:**

| Brick class | Maximum water absorption (24-hour immersion) |
|---|---|
| **FIRST class** | **15 %** ← |
| **SECOND class** | **20 %** |
| **THIRD class** | **25 %** |

> **The source gives exactly this table, and notes that where an IS code is not specified the NS (Nepal Standard) code is followed.**

> **Every option in this question is one row of that table**, so the whole set must be known — and the progression 15, 20, 25 is regular enough to hold easily.

**Why water absorption is the key durability test for a brick:**

> **Absorption measures POROSITY, and porosity is what admits the agents that destroy masonry.**

| Damage mechanism | Needs water inside the brick |
|---|---|
| **FROST damage** | **Water in the pores expands 9 % on freezing and spalls the face** |
| **EFFLORESCENCE** | **Soluble salts dissolve, migrate to the surface and crystallise there** |
| **Sulphate attack on the mortar** | Water carries the sulphates |
| **Reduced strength when wet** | A saturated brick is weaker than a dry one |
| **Rising damp** | **A porous brick wicks water upward far more readily** |

> **So a single cheap test screens against several unrelated failure modes at once**, because they all require the same precondition — **water getting inside.**

> **That is why absorption, rather than strength, is the test that best predicts a brick's durability.** A strong but porous brick will decay; a moderately strong dense one will not.

**The other requirements for a first class brick, since absorption is one of several:**

| Requirement | First class brick |
|---|---|
| **WATER ABSORPTION** | **Not more than 15 %** ← |
| **Minimum COMPRESSIVE STRENGTH** | **10.5 N/mm² (some standards 7.5-10 N/mm²)** |
| **Shape** | **Sharp, well-defined EDGES and true right-angled CORNERS** |
| **Surfaces** | **Plane, parallel, free from cracks and flaws** |
| **Colour** | **Uniform deep red or cherry** |
| **SOUND when struck** | **A clear METALLIC RING — a dull thud indicates under-burning or cracks** ← |
| **Efflorescence** | Nil to slight |
| Fingernail test | **No impression when scratched with a fingernail** |

> **The RINGING SOUND test is the one worth knowing because it needs no equipment at all: strike two bricks together and a well-burnt brick rings while an under-burnt one thuds.**

> **It works because a properly vitrified brick is dense and continuous, so it sustains a vibration; an under-burnt or cracked one does not.**

> **That kind of field test — no instrument, immediate answer — is worth more on a remote site than a laboratory certificate for a different batch.**

**The classes and where each is used:**

| Class | Character | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **FIRST** | **Well burnt, uniform, low absorption** | **EXPOSED masonry, load-bearing work, facing** |
| **SECOND** | Slightly irregular, higher absorption | **Work to be PLASTERED; internal walls** |
| **THIRD** | Under-burnt, soft, high absorption | **Temporary work; unimportant structures in dry situations** |
| **Fourth (jhama / over-burnt)** | **Over-burnt, distorted, very hard** | **BROKEN as AGGREGATE for lime concrete or road sub-base** ← |

> **The fourth class is worth naming because it is not simply waste: over-burnt brick is hard and durable, merely mis-shapen** — so it is broken down and used as aggregate rather than discarded. **Brick aggregate (surkhi and brick ballast) has a genuine role in lime concrete and in road foundations.**

**And the practical rule that follows from the absorption figure:**

> **BRICKS MUST BE SOAKED BEFORE LAYING**, and the reason follows directly from their absorption.

> **A dry brick with 15 per cent absorption will suck water OUT of the mortar the moment it is laid.**

> **The mortar is then DEWATERED before the cement can hydrate — and cement that never had water when it needed it does not gain strength later, however carefully the wall is cured afterwards.**

| Practice | Note |
|---|---|
| **Soak until bubbles cease** | Typically several hours |
| **Lay in a damp, not dripping, condition** | A dripping brick floats on the mortar |
| **Do not soak over-burnt or very dense brick as long** | Little absorption to satisfy |

> **The soaking rule is the most consequential and most ignored instruction in brickwork**, and its failure is invisible: the wall looks correct and its mortar is permanently weak.

> **Which is a general point worth carrying: the defects that matter most in construction are often the ones that leave no trace.**

examTip.trick: **15 %, 20 %, 25 % for first, second and third class.** Every option is a row of that table, so learn the progression rather than one figure.
examTip.trap: **Absorption predicts DURABILITY better than strength does**, because frost damage, efflorescence, sulphate attack and rising damp all need the same precondition — water inside the brick. A strong porous brick still decays.
examTip.mnemonic: **Strike two bricks: a well-burnt one RINGS, an under-burnt one THUDS** — a field test needing no equipment. And **soak bricks before laying**, or the dry brick dewaters the mortar before the cement can hydrate.

questions.stem: The following operations are required for tunnelling in rocky terrain: 1. Removing the foul gases, 2. Marking the tunnel profile, 3. Setting up and drilling, 4. Checking misfire, 5. Mucking. The correct sequence is:
questions.solution:
**2, 3, 1, 4, 5 — mark the profile, drill, ventilate, check for misfires, then muck out.**

**The drill-and-blast cycle, in order, with the reason for each position:**

| Step | Operation | Why it comes here |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **MARKING the tunnel profile (2)** | **Nothing can be drilled until the face is marked out — this must be first** |
| **2** | **SETTING UP and DRILLING (3)** | Drill the blast-hole pattern to the marked profile; charge and fire |
| **3** | **REMOVING the FOUL GASES (1)** | **VENTILATE after the blast — the air is unbreathable and must be cleared before anyone approaches the face** ← |
| **4** | **CHECKING for MISFIRE (4)** | **Once the air is safe to enter, inspect for unexploded charges BEFORE any mucking begins** |
| **5** | **MUCKING (5)** | Remove the broken rock; the cycle then repeats |

> **The sequence is bounded at both ends by logic rather than convention: MARKING must be first because nothing else can be done without it, and MUCKING must be last because the rock does not exist until the blast has broken it.**

**Why the middle order is the safety-critical part — and this is what the question really tests:**

> **VENTILATION (1) must come BEFORE the misfire check (4), and both must come BEFORE mucking (5).**

> **The reasoning is a sequence of hazards:**

| Hazard | Controlled by | Must happen |
|---|---|---|
| **Blast fumes — CO, NO₂, unburnt explosive vapour** | **VENTILATION** | **Before anyone enters the face at all** |
| **UNEXPLODED CHARGE (misfire)** | **INSPECTION for misfires** | **Before any mechanical work disturbs the rock** |
| Loose rock at the crown | Scaling | Before working beneath |

> **A misfire is an unexploded charge sitting in the broken rock.**

> **If mucking begins before it is found, the excavator will strike it — and it may detonate.** That is the reason for the ordering, and it is not a procedural nicety.

> **So mucking cannot precede the misfire check.** Option (b), which places mucking (5) before the misfire check (4), is therefore not merely out of order — **it describes an unsafe sequence, and that is the strongest reason to reject it.**

> **Similarly the misfire check cannot precede ventilation, because the inspection requires a person at the face and the air is not yet breathable.**

**Why each distractor fails:**

| Option | Fault |
|---|---|
| **1, 2, 3, 4, 5** | **Ventilation FIRST, before there has been a blast to ventilate** — nothing to remove yet |
| **2, 3, 5, 4, 1** | **MUCKING before the misfire check — UNSAFE** ← and ventilation last, after people have worked at the face |
| **4, 2, 1, 3, 5** | **Misfire check FIRST, before any blast has been fired** — nothing to check |
| **2, 3, 1, 4, 5** | ✓ |

> **Options (a) and (c) both fail on the same logical point: they place a POST-BLAST operation before the blast.** Recognising which operations are inherently post-blast (ventilation, misfire check, mucking) orders the sequence almost completely without any tunnelling knowledge.

> **That is the general technique for sequence questions: identify which steps are logically impossible in a given position, and the order usually falls out.**

**The full tunnelling cycle, for context:**

| Stage | Note |
|---|---|
| **SURVEY and set out the profile** | Line, level and shape |
| **DRILLING the blast pattern** | **The cut holes fire first to create a free face, then easers, then trimmers** |
| **CHARGING and STEMMING** | Explosive placed and holes plugged |
| **BLASTING** | **Fired in a designed DELAY sequence** |
| **VENTILATION** | **Clear the fumes** |
| **Misfire inspection** | Safety |
| **SCALING** | **Bring down loose rock from the crown and walls** |
| **MUCKING and haulage** | Remove the spoil |
| **SUPPORT — rock bolts, shotcrete, steel sets, lagging** | **Installed as soon as the face is safe** |
| Repeat | The next round |

> **The DELAY SEQUENCE in blasting is worth a note: the holes are not fired simultaneously.**

> **The central "cut" holes fire first to create a free face for the rock to move into, and the remaining holes fire in millisecond delays working outward.**

> **Without a free face, rock cannot be displaced — it is confined on all sides — so a simultaneous blast would simply shatter in place.** The delay pattern is what makes drill-and-blast work at all.

**And the alternative method, since it explains why drill-and-blast persists:**

> **A TUNNEL BORING MACHINE (TBM) excavates continuously, with no blasting, less overbreak and less disturbance to the surrounding rock.**

| | **DRILL AND BLAST** | **TBM** |
|---|---|---|
| **Capital cost** | **LOW — drills and explosives** | **VERY HIGH — a machine built for one tunnel's diameter** |
| **Suits** | **Short tunnels; VARIABLE ground; any shape** | **LONG tunnels in predictable ground; circular only** |
| **Progress rate** | Slower | Much faster |
| **Overbreak and rock damage** | **Higher** | Minimal |
| **Flexibility to change section** | **HIGH** | None |

> **The break-even is essentially a matter of LENGTH: a TBM's cost is largely fixed, so it is justified only over a long drive.**

> **Which is why Nepal's hydropower headrace tunnels — often several kilometres and in variable Himalayan geology — have used both**, and why drill-and-blast remains the standard for shorter drives and for adits.

examTip.trick: **Marking must be FIRST (nothing can be drilled without it) and mucking LAST (the rock does not exist until the blast).** In between: ventilate, then check misfires, then muck.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) places MUCKING before the misfire check — an UNSAFE sequence**, since the excavator would strike an unexploded charge. And (a) and (c) both put a POST-BLAST step before the blast.
examTip.mnemonic: **Identify which steps are inherently POST-BLAST** — ventilation, misfire check, mucking — and the order falls out with no tunnelling knowledge. And blast holes fire in DELAYS, because rock cannot move without a free face.

questions.stem: For a simply supported beam with a point load at the centre, the strain energy will be:
questions.solution:
**U = W²L³ / (96 EI).**

**Where it comes from — Castigliano's theorem gives it in one line:**

> **Strain energy in bending:  U = ∫ M² ds / (2EI)**

> **For a simply supported beam with a central point load W, take one half and double:**

> **M(x) = (W/2)x  for 0 ≤ x ≤ L/2**

> **U = 2 × ∫₀^{L/2} (Wx/2)² dx / (2EI)**

> **= 2 × (W²/4) × [x³/3]₀^{L/2} / (2EI)**

> **= (W²/4) × (L³/24) / EI**

> **= W²L³ / (96 EI)** ✓

> **The source gives it directly, together with the udl case: U = w²L⁵/(240 EI).**

**The DIMENSIONAL check, which eliminates half the options instantly:**

> **W is a POINT LOAD (a force); w is a DISTRIBUTED load (force per length).** Those are different quantities, and the question's stem says POINT LOAD.

| Option | Load type implied | Power of L | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| **W²L⁵/240EI** | **Written with W but has L⁵ — the UDL form** | **L⁵** | **Wrong: L⁵ belongs with w², not W²** ← |
| **W²L⁵/480EI** | Same problem | **L⁵** | **Wrong** |
| **W²L³/48EI** | **Correct form, wrong constant** | **L³** | Dimensionally OK |
| **W²L³/96EI** | ✓ | **L³** | **Correct** |

> **Check the dimensions properly. Strain energy has units of force × length.**

> **W²L³/EI:  (force)² × (length)³ ÷ [(force/length²) × (length)⁴] = (force)² × (length)³ × (length)²/[(force)(length)⁴] = force × length** ✓

> **W²L⁵/EI would give force × length³ — NOT an energy.** ✗

> **So options (a) and (b) fail on dimensions**, and the reason is that L⁵ belongs with a DISTRIBUTED load (whose square carries an extra 1/length²), not with a point load.

> **That leaves the constant, 48 or 96 — and dimensions cannot settle a dimensionless constant, which is why it must be derived or remembered.**

**The relation that makes the constant memorable — Castigliano's theorem:**

> **∂U/∂W = δ, the deflection at the load.**

> **Differentiate the answer: ∂/∂W [W²L³/96EI] = 2WL³/96EI = WL³/48EI** ✓

> **And WL³/48EI is exactly the known central deflection of a simply supported beam under a central point load.**

> **So the strain energy's constant (96) is TWICE the deflection's constant (48)** — because differentiating W² brings out a factor of 2.

> **That relation is the reliable way to recover the constant: remember the DEFLECTION formula (which is used far more often) and double the denominator.**

> **It also explains option (c) 48: that is the deflection's constant, offered as the energy's — a well-made trap for anyone who half-remembers the pair.**

**Castigliano's theorem in general, since it is the tool this question sits on:**

| Form | Statement |
|---|---|
| **First theorem** | **∂U/∂δ = P — the force is the derivative of energy with respect to displacement** |
| **SECOND theorem** | **∂U/∂P = δ — the DISPLACEMENT is the derivative of energy with respect to the load** ← |

> **The second theorem is the one used in practice, and its power is that it gives a deflection at ANY point WITHOUT integrating a deflection curve.**

> **The technique for a point where there is no load: apply a FICTITIOUS load Q there, differentiate, then set Q = 0.** That trick makes the theorem general.

> **And for a REDUNDANT force in an indeterminate structure, ∂U/∂R = 0** — because the redundant's corresponding displacement is zero. **That is how the horizontal thrust of a two-hinged arch is derived, which appears elsewhere in this series of papers.**

**The strain energy expressions, gathered:**

| Loading | Strain energy |
|---|---|
| **AXIAL load P on a bar** | **U = P²L/(2AE)** |
| **BENDING, general** | **U = ∫M²ds/(2EI)** |
| **SSB, central point load W** | **U = W²L³/(96EI)** ← |
| **SSB, udl w** | **U = w²L⁵/(240EI)** |
| **Cantilever, end load W** | **U = W²L³/(6EI)** |
| **TORSION, torque T** | **U = T²L/(2GJ)** |
| **SHEAR** | U = ∫V²ds/(2AG) — usually negligible in beams |

> **Note that every expression has the form (load)²(length)/(2 × stiffness)** — axial, bending and torsional alike.

> **That common structure is worth seeing: strain energy is always the square of the action divided by twice the relevant rigidity**, which is the same form as ½kx² for a spring. **A structure is a spring, and this is its energy.**

examTip.trick: **U = ∫M²ds/2EI with M = Wx/2 over each half gives W²L³/96EI.** And the constant is recoverable: **∂U/∂W must equal the known deflection WL³/48EI**, so the energy's 96 is twice the deflection's 48.
examTip.trap: **Options (a) and (b) have L⁵, which belongs with a DISTRIBUTED load w², not a point load W².** Dimensional check: W²L³/EI is force × length (an energy); W²L⁵/EI is not. And option (c) 48 is the DEFLECTION's constant.
examTip.mnemonic: **Every strain energy has the form (action)²(length)/(2 × rigidity)** — P²L/2AE, T²L/2GJ, ∫M²ds/2EI. A structure is a spring, and this is its ½kx².

questions.stem: The value of a property determined by what it fetches in the open market is called:
questions.solution:
**Market value.**

**The definition:**

> **MARKET VALUE is the price a property would fetch if SOLD IN THE OPEN MARKET** — that is, what a willing buyer would pay a willing seller, neither being under compulsion.

> **It is determined by the market rather than by any calculation, which is what distinguishes it from every other value in the list.**

> **The source states the contrast directly: market value is pricing from the market, while BOOK VALUE is the actual worth recorded in the account book.**

**The family of values, which is what this corner of the syllabus is about:**

| Value | Definition | Determined by |
|---|---|---|
| **MARKET value** | **What it fetches in the OPEN MARKET** | **The market** ← |
| **BOOK value** | **Original cost LESS accumulated depreciation — the figure in the accounts** | **An accounting calculation** |
| **SALVAGE value** | **The value at the end of its useful life, WITHOUT dismantling — it can still be used or sold as it stands** | Estimate |
| **SCRAP value** | **The value of the DISMANTLED materials — what the pieces fetch** | **Estimate, commonly ~10 % of the cost of the structure** |
| **DISTRESS value** | **A price BELOW market value, because the owner must sell in a hurry** | Circumstance |
| **Sentimental value** | Above market value, for personal reasons | Circumstance |
| **Replacement value** | Cost to build the same thing today | Estimate |
| **Assessed / rateable value** | For taxation | The authority |

> **The SALVAGE / SCRAP distinction is the one most often confused, and the test is whether the thing is DISMANTLED:**

> **SALVAGE value assumes the asset is still whole and can be sold or used as it is.**

> **SCRAP value assumes it is broken up and only the materials are worth anything.**

> **So scrap value is normally the LOWER of the two**, and an asset can have a salvage value well above its scrap value — a used machine still worth selling, whose metal alone would fetch little.

**Why book value and market value diverge — and they usually do:**

> **BOOK VALUE follows a depreciation schedule chosen when the asset was bought.**

> **MARKET VALUE follows what buyers will actually pay.**

> **Nothing links the two, so they drift apart:**

| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| **Property in a rising market** | **MARKET value far exceeds book value** |
| **Equipment made OBSOLETE by a better model** | **MARKET value collapses BELOW book value, though the asset is undamaged** ← |
| **A well-maintained machine at the end of its depreciated life** | **Book value near zero; market value real** |

> **The obsolescence row is the one that catches engineers, because it has nothing to do with the asset's condition.**

> **DEPRECIATION is loss of value from use, age and wear — predictable and gradual.**

> **OBSOLESCENCE is loss of value because something BETTER exists — sudden, and no maintenance regime protects against it.**

> **A perfectly serviceable machine can be worth scrap value the day a better one is marketed**, and that is a risk to be recognised in a replacement decision rather than a fault to be avoided.

**Why an engineer needs these definitions at all:**

| Use | Which value |
|---|---|
| **Valuation of a property for sale or mortgage** | **MARKET value** |
| **Depreciation and the accounts** | **BOOK value** |
| **Replacement decision** | **Market value of the old plus the cost of the new** |
| **Insurance** | Replacement value |
| **End-of-life estimate in a depreciation calculation** | **SALVAGE or SCRAP value** |
| **Compulsory acquisition compensation** | Market value, statutorily assessed |
| Rate analysis for plant hire | Book value, through the depreciation charge |

> **The salvage/scrap value matters in the depreciation calculation specifically: the DEPRECIABLE AMOUNT is the cost MINUS the salvage value**, not the cost itself.

> **So an asset costing Rs 500,000 with a salvage value of Rs 50,000 depreciates only Rs 450,000 over its life** — and forgetting to subtract the salvage value is the commonest error in a straight-line depreciation problem.

**And the valuation methods, since market value must still be estimated in practice:**

| Method | Basis |
|---|---|
| **COMPARISON (market) method** | **Recent sale prices of comparable properties — the primary method where a market exists** |
| **COST (contractor's) method** | **Replacement cost of the structure, LESS depreciation, PLUS the land value** |
| **INCOME (rental) capitalisation** | **Net annual income × YEARS' PURCHASE — for income-producing property** |
| **Profit-based method** | For a business premises whose value derives from its trade |
| **Development method** | For land with development potential |

> **YEARS' PURCHASE is the multiplier that converts an annual income into a capital value, and it is simply the present worth of an annuity: YP = 1/i for a perpetuity.**

> **So at a 5 per cent expected return, YP = 20 — and a property yielding Rs 100,000 a year is worth about Rs 2,000,000.** That single relation is the whole of income-based valuation, and it makes the connection between valuation and the interest-rate arithmetic of engineering economics explicit.

examTip.trick: **MARKET value is set by the market; BOOK value by an accounting calculation.** Nothing links them, so they drift apart.
examTip.trap: **SALVAGE assumes the asset is still WHOLE and usable; SCRAP assumes it is DISMANTLED and only the materials count** — so scrap is normally the lower. The test is whether it is broken up.
examTip.mnemonic: **The depreciable amount is COST MINUS SALVAGE**, not cost — the commonest error in a straight-line problem. And **OBSOLESCENCE has nothing to do with condition**: a perfect machine can be worth scrap the day a better one appears.

questions.stem: The value at which the owner sells the property for less than the market value is called:
questions.solution:
**Distress value.**

**The definition:**

> **DISTRESS VALUE is the price at which a property is sold when the owner is UNDER COMPULSION to sell** — and it is therefore BELOW the market value.

> **The source states it directly: the owner sells the property for less than the market value, and that is called distress value.**

**Why a distressed sale fetches less — the reason is the absence of one condition of market value:**

> **MARKET VALUE assumes a WILLING buyer and a WILLING seller, NEITHER UNDER COMPULSION, with adequate time for the property to be exposed to the market.**

> **Remove any one of those conditions and the price falls:**

| Cause of distress | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Urgent need for cash** | No time to wait for the right buyer |
| **Forced sale — bankruptcy, court order, auction** | **A compressed timescale and a limited pool of bidders** ← |
| **Foreclosure by a lender** | The lender wants recovery, not the best price |
| **Emigration or death in the family** | Sale must complete by a date |
| Legal dispute over the title | Buyers discount for the risk |

> **The common factor is TIME.** A property's market value assumes it can be offered until the right buyer appears; **a distressed sale cannot wait, so it accepts whoever is available.**

> **That is why the discount can be large — commonly 10 to 30 per cent below market value, and much more at a forced auction.**

> **And it explains the mirror-image concept: SENTIMENTAL VALUE, a price ABOVE market value paid by a buyer with a personal reason to want that particular property.** Both are departures from market value caused by the parties' circumstances rather than by the property.

**The full family of values, since this and the previous question are drawn from it:**

| Value | Relation to market value |
|---|---|
| **MARKET value** | **The reference — willing buyer, willing seller, no compulsion, adequate time** |
| **DISTRESS value** | **BELOW market value — the seller is compelled** ← |
| **Sentimental value** | **ABOVE market value — the buyer is attached** |
| **BOOK value** | **Unrelated — cost less accumulated depreciation, an accounting figure** |
| **SALVAGE value** | End of useful life, NOT dismantled |
| **SCRAP value** | End of life, DISMANTLED — normally the lowest |
| **Replacement value** | Cost to rebuild the same thing today |
| **Assessed value** | Set by an authority for taxation |

> **Note that BOOK VALUE is the odd one out: it is not a price at all.** It is a number in the accounts, derived from a depreciation schedule chosen years earlier, and it may bear no relation to what anyone would pay.

> **Options (a) and (c) both fail for that reason — they are not market-related prices**, while the question asks about a price relative to the market.

**Why a valuer must be explicit about which value is being reported:**

> **A valuation report that does not state its BASIS is worthless, because the same property has several defensible values at the same moment.**

| Purpose of the valuation | Basis required |
|---|---|
| **Sale between willing parties** | **Market value** |
| **Mortgage security** | **Market value, sometimes with a forced-sale (distress) value alongside** ← |
| **Insurance** | **Replacement (reinstatement) value** |
| **Compulsory acquisition** | **Market value, statutorily assessed, plus compensation for disturbance** |
| **Accounts and depreciation** | **Book value** |
| **Taxation** | Assessed value |

> **The mortgage row is worth noticing because it is where distress value has a formal role: a lender wants to know the market value AND what the property would fetch if it had to be sold quickly**, because that is the sum the lender might actually recover.

> **So distress value is not merely a curiosity — it is a required figure in lending, and reporting only the market value understates the lender's risk.**

**The valuation methods, since market value must be estimated before a distress discount can be applied:**

| Method | Basis |
|---|---|
| **COMPARISON (market)** | **Recent sales of comparable properties — the primary method** |
| **COST (contractor's)** | Replacement cost less depreciation, plus land value |
| **INCOME (rental) capitalisation** | **Net annual income × YEARS' PURCHASE** |
| **Development** | Residual value of land with development potential |
| Profit-based | Where value derives from the trade carried on |

> **YEARS' PURCHASE converts an income into a capital value, and for a perpetuity YP = 1/i.**

> **At a 5 per cent expected return YP = 20, so a property yielding Rs 100,000 a year is worth about Rs 2,000,000** — and at 8 per cent, YP = 12.5 and the same income is worth only Rs 1,250,000.

> **That sensitivity is worth noticing: the CAPITAL value of an income-producing property depends as much on the prevailing interest rate as on the income itself**, which is why property values move when rates move even though nothing about the buildings has changed.

> **And it connects this topic directly to the discounting arithmetic of engineering economics — years' purchase is simply the present-worth factor for an annuity, wearing a different name.**

examTip.trick: **Market value assumes a willing seller with ADEQUATE TIME.** Remove the time and the price falls — that is distress value, commonly 10-30 % below market and more at a forced auction.
examTip.trap: **Book value and salvage value are not market-related prices at all** — book value is an accounting figure from a schedule chosen years earlier. The question asks about a price relative to the market.
examTip.mnemonic: **DISTRESS is below market (compelled SELLER); SENTIMENTAL is above (attached BUYER)** — both caused by the parties, not the property. And a lender needs BOTH figures, because the distress value is what it might actually recover.

questions.stem: In a hydel system, a forebay connects:
questions.solution:
**The headrace channel and the penstock.**

**Where the forebay sits in the water conveyance chain:**

> **INTAKE → settling basin → HEADRACE (power) CHANNEL → FOREBAY → PENSTOCK → TURBINE → tailrace → river**

> **The forebay is the transition between the low-velocity OPEN CHANNEL and the high-velocity CLOSED PENSTOCK.**

> **The source states it directly: the forebay connects the headrace channel and the penstock.**

**What the forebay does — it has four distinct jobs:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Provide short-term STORAGE (pondage)** | **Absorbs the mismatch between the steady channel flow and the varying turbine demand** ← the primary purpose |
| **Settle remaining SEDIMENT** | A final settling opportunity before the water reaches the runner |
| **House the TRASHRACK** | Screens debris out of the penstock intake |
| **Provide a SPILLWAY** | Sheds surplus when the turbine takes less than the channel delivers |
| Allow air release and act as a transition | The water surface breaks the connection between channel and pipe |

> **The STORAGE function is the one that explains why the forebay exists at all.**

> **A headrace channel delivers a roughly CONSTANT flow — it is fed by a fixed diversion.**

> **The turbine's demand VARIES with the electrical load, minute by minute.**

> **Something must absorb the difference, and the forebay is it: when demand falls the pond rises and the surplus spills; when demand rises the pond drops and supplies the shortfall until the channel catches up.**

> **Without it the channel would overtop on every load rejection and the penstock would draw air on every load increase.**

**The crucial distinction — FOREBAY versus SURGE TANK:**

| | **FOREBAY** | **SURGE TANK** |
|---|---|---|
