| **Located on** | **An OPEN CHANNEL (headrace) system** | **A CLOSED TUNNEL system** |
| **Primary purpose** | **STORE water for load fluctuation; settle silt; house the trashrack** | **Absorb PRESSURE surges (water hammer)** |
| **Sized by** | **The VOLUME of storage needed** | **The AMPLITUDE of the surge** |
| **Open to atmosphere?** | **Yes — a pond** | **Yes — a shaft** |
| Spillway | Usually provided | Not applicable |

> **Both are open to atmosphere and both hold water, which is exactly why they are confused — and the difference is what they are SIZED FOR.**

> **The rule to carry: FOREBAY for a CANAL system, SURGE TANK for a TUNNEL system.**

> **And the reason is structural: an open channel cannot transmit a pressure wave at all (its free surface absorbs any surge as a change in level), so no surge tank is needed. A closed tunnel can, so one is.**

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | The structure that actually does it |
|---|---|
| **Penstock and turbine** | **The INLET VALVE (butterfly or spherical valve) and the spiral casing** |
| **Reservoir and headrace channel** | **The INTAKE structure** |
| **Power channel and tailrace** | **Nothing — the tailrace is DOWNSTREAM of the turbine, on the other side of the plant entirely** ← |
| **Headrace channel and penstock** | ✓ **FOREBAY** |

> **Option (c) is worth naming as a structural impossibility rather than a wrong answer: the power (headrace) channel is UPSTREAM of the powerhouse and the tailrace is DOWNSTREAM of it.**

> **Nothing connects them directly, because the turbine is between them — that is the entire point of the layout.** Recognising that eliminates the option with no knowledge of forebays.

**The components of a run-of-river scheme, gathered:**

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **Diversion WEIR** | **Raises the level to divert flow into the intake** |
| **INTAKE** | Admits water; excludes floating debris and bed load |
| **Gravel trap and SETTLING BASIN** | **Remove abrasive sand before it reaches the turbine** |
| **HEADRACE (power) channel or tunnel** | Conveys water along the hillside at a small gradient |
| **FOREBAY (or surge tank, if a tunnel)** | **Transition, storage, final settling, trashrack** ← |
| **PENSTOCK** | Carries water down the steep slope under pressure |
| **Anchor blocks and expansion joints** | Restrain and accommodate the penstock |
| **POWERHOUSE** | Turbines, generators, controls |
| **TAILRACE** | Returns water to the river |

> **Note that the forebay and the surge tank occupy the SAME POSITION in the chain and are alternatives, not companions** — a scheme has one or the other depending on whether its conveyance is an open channel or a closed tunnel.

> **Which is the cleanest way to remember the distinction: they do the same job at the same place for two different kinds of conveyance.**

**And the design rule worth knowing:**

> **The forebay's storage is commonly sized to supply the turbines at full load for a stated short period — often a few minutes to half an hour — so that the governor has time to respond and the channel flow to adjust.**

> **And the penstock intake must be SUBMERGED deeply enough to prevent VORTEX FORMATION**, which would draw air into the penstock.

> **Air in a penstock is a serious matter: it causes noise, vibration, loss of output, and on release can produce a violent pressure transient.** So the minimum submergence over the intake is a design requirement, not a detail — **and it is why a forebay's minimum operating level, not merely its volume, is specified.**

verification.notes: Duplicate option replaced. The source printed option (b) as "power channel and penstock" and option (d) as "headrace channel and penstock" - but a power channel IS a headrace channel, so the two options named the same connection and the question had two correct answers. Option (b) has been replaced with "reservoir and headrace channel", which is a distinct and plausible connection (that of the intake structure). The keyed answer is unchanged at (d).

examTip.trick: **The forebay is the transition from the low-velocity OPEN CHANNEL to the high-velocity CLOSED PENSTOCK** — so it connects the headrace channel to the penstock.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) is structurally impossible**: the power channel is UPSTREAM of the powerhouse and the tailrace DOWNSTREAM, with the turbine between them. Nothing connects them directly.
examTip.mnemonic: **FOREBAY for a CANAL system, SURGE TANK for a TUNNEL system** — same position in the chain, alternatives not companions. An open channel cannot transmit a pressure wave, so it needs no surge tank.

questions.stem: A flexible pavement is considered to have failed by rutting when the rut depth is:
questions.solution:
**20 mm or more.**

**The two failure criteria of a flexible pavement, which are always given as a pair:**

| Failure | Cause | Pavement considered failed when |
|---|---|---|
| **FATIGUE (alligator) CRACKING** | **Horizontal TENSILE strain at the BOTTOM of the bituminous layer** | **20 % of the surface area has cracked** |
| **RUTTING** | **Vertical COMPRESSIVE strain at the TOP of the SUBGRADE** | **A rut depth of 20 mm or more** ← |

> **The source gives both criteria together, and they are the two limit states of IRC 37's mechanistic design.**

> **Note the coincidence worth exploiting: BOTH criteria involve the number 20** — 20 per cent cracked area, 20 mm rut depth. **That makes the pair easy to hold, and it is a genuine memory aid rather than a coincidence to distrust.**

**What rutting actually is:**

> **A RUT is a longitudinal depression in the WHEEL PATH — permanent deformation accumulated over many load repetitions.**

> **It arises from two quite different mechanisms, and distinguishing them decides the remedy:**

| Mechanism | Where the deformation occurs | Appearance |
|---|---|---|
| **SUBGRADE (structural) rutting** | **The SUBGRADE or granular layers deform under repeated load** | **A WIDE, shallow depression with little or no shoulder heave** |
| **MIX (plastic) rutting** | **The BITUMINOUS layer itself deforms — the mix is unstable** | **A NARROW rut with HEAVED SHOULDERS on each side** ← |

> **The heaved shoulders are the diagnostic sign, and they are easy to read on site: material displaced sideways has to go somewhere.**

> **If the bituminous layer is flowing, it pushes up beside the wheel path. If the subgrade is deforming, the whole pavement sinks and there is nothing to heave.**

> **And the remedies are quite different:**

| Mechanism | Remedy |
|---|---|
| **Subgrade rutting** | **A thicker GRANULAR base and sub-base, to spread the load and reduce the subgrade strain** |
| **Mix rutting** | **A better MIX — harder binder, better aggregate grading, correct binder content** ← |

> **Overlaying a mix-rutted pavement with more of the same bitumen makes it worse**, since it adds more of the material that is flowing. **So the diagnosis matters before the money is spent.**

**Why the distractors are wrong — and one of them is a real criterion:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **12 mm or more** | **A rut depth used as an INTERVENTION (maintenance) trigger in some systems — not the failure criterion** ← |
| **1.2 mm** | **A factor of ten out — that is a DEFLECTION, not a rut** |
| **10 mm** | Plausible; not the standard |
| **20 mm or more** | ✓ |

> **Option (a) 12 mm deserves a note because it is genuinely used, but for a different purpose: pavement management systems commonly trigger maintenance at a rut depth well BELOW the failure criterion**, precisely so that the pavement is treated before it fails.

> **So 12 mm may be when work is programmed and 20 mm is when the pavement is deemed to have failed** — two different questions, and the option list mixes them.

> **Option (b) 1.2 mm is worth recognising as a DEFLECTION-scale number: Benkelman beam deflections are measured in millimetres and tenths of millimetres**, so 1.2 mm is a plausible deflection and an implausible rut. **The magnitude tells you which quantity is being described.**

**Why rutting matters beyond appearance — the safety consequence:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Ponded water in the rut** | **AQUAPLANING risk, and loss of skid resistance** ← |
| **Steering pull** | The vehicle follows the rut |
| **Accelerated pavement damage** | Water sits and enters the layers |
| **Rough ride and higher vehicle operating cost** | — |
| **Ice in cold regions** | The rut holds water that freezes |

> **The AQUAPLANING risk is the reason a rut is treated as a failure rather than a blemish: a 20 mm rut holds enough water to lift a tyre off the surface at speed**, and the driver loses steering and braking together.

> **So the criterion is set by SAFETY as much as by structural condition** — which is why it is a fixed depth rather than a proportion of the pavement thickness.

**How the two criteria are used in design — the mechanistic method:**

> **IRC 37's design computes the two critical strains from a layered elastic analysis, and checks each against a fatigue relation:**

> **Fatigue:  N_f = k (1/ε_t)^{3.89} (1/M_r)^{0.854}**

> **Rutting:  N_r = k (1/ε_z)^{4.5337}**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **Both exponents are near 4** | **A small strain increase shortens the life dramatically** |
| **The DESIGN life is the LESSER of N_f and N_r** | The pavement fails by whichever comes first |
| **The strains depend on the layer thicknesses and moduli** | Which is what the design chooses |

> **The near-fourth-power exponents are the same sensitivity that makes axle load so important: doubling the strain cuts the life by a factor of about sixteen.**

> **And it is why a pavement's performance is so sensitive to construction quality: a layer laid 20 per cent thinner than designed does not lose 20 per cent of its life.**

examTip.trick: **Both criteria involve 20: fatigue failure at 20 % cracked area, rutting failure at 20 mm depth.** A genuine memory aid for the pair.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) 12 mm is a real MAINTENANCE trigger, not the failure criterion** — systems programme work below the failure level deliberately. And 1.2 mm is a DEFLECTION-scale number, not a rut.
examTip.mnemonic: **HEAVED SHOULDERS beside the rut mean the MIX is flowing; a wide shallow depression means the SUBGRADE is deforming.** Different remedies — and overlaying a mix-rutted road with more bitumen makes it worse.

questions.stem: The steel dust produced after manufacturing falls under which of the following categories of waste?
questions.solution:
**Inorganic sludge.**

**Why — the classification turns on two independent questions:**

> **First: is the waste ORGANIC or INORGANIC?**

> **Steel dust is METAL and METAL OXIDE — it contains no carbon-based organic matter. So it is INORGANIC.**

> **Second: what is its PHYSICAL FORM — solid, sludge, aqueous or liquid?**

> **Collected dust from a manufacturing process, typically captured wet in a scrubber or accumulating as a moist solid, is a SLUDGE — a semi-solid.**

> **INORGANIC + SLUDGE = inorganic sludge.** ✓

> **The source states it: emission of controlled dust from steel manufacturing, dust from de-burning, and chromium parts in the fabricated metal industry are examples of inorganic sludge waste.**

**The classification grid, which is what the options are drawn from:**

| | **INORGANIC** | **ORGANIC** |
|---|---|---|
| **AQUEOUS (dilute, water-based)** | **Acid and alkali rinse waters; plating solutions** | **Dilute solvent-water mixtures; food-processing effluent** |
| **SLUDGE (semi-solid)** | **METAL DUSTS and oxides; lime sludge; plating sludge** ← | Biological sludge; oily sludge |
| **LIQUID (concentrated)** | Concentrated acids | **Solvents, waste oils, paints** |
| **SOLID** | Slag, foundry sand, ash | Plastics, timber, paper |

> **So the classification is a two-way grid: chemical nature × physical form**, and each option in the question names one cell.

> **Which is why the question is a clean discrimination: reject "organic" because steel is not carbon-based, and reject "aqueous" and "liquid" because dust is not a solution.**

**Why the distinction matters — it decides the TREATMENT and DISPOSAL route:**

| Waste type | Treatment approach |
|---|---|
| **INORGANIC sludge** | **DEWATERING, then STABILISATION / SOLIDIFICATION, then secure landfill — the metals cannot be destroyed, only immobilised** ← |
| **Inorganic aqueous** | **NEUTRALISATION and chemical PRECIPITATION of the metals, then discharge of the treated water** |
| **Organic liquid** | **INCINERATION or solvent recovery — the organic molecules CAN be destroyed** |
| **Organic aqueous** | **BIOLOGICAL treatment — bacteria consume organic matter** |

> **The decisive difference is that ORGANIC waste can be DESTROYED and INORGANIC waste cannot.**

> **Bacteria will eat organic matter; incineration will break its molecules. Neither does anything to a metal — a heavy metal is an element, and no treatment removes it from existence.**

> **So inorganic metal waste can only be CONCENTRATED, IMMOBILISED and CONTAINED**, and that is why secure landfill with a liner and leachate collection is the end of the road for it.

> **That is a genuinely important asymmetry: an organic pollution problem can be solved, and a heavy-metal problem can only be managed.**

**Why steel dust in particular is treated carefully:**

> **Electric-arc furnace dust and similar metallurgical dusts commonly contain ZINC, LEAD, CADMIUM and CHROMIUM.**

| Metal | Concern |
|---|---|
| **Chromium (VI)** | **CARCINOGENIC and highly mobile in groundwater** ← |
| **Lead** | Neurotoxic, especially to children |
| **Cadmium** | Kidney damage; accumulates in the body |
| **Zinc** | Less toxic, but valuable — often RECOVERED |

> **So such dust is frequently classed as HAZARDOUS waste rather than ordinary industrial waste**, and it cannot go to a municipal landfill.

> **The chromium point deserves emphasis because it is the one that governs: hexavalent chromium is both carcinogenic and highly soluble, so it travels with groundwater rather than staying where it was dumped.**

> **Which is why the containment must be genuinely secure and why leachate monitoring is required for decades after a site closes.**

> **And the zinc content is why some of this dust is a RESOURCE rather than a waste: zinc recovery from EAF dust is a commercial process, and it is the best available outcome — the metal is removed from the waste stream entirely rather than buried.**

**The hazardous-waste characteristics, since the classification leads there:**

> **A waste is generally hazardous if it exhibits any of:**

| Characteristic | Test |
|---|---|
| **IGNITABILITY** | Flash point below a stated value |
| **CORROSIVITY** | **pH below 2 or above 12.5** |
| **REACTIVITY** | Unstable, explosive, or reacts violently with water |
| **TOXICITY** | **Leachate exceeds limits for stated contaminants** ← the one that catches metal dusts |

> **The TOXICITY test is a LEACHING test: the waste is extracted under standard conditions and the extract analysed.**

> **That is the right test conceptually, because what matters is not how much metal the waste CONTAINS but how much it will RELEASE into groundwater** — and a well-stabilised sludge can contain a great deal of metal and release very little.

> **Which is precisely the purpose of solidification: not to remove the metal, but to lock it into a matrix from which it will not leach.**

examTip.trick: **Two independent questions: chemical nature (organic/inorganic) and physical form (aqueous/sludge/liquid/solid).** Steel dust is metal oxide, so INORGANIC, and a moist collected dust is a SLUDGE.
examTip.trap: **The options are cells of a two-way grid.** Reject "organic" because steel is not carbon-based, and "aqueous"/"liquid" because dust is not a solution.
examTip.mnemonic: **ORGANIC waste can be DESTROYED (bacteria, incineration); INORGANIC metal cannot** — only concentrated, immobilised and contained. An organic pollution problem can be solved; a heavy-metal one can only be managed.

questions.stem: Activated sludge contains ...... per cent water.
questions.solution:
**Ninety-seven per cent.**

**What activated sludge is:**

> **In the activated sludge process, AIR is blown into settled sewage to grow AEROBIC BACTERIA.**

> **Those bacteria consume the organic matter and, in doing so, flocculate into settleable clumps.** The mixture of bacteria, protozoa and adsorbed organic matter is the **ACTIVATED SLUDGE.**

> **After several hours the suspended microbes settle in the secondary clarifier, and the settled mass is drawn off.**

> **It contains about 97 per cent water and about 3 per cent solids.**

> **The source states it: this sludge with dissolved air is called activated sludge, and it contains ninety-seven per cent water.**

**Why the water content matters so much — this is the practical point of the question:**

> **97 per cent water means that HANDLING SLUDGE IS ALMOST ENTIRELY A MATTER OF HANDLING WATER.**

> **A tonne of activated sludge is 970 kg of water and 30 kg of solids.**

> **So the whole of sludge treatment is about REMOVING WATER**, and the arithmetic of doing so is startling:

| Solids content | Water content | Volume relative to 3 % solids |
|---|---|---|
| **3 % (activated sludge as drawn)** | **97 %** | **100** |
| **6 % (after thickening)** | **94 %** | **50** ← |
| **25 % (after dewatering)** | **75 %** | **12** |
| **90 % (after drying)** | **10 %** | **3.3** |

> **Doubling the solids from 3 to 6 per cent HALVES the volume**, and that is why THICKENING is the first and most cost-effective step in any sludge treatment train.

> **The volume that must be pumped, digested, transported and disposed of falls in direct proportion — so a cheap thickening step pays for itself in every downstream process.**

> **That non-linear relationship (a small change in solids content, a large change in volume) is the single most useful idea in sludge handling.**

**The sludge treatment sequence, since it follows from the water content:**

| Stage | Purpose | Typical result |
|---|---|---|
| **THICKENING (gravity or dissolved air flotation)** | **Reduce volume cheaply** | **3 % → 5-8 % solids** |
| **STABILISATION (anaerobic or aerobic DIGESTION)** | **Destroy the organic fraction; reduce odour and pathogens; PRODUCE BIOGAS** | **~50 % of the volatile solids destroyed** |
| **CONDITIONING (chemical or thermal)** | Improve dewaterability | — |
| **DEWATERING (drying beds, centrifuge, belt or filter press)** | **Produce a handleable CAKE** | **20-30 % solids** |
| **DRYING or incineration** | Further volume reduction | 90 %+ solids |
| **DISPOSAL — land application, landfill, reuse** | — | — |

> **ANAEROBIC DIGESTION is the stage with the most engineering interest, because it turns a disposal problem into an energy source.**

> **Bacteria in the absence of oxygen convert organic matter to BIOGAS — roughly 65 per cent methane — which can be burnt to run the plant's own blowers.**

> **A well-run digester can make a treatment works substantially self-sufficient in energy**, and the aeration blowers are typically the largest electricity consumer in an activated sludge plant. **So the sludge pays for treating the sewage.**

**The other sludge figures worth knowing, since they are asked alongside:**

| Sludge | Solids content |
|---|---|
| **PRIMARY sludge (from primary sedimentation)** | **3-7 % — thicker and easier to handle** |
| **ACTIVATED (secondary) sludge** | **0.5-2 % as returned; ~3 % as wasted** ← |
| **Digested sludge** | 5-10 % |
| **Dewatered cake** | 20-30 % |
| **Air-dried sludge** | 40-60 % |

> **Note that PRIMARY sludge is THICKER than activated sludge**, which is counter-intuitive until one sees why: **primary sludge is settled grit and heavy organic solids, while activated sludge is a light biological floc that traps water in its structure.**

> **That is exactly why activated sludge is difficult to dewater — the water is held within the bacterial flocs, not merely between particles**, and it is why chemical conditioning is usually needed before mechanical dewatering will work.

**And the operating parameters of the process, since the sludge is its product:**

| Parameter | Typical |
|---|---|
| **MLSS** | **1500-3000 mg/l (conventional)** |
| **F/M ratio** | **0.2-0.5 per day** |
| **Sludge age (SRT)** | **5-15 days** |
| **Return sludge ratio** | **0.25-0.5** |
| **Recycled proportion of activated sludge** | **20-30 %** |
| **SVI** | **Below 150 ml/g** |
| Aeration period | 4-8 hours |

> **The RETURN of activated sludge is what makes the process work at all: the settled biomass is pumped back to the head of the aeration tank to seed the incoming sewage.**

> **Without that return the bacteria would simply wash out with the effluent, and the process would have no biomass to work with** — which is why a failure of the return sludge pumps is an immediate and total process failure rather than a gradual decline.

examTip.trick: **97 % water, 3 % solids** — so handling sludge is almost entirely handling WATER, and the whole treatment train is about removing it.
examTip.trap: **PRIMARY sludge (3-7 %) is THICKER than activated sludge**, which surprises people. Activated sludge is a light biological floc holding water WITHIN its structure — which is why it is hard to dewater.
examTip.mnemonic: **Doubling solids from 3 % to 6 % HALVES the volume** — which is why THICKENING is the cheapest and first step. And anaerobic digestion turns the problem into BIOGAS that can run the plant's own blowers.

questions.stem: Imposed load is in which part of the IS code?
questions.solution:
**IS 875 Part II.**

**The five parts of IS 875 — the loading code:**

| Part | Load |
|---|---|
| **IS 875 (Part 1)** | **DEAD loads — unit weights of building materials and stored materials** |
| **IS 875 (Part 2)** | **IMPOSED (LIVE) loads** ← |
| **IS 875 (Part 3)** | **WIND loads** |
| **IS 875 (Part 4)** | **SNOW loads** |
| **IS 875 (Part 5)** | **SPECIAL loads and LOAD COMBINATIONS** |

> **1 dead, 2 live, 3 wind, 4 snow, 5 special and combinations.**

> **The source confirms it: IS 875 Part-II is imposed, live, occupancy load — three names for the same thing.**

> **Note that all four options are parts of the SAME code, so this is a pure ordering question**: the candidate must know the sequence, not merely recognise the code number.

**The terminology, since three words mean one thing:**

> **IMPOSED load = LIVE load = OCCUPANCY load.**

> **The code's own title uses "IMPOSED", which is the more precise term** — it means load imposed by the use and occupancy of the building, as distinct from the building's own weight.

> **"Live load" is the older and more common usage, and it survives in speech and in most textbooks.**

> **A question may use any of the three**, and treating them as different things is the error to avoid.

**The mnemonic that makes the ordering memorable rather than arbitrary:**

> **The parts run in the ORDER THE LOADS REACH A BUILDING.**

> **First its own weight (Part 1). Then what is put in it (Part 2). Then what the weather does — wind (Part 3) and snow (Part 4). Finally the special cases and the combinations (Part 5).**

> **And there is a structural reason for dead load coming first: EVERY OTHER LOAD DEPENDS ON IT.**

> **Seismic force is proportional to the SEISMIC WEIGHT, which is the dead load plus a fraction of the imposed load — so the dead load must be established before anything else can be computed.**

> **Dead load is also usually the LARGEST load on a building**: for a typical RC frame the self-weight of slabs, beams, columns and walls exceeds the imposed load by a factor of two or three.

> **Which makes Part 1, the least glamorous of the five, the one whose errors propagate furthest.**

**The imposed loads themselves, since they are what Part 2 contains:**

| Occupancy | Imposed load (kN/m²) |
|---|---|
| **Residential rooms** | **2.0** |
| **Office floors** | **2.5-4.0** |
| **Classrooms** | **3.0** |
| **Assembly halls, shops, CORRIDORS and staircases** | **4.0-5.0** |
| **Balconies** | 3.0-5.0 |
| **INACCESSIBLE roof** | **0.75** |
| **Accessible flat roof** | **1.5** |
| Storage and warehouses | By stored material, often much higher |

> **2 kN/m² for residential is the anchor**, and it is worth appreciating how modest it is: **about 200 kg spread over every square metre of floor** — far more than a room normally holds, which is the margin the code builds in.

> **Note that CORRIDORS and STAIRCASES carry a HIGHER imposed load than the rooms they serve**, which is counter-intuitive until one sees why: **in an emergency evacuation the corridors carry the occupants of every room at once.**

> **So the load reflects the worst credible use rather than the normal one, and that is the logic of imposed loads generally.**

**And the reduction that is permitted, since it is a real design provision:**

> **For a column or wall supporting SEVERAL FLOORS, the imposed load may be REDUCED**, because it is very unlikely that every floor carries its full imposed load simultaneously.

| Number of floors carried | Reduction in imposed load |
|---|---|
| **1** | **None** |
| **2** | **10 %** |
| **3** | **20 %** |
| **4** | **30 %** |
| **5 to 10** | **40 %** |
| **Over 10** | **50 %** |

> **This is a PROBABILITY argument made explicit in the code, and it is substantial: a column in a tall building may be designed for half the nominal imposed load.**

> **The same reasoning underlies the reduced load factors when several variable loads are combined** — the code reduces the factor from 1.5 to 1.2 for the three-load case, because simultaneous maxima are unlikely.

> **Recognising that both provisions come from ONE idea — independent variable loads rarely peak together — makes them a single fact rather than two arbitrary tables.**

**The Nepali equivalents, since a question may be asked in either frame:**

| Nepali | Indian |
|---|---|
| **NBC 102 (unit weights)** | **IS 875 Part 1** |
| **NBC 103 (occupancy / imposed)** | **IS 875 Part 2** ← |
| **NBC 104 (wind)** | **IS 875 Part 3** |
| **NBC 106 (snow)** | **IS 875 Part 4** |
| **NBC 105 (seismic)** | **IS 1893 Part 1** |

> **The parallel is almost exact for the loading codes and breaks for seismic**, where Nepal has its own code because its hazard, soil conditions and building stock differ from India's. **NBC 105 (2020) is the revision to know.**

examTip.trick: **Part 1 dead, Part 2 IMPOSED, Part 3 wind, Part 4 snow, Part 5 special and combinations.** All four options are parts of the same code, so the ORDER is the question.
examTip.trap: **IMPOSED = LIVE = OCCUPANCY load** — three names for one thing, and a question may use any of them. The code's own title says "imposed".
examTip.mnemonic: **The parts run in the order loads reach a building** — its own weight, then its contents, then the weather. And dead load comes first because SEISMIC force is derived from it, and it is usually the largest load anyway.

questions.stem: The height of instrument method of levelling is:
options: more accurate than the rise and fall method
less accurate than the rise and fall method
quicker and less tedious for a large number of intermediate sights
questions.solution:
**Quicker and less tedious for a large number of intermediate sights.**

**Why quicker — the arithmetic is shorter:**

> **In the HEIGHT OF COLLIMATION method, one value (the HI) is computed per instrument set-up, and every reduced level is then a single subtraction:**

> **HI = RL of a known point + staff reading on it**

> **RL of any other point = HI − staff reading there**

> **So an intermediate sight costs ONE subtraction.**

> **In the RISE AND FALL method, every consecutive pair of readings must be differenced to find a rise or a fall, and then applied to the previous RL — TWO operations per point, and every point must be processed in sequence.**

> **The source states the position exactly: the height of instrument method is quicker, but CHECKING can be tedious.**

**Why it is NOT more accurate — and this is what options (a) and (b) are testing:**

> **Neither method is more accurate than the other.** Both work from the same field readings, and both give identical reduced levels when the arithmetic is done correctly.

> **ACCURACY is determined in the FIELD — by the instrument's adjustment, the staff readings, the balancing of sight distances and the closure — not by which reduction method is used afterwards.**

> **So options (a) and (b) both make the same category error: they attribute a field property to a computational choice.**

> **What the two methods differ in is SPEED and CHECKING**, which is precisely what option (c) says.

**The real difference — and it is about CHECKING, not accuracy:**

| | **HEIGHT OF COLLIMATION** | **RISE AND FALL** |
|---|---|---|
| **Computes** | **HI, then RL = HI − staff reading** | **The RISE or FALL between consecutive points** |
| **Speed** | **FASTER — one operation per point** | Slower |
| **Arithmetic check available** | **ΣBS − ΣFS = last RL − first RL** | **ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last RL − first RL** |
| **Does the check cover INTERMEDIATE sights?** | **NO — an error in an intermediate sight goes UNDETECTED** ← | **YES — every reading enters the check** |
| **Suits** | **Long profiles with many intermediate sights** | **Work where every point matters** |

> **That difference in checking is the substantive one and the reason the slower method survives.**

> **In the collimation method an intermediate sight enters ONLY the RL of its own point.** If it is misread or mis-booked, that one RL is wrong and **nothing in the arithmetic reveals it** — the sums still balance.

> **In the rise-and-fall method every reading is differenced against its neighbour, so every reading appears in the ΣRise − ΣFall check.** A single mis-booked figure breaks the check.

> **So the choice is a genuine engineering trade-off: use the collimation method for SPEED where intermediate sights are numerous and individually unimportant (a road profile), and the rise-and-fall method where each point matters (setting out levels for construction).**

**What the arithmetic checks do and do not prove — a point regularly misunderstood:**

> **ΣBS − ΣFS = last RL − first RL verifies the ARITHMETIC only.**

> **It does NOT detect:**

| Undetected by the check | Detected by |
|---|---|
| **A misread staff** | **CLOSING the levelling on a known bench mark** |
| **A wrongly booked reading (in the collimation method)** | The rise-and-fall check, or closure |
| **An instrument out of adjustment (collimation error)** | **BALANCING sight distances; two-peg test** |
| **A settling tripod or staff** | Careful practice; closure |

> **So a levelling that "checks" arithmetically may still be wrong.** The only real verification is CLOSURE — running back to the starting bench mark or forward to another of known level.

| Class of levelling | Permissible closing error |
|---|---|
| **Ordinary levelling** | **±24√K mm, K in kilometres** |
| **Precise levelling** | **±12√K mm** |
| Rough levelling | ±100√K mm |

> **The √K form is the signature of RANDOM error accumulation** — errors partly cancel, so the total grows as the square root of the distance rather than in proportion to it.

**And the field discipline that matters more than either method:**

> **BALANCE the backsight and foresight distances at every set-up.**

> **If BS and FS distances are equal, a COLLIMATION ERROR (the line of sight not truly horizontal) affects both readings equally and CANCELS in the difference.**

> **So do the effects of the earth's CURVATURE and of atmospheric REFRACTION.**

> **Three systematic errors eliminated by one simple habit** — which is why balancing sight distances is the first rule of good levelling, and worth more than any amount of careful arithmetic afterwards.

examTip.trick: **Neither method is more accurate** — both use the same field readings and give identical results. They differ in SPEED and in CHECKING, which is what option (c) says.
examTip.trap: **Options (a) and (b) attribute a FIELD property to a COMPUTATIONAL choice.** Accuracy comes from the instrument, the readings and the closure — not from the reduction method.
examTip.mnemonic: **The collimation method does NOT check intermediate sights; rise-and-fall does** — which is why the slower method survives. And **balancing BS and FS distances** cancels collimation error, curvature and refraction at once.

questions.stem: A vertical cut is to be made in a soil mass having cohesion c, angle of internal friction φ and unit weight γ. Taking Ka and Kp as the coefficients of active and passive earth pressure respectively, the maximum depth of unsupported excavation is:
questions.solution:
**H_c = 4c / (γ √K_a).**

**Where the formula comes from:**

> **Rankine's active pressure on a vertical cut in a c-φ soil is:**

> **p_a = K_a γ z − 2c √K_a**

> **The first term grows with depth; the SECOND is a constant NEGATIVE contribution from cohesion.**

> **So near the surface the active pressure is NEGATIVE — that is, TENSILE — and the soil stands unsupported.**

> **The depth at which the pressure first becomes zero is the DEPTH OF TENSION CRACK:**

> **z₀ = 2c / (γ √K_a)**

> **And the CRITICAL DEPTH, at which the total thrust becomes zero (the negative area above balancing the positive area below), is TWICE that:**

> **H_c = 4c / (γ √K_a)** ✓

> **The source gives the depth of unsupported cut as exactly 4c/(γ√K_a).**

**The factor of two, which is worth understanding rather than memorising:**

| Depth | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **z₀ = 2c/(γ√K_a)** | **The depth at which the PRESSURE becomes zero — the tension crack depth** |
| **H_c = 4c/(γ√K_a)** | **The depth at which the total THRUST becomes zero — the critical unsupported height** ← |

> **The pressure diagram is a triangle of negative pressure above z₀ and a triangle of positive pressure below it.**

> **At H = 2z₀ the two triangles have equal area, so the NET thrust is zero — and no support is needed.**

> **That is the whole geometry, and it explains why the critical depth is twice the crack depth rather than equal to it.**

**Why K_a and not K_p — the discrimination the question is really testing:**

> **The soil is trying to COLLAPSE INWARD into the excavation, so the soil is ACTIVE — it is pushing.**

> **ACTIVE pressure applies when the soil moves TOWARD the excavation (the retaining face moves away from the soil).**

> **PASSIVE pressure applies when something pushes INTO the soil.**

> **A vertical cut is unambiguously an active case, so K_a is correct and options (c) and (d) are wrong.**

> **And since K_a < 1 while K_p > 1, using K_p would give a much smaller (and unsafe) depth:**

| For φ = 30° | Value | H_c with q/γ = 9 m analogue |
|---|---|---|
| **K_a = 1/3, √K_a = 0.577** | **H_c = 4c/(0.577γ) = 6.93c/γ** | Larger |
| **K_p = 3, √K_p = 1.732** | 4c/(1.732γ) = 2.31c/γ | **Three times smaller** |

> **So the K_p versions are not merely wrong — they are unconservatively wrong by a factor of three**, which is the kind of error that matters.

**Why options (b) and (d) fail on DIMENSIONS — a free check:**

> **H_c must be a LENGTH.**

> **c has units of stress (kN/m²) and γ of unit weight (kN/m³), so c/γ has units of METRES.** ✓

> **In options (a) and (c) the K term is in the DENOMINATOR with γ, so the expression is (c/γ) × (1/√K) — a length times a dimensionless number.** ✓ **Valid.**

> **In options (b) and (d) the K term MULTIPLIES c, giving (c√K)/γ — also a length times a dimensionless number.** ✓ **Also dimensionally valid.**

> **So dimensions do NOT discriminate here, which is worth knowing rather than discovering.** The discrimination is whether √K belongs above or below the line.

> **The physical check settles it: a soil with a HIGHER φ (larger K_p, SMALLER K_a) should stand to a GREATER depth.**

| Option | As φ increases (K_a falls) | Correct behaviour? |
|---|---|---|
| **4c/(γ√K_a)** | **K_a falls, so √K_a falls, so H_c RISES** ✓ | **YES — a stronger soil stands deeper** |
| **(4c√K_a)/γ** | **K_a falls, so H_c FALLS** ✗ | **NO — backwards** |

> **That is the decisive test and it needs no recall: a better soil must stand to a greater unsupported depth**, so K_a must be in the denominator.

**The practical warning, which matters more than the formula:**

> **This critical depth is a THEORETICAL maximum with a factor of safety of exactly ONE.** It is the depth at which the cut is on the point of collapse.

> **No excavation should ever be taken to it.** In practice a factor of safety of at least 1.5 is applied, giving a safe unsupported depth of about **H_c/1.5 = 2.67c/(γ√K_a)**.

> **And even that assumes conditions the formula does not check:**

| Assumption | Why it fails in practice |
|---|---|
| **The cohesion c is reliable and PERMANENT** | **Cohesion in clay FALLS with time as the soil softens and swells** ← |
| **No water pressure in the tension crack** | **Rain filling the crack adds hydrostatic thrust and is a common trigger for collapse** |
| **No surcharge at the top** | Spoil, plant or a stockpile beside the cut |
| **No vibration** | Traffic or plant nearby |
| Uniform soil, no fissures | Fissured clay is far weaker in mass than in a sample |

> **The first two are the ones that kill people.** A trench cut in stiff clay stands for days and then fails — **because the clay has softened and because rain has filled the tension crack.**

> **Which is why trench support is a legal requirement rather than a matter of judgement in most jurisdictions**, and why "it stood yesterday" is the reasoning behind a large proportion of excavation fatalities.

> **So this formula's real use is to show that an unsupported vertical cut in clay of even modest cohesion appears safe to a considerable depth — and to explain why that appearance is dangerous.**

examTip.trick: **H_c = 4c/(γ√K_a), which is TWICE the tension-crack depth z₀ = 2c/(γ√K_a)** — because the negative and positive pressure triangles have equal area at H = 2z₀.
examTip.trap: **Dimensions do NOT discriminate here** — all four options are lengths. The physical test does: a soil with HIGHER φ (smaller K_a) must stand DEEPER, so √K_a belongs in the DENOMINATOR. And using K_p is unconservative by a factor of three.
examTip.mnemonic: **This depth has a factor of safety of exactly ONE** — the point of collapse. And the formula assumes the cohesion is permanent and the crack dry, which is why a clay trench stands for days and then fails after rain.

questions.stem: If the area is 72 hectares, the intensity of rainfall is 10 cm/hr and the runoff coefficient is 0.5, then the discharge of storm water is:
questions.solution:
**10 m³/s.**

**The RATIONAL FORMULA:**

> **Q = C i A**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **C** | **RUNOFF COEFFICIENT (dimensionless)** | **0.5** |
| **i** | **Intensity of rainfall** | **10 cm/hr** |
| **A** | **Catchment AREA** | **72 hectares** |

**Step 1 — convert the intensity to metres per second:**

> **i = 10 cm/hr = 0.10 m/hr = 0.10 / 3600 m/s = 1/36,000 m/s**

**Step 2 — convert the area to square metres:**

> **A = 72 hectares = 72 × 10,000 = 720,000 m² = 72 × 10⁴ m²**

**Step 3 — substitute:**

> **Q = 0.5 × (1/36,000) × 720,000**

> **= 0.5 × 20 = 10 m³/s** ✓

> **The arithmetic is clean because 720,000/36,000 = 20 exactly**, and the source's working follows exactly this route.

**The unit conversions are the whole question, so do them deliberately:**

| Conversion | Factor |
|---|---|
| **1 hectare** | **10,000 m²** |
| **1 hour** | **3600 s** |
| **1 cm** | **0.01 m** |

> **Every one of the four options is what you get from a different combination of these**, which is why the question punishes carelessness rather than ignorance:

| Option | Likely slip |
|---|---|
| **1.0 m³/s** | A factor of ten out — cm/m conversion mishandled |
| **10 m³/s** | ✓ |
| **11 m³/s** | Rounding of an intermediate step |
| **100 m³/s** | **The runoff coefficient omitted AND a factor of ten** — or using i = 10 m/hr |

> **A useful discipline: reduce everything to SI units FIRST, then multiply once.** Mixing hectares with cm/hr invites exactly these errors.

**A convenient shortcut worth knowing, since it removes the conversions:**

> **In practical units, Q (m³/s) = C × i (mm/hr) × A (hectares) / 360**

> **Check it: 0.5 × 100 × 72 / 360 = 3600/360 = 10 m³/s** ✓

> **The 360 absorbs all three conversions at once, and this form is the one used in drainage practice** — intensity in mm/hr and area in hectares are the units data actually arrives in.

**What the runoff coefficient represents:**

> **C is the fraction of rainfall that becomes SURFACE RUNOFF rather than infiltrating, evaporating or being intercepted.**

| Surface | C |
|---|---|
| **Watertight roofs** | **0.70-0.95** |
| **Asphalt and concrete pavement** | **0.85-0.90** |
| **Closely built urban area** | **0.70-0.90** |
| **Residential, moderately built** | **0.40-0.60** |
| **Parks, lawns, gardens** | **0.05-0.25** |
| **Wooded land** | **0.01-0.20** |
| Bare uncultivated soil | 0.20-0.60 |

> **The urban/rural contrast is the important one, and it is the reason urban drainage is such a large problem: paving a catchment can raise C from 0.2 to 0.9 — a FOUR- OR FIVE-FOLD increase in peak runoff from the same rainfall.**

> **And the increase is not only in volume but in TIMING: an impervious catchment concentrates its runoff much faster, so the peak is both larger and earlier.**

> **That is why urbanisation upstream causes flooding downstream even where no additional rain has fallen** — and why modern practice requires attenuation storage to hold the difference back.

**The formula's most important assumption — the TIME OF CONCENTRATION:**

> **The rational formula assumes the rainfall lasts AT LEAST as long as the TIME OF CONCENTRATION t_c — the time for runoff to travel from the most remote point of the catchment to the outlet.**

> **Only then is the WHOLE catchment contributing simultaneously, which is what makes Q = CiA valid.**

> **And the design intensity i must be the intensity for a storm of duration t_c**, taken from an intensity-duration-frequency relation:

> **i = a / (t + b)^n**, a common form being **i = 254 / (t + 20)** or similar, with t in minutes.

> **Since intensity FALLS as duration rises, using t_c gives the highest intensity for which the whole catchment still contributes — which is the critical condition.**

> **Using a shorter storm gives a higher intensity but only part of the catchment contributing; a longer one gives the whole catchment but a lower intensity.** The peak occurs at t = t_c, and that is why the time of concentration is the pivot of the whole method.

**And the limitation to state honestly:**

> **The rational formula is valid for SMALL catchments — commonly quoted as up to about 50 hectares, and stretched to a few hundred.**

> **Beyond that its assumptions fail: rainfall is not uniform over a large area, the runoff coefficient is not constant, and channel storage attenuates the peak.**

> **For larger catchments a UNIT HYDROGRAPH or a flood-frequency method is needed** — which is why the rational formula belongs to urban drainage and small culvert design rather than to river hydrology.

examTip.trick: **Q = CiA in SI: i = 0.10/3600 m/s, A = 720,000 m², so Q = 0.5 × 720,000/36,000 = 10 m³/s.** Or use the practical form **Q = CiA/360** with i in mm/hr and A in hectares.
examTip.trap: **All four options come from different combinations of the three conversions** (hectare = 10⁴ m², hour = 3600 s, cm = 0.01 m). Reduce everything to SI FIRST, then multiply once.
examTip.mnemonic: **The design intensity must be that of a storm lasting the TIME OF CONCENTRATION** — only then is the whole catchment contributing. And paving a catchment raises C from ~0.2 to ~0.9: a four- or five-fold peak increase from the same rain.

questions.stem: Find the volume of stone required for the pitching on the sloping side of a guide bund of slope 2:1, having length 100 m, height 5 m and thickness 1 m.
questions.solution:
**Of the order of 1184 m³ (computed 1118 m³).**

**The calculation:**

> **Stone pitching is laid on the SLOPING FACE, so the area to be covered is the SLANT area, not the vertical projection.**

> **Slant length of the slope = h √(1 + z²)**, with z the horizontal run per unit rise.

> **For a slope of 2:1 (H:V), z = 2:**

> **Slant length = 5 √(1 + 2²) = 5 √5 = 5 × 2.2361 = 11.18 m**

> **Area of pitching = slant length × length of bund = 11.18 × 100 = 1118 m²**

> **Volume = area × thickness = 1118 × 1 = 1118 m³**

> **The nearest option is (d) 1184 m³.** ✓

> **The source's own working sets out exactly this route — 5√5 × 100 × 1 — and then prints the product as 1184 m³, where the multiplication actually gives 1118 m³. The keyed letter is right; only the printed arithmetic is slightly wrong, and no option carries the exact value.**

**Why option (a) 11.84 m³ is the designed trap:**

> **It is the answer with a factor of a HUNDRED lost — essentially the slant length alone, mistaken for a volume.**

> **The magnitude check disposes of it immediately: a bund 100 m long and 5 m high covered in stone 1 m thick is a substantial structure, and 11.84 m³ is about five wheelbarrow loads.**

> **Options (b) 250 and (c) 500 are also far too small: 500 m³ would be the volume if the slant area were only 500 m², that is, a slant length of 5 m — the height, with no slope allowance at all.**

> **So option (c) is what you get by using the VERTICAL height instead of the SLANT length**, which is the substantive conceptual error the question is testing.

**The √(1+z²) factor — why it appears and where else it does:**

> **It is Pythagoras on the slope: for a rise h the horizontal run is zh, so the slant is √(h² + z²h²) = h√(1+z²).**

> **So √(1+z²) is the SLANT LENGTH PER UNIT RISE**, and it appears wherever a sloping face's true length is needed:

| Application | Where √(1+z²) appears |
|---|---|
| **Stone pitching on a slope** | **Slant area = h√(1+z²) × length** ← |
| **WETTED PERIMETER of a trapezoidal channel** | **P = B + 2y√(1+z²)** |
| **Area of side slopes of an embankment or canal** | 2 × L × y√(1+z²) |
| Length of a slope for turfing or geotextile | Same |

> **For the common slopes it is worth having the values:**

| Slope (H:V) | z | √(1+z²) |
|---|---|---|
| **1:1** | **1** | **1.414** |
| **1.5:1** | **1.5** | **1.803** |
| **2:1** | **2** | **2.236** ← |
| **2.5:1** | 2.5 | 2.693 |
| **3:1** | **3** | **3.162** |

> **Note that for flat slopes √(1+z²) approaches z**, so the slant length approaches the horizontal run — which is a useful approximation for very flat slopes and a bad one for steep ones.

**Why guide bunds need pitching at all:**

> **A guide bund is an EARTH embankment placed in a river to guide the flow into the waterway and prevent OUTFLANKING.**

> **Earth in a river erodes, so the exposed faces must be ARMOURED:**

| Element | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **STONE PITCHING on the river-side slope** | **Resists direct attack by the current and by waves** ← |
| **LAUNCHING APRON at the toe** | **Stone laid on the bed, which slides into the scour hole as it develops** |
| Turfing on the rear slope | Protects against rain erosion |
| Filter layer beneath the pitching | **Prevents the fine embankment soil washing out through the stone** |

> **The FILTER LAYER is the element most often omitted and most consequential: without it the current sucks fine soil out through the voids between the stones, the pitching settles into the resulting cavity, and the protection fails from beneath while looking intact from above.**

> **A graded granular filter, or a geotextile, is what prevents that** — and it is a genuine case where the invisible layer matters more than the visible one.

**The design proportions of a guide bund, since this question concerns one:**

| Element | Value |
|---|---|
| **UPSTREAM length** | **1.0 to 1.5 L (generally 1.25 L)** |
| **DOWNSTREAM length** | **0.2 to 0.4 L (generally 0.25 L)** |
| **Radius of the upstream curved head** | **0.4 to 0.5 L** |
| **Sweep angle, upstream head** | **120° to 145°** |
| **Side slopes** | **2:1 to 3:1** ← the 2:1 of this question |
| **Pitching thickness** | **0.3 to 1.0 m, by the velocity and stone size** |
| **Apron thickness** | **1.5 to 2.25 × the pitching thickness** |
| Free board above HFL | 1.5 to 2 m |

> **The stone SIZE matters as much as the thickness, and it is sized from the velocity — roughly d ≈ τ/(0.06(γ_s − γ)) from Shields' criterion, giving about a 100 mm stone for a bed shear of 100 N/m².**

> **An undersized stone will simply be carried away, however thick the layer is laid** — so pitching design is a matter of stone size first and thickness second.

The source's own working is the correct method - slant length 5 root5 = 11.18 m, times 100 m length, times 1 m thickness - but it prints the product as 1184 m3 where the multiplication gives 1118 m3. No option carries 1118, and option (d) 1184 is both the nearest offered value and the source's keyed answer, so the key is retained. The solution states the computed figure of 1118 m3 openly rather than reproducing the source's arithmetic.

questions.stem: Which of the following sets of equations represents a possible 2-D incompressible flow?
questions.solution:
**∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 0.**

**The continuity equation for two-dimensional incompressible flow:**

> **∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 0**

> **The pairing is the whole point: u (the x-component of velocity) is differentiated with respect to x, and v (the y-component) with respect to y.**

> **EACH VELOCITY COMPONENT IS DIFFERENTIATED ALONG ITS OWN DIRECTION.**

> **The source confirms it: for a steady, incompressible, plane two-dimensional flow the equation reduces to ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 0.**

**What the equation MEANS — conservation of mass:**

> **∂u/∂x is the rate at which the flow STRETCHES in the x-direction; ∂v/∂y the rate in the y-direction.**

> **For an incompressible fluid, whatever flows into a small element must flow out of it — the element's volume cannot change.**

> **So if the flow stretches in one direction it must CONTRACT in the other by exactly the same amount, and the two terms must sum to zero.**

> **That is why the equation is a sum rather than a difference, and why it equals zero rather than a constant.**

**Why each distractor is wrong — and each is a specific, recognisable error:**

| Option | The mistake |
|---|---|
| **∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 0** | ✓ **Correct pairing** |
| **∂u/∂y + ∂v/∂x = 0** | **The pairing SWAPPED — each component differentiated along the OTHER direction** ← the substantive trap |
| **∂u/∂v + ∂x/∂y = 0** | **Differentiating a velocity with respect to a VELOCITY, and a coordinate with respect to a coordinate — meaningless** |
| **∂v/∂u + ∂y/∂x = 0** | Same category error |

> **Option (b) is the designed trap and it deserves attention, because the expression it writes is NOT meaningless — it is a real and important quantity.**

> **∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y is the VORTICITY (twice the rotation), and the condition ∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y = 0 is the condition for IRROTATIONAL flow.**

> **So the swapped pairing with a MINUS sign is irrotationality; with a PLUS sign, as option (b) writes it, it is neither continuity nor irrotationality but a combination with no standard meaning.**

> **Which makes the discrimination worth stating precisely:**

| Condition | Equation | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **CONTINUITY (incompressible)** | **∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 0** | **Mass is conserved** ← |
| **IRROTATIONALITY** | **∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y = 0** | **No net rotation of a fluid element** |

> **These are INDEPENDENT conditions.** A flow can satisfy either, both, or neither — **and only a flow satisfying BOTH admits a velocity potential as well as a stream function.**

> **Options (c) and (d) can be dismissed on a category error alone: ∂u/∂v differentiates one velocity component with respect to another, which is not a meaningful field operation**, and ∂x/∂y differentiates one independent coordinate with respect to another, which is zero by definition.

> **Recognising a malformed expression is a legitimate technique, and it disposes of half the options here without any fluid mechanics.**

**The full family of continuity equations, since the question specifies one case:**

| Case | Continuity equation |
|---|---|
| **2-D INCOMPRESSIBLE (steady or unsteady)** | **∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 0** ← |
| **3-D incompressible** | **∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y + ∂w/∂z = 0** |
| **3-D COMPRESSIBLE, unsteady** | **∂ρ/∂t + ∂(ρu)/∂x + ∂(ρv)/∂y + ∂(ρw)/∂z = 0** |
| Cylindrical, 2-D axisymmetric | ∂(r v_r)/∂r + ∂(r v_z)/∂z = 0 |
| **1-D pipe or channel flow** | **A₁V₁ = A₂V₂ (the familiar form)** |

> **Note that the incompressible form has NO TIME TERM.**

> **Incompressibility makes continuity a CONSTRAINT on the velocity field at every instant, rather than an equation describing how anything evolves.**

> **So an UNSTEADY incompressible flow satisfies exactly the same continuity equation as a steady one** — which surprises candidates and is worth holding, because it means the word "steady" in the stem is not what makes the equation valid.

> **What incompressibility requires is that ρ be constant, so it can be divided out of the compressible form.** The time derivative ∂ρ/∂t then vanishes because ρ does not change.

**And the STREAM FUNCTION, which exists precisely because of this equation:**

> **If a function ψ is defined so that  u = ∂ψ/∂y  and  v = −∂ψ/∂x**, then:

> **∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = ∂²ψ/∂x∂y − ∂²ψ/∂y∂x = 0  AUTOMATICALLY.**

> **So any flow described by a stream function satisfies continuity identically** — the equation is built into the definition.

> **That is the whole reason the stream function is useful: it reduces two unknown velocity components to ONE unknown function, and it does so by satisfying continuity for free.**

> **And lines of constant ψ are STREAMLINES**, with the difference in ψ between two streamlines equal to the discharge between them — which is why a flow net's flow channels each carry an equal share.

examTip.trick: **Each velocity component is differentiated along ITS OWN direction: ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 0.** It says that stretching in one direction must be matched by contraction in the other, since volume cannot change.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) swaps the pairing** — and the SWAPPED form with a MINUS sign (∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y = 0) is IRROTATIONALITY, a real and different condition. Continuity and irrotationality are independent.
examTip.mnemonic: **The incompressible form has NO time term** — it constrains the field at every instant, so unsteady flow obeys the same equation as steady. And any flow with a STREAM FUNCTION satisfies it automatically, which is why ψ is useful.

questions.stem: If an irrigation channel has a side slope of z:1, bed width b, depth y and length L, then the area of the side slopes of the trapezoidal channel (both sides) is:
questions.solution:
**A = 2 L y √(1 + z²).**

**Building the expression from the geometry:**

> **Take the sloping face of one side of the channel. Its two dimensions are:**

| Dimension | Value |
|---|---|
| **Along the channel** | **L (the length)** |
| **Up the slope (the SLANT length)** | **y √(1 + z²)** |

> **The slant length comes from Pythagoras: for a depth y the horizontal run is zy, so the slant is √(y² + z²y²) = y√(1+z²).**

> **Area of ONE side = L × y√(1+z²)**

> **Area of BOTH sides = 2 L y √(1+z²)** ✓

> **The source's own derivation is exactly this: s² = y² + (yz)², so s = y√(1+z²), and Area = 2 × l × y√(1+z²) for both sides.**

**Three checks that identify the answer with no recall:**

> **CHECK 1 — the factor 2.** There are TWO sloping sides, so the expression must carry a 2. **Option (c) counts only one.** ✓ eliminated

> **CHECK 2 — which dimension is on the slope.** The slope rises through the DEPTH y, not across the bed width b. **Option (b) uses b, which is the bed — a horizontal dimension that has nothing to do with the sloping face.** ✓ eliminated

> **CHECK 3 — the limiting case z = 0 (vertical sides).** Then √(1+0) = 1 and A = 2Ly — which is correct: two vertical rectangular faces of height y and length L. ✓ **Option (a) passes.**

> **Three checks, and only option (a) survives** — which is a better method than recall, because it also confirms the expression means what it should.

**Where √(1+z²) appears elsewhere — it is one factor doing several jobs:**

| Application | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Area of the side slopes** | **2Ly√(1+z²)** ← |
| **WETTED PERIMETER of a trapezoidal channel** | **P = b + 2y√(1+z²)** |
| **Stone pitching on an embankment slope** | Slant length × length × thickness |
| Length of a slope for turfing or geotextile | Same |

> **In every case √(1+z²) is the SLANT LENGTH PER UNIT OF DEPTH**, and recognising it as one quantity rather than four formulae is worth the effort.

> **The values for the common slopes:**

| Slope (H:V) | z | √(1+z²) |
|---|---|---|
| **Vertical** | **0** | **1** |
| **1:1** | **1** | **1.414** |
| **1.5:1** | 1.5 | 1.803 |
| **2:1** | **2** | **2.236** |
| **3:1** | 3 | 3.162 |

> **Note the contrast with the AREA of the channel section, which uses z DIRECTLY: A = by + zy².**

> **The area needs only the HORIZONTAL RUN of the triangular parts (zy); the perimeter and the sloping face need the SLANT length (y√(1+z²)).**

> **Confusing the two — putting √(1+z²) in the cross-sectional area, or z in the perimeter — is the standard error, and the check is that the area's side term must vanish at z = 0 while the perimeter's must reduce to 2y.**

**Why the side-slope area matters in practice:**

> **It is the quantity that determines the cost of LINING and of protection:**

| Item priced by side-slope area | Note |
|---|---|
| **Canal LINING (concrete, brick or membrane)** | **The dominant cost item in a lined canal** ← |
| **Turfing or grassing of an earth channel** | Erosion protection |
| **Stone pitching** | Where velocities are high |
| Excavation of the slope face | Part of the earthwork |

> **And that connects directly to the MOST ECONOMICAL SECTION.**

> **Minimising the WETTED PERIMETER for a given area maximises the discharge — and it also minimises the LINING MATERIAL, since both depend on the same perimeter.**

> **So hydraulic efficiency and construction cost point the SAME WAY here**, which is unusual in engineering and worth noticing when it happens.

> **The most economical trapezoidal section is HALF A REGULAR HEXAGON, with:**

| Condition | Value |
|---|---|
| **Side slope** | **z = 1/√3 ≈ 0.577 (sides at 60° to the horizontal)** |
| **Hydraulic radius** | **R = y/2** |
| A circle inscribed in the section | Touches the bed and both sides |

> **But the SOIL usually overrides it: z = 0.577 is a slope of about 1.73 horizontal to 1 vertical, steeper than most earth will stand.**

> **Practical canal side slopes are 1.5:1 to 2:1 in ordinary soil and flatter in soft ground** — so the hexagonal optimum is a benchmark rather than a specification, and a real canal is the closest practicable approach to it.

> **Which is why LINING changes the answer: a lined canal can hold a steeper slope than an unlined one, so lining buys not only reduced seepage but a more efficient section as well.**

verification.notes: Duplicate option removed and a lost radical restored. The source printed options (c) and (d) IDENTICALLY as A = L*y(1+z^2), leaving only three distinct choices; option (d) has been replaced with "None of the above". The source also printed every option with (1+z^2) rather than root(1+z^2), although its own worked derivation gives s = y root(1+z^2) and Area = 2*l*y root(1+z^2) - so the radical had been lost in typesetting throughout. It has been restored in the options. The keyed answer is unchanged at (a).

examTip.trick: **One side's face is L by the SLANT length y√(1+z²); there are two sides, so A = 2Ly√(1+z²).**
examTip.trap: **Three checks with no recall: the factor must be 2 (two sides); the slope rises through the DEPTH y, not the bed width b; and at z = 0 it must reduce to 2Ly (two vertical faces).**
examTip.mnemonic: **AREA of the section uses z directly (by + zy²); PERIMETER and the sloping FACE use the slant √(1+z²)** — the area needs the horizontal run, the others the true slope length. Check: the area term vanishes at z = 0, the perimeter's reduces to 2y.

questions.stem: Spot welding is used when two plates are placed:
options: At right angles to each other
questions.solution:
**One below the other — that is, overlapping.**

**How spot welding works, and why the geometry follows:**

> **SPOT WELDING (properly RESISTANCE spot welding) presses two OVERLAPPING sheets between a pair of COPPER ELECTRODES and passes a heavy electric current through them.**

> **The electrical RESISTANCE at the INTERFACE between the two sheets generates enough heat to melt a small volume of metal there — the "spot" — which then solidifies under the electrode pressure to form a weld nugget.**

> **The source's own figure shows exactly this: copper electrodes above and below, pressure applied from both sides, and the electrical current passing through the overlapped sheets.**

> **So the two sheets MUST OVERLAP — one lying on the other — because the weld forms at the surface where they touch.**

> **Two plates butting edge to edge have no overlapping interface to melt, and two plates at right angles cannot be gripped between a pair of opposed electrodes.**

> **The geometry is therefore not a preference but a requirement of the process.**

**Why each distractor is wrong — and each names a real joint for a different process:**

| Option | The joint it describes | Welded by |
|---|---|---|
| **One below the other (LAP joint)** | ✓ **Overlapping** | **SPOT welding, or a fillet weld** |
| **One BUTTING against the other (butt joint)** | **Edge to edge** | **BUTT weld — groove or square butt, with a full-penetration weld** ← |
| **One next to the other** | Loosely the same as a butt joint | — |
| **At RIGHT ANGLES (tee or corner joint)** | **Perpendicular** | **FILLET weld** |

> **So the options are a survey of joint TYPES, and the question tests which type the process demands.**

> **That framing is worth noticing, because the joint types and the weld types are two separate classifications that are constantly conflated:**

| **JOINT type (the geometry of the parts)** | **WELD type (the shape of the deposited metal)** |
|---|---|
| **Butt** | **Groove (butt) weld — square, V, U, J, bevel** |
| **LAP** | **FILLET weld, or SPOT weld** ← |
| **Tee** | **Fillet weld, or groove weld** |
| **Corner** | Fillet or groove |
| **Edge** | Groove |

> **A LAP joint can carry either a fillet weld along its edges or spot welds through its overlap** — so naming the joint does not name the weld, and vice versa.

**Where spot welding belongs in construction — and its limits:**

| Suits | Note |
|---|---|
| **THIN sheet metal** | **Typically up to about 3 mm per sheet** ← |
| **Cold-formed light gauge sections** | Purlins, sheeting rails, decking |
| **Repetitive factory production** | Fast, automated, no filler metal or flux |
| Non-structural and lightly loaded connections | — |

| Does NOT suit | Why |
|---|---|
| **THICK structural plate** | **The current cannot heat the interface of thick material effectively** |
| **Main structural connections** | **A spot weld carries load in SHEAR at a small area and is not designed as a structural weld** |
| Joints needing a continuous seal | Spots leave gaps between them |
| Site work | Requires heavy fixed equipment and a large power supply |

> **So spot welding is a SHEET-METAL and FACTORY process, not a structural steelwork one** — which is why it appears in the syllabus as one of a family of processes rather than as a design method.

**The welding processes worth knowing, for context:**

| Process | Note |
|---|---|
| **SMAW (manual metal arc / stick)** | **The workhorse of site steelwork — a flux-coated consumable electrode** |
| **Submerged arc (SAW)** | **Automatic, deep penetration, for long shop welds** |
| **MIG / MAG (gas metal arc)** | Continuous wire, shielding gas; fast |
| **TIG (gas tungsten arc)** | High quality, thin material, non-consumable electrode |
| **RESISTANCE SPOT welding** | **No filler metal; sheet material; overlapping joint** ← |
| **Oxy-acetylene (gas) welding** | Now mainly for cutting and repair |
| Stud welding | Shear studs on composite beams |

> **Note that spot welding is the odd one out: it uses NO FILLER METAL and NO ARC.** The parent material itself melts, and the heat comes from ohmic resistance rather than from an arc.

> **That is why it needs no flux, no shielding gas and no consumable — and why it leaves no visible weld bead**, only a small indentation from the electrode.

**And the inspection consequence, which is a genuine drawback:**

> **A spot weld's nugget is INSIDE the joint and cannot be seen.**

| Inspection method | Note |
|---|---|
| **Visual** | **Shows only the electrode indentation, not the nugget** |
| **PEEL or chisel test** | **DESTRUCTIVE — tears one sheet to expose the nugget** |
| **Ultrasonic** | Possible but difficult on thin sheet |
| **Process monitoring (current, time, force)** | **The practical route — control the process rather than inspect the product** ← |

> **So spot-weld quality is assured by CONTROLLING THE PROCESS rather than by inspecting each weld**, with destructive tests on samples to confirm the settings.

> **That is a general pattern worth recognising: where a product cannot be inspected, quality must be built in by process control** — the same argument that makes QA (process-oriented) necessary alongside QC (product-oriented).

examTip.trick: **The weld forms at the INTERFACE where the two sheets touch, so they must OVERLAP** — one below the other, gripped between opposed copper electrodes. Butting plates have no interface to melt.
examTip.trap: **JOINT type and WELD type are separate classifications.** A LAP joint can carry a fillet weld OR spot welds; naming the joint does not name the weld.
examTip.mnemonic: **Spot welding uses NO filler, NO arc and NO flux** — the parent metal melts from ohmic resistance. It suits THIN sheet (up to ~3 mm) in a factory, not structural plate. And its nugget is invisible, so quality comes from PROCESS control.

questions.stem: If σx and τxy are the normal and shear stress respectively, then the minor principal stress will be:
questions.solution:
**σ_minor = σx/2 − √(σx²/4 + τxy²).**

**Where it comes from — the general principal stress result with σy = 0:**

> **For a general two-dimensional stress state:**

> **σ₁,₂ = (σx + σy)/2 ± √[((σx − σy)/2)² + τxy²]**

> **With σy = 0 — a single direct stress accompanied by shear, which is the commonest practical case:**

> **σ₁,₂ = σx/2 ± √(σx²/4 + τxy²)**

| Which sign | Which stress |
|---|---|
| **PLUS the radical** | **MAJOR principal stress (the larger)** |
| **MINUS the radical** | **MINOR principal stress (the smaller)** ← |

> **The source gives both lines: minor = σx/2 − √(σx²/4 + τxy²), major = σx/2 + √(σx²/4 + τxy²).**

**Two things must be got right, and the option list tests each separately:**

> **FIRST — the SIGN OUTSIDE the radical.** Minor means the SMALLER, so the radical is SUBTRACTED.

> **That eliminates options (a) and (c), which both ADD it.**

> **SECOND — the SIGN INSIDE the radical.** The τxy² term is ADDED to σx²/4, never subtracted.

> **That eliminates option (b), which subtracts it — leaving only option (d).**

> **So the question is a clean two-way discrimination, and each wrong option fails on exactly one of the two signs.**

**Why the term inside must be a SUM — the reason is geometric:**

> **On MOHR'S CIRCLE, the radical is the RADIUS.**

| Mohr's circle element | Expression (for σy = 0) |
|---|---|
| **CENTRE** | **(σx + σy)/2 = σx/2** |
| **RADIUS** | **√[((σx − σy)/2)² + τxy²] = √(σx²/4 + τxy²)** |
| **Major principal stress** | **Centre + radius** |
| **Minor principal stress** | **Centre − radius** ← |
| **Maximum shear stress** | **THE RADIUS itself** |

> **A radius is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are σx/2 and τxy — so by Pythagoras the two must be SQUARED AND ADDED.**

> **A radius can never be reduced by adding a perpendicular component**, which is why option (b)'s subtraction is geometrically impossible rather than merely wrong.

> **And there is a decisive practical consequence: if the term were a difference, the radical could become IMAGINARY when τxy exceeds σx/2** — and a principal stress is always real. **That impossibility is the fastest way to reject (b).**

**The PURE SHEAR check, which verifies the whole formula in seconds:**

> **Set σx = 0. For pure shear the principal stresses are known to be exactly ± τxy.**

| Option | At σx = 0 | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| (a) 0 + √τxy² = **+τxy** | Correct in magnitude | **This is the MAJOR stress, not the minor** |
| (b) 0 − √(−τxy²) = **imaginary** | **IMPOSSIBLE** | **Fails** |
| (c) 0 + √(−τxy²) = **imaginary** | **IMPOSSIBLE** | **Fails** |
| **(d) 0 − √τxy² = −τxy** | ✓ | **CORRECT — the minor stress in pure shear** |

> **The pure-shear check is decisive and takes ten seconds.** It is the check to reach for whenever a principal-stress formula must be identified from options.

> **Note that setting τxy = 0 does NOT discriminate: every option then gives σx/2 ± σx/2, which is σx or 0 — and both are legitimate principal stresses for uniaxial tension.** So that check is useless here, which is worth knowing in advance rather than discovering mid-examination.

**The companion results, since they come from the same circle:**

| Quantity | Expression (σy = 0) |
|---|---|
| **Major principal stress** | **σx/2 + √(σx²/4 + τxy²)** |
| **MINOR principal stress** | **σx/2 − √(σx²/4 + τxy²)** ← |
| **MAXIMUM SHEAR stress** | **√(σx²/4 + τxy²) = (σ₁ − σ₂)/2** |
| **Orientation of the principal planes** | **tan 2θ = 2τxy/(σx − σy)** |

> **Note that τ_max is exactly the RADICAL** — and equals half the difference of the principal stresses.

> **Two facts worth carrying:**

> **PRINCIPAL PLANES CARRY NO SHEAR — that is their definition**, and it is why the principal stresses are the extreme values of direct stress.

> **The planes of MAXIMUM SHEAR lie at 45° to the principal planes, and they carry a direct stress of (σ₁+σ₂)/2 — NOT zero.** A common error is to assume the maximum-shear plane is free of direct stress; it is not.

**And where this is used, since it looks abstract:**

> **A SHAFT under combined bending moment M and torque T has σx = 32M/πd³ and τxy = 16T/πd³.**

> **Substituting into the formulae above gives the standard results:**

> **EQUIVALENT BENDING MOMENT  M_e = ½(M + √(M² + T²))**

> **EQUIVALENT TORQUE  T_e = √(M² + T²)**

> **Those two expressions are this question's formula in disguise**, and recognising that saves learning them as separate results.

> **The same analysis underlies the design of any member carrying combined direct and shear stress — a beam web, a bolt in tension and shear, a pressure vessel with a torsional load.**

examTip.trick: **Minor means SMALLER, so SUBTRACT the radical; and the τxy² term is always ADDED inside it.** Each wrong option fails on exactly one of those two signs.
examTip.trap: **Setting τxy = 0 does NOT discriminate** — every option gives σx or 0. Use PURE SHEAR (σx = 0) instead: the answer must be −τxy, and options (b) and (c) go IMAGINARY, which is impossible for a principal stress.
examTip.mnemonic: **The radical IS Mohr's radius**, the hypotenuse of legs σx/2 and τxy — so Pythagoras requires a SUM. And **τ_max equals that radius**, while the maximum-shear plane carries a direct stress of (σ₁+σ₂)/2, not zero.

questions.stem: When the barometer reads 740.0 mm of mercury, a pressure of 10 kPa suction at that location is equivalent to:
questions.solution:
**88.72 kPa absolute.**

**Step 1 — convert the barometric reading to a pressure:**

> **p_atm = ρ_mercury × g × h**

> **= 13,600 kg/m³ × 9.81 m/s² × 0.740 m**

> **= 98,722 Pa = 98.72 kPa**

> **The source's working gives exactly this: 0.740 × 13600 × 9.81 = 98.72 kPa.**

> **Note that this is NOT the standard 101.325 kPa, because the barometer reads 740 mm rather than the standard 760 mm** — the location is above sea level, or the weather is low. **That is the point of giving the barometric reading at all.**

**Step 2 — convert the suction to an absolute pressure:**

> **A SUCTION (vacuum) is a pressure BELOW atmospheric, so it is SUBTRACTED:**

> **p_absolute = p_atmospheric − p_vacuum**

> **= 98.72 − 10 = 88.72 kPa (absolute)** ✓

**Why the subtraction is the whole question:**

> **The pressure vocabulary must be secure:**

| Term | Measured from | Relation |
|---|---|---|
| **ABSOLUTE pressure** | **A PERFECT VACUUM as zero** | — |
| **GAUGE pressure** | **ATMOSPHERIC as zero** | **p_abs = p_atm + p_gauge** |
| **VACUUM (suction)** | **Atmospheric, measured DOWNWARD** | **p_abs = p_atm − p_vacuum** ← |

> **So a suction is simply a NEGATIVE GAUGE PRESSURE, and "10 kPa suction" means a gauge pressure of −10 kPa.**

> **Substituting into the first relation: p_abs = 98.72 + (−10) = 88.72 kPa.** ✓ **The two forms are the same statement.**

> **The absolute pressure must be LESS than atmospheric, because a suction is below it** — and that single observation is the check that catches the wrong direction.

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **10.02 m of water (abs)** | **Converting 98.72 kPa to metres of water gives 98,720/9810 = 10.06 m — so this is roughly the ATMOSPHERIC pressure expressed as a water column, not the answer** ← |
| **9.87 m of water** | **98.72/9.81 ≈ 10.06, and 9.87 is close to 98.72/10 — a decimal artefact of the atmospheric figure** |
| **88.72 kPa (abs)** | ✓ |
| **0.043 kPa (abs)** | Not a meaningful intermediate |

> **Options (a) and (b) are both near the ATMOSPHERIC pressure expressed in metres of water, and neither accounts for the suction at all.**

> **They are also the wrong KIND of answer: the question asks for an equivalent pressure, and a head of water is a legitimate way to express one — but these particular values correspond to the atmospheric pressure rather than to the absolute pressure after the suction.**

> **Converting the correct answer would give 88.72/9.81 = 9.04 m of water absolute**, which is not offered — confirming that the intended answer is the kPa form.

**The pressure conversions worth having automatically:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **Standard atmosphere** | **101.325 kPa = 1.01325 bar = 760 mm Hg = 10.33 m of water** |
| **1 bar** | **100 kPa** |
| **1 m of water** | **9.81 kPa** |
| **1 mm of mercury (torr)** | **133.3 Pa** |
| **Density of mercury** | **13,600 kg/m³ (13.6 × water)** |

> **The mercury density of 13.6 relative to water is the key number**, and it explains why mercury is used in barometers at all: **a water barometer would need a tube over 10 metres tall, while a mercury one needs only 0.76 m.**

**Why the ABSOLUTE pressure matters — and it is not bookkeeping:**

| Use | Which pressure |
|---|---|
| **Pipe and vessel wall stress** | **GAUGE — the wall feels the difference across it** |
| **PUMP SUCTION calculations, NPSH** | **ABSOLUTE — because VAPOUR PRESSURE is an absolute quantity** ← |
| **Gas law calculations (pV = nRT)** | **ABSOLUTE, always** |
| Hydraulic head and energy equations | Gauge, conventionally |

> **The NPSH case is where the distinction earns its place, and it is exactly the situation this question describes — a suction.**

> **CAVITATION occurs when the ABSOLUTE pressure falls to the liquid's vapour pressure**, which for water at 20 °C is about 2.34 kPa absolute.

> **So the 88.72 kPa absolute computed here is comfortably above vapour pressure — but a suction of 90 kPa at the same location would leave only 8.7 kPa absolute, close to the limit.**

> **A suction calculation done in gauge pressure would be wrong by one whole atmosphere, which is the entire available margin** — and that is why the absolute value is the one that must be computed.

**And the limit this sets on any suction lift:**

> **Since the atmosphere here supplies only 98.72 kPa = 10.06 m of water, NO PUMP AT THIS LOCATION CAN LIFT WATER BY SUCTION MORE THAN 10.06 m, EVEN WITH A PERFECT VACUUM.**

> **In practice the limit is 6 to 7 m**, after allowing for friction in the suction pipe, the water's vapour pressure, and a margin against cavitation.

> **And note that the limit FALLS WITH ALTITUDE**, because the atmosphere supplying the push is thinner. **A pump that lifts 6 m in the Terai will lift appreciably less in Kathmandu and much less at 3000 m** — which is a real design consideration in Nepal and follows directly from the barometric reading this question begins with.

examTip.trick: **p_atm = 13,600 × 9.81 × 0.740 = 98.72 kPa, then p_abs = 98.72 − 10 = 88.72 kPa.** A suction is subtracted, so the absolute pressure must be BELOW atmospheric.
examTip.trap: **Options (a) and (b) are near the ATMOSPHERIC pressure expressed in metres of water** and ignore the suction entirely. Note also that 740 mm is not the standard 760 — the reading is given because it matters.
examTip.mnemonic: **Use ABSOLUTE pressure for NPSH and gas laws** — a suction calculation in gauge pressure is wrong by a whole atmosphere, which is the entire margin. And the suction lift limit FALLS with altitude: less in Kathmandu than in the Terai.

questions.stem: The stiffness of a member at its free end, if the far end is fixed, is:
questions.solution:
**4EI/L.**

**The four values, one for each FAR-END condition:**

| Far end | Stiffness | Relative stiffness |
|---|---|---|
| **FIXED** | **4EI/L** ← | **1** |
| **HINGED (pinned)** | **3EI/L** | **3/4** |
| **GUIDED ROLLER** | **EI/L** | 1/4 |
| **FREE** | **0** | 0 |

> **STIFFNESS is the moment required AT A JOINT to produce UNIT ROTATION at that joint.**

> **The stem specifies that the FAR end is FIXED, so the answer is 4EI/L.**

> **The source lists all four values exactly, and every option in this question is one of them** — so the whole set must be known, not one figure.

**Reading the stem carefully, because the wording is the difficulty:**

> **The phrase is "the stiffness ... at its FREE END, if the FAR END is FIXED".**

> **"Free end" here means the end being ROTATED — the end at which the moment is applied and the unit rotation imposed.** It is free to rotate, which is what makes the question meaningful: a stiffness is defined by rotating something.

> **"Far end" means the OTHER end, and its condition is what determines the stiffness.**

> **So the classification is always by the condition of the FAR end, never of the near one** — and reading which end the stem describes is the whole question.

> **Option (a) 0 is the designed trap for anyone who reads "free end" as the far-end condition**, since a member with a FREE far end has zero stiffness (there is nothing to rotate against).

> **That is a genuinely easy misreading, and it is why the source's own list is phrased consistently as "if the farther end is ...".**

**Why the fixed case gives 4EI/L — the slope-deflection result:**

> **For a member AB with A rotated by θ and B FIXED:**

> **M_AB = (4EI/L)θ**  and  **M_BA = (2EI/L)θ**

> **So the moment needed at A for unit rotation is 4EI/L, and half of it appears at the far end — the CARRY-OVER FACTOR of 1/2.**

> **And the hinged case follows by releasing that far-end moment:**

> **Releasing M_BA carries HALF of it back to A, OPPOSING the applied moment:**

> **carry-back = ½ × (2EI/L)θ = (EI/L)θ**
