> **Net moment needed = 4EI/L − EI/L = 3EI/L** ✓

> **So the 3/4 factor is not arbitrary: it is 1 minus the product of the two carry-over halves**, and deriving it once makes both values secure.

**How stiffness is used — the distribution factor:**

> **DF for a member at a joint = (its stiffness) / (sum of stiffnesses of all members at that joint)**, and **ΣDF at any joint = 1.**

> **The stiffnesses above are what go into that sum**, which is why the four values matter.

**A caution on distribution factors AT supports, because the notes state this badly:**

| Support at the joint | Distribution factor of the member there |
|---|---|
| **FIXED support** | **0 — the support is infinitely stiff and absorbs everything** |
| **HINGED or ROLLER END support** | **1 — the support takes no moment, so the member takes all of it** |

> **Those are the standard convention, and the underlying rule settles them without memorising either: DF = member stiffness / joint stiffness.**

> **A FIXED support contributes INFINITE stiffness to that sum, driving the member's fraction to zero.**

> **A HINGED end support contributes NONE, leaving the member as the only term and its fraction equal to one.**

> **So the two facts to keep apart are: STIFFNESS of a member with a HINGED FAR END is 3EI/L, and the DF of a member AT a hinged end support is 1.** Both concern hinges and answer different questions.

**The related quantities, since they are used together:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **Stiffness, far end FIXED** | **4EI/L** ← |
| **Stiffness, far end hinged** | **3EI/L** |
| **CARRY-OVER factor, far end fixed** | **+1/2** |
| **Carry-over factor, far end hinged** | **0** |
| **FEM, udl, both ends fixed** | **wL²/12** |
| **FEM, udl, one end hinged** | **wL²/8 at the fixed end** |
| **FEM, central point load, both fixed** | **WL/8** |

> **Notice the pattern in the fixed-end moments: releasing one end RAISES the moment at the other from wL²/12 to wL²/8 — a 50 per cent increase, because the released end's moment has to go somewhere.**

> **The same logic that gives 3EI/L gives that too**, which is why the two sets of numbers are worth learning together rather than as separate tables.

**And the practical point about using the modified stiffness:**

| Approach | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Use 4EI/L throughout and distribute the far-end moment each cycle** | Correct, but wastes cycles |
| **Use the MODIFIED 3EI/L once for a hinged far end, with zero carry-over** | **Correct and finishes the hinge in ONE step** ← |

> **That is the practical reason for knowing the modified value at all: it removes the hinged member from the iteration entirely**, which on a hand calculation is a substantial saving and on a large frame the difference between a tractable and an intractable problem.

examTip.trick: **Classification is always by the FAR end's condition: fixed 4EI/L, hinged 3EI/L, guided roller EI/L, free 0.** The stem says the far end is FIXED.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) 0 is the trap for reading "free end" as the FAR-end condition.** "Free end" here means the end being ROTATED; the far end is what determines the stiffness.
examTip.mnemonic: **Releasing a fixed far end carries back half of 2EI/L against the applied moment: 4 − 1 = 3.** And keep two hinge facts apart — **stiffness with a hinged FAR end is 3EI/L; DF of a member AT a hinged end support is 1.**

questions.stem: When the water table rises to the ground level, the ultimate bearing capacity of a shallow foundation on sand is reduced to about:
questions.solution:
**50 per cent — the capacity is roughly HALVED.**

**Why — the reason is that both surviving terms use the SUBMERGED unit weight:**

> **Terzaghi's ultimate bearing capacity:**

> **q_u = c N_c + γ D_f N_q + 0.5 γ B N_γ**

> **FOR SAND, c = 0, so the cohesion term vanishes and only two terms remain — and BOTH contain γ:**

> **q_u = γ D_f N_q + 0.5 γ B N_γ**

> **When the water table rises to the ground surface, the soil is submerged throughout, and the SUBMERGED unit weight replaces the bulk one:**

> **γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w ≈ 0.5 γ**

> **Substituting:**

> **q_u(submerged) = 0.5γ D_f N_q + 0.5 × 0.5γ B N_γ = 0.5 (γ D_f N_q + 0.5 γ B N_γ) = 0.5 q_u** ✓

> **The factor of 0.5 comes OUTSIDE the bracket because it multiplies BOTH terms equally** — which is exactly the source's own derivation.

**Why γ′ is about half of γ — the arithmetic behind the approximation:**

| Quantity | Typical value for sand |
|---|---|
| **Saturated unit weight γ_sat** | **19-21 kN/m³** |
| **Unit weight of water γ_w** | **9.81 kN/m³** |
| **SUBMERGED unit weight γ′** | **9-11 kN/m³** |
| **Ratio γ′/γ_sat** | **~0.5** ← |

> **So "halved" is an approximation resting on the fact that soil is about twice as dense as water** — which is true for most soils, since the solids' specific gravity is around 2.65 and the voids are water-filled.

> **The approximation is good enough for the standard examination answer and worth stating as an approximation rather than an identity.**

**The crucial contrast with CLAY, which is what makes this question about sand specifically:**

| | **SAND (c = 0)** | **CLAY (undrained, φ = 0)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Surviving terms** | **γD_f N_q + 0.5γB N_γ — BOTH contain γ** | **c_u N_c — contains NO γ** |
| **Effect of a rising water table** | **Capacity HALVED** ← | **Capacity essentially UNCHANGED** |
| **Why** | **Both terms scale with the unit weight** | **Undrained cohesion does not depend on the unit weight** |

> **So the water table's effect is dramatic in sand and negligible in clay (in the short term)** — and that asymmetry is the substance of the topic.

> **The reason is physical: sand's strength is FRICTIONAL, and friction needs effective confining stress, which the water reduces.** Clay's undrained strength is cohesive and does not.

> **Which means a foundation design on sand MUST state its groundwater assumption**, and a design that assumed a deep water table is unsafe if the table rises.

**When the water table is at an INTERMEDIATE depth — the general case:**

> **Three positions must be distinguished, and only the last is the question's case:**

| Water table position | Effect |
|---|---|
| **At or BELOW a depth of about (D_f + B) below the footing** | **NO effect — the water is below the zone of influence** |
| **BETWEEN the footing base and (D_f + B)** | **PARTIAL reduction — the N_γ term is affected proportionally** |
| **At or ABOVE the footing base** | **Both terms affected; at ground level the capacity is HALVED** ← |

> **The depth (D_f + B) matters because the failure zone beneath a footing extends roughly one footing width below it.** Water deeper than that does not enter the mechanism at all.

> **So a rising water table has NO effect until it reaches the zone of influence, then a progressively larger one** — which is why the correction is applied through a reduction factor rather than as a switch.

**The practical consequences, which are the reason this matters:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Design for the HIGHEST credible water table** | **Not the level found on the day of the site investigation** ← |
| **A borehole in the dry season understates the risk** | **The monsoon table may be metres higher** |
| **Post-construction rises must be anticipated** | Irrigation, leaking mains, urbanisation, a new reservoir |
| **Permanent dewatering is rarely acceptable** | It settles the surroundings and must run for ever |

> **The seasonal point is the one that catches designs in Nepal specifically: a site investigated in March may show a water table several metres below the level it reaches in August.**

> **Recording only the observed level, without asking what the highest level is, halves the design capacity without anyone noticing** — and the failure appears in the first monsoon after construction.

> **So the groundwater observation must be accompanied by a judgement about the seasonal maximum**, from local wells, from the site's own history, or from a piezometer left in place.

**And the wider principle this illustrates:**

> **The water table controls EFFECTIVE STRESS, and effective stress controls almost everything in soil mechanics.**

| Quantity | Effect of a rising water table |
|---|---|
| **Bearing capacity of sand** | **HALVED** ← |
| **Slope stability** | **Factor of safety can be halved** |
| **Settlement** | Reduced (less effective stress increase) |
| **Uplift on a basement or empty tank** | **INCREASED — a flotation risk** |
| Liquefaction potential | **Increased — saturation is a precondition** |

> **Every row is a design case in its own right, and every one turns on the same variable** — which is why the groundwater level is the single most consequential number in a site investigation report.

examTip.trick: **For sand, c = 0, so both surviving terms contain γ** — and γ′ ≈ 0.5γ, so the 0.5 factors out of the whole bracket. Capacity halved.
examTip.trap: **In CLAY the effect is negligible**, because the undrained term c_u N_c contains no γ at all. So the question's answer depends entirely on the soil being SAND.
examTip.mnemonic: **Design for the HIGHEST credible water table, not the level found on the day.** A dry-season borehole in Nepal can understate the monsoon level by metres — and that silently halves the design capacity.

questions.stem: The solid content of sewage is usually:
questions.solution:
**0.1 per cent.**

**The composition of domestic sewage:**

> **Sewage is about 99.9 PER CENT WATER and 0.1 PER CENT SOLIDS** — the solids being partly organic and partly inorganic.

> **The source states it exactly: it contains 99.9 % water and 0.1 % solids, partly organic and partly inorganic.**

> **In concentration terms, 0.1 per cent is about 1000 mg/l of total solids**, which is the figure a laboratory would report.

**Why so dilute — and why that is the central fact about sewage treatment:**

> **A person produces perhaps 100 to 150 grams of dry solid waste a day and uses 100 to 200 litres of water to carry it away.**

> **So the carriage water outweighs the waste by a factor of about a thousand.**

> **The consequence is the defining feature of the whole subject: SEWAGE TREATMENT IS ALMOST ENTIRELY THE TREATMENT OF WATER.**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **The plant's SIZE is set by the water volume, not the pollutant mass** | **Every tank, channel and pump handles 1000 times more water than waste** ← |
| **The energy cost is dominated by moving and aerating water** | Aeration blowers are the largest consumer |
| **Concentrating the solids is the first objective** | Sedimentation, thickening |
| **A small reduction in water use has a large effect** | Less to pump and treat |

> **And it explains why SEPARATE sewerage systems are preferred: adding stormwater to sewage dilutes it further and multiplies the volume to be handled, without adding any treatable load.**

**The breakdown of the solids, since 0.1 per cent is subdivided:**

| Fraction | Proportion of total solids |
|---|---|
| **Total solids** | **100 % (~1000 mg/l)** |
| **SUSPENDED solids** | **~30 % (~300 mg/l)** |
| **DISSOLVED solids** | **~70 % (~700 mg/l)** |
| **Of the suspended: SETTLEABLE** | **~60 % — removed by primary sedimentation** |
| **VOLATILE (organic) fraction of total solids** | **~50-70 %** |

> **The SETTLEABLE fraction is what primary sedimentation removes, and it explains the plant's typical performance: primary treatment removes about 60-70 per cent of suspended solids and only 30-40 per cent of BOD.**

> **The reason for that difference is that much of the BOD is DISSOLVED, and dissolved matter does not settle whatever the tank's size.**

> **Which is precisely why SECONDARY (biological) treatment is necessary: bacteria can consume dissolved organic matter, and sedimentation cannot remove it.**

**The characteristic strengths of sewage, since the solids figure sits among them:**

| Parameter | Weak | Medium | Strong |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Total solids (mg/l)** | **350** | **720** | **1200** |
| **Suspended solids** | **100** | **220** | **350** |
| **BOD₅** | **110** | **220** | **400** |
| **COD** | **250** | **500** | **1000** |
| **Total nitrogen** | **20** | **40** | **85** |
| Total phosphorus | 4 | 8 | 15 |

> **The BOD figure of about 200-250 mg/l for medium-strength domestic sewage is the anchor to remember**, and the per-capita load of about 45-55 grams of BOD per person per day with it.

> **And note the BOD:COD ratio: roughly 0.5 for domestic sewage.**

> **That ratio is diagnostic of BIODEGRADABILITY: a ratio near 0.5 or above means the waste is readily biodegradable and suits biological treatment.**

> **A much lower ratio — say 0.2 — signals INDUSTRIAL waste containing material bacteria cannot digest**, and it warns that biological treatment alone will not work. **So the two tests together tell you something neither tells alone.**

**Why the dilution has a further consequence worth knowing:**

> **Because sewage is so dilute, it is easily made MORE dilute — and infiltration does exactly that.**

| Source of additional flow | Effect |
|---|---|
| **INFILTRATION of groundwater through joints and cracks** | **Increases the volume without adding load — the plant treats clean water** ← |
| **Illegal stormwater connections** | Sudden large dilution and hydraulic overload |
| **Industrial cooling water** | Volume without load |

> **Infiltration is the quiet cost of an old sewerage system: it can EXCEED the sanitary flow itself in a system below the water table**, and every litre of it is pumped, treated and discharged at full cost for no benefit.

> **Which makes sewer rehabilitation — relining, joint sealing — a treatment-capacity project as much as a maintenance one**, in the same way that leak detection is a supply-capacity project on the water side.

> **That symmetry is worth noticing: on the supply side we lose treated water we paid to make; on the sewerage side we treat clean water we never wanted.** Both are failures of pipe integrity, and both are cheaper to fix than to build around.

examTip.trick: **99.9 % water, 0.1 % solids** — about 1000 mg/l of total solids. The carriage water outweighs the waste by roughly a thousand to one.
examTip.trap: **Sewage treatment is therefore almost entirely the treatment of WATER** — every tank and pump handles a thousand times more water than waste, which is why plant size follows volume rather than pollutant mass.
examTip.mnemonic: **Primary sedimentation removes ~65 % of SS but only ~35 % of BOD**, because much of the BOD is DISSOLVED — which is exactly why biological secondary treatment is needed. And **BOD:COD ≈ 0.5** signals a biodegradable waste.

questions.stem: What is the moment of inertia of a rectangular section about a horizontal axis through the centroid?
questions.solution:
**bd³/12.**

**The two values for a rectangle, which the first two options set against each other:**

| Axis | Moment of inertia |
|---|---|
| **Through the CENTROID, parallel to b** | **bd³/12** ← |
| **Along the BASE** | **bd³/3** |

> **The source gives both: about the C.G., I = bd³/12; about the base, I = bd³/3.**

> **So option (b) is not wrong — it is the value about a DIFFERENT axis**, and the stem's phrase "through the centroid" is the whole discrimination.

**Where the base value comes from — the parallel axis theorem:**

> **I_base = I_centroid + A d²**, with d the distance between the axes.

> **= bd³/12 + (bd)(d/2)²**

> **= bd³/12 + bd³/4**

> **= bd³/12 + 3bd³/12 = 4bd³/12 = bd³/3** ✓

> **So shifting the axis from the centroid to the base multiplies I by FOUR.**

> **That factor of four is worth noticing, because it shows how strongly I depends on the axis position — and it is why locating the centroid is the first step in any compound-section calculation.**

> **It also gives a free check on any I: since A d² is never negative, I IS ALWAYS LEAST ABOUT THE CENTROIDAL AXIS.** A computed value smaller than the centroidal one is an arithmetic error.

**Why the other two options are wrong — and each is a real formula:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **bd³/12** | ✓ **Rectangle about its centroid** |
| **bd³/3** | **Rectangle about its BASE** ← |
| **bd³/36** | **TRIANGLE about its centroidal axis (bh³/36)** ← |
| **bd²/6** | **The SECTION MODULUS of a rectangle, Z — not a moment of inertia at all** ← |

> **Option (d) is the most instructive distractor, and it fails on DIMENSIONS:**

> **A moment of inertia has dimensions of LENGTH⁴; a section modulus has LENGTH³.**

> **bd²/6 is length³, so it cannot be an I** — and that check costs no time at all.

> **The relation between them confirms it: Z = I/y_max = (bd³/12)/(d/2) = bd²/6.** ✓ **So option (d) is the answer to the neighbouring question.**

**The section properties worth having memorised:**

| Section | I about the centroid | y_max | Z |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RECTANGLE b × d** | **bd³/12** | **d/2** | **bd²/6** |
| **Rectangle about its base** | **bd³/3** | — | — |
| **CIRCLE, diameter d** | **πd⁴/64** | **d/2** | **πd³/32** |
| **Hollow circle, D and d** | **π(D⁴−d⁴)/64** | D/2 | π(D⁴−d⁴)/32D |
| **TRIANGLE, base b, height h** | **bh³/36** | **2h/3** | **bh²/24** |
| **Semicircle about its diameter** | **πd⁴/128** | — | — |

> **The TRIANGLE is the one to be careful with: its centroid is h/3 from the base, so y_max is the LARGER distance 2h/3** — giving Z = bh²/24 rather than bh²/12.

> **And that is why option (c) bd³/36 is a well-made distractor: /36 is unmistakably a triangle's denominator, and a candidate who remembers "12, 3, 36" without attaching each to its shape and axis will guess.**

**The rule that generates the rectangle's formula, so it need not be memorised:**

> **I = (dimension PARALLEL to the axis) × (dimension PERPENDICULAR to the axis)³ / 12**

> **The CUBED dimension is always the one measured PERPENDICULAR to the axis of bending**, because a fibre's contribution goes as the square of its distance, integrated over the area.

> **So for a horizontal axis, the DEPTH d is cubed: bd³/12.** And about the perpendicular centroidal axis it is **db³/12** — the same formula with b and d exchanged.

**Why the CUBE matters more than anything else in beam design:**

| Change | Effect on I |
|---|---|
| **Double the WIDTH** | **I × 2** |
| **Double the DEPTH** | **I × 8** |
| **Increase the depth by 26 % (one standard size)** | **I × 2** |

> **Depth is EIGHT TIMES more effective than width**, per unit of extra material in that direction.

> **Which is why beams are deep and narrow rather than wide and shallow, why an I-section pushes its flanges as far apart as it can, and why the practical limit on beam depth is architectural (headroom) rather than structural.**

> **And the corollary for strength: Z = bd²/6 goes as the SQUARE of the depth**, so doubling the depth quadruples the moment capacity while only doubling the material.

> **Stiffness gains by d³ and strength by d² — both favour depth, and stiffness favours it more.** Which is why a deflection problem is almost always solved by adding depth rather than by adding material anywhere else.

examTip.trick: **bd³/12 about the centroid; bd³/3 about the BASE** — a factor of four, from the parallel axis theorem A(d/2)². The stem's "through the centroid" is the discrimination.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) bd²/6 is the SECTION MODULUS, dimension length³, not length⁴** — a free dimensional check. And /36 in option (c) is unmistakably a TRIANGLE's denominator.
examTip.mnemonic: **The CUBED dimension is the one PERPENDICULAR to the axis.** Double the width, I × 2; double the DEPTH, I × 8. And **I is always LEAST about the centroidal axis**, since Ad² is never negative — a free check.

questions.stem: A plane truss consists of an apex joint connected by three members — two inclined members running down to the two outer base joints and one vertical member running down to a middle base joint. All three base joints are PINNED supports. The degree of static indeterminacy of the structure is:
questions.solution:
**1.**

**Counting the members, joints and reactions:**

| Quantity | Count |
|---|---|
| **MEMBERS, m** | **3 — two inclined and one vertical** |
| **JOINTS, j** | **4 — the apex plus the three base joints** |
| **REACTIONS, r** | **6 — three PINNED supports, each providing 2** |

> **The source's own working gives exactly these: m = 3, r = 2 + 2 + 2 = 6, j = 4.**

**Applying the plane-truss criterion:**

> **D_s = m + r − 2j**

> **= 3 + 6 − 2(4)**

> **= 9 − 8 = 1** ✓

> **So the truss is INDETERMINATE TO THE FIRST DEGREE.**

**Why the criterion takes that form — counting unknowns against equations:**

| Side | Count |
|---|---|
| **UNKNOWNS** | **m member forces + r reaction components = 3 + 6 = 9** |
| **EQUATIONS** | **2 per joint (ΣH = 0 and ΣV = 0 at each pin) = 2 × 4 = 8** |
| **EXCESS unknowns** | **9 − 8 = 1 → indeterminate to the FIRST degree** |

> **So the degree of indeterminacy is simply the number of unknowns that equilibrium cannot determine** — and it is the number of additional compatibility conditions needed to solve the structure.

**Where the indeterminacy comes from in this particular truss — worth seeing physically:**

> **The excess lies in the SUPPORTS.**

> **Split the indeterminacy into its two parts:**

| Part | Expression | Value here |
|---|---|---|
| **EXTERNAL, D_se** | **r − 3** | **6 − 3 = 3** |
| **INTERNAL, D_si** | **m − (2j − 3)** | **3 − (8 − 3) = 3 − 5 = −2** |
| **TOTAL** | **D_se + D_si** | **3 + (−2) = 1** ✓ |

> **The total is right, and the split is revealing: the structure is EXTERNALLY over-supported (three pinned supports give six reactions where three would suffice) and INTERNALLY deficient in members.**

> **A negative internal indeterminacy means the member arrangement alone would be a MECHANISM — three members and four joints cannot form a rigid truss by themselves.**

> **What holds the structure together is the SUPPORTS, not the triangulation** — which is why it is more accurately described as three separate members each pinned at both ends than as a truss in the usual sense.

> **That is a genuine and instructive feature of this particular arrangement, and it is worth noticing that the counting criterion gives the right total even though neither part is positive.**

**Why the counting criterion is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT:**

> **A structure can satisfy the count and still be unstable, if the members are badly arranged.**

| Defect | Example |
|---|---|
| **One panel left unbraced while another is over-braced** | **The count balances but one panel is a mechanism and the other redundant** |
| **Three COLLINEAR support reactions** | **Cannot resist a force along that line — externally unstable whatever the count** |
| **Three PARALLEL reactions** | Cannot resist a force perpendicular to them |
| A joint with two collinear members and a load | Local mechanism |

> **So the count identifies the ARITHMETIC of stability, and the ARRANGEMENT must then be checked by inspection.**

> **The classic demonstration is a truss with one square panel left undiagonalised and another given two diagonals: m + r = 2j exactly, and the structure folds up.**

> **Which is why option (a) 0 could never be ruled out by counting alone in a general case, and why a well-set question either supplies a figure or describes the arrangement — as this one now does.**

**The classification, for completeness:**

| Condition | Classification |
|---|---|
| **m + r < 2j** | **UNSTABLE — a mechanism; fewer unknowns than equations** |
| **m + r = 2j** | **JUST DETERMINATE (if properly arranged)** |
| **m + r > 2j** | **INDETERMINATE, to degree (m + r − 2j)** ← |

> **And the corresponding criterion for a plane FRAME (rigid joints rather than pins) is different and worth keeping apart:**

> **D_s = 3m + r − 3j** for a rigid-jointed plane frame, because each member carries three internal forces (axial, shear, moment) and each rigid joint supplies three equations.

> **Using the truss formula on a frame, or the reverse, is a standard error** — and the tell is whether the joints are PINNED (truss, 2 equations each) or RIGID (frame, 3 equations each).

**And how an indeterminate truss is actually solved, since the count is only the first step:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **Method of consistent deformation (flexibility)** | **Release the redundant, compute the displacement, restore compatibility** |
| **Castigliano's theorem** | **∂U/∂R = 0 for a redundant force whose displacement is zero** |
| **Unit load method** | The practical hand technique |
| **Stiffness (matrix) method** | What software uses |

> **The flexibility approach is the natural one for a first-degree indeterminate structure: release the one redundant, analyse the resulting determinate truss, and impose the condition that the released displacement is actually zero.**

> **One redundant means ONE compatibility equation** — which is why the degree of indeterminacy is precisely the amount of extra work required, and therefore worth computing before beginning.

verification.notes: Figure-dependent question rewritten in text. The source stem read only "Degree of static indeterminacy of the given structure" and referred to a figure. The figure appears both in the question page and again in the source's own answer, showing an apex joint with two inclined members to the outer base joints and one vertical member to a middle base joint, all three base supports pinned; the source's working (m = 3, r = 2+2+2 = 6, j = 4, DSI = 3 + 6 - 8 = 1) confirms both the geometry and the keyed answer (b). The stem now describes that arrangement in words. Options and answer are unchanged.

examTip.trick: **D_s = m + r − 2j = 3 + 6 − 8 = 1.** Unknowns are member forces plus reactions; equations are two per pinned joint. Three pinned supports give SIX reactions, not three.
examTip.trap: **Counting is NECESSARY but not SUFFICIENT.** A truss with one unbraced panel and another double-braced satisfies m + r = 2j exactly and still folds up. Three collinear or parallel reactions are unstable whatever the count.
examTip.mnemonic: **Keep the two criteria apart: TRUSS (pinned joints) is m + r − 2j; rigid-jointed FRAME is 3m + r − 3j.** The tell is whether joints supply two equations or three.

questions.stem: Flow in a channel is called laminar flow if the Reynolds number is:
questions.solution:
**Re < 500.**

**The transition values for OPEN CHANNEL flow:**

| Reynolds number | Regime |
|---|---|
| **Re < 500** | **LAMINAR** ← |
| **500 < Re < 2000** | **TRANSITIONAL** |
| **Re > 2000** | **TURBULENT** |

> **The source states all three: below 500 laminar, above 2000 turbulent, and between them transitional.**

> **So options (b) and (c) are the OTHER TWO REGIMES from the same table** — which makes this a matching question, and the whole set must be known.

> **Option (d) "all of the above" is self-contradictory: the three ranges are mutually exclusive by construction, so a flow cannot be laminar in all of them.**

**The crucial contrast with PIPE flow — and this is what the question is really testing:**

| | **OPEN CHANNEL** | **PIPE** |
|---|---|---|
| **Laminar** | **Re < 500** | **Re < 2000** |
| **Transitional** | **500-2000** | **2000-4000** |
| **Turbulent** | **Re > 2000** | **Re > 4000** |
| **Characteristic length in Re** | **HYDRAULIC RADIUS R** | **DIAMETER D** |

> **The numbers differ by a factor of about four, and the reason is the LENGTH SCALE used in the Reynolds number.**

> **For a pipe:  Re = VD/ν**

> **For an open channel:  Re = VR/ν**, with R the hydraulic radius.

> **And for a full circular pipe, R = A/P = (πD²/4)/(πD) = D/4.**

> **So the channel Reynolds number is one QUARTER of the pipe Reynolds number for the same flow** — which is exactly why the transition values are a quarter as large.

> **The physics has not changed; only the yardstick has.** Recognising that makes the two sets of numbers one fact rather than two, and it is the reliable way to avoid quoting the pipe values for a channel.

> **A candidate who answers 2000 for a channel has quoted the PIPE laminar limit, and option (b) is placed to catch exactly that.**

**What the Reynolds number means:**

> **Re = (INERTIAL forces) / (VISCOUS forces) = VL/ν**

| Regime | Which dominates |
|---|---|
| **LAMINAR (low Re)** | **VISCOUS forces dominate — the flow moves in orderly layers and damps out disturbances** |
| **TURBULENT (high Re)** | **INERTIAL forces dominate — disturbances grow into eddies** |

> **So the transition is the point at which viscosity can no longer suppress a disturbance**, and the Reynolds number measures which side of that balance the flow is on.

> **Note that ν (KINEMATIC viscosity) appears, not μ** — because the ratio of inertia to viscosity naturally produces μ/ρ. **That is why kinematic viscosity is the one tabulated for such calculations, and why ν = 10⁻⁶ m²/s for water is the number to have automatically.**

**Why laminar open-channel flow is almost never encountered in practice:**

> **Consider a modest channel: R = 0.5 m and V = 0.5 m/s.**

> **Re = 0.5 × 0.5 / 10⁻⁶ = 250,000** — over five hundred times the turbulent threshold.

> **To get Re below 500 with water would require an extraordinarily thin or slow flow:** at R = 0.001 m (a 1 mm film), V would still need to be below 0.5 m/s.

| Situation | Regime |
|---|---|
| **Any canal, river or sewer** | **TURBULENT, overwhelmingly** |
| **Sheet flow over a pavement or roof** | **Can be laminar or transitional — a very thin film** ← |
| **Overland flow at the start of runoff** | Laminar initially |
| Flow of a viscous liquid or in a laboratory flume | Can be laminar |

> **So the laminar range matters for OVERLAND SHEET FLOW — the first metres of runoff on a paved surface — and essentially nowhere else in open-channel hydraulics.**

> **Which is worth knowing, because it means every practical channel calculation assumes turbulent flow**, and that assumption is what justifies using Manning's equation at all.

**Why that matters for Manning's equation specifically:**

> **Manning's n is a constant for a given surface ONLY IN FULLY TURBULENT FLOW.**

> **In laminar or transitional flow the resistance depends on the Reynolds number, and a fixed n is meaningless.**

> **So Manning's equation is a TURBULENT-FLOW formula, and its universal use in channel design rests on the observation above — that real channels are always turbulent.**

> **The same is true of Chezy's C, and it is why both are described as empirical: they were fitted to turbulent field data and carry that regime as an unstated assumption.**

**And the other dimensionless number that governs open channels, since the two are often confused:**

| Number | Form | Compares | Governs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **REYNOLDS** | **Re = VR/ν** | **Inertia to VISCOSITY** | **Laminar / turbulent** |
| **FROUDE** | **Fr = V/√(gy)** | **Inertia to GRAVITY** | **Subcritical / supercritical** ← |

> **The FROUDE number is far more important in open-channel flow than the Reynolds number**, precisely because the flow is always turbulent and so Re rarely decides anything.

> **Fr < 1 subcritical, Fr = 1 critical, Fr > 1 supercritical** — and that distinction governs the flow profile, the direction of control, and whether a hydraulic jump forms.

> **So a candidate should know the Reynolds thresholds and understand that in practice the Froude number is the number that matters.** That is the honest hierarchy of the subject.

examTip.trick: **Channel: laminar Re < 500, turbulent Re > 2000. Pipe: laminar Re < 2000, turbulent Re > 4000.** The factor of four comes from the LENGTH SCALE — for a full pipe R = D/4, so Re_channel = Re_pipe/4.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) Re > 2000 is the PIPE laminar limit**, placed to catch anyone quoting pipe values for a channel. Options (b) and (c) are the other two regimes from the same table.
examTip.mnemonic: **Real channels are ALWAYS turbulent** — a modest canal gives Re ≈ 250,000. Laminar open-channel flow matters only for thin SHEET FLOW on pavements. Which is why Manning's n is valid at all, and why the **FROUDE** number is the one that actually decides things.

questions.stem: In influence line diagrams (ILD):
options: Points remain fixed, position of load changes
Points change, position of loads remain fixed
questions.solution:
**The point remains FIXED and the position of the load CHANGES.**

**The definition, and the distinction it rests on:**

> **An INFLUENCE LINE shows how a quantity AT ONE FIXED POINT varies as a UNIT LOAD MOVES across the structure.**

> **So the SECTION is fixed and the LOAD travels.**

> **The source states it exactly: influence line diagrams show how a specific function at a point varies with the position of a unit load moving across the structure — the points on the structure remain fixed while the position of the unit load changes.**

**The contrast with an ordinary SF or BM diagram, which is the whole point:**

| | **SHEAR FORCE / BENDING MOMENT diagram** | **INFLUENCE LINE diagram** |
|---|---|---|
| **The LOAD** | **FIXED in position** | **MOVES across the span** |
| **The SECTION** | **VARIES along the span** | **FIXED at one point** |
| **The ordinate represents** | **The quantity AT THAT SECTION, for the given load** | **The quantity AT THE FIXED POINT, for a unit load AT THAT POSITION** |
| **Answers the question** | **"What is the moment everywhere, for this load?"** | **"What is the moment HERE, for a load anywhere?"** ← |

> **The two diagrams look similar and mean opposite things, and that is why the distinction is worth stating carefully.**

> **On a BM diagram, the horizontal axis is the SECTION LOCATION.**

> **On an influence line, the horizontal axis is the LOAD LOCATION.**

> **Reading an influence line as though it were a moment diagram is the standard error in this topic, and it produces answers that are wrong by more than a sign.**

**Why influence lines exist — the problem they solve:**

> **A bridge is not loaded by a fixed set of forces. It is loaded by whatever crosses it, in whatever position does the most harm.**

> **So the designer must find the WORST POSITION of a moving load system — and an ordinary BM diagram, drawn for one load position, cannot answer that.**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **Position a moving load for MAXIMUM effect** | **The reason they exist — bridges, cranes, gantries, trains** ← |
| **Compute the effect of a set of loads** | **Multiply each load by the ordinate UNDER IT and add** |
| **Compute the effect of a udl over part of the span** | **Intensity × AREA of the influence line under the loaded length** |
| Identify which spans to load in a continuous beam | Load where the ordinate has the sign you want |

> **The udl rule is the most useful single result: effect = intensity × area under the influence line.**

> **And it gives the standard bridge-loading conclusion immediately: to MAXIMISE a quantity, load exactly the length over which the influence line has the sign you want, and no more.**

> **Which is why a continuous beam is loaded in ALTERNATE spans — a chequerboard pattern — for maximum sagging moment: the influence line changes sign from span to span, so loading every span would let the negative parts cancel the positive.**

**MÜLLER-BRESLAU'S PRINCIPLE, which is how influence lines are drawn:**

> **The influence line for a force quantity is the DEFLECTED SHAPE the structure takes when the corresponding RESTRAINT IS RELEASED and a UNIT DISPLACEMENT is applied in the direction of that force.**

| Quantity wanted | Release and impose |
|---|---|
| **REACTION at a support** | **Remove the support; lift it by unity** |
| **SHEAR at a section** | **Cut the section; impose a unit RELATIVE VERTICAL displacement, faces kept PARALLEL** |
| **BENDING MOMENT at a section** | **Insert a hinge; impose a unit RELATIVE ROTATION** |

> **The principle turns a load-position problem into a geometry problem**, which is why it is so powerful — and why influence lines for determinate structures are always made of STRAIGHT LINES.

> **Curved influence lines appear only for INDETERMINATE structures, where the released deflected shape is itself a bending curve.**

**The standard influence lines worth knowing:**

| Structure and quantity | Influence line |
|---|---|
| **SSB, reaction at A** | **Triangle: 1 at A, 0 at B** |
| **SSB, shear at section C** | **Two triangles of OPPOSITE sign, with a UNIT JUMP at C** |
| **SSB, moment at C (distances a, b)** | **Triangle, peak ab/L at C** |
| **CANTILEVER, shear at the fixed end** | **RECTANGLE of height 1** |
| **Cantilever, moment at the fixed end** | **Triangle, peak L at the support** |

> **The unit JUMP in the shear influence line is its characteristic feature**, and it is why a shear influence line for a simply supported beam is never a single triangle.

**Why options (b), (c) and (d) are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Points fixed, load moves** | ✓ |
| **Points change, load fixed** | **That describes an ordinary SF or BM DIAGRAM** ← the substantive trap |
| **Both change** | Would describe no coherent diagram |
| **Neither changes** | Would give a single number, not a diagram |

> **Option (b) is the designed trap because it is a correct description of the OTHER diagram**, and the two are studied together.

> **Options (c) and (d) can be dismissed on structure: a DIAGRAM requires exactly one variable to plot against.** If both change there are two variables and no single curve; if neither changes there is nothing to plot.

> **Recognising that a diagram needs one and only one independent variable disposes of half the options with no knowledge of influence lines at all.**

examTip.trick: **On a BM diagram the horizontal axis is the SECTION location; on an influence line it is the LOAD location.** The section is fixed and the load travels.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) correctly describes an ordinary SF/BM DIAGRAM** — the two are studied together and look similar while meaning opposite things. And (c)/(d) fail structurally: a diagram needs exactly ONE independent variable.
examTip.mnemonic: **Effect of a udl = intensity × AREA under the influence line** — so load exactly the length where the sign helps and no more. Which is why a continuous beam is loaded in ALTERNATE spans for maximum sagging moment.

questions.stem: What percentage of activated sludge is recycled?
questions.solution:
**20 to 30 per cent.**

**What is being recycled and why:**

> **In the activated sludge process, the sludge settled in the secondary clarifier is PUMPED BACK to the head of the aeration tank.**

> **That flow is the RETURN ACTIVATED SLUDGE (RAS), and it is expressed as a percentage of the incoming sewage flow — typically 20 to 30 per cent.**

> **The source keys 20-30 per cent.**

**Why the return is essential — not an optimisation but a necessity:**

> **The process works by maintaining a large population of aerobic bacteria in the aeration tank — the MIXED LIQUOR SUSPENDED SOLIDS, typically 1500 to 3000 mg/l.**

> **But the incoming sewage carries almost no bacteria, and the aeration tank's contents flow continuously out to the clarifier.**

> **Without the return, the biomass would simply WASH OUT with the effluent within a few hours, and the tank would be left with nothing but sewage and air.**

> **So the return is what SEEDS the incoming sewage and holds the biomass in the system.**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Return sludge pumps fail** | **IMMEDIATE and TOTAL process failure — not a gradual decline** ← |
| **Return rate too low** | MLSS falls; treatment deteriorates; the clarifier's sludge blanket rises |
| **Return rate too high** | Wastes pumping energy; hydraulically overloads the clarifier |

> **That the failure is immediate rather than gradual is worth stating: an operator who stops the RAS pumps has stopped the treatment plant, even though the aeration blowers are still running and the tank still looks correct.**

**The distinction between RETURN and WASTE sludge, which is the pair to keep straight:**

| | **RETURN activated sludge (RAS)** | **WASTE activated sludge (WAS)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Where it goes** | **BACK to the aeration tank** | **OUT to sludge treatment** |
| **Purpose** | **Maintain the MLSS — hold the biomass in the system** | **Remove the EXCESS biomass the bacteria have grown** |
| **Quantity** | **20-30 % of the sewage flow (sometimes up to 100 %)** | **A small fraction — typically 1-2 % of the sewage flow** |
| **Controls** | **The MLSS concentration** | **The SLUDGE AGE (and hence the F/M ratio)** ← |

> **The WASTE rate is the process's principal control handle**, and that is the substantive point:

> **Bacteria GROW by consuming the sewage's organic matter, so the biomass increases continuously.**

> **If none were wasted, the MLSS would rise without limit until the clarifier could no longer settle it.**

> **So wasting is how the operator sets the SLUDGE AGE — the average time a bacterium stays in the system:**

> **SLUDGE AGE (SRT) = (mass of MLSS in the aeration tank) ÷ (mass of solids wasted per day)**

| Waste more sludge | Waste less sludge |
|---|---|
| **Sludge age FALLS** | **Sludge age RISES** |
| **F/M ratio RISES** | F/M ratio falls |
| **Younger, faster-growing biomass** | Older, more stable biomass |
| **NITRIFICATION lost below ~8 days** | **Nitrification achieved above ~8-15 days** ← |

> **The nitrification threshold is the one with real consequence: nitrifying bacteria grow SLOWLY, so they can only be retained if the sludge age is long enough.**

> **Waste too aggressively and the nitrifiers wash out — the plant still removes BOD but stops converting ammonia**, and the effluent's ammonia consent is breached without any visible change in the plant.

> **So a single operational lever, the wasting rate, decides whether the plant nitrifies.** That is why sludge age is the parameter an operator actually controls to.

**The full set of operating parameters, for context:**

| Parameter | Typical (conventional) |
|---|---|
| **MLSS** | **1500-3000 mg/l** |
| **F/M ratio** | **0.2-0.5 per day** |
| **Sludge age (SRT)** | **5-15 days** |
| **RETURN sludge ratio** | **0.25-0.5 (i.e. 25-50 %); commonly quoted 20-30 %** ← |
| **Aeration period** | **4-8 hours** |
| **SVI** | **Below 150 ml/g** |
| Activated sludge water content | **97 %** |

> **And the process variants are defined by where they sit on the F/M scale:**

| Variant | F/M | Sludge age | Character |
|---|---|---|---|
| **HIGH-RATE** | **High (1.5-3)** | **Short (0.5-2 days)** | **Small tank, more sludge, no nitrification, less stable** |
| **CONVENTIONAL** | **0.2-0.5** | **5-15 days** | The standard |
| **EXTENDED AERATION** | **Low (0.05-0.15)** | **Long (20-30 days)** | **Big tank, little sludge, tolerant, nitrifies; suits small works** |

> **EXTENDED AERATION is the variant most used for small Nepali and Indian plants**, and the reason is operational rather than technical: **a long sludge age makes the process tolerant of shock loads, produces little sludge to dispose of, and forgives inconsistent operation.**

> **Its cost is a much larger aeration tank and more air per unit of BOD removed** — which is a fair trade where land is cheaper than skilled operators.

examTip.trick: **20-30 % of the sewage flow is RETURNED to the aeration tank**, to hold the biomass in the system. Without it the bacteria wash out with the effluent within hours.
examTip.trap: **Keep RETURN and WASTE sludge apart.** RAS (20-30 %) maintains the MLSS; WAS (1-2 %) removes the excess growth and is what sets the SLUDGE AGE.
examTip.mnemonic: **Wasting rate is the operator's real control handle** — and below a sludge age of ~8 days the slow-growing NITRIFIERS wash out. The plant still removes BOD and silently stops converting ammonia.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not included in the three R's?
questions.solution:
**Recover.**

**The three R's:**

> **REDUCE — REUSE — RECYCLE.**

> **"Recover" is not one of them.**

> **The source defines the three: REDUCE (reducing the amount of waste produced), REUSE (using things again instead of throwing them away) and RECYCLE (recycling items to make new products out of them).**

**What each one means, and why the ORDER is the substance of the concept:**

| R | Meaning | Position |
|---|---|---|
| **REDUCE** | **Do not generate the waste in the first place** | **FIRST — and by far the most effective** |
| **REUSE** | **Use the item AGAIN in its existing form, without reprocessing** | **SECOND** |
| **RECYCLE** | **Break the item down and REPROCESS the material into something new** | **THIRD** |

> **The three are a HIERARCHY, not a list — they are deliberately in descending order of preference.**

> **REDUCE is best because waste that is never created needs no collection, no transport, no processing and no disposal.** It also avoids the resources and energy used in making the item.

> **REUSE comes next because the item keeps its form and function, so almost no energy is spent.**

> **RECYCLE is last of the three because it requires COLLECTION, SORTING, TRANSPORT and REPROCESSING** — all of which consume energy and produce their own emissions.

> **That ordering is the point of the concept, and it is why "recycling" being the most publicly visible of the three is slightly unfortunate: it is the LEAST preferred of them.**

**Why "RECOVER" is a well-made distractor — because it is a real term:**

> **RECOVERY is a genuine stage of the waste management hierarchy — it simply is not one of the three R's.**

> **The FULL hierarchy, of which the three R's are the top:**

| Rank | Stage | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **PREVENT / REDUCE** | **Best — the waste never exists** |
| **2** | **REUSE** | Same item, used again |
| **3** | **RECYCLE** | Material reprocessed |
| **4** | **RECOVER** | **ENERGY recovery — incineration with heat or power generation; composting; biogas** ← |
| **5** | **DISPOSE** | **Landfill — the LAST resort** |

> **So "recover" sits IMMEDIATELY BELOW the three R's, which is exactly why it feels as though it belongs to them.**

> **It is often written as a fourth R, giving "the four R's" — and some formulations add REFUSE, REPAIR or REPURPOSE, producing five or more.**

> **But the classical and universally quoted set is THREE: reduce, reuse, recycle** — and the question asks about that set.

> **Option (d) "Reduced" is the same word as "Reduce" in a different grammatical form, so it IS one of the three despite the awkward wording** — and a candidate reading quickly might reject it for the tense rather than the meaning.

**Why recovery is ranked below recycling — the reasoning is worth knowing:**

> **Energy recovery DESTROYS the material and keeps only its energy content.**

> **Recycling keeps the MATERIAL, which is worth far more than the energy in it: making aluminium from recycled metal uses about 5 per cent of the energy needed to make it from ore.**

> **So burning an aluminium can for its energy content throws away the far larger saving that recycling it would have delivered.**

> **That is the argument for the ordering, and it is a quantitative one rather than a sentiment.**

**Where solid waste management fits in a civil engineer's work:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **Waste GENERATION rate** | **0.2-0.5 kg per person per day in Nepali towns; higher in cities** |
| **COLLECTION and transport** | **Usually 60-80 % of the total cost of the system** ← |
| **Transfer stations** | Where haul distances are long |
| **SANITARY LANDFILL** | **Liner, leachate collection and treatment, gas venting, daily cover, final capping** |
| **Composting** | **Suits the HIGH ORGANIC FRACTION of South Asian waste** |
| Waste-to-energy | Needs a high calorific value — often unsuitable for wet organic waste |

> **The collection cost dominating the system is the fact with the most practical weight: reducing the QUANTITY of waste saves collection cost, which is where most of the money goes.**

> **And the composition point matters for technology choice: South Asian municipal waste is typically 50-70 per cent ORGANIC and WET, with a low calorific value.**

> **So imported waste-to-energy incineration frequently fails here — the waste will not burn without auxiliary fuel — while COMPOSTING and BIOGAS suit it well.**

> **That is a genuine engineering judgement rather than a preference: the right technology follows from the waste's actual composition, not from what works elsewhere.**

> **And it is the same reasoning as source segregation: a mixed wet-and-dry waste stream is hard to treat by any route, while segregated organic waste composts readily and segregated dry recyclables have a market.** Which brings the argument back to the top of the hierarchy — **the cheapest treatment is the waste you never mixed.**

examTip.trick: **REDUCE, REUSE, RECYCLE** — and they are a HIERARCHY in descending order of preference, not a list.
examTip.trap: **"Recover" is a REAL stage of the waste hierarchy — energy recovery — sitting immediately BELOW the three R's**, which is exactly why it feels as though it belongs. And "Reduced" is just "Reduce" in another tense, so it IS one of the three.
examTip.mnemonic: **Recycling keeps the MATERIAL; recovery keeps only its ENERGY** — and recycled aluminium takes ~5 % of the energy of primary metal. That quantitative gap is why recovery ranks below recycling.

questions.stem: The design speed of a rotary in an urban road is:
questions.solution:
**30 km/h.**

**The recommended design speeds for a rotary:**

| Situation | Design speed |
|---|---|
| **URBAN roads** | **30 km/h** ← |
| **RURAL roads** | **40 km/h** |

> **The source states it: IRC recommends a 30 km/h design speed for the design of rotaries.**

> **Note that the RURAL figure of 40 km/h is offered as option (c)** — so the question tests whether the urban/rural distinction is known, not merely the number.

**Why a rotary's design speed is so LOW — the reason is the mechanism:**

> **A ROTARY (roundabout) works by converting CROSSING conflicts into MERGING and DIVERGING ones.**

> **At a conventional crossroads, vehicle paths CROSS at large angles, and a crossing conflict at speed is the most dangerous kind of collision.**

> **At a rotary, every vehicle enters the circulating stream by MERGING at a small angle, travels round, and leaves by DIVERGING.** No path crosses another.

> **But merging safely requires drivers to adjust their speed to the circulating stream and to accept gaps in it — and that is only possible at LOW SPEED.**

> **So the low design speed is not a limitation of the rotary; it is the CONDITION on which it works.** A high-speed rotary would reintroduce the very conflicts it exists to remove.

**How the geometry ENFORCES the speed — this is the design idea worth understanding:**

> **A rotary does not rely on a speed limit sign. Its GEOMETRY makes high speed impossible.**

| Element | How it controls speed |
|---|---|
| **The central ISLAND** | **Forces every vehicle to deflect — a curved path cannot be taken fast** ← |
| **ENTRY radius (smaller than the exit radius)** | **Slows vehicles entering; speeds them leaving** |
| **WEAVING length** | Must be long enough for a merge and a diverge to complete |
| **Deflection angle at entry** | The larger the deflection, the lower the achievable speed |

> **The asymmetry between entry and exit radii is deliberate and instructive: a SMALL entry radius slows the vehicle down, and a LARGER exit radius lets it accelerate away cleanly.**

> **So the geometry is not symmetrical even though the rotary looks it** — and a rotary built with generous entry radii will be driven fast, whatever the signs say.

> **Which is the general principle: SELF-ENFORCING geometry beats regulation.** A design that makes the unsafe behaviour physically awkward does not depend on compliance.

**The rotary design elements, since they follow from the speed:**

| Element | Typical value |
|---|---|
| **Design speed, urban** | **30 km/h** ← |
| **Design speed, rural** | **40 km/h** |
| **Radius of the central island** | **1.33 × the radius of the entry curve** |
| **Entry curve radius, urban** | **15-25 m** |
| **Exit curve radius** | **1.5-2 × the entry radius** |
| **WEAVING angle** | **About 15° or less** |
| **Weaving length, urban** | **18-30 m** |
| **Width of the rotary roadway** | **Wider than the approach — allows weaving** |

> **The weaving length is the element that most often governs the rotary's overall size**, since it must accommodate a merge followed by a diverge within one segment.

**When a rotary is the right choice — and when it is not:**

| Suits a rotary | Does NOT suit a rotary |
|---|---|
| **Intersections of FOUR OR MORE approaches** | **Very HIGH traffic volumes — the rotary saturates and locks up** ← |
| **Roughly EQUAL flows on all approaches** | **One dominant flow — it monopolises the circulating carriageway** |
| **Moderate total volume** | **Heavy PEDESTRIAN movement — crossing a rotary is difficult** |
| **Where a signal is undesirable (no power, no maintenance)** | **Restricted land — a rotary needs a large area** |
| Where turning movements are numerous | Steep approach gradients |

> **The saturation failure is the important limitation and it is abrupt rather than gradual: once the circulating carriageway is full, entering vehicles cannot find gaps, queues build on every approach simultaneously, and the rotary LOCKS.**

> **A signalised junction degrades gracefully under overload; a rotary does not.** Which is why many urban rotaries built decades ago have since been signalised or replaced — the traffic outgrew the form.

> **And the pedestrian objection is a real one in a Nepali urban context: a rotary offers no controlled crossing point**, so pedestrians must find gaps in a continuously circulating stream. **A signalised junction gives them a phase; a rotary gives them nothing.**

> **So the rotary suits a particular window of conditions — moderate, balanced, vehicle-dominated flows with land available — and outside that window it is the wrong form of junction rather than a poorly designed one.**

examTip.trick: **30 km/h urban, 40 km/h rural.** Option (c) 40 is the RURAL figure, so the question tests the distinction rather than the number.
examTip.trap: **The low speed is the CONDITION on which a rotary works, not a limitation** — merging requires drivers to accept gaps, which is only possible slowly. A fast rotary reintroduces the crossing conflicts it exists to remove.
examTip.mnemonic: **The GEOMETRY enforces the speed, not the signs** — the central island forces deflection, and the entry radius is deliberately SMALLER than the exit radius. And a rotary **LOCKS abruptly** at saturation, where a signal degrades gracefully.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an assumption of Terzaghi's theory of one-dimensional consolidation?
options: Darcy's law is valid for the hydraulic gradient
questions.solution:
**Stokes' law is valid — that belongs to a different test altogether.**

**Where Stokes' law actually belongs:**

> **STOKES' LAW gives the terminal settling velocity of a small sphere in a viscous fluid:**

> **v = (γ_s − γ_w) d² / (18 μ)**

> **It is the basis of the HYDROMETER (sedimentation) ANALYSIS — the method for determining the PARTICLE SIZE DISTRIBUTION of the fine fraction of a soil, below 75 microns, where sieving is impossible.**

> **So Stokes' law is about GRADING, not about consolidation.** It concerns how fast individual particles fall through water in a measuring cylinder.

> **Consolidation concerns how fast WATER is squeezed OUT of a soil mass under load.** The two have nothing to do with each other beyond both involving water and soil.

> **That is a clean category discrimination, and it is why option (a) is the answer.**

**The genuine assumptions of Terzaghi's theory, which the source lists in full:**

| Assumption | Note |
|---|---|
| **The soil is HOMOGENEOUS and ISOTROPIC** | ← option (c) |
| **The soil is FULLY SATURATED** | ← option (b) |
| **The solid particles are INCOMPRESSIBLE** | Only the void volume changes |
| **Compression and flow are ONE-DIMENSIONAL (vertical)** | The theory's name |
| **Strains are SMALL** | So the geometry does not change appreciably |
| **DARCY'S LAW is valid at all hydraulic gradients** | ← option (d) |
| **The coefficient of PERMEABILITY and the coefficient of VOLUME COMPRESSIBILITY remain CONSTANT** | Through the whole process |
| **A unique, time-independent relation between VOID RATIO and EFFECTIVE STRESS** | The e-log σ′ curve |

> **So three of the four options are genuine assumptions and one is from another topic entirely** — which makes this a clean elimination rather than a matter of degree.

**Which of the real assumptions are most doubtful, stated honestly:**

> **The theory is remarkably successful for a model resting on assumptions this strong, and it is worth knowing which ones actually fail:**

| Assumption | How it fails in practice |
|---|---|
| **k and m_v constant** | **Both CHANGE as the soil consolidates — permeability falls as the voids close** ← the most significant departure |
| **Fully saturated** | **Partly saturated soil consolidates quite differently; air compresses immediately** |
| **One-dimensional** | **True beneath a WIDE loaded area; false beneath a narrow footing, where drainage is also lateral** |
| **Unique e-σ′ relation, time-independent** | **SECONDARY consolidation (creep) continues after primary consolidation ends, so the relation is NOT time-independent** |
| **Small strains** | Fails for very soft, highly compressible deposits |

> **The k and m_v assumption is the one that matters most: as a clay consolidates, its void ratio falls, and its permeability falls with it.**

> **So consolidation SLOWS as it proceeds, more than the theory predicts** — and the theory's coefficient of consolidation c_v = k/(m_v γ_w) is treated as constant only because both k and m_v fall together and the ratio changes less than either.

> **That partial cancellation is why the theory works as well as it does**, and it is a fair example of a model surviving on a fortunate coincidence rather than on the truth of its assumptions.

> **And the SECONDARY consolidation point is a genuine limitation rather than a refinement: Terzaghi's theory describes PRIMARY consolidation only — the dissipation of excess pore pressure.** Creep continues afterwards, at constant effective stress, and for organic and highly plastic soils it can exceed the primary settlement.

**The theory's central results, since they are what the assumptions buy:**

> **The governing equation:  ∂u/∂t = c_v (∂²u/∂z²)**

> **with the COEFFICIENT OF CONSOLIDATION  c_v = k / (m_v γ_w)**

> **And the solution is expressed through two dimensionless quantities:**

| Quantity | Definition |
|---|---|
| **TIME FACTOR** | **T_v = c_v t / d²** |
| **Degree of consolidation** | **U — the fraction of the ultimate settlement achieved** |

> **The relation between them is tabulated, with two values worth remembering:**

| U | T_v |
|---|---|
| **50 %** | **0.197** |
| **90 %** | **0.848** |

> **The most consequential result follows from the d² in the time factor:**

> **t = T_v d² / c_v** — so **CONSOLIDATION TIME VARIES AS THE SQUARE OF THE DRAINAGE PATH LENGTH.**

| Change | Effect on time |
|---|---|
| **HALVE the drainage path** | **Time falls to a QUARTER** ← |
| **Double the layer thickness (one-way drainage)** | **Time × 4** |
| **Add drainage at both faces (halving d)** | **Time × 1/4** |

> **That square relation is the entire basis of VERTICAL DRAINS (sand drains and prefabricated band drains).**

> **A 10 m thick clay layer draining vertically has d = 5 m if drained both ways. Install band drains at 1.5 m spacing and the water flows HORIZONTALLY to the nearest drain — a path of about 0.75 m.**

> **The path falls by a factor of nearly seven, so the time falls by a factor of about forty.** A settlement that would have taken decades takes months.

> **Which is why preloading with vertical drains is such a powerful ground-improvement technique**, and why the d² term is the most useful single thing to take from the theory.

**And the note on the drainage path itself, since it is easy to get wrong:**

| Drainage condition | d |
|---|---|
| **Drained at BOTH faces (sand above and below)** | **HALF the layer thickness** |
| **Drained at ONE face only (rock or impervious layer beneath)** | **The FULL layer thickness** |

> **Getting that wrong changes the predicted time by a factor of FOUR**, and it depends entirely on what lies beneath the clay — which is precisely the kind of thing a borehole must establish and a shallow investigation may miss.

examTip.trick: **Stokes' law belongs to the HYDROMETER analysis — particle SIZE of the fine fraction — not to consolidation.** A clean category discrimination: grading versus rate of water expulsion.
examTip.trap: **Three of the four options ARE genuine Terzaghi assumptions** (saturated, homogeneous and isotropic, Darcy valid), so the question is an elimination rather than a matter of degree.
examTip.mnemonic: **Time varies as the SQUARE of the drainage path** — halve the path, quarter the time. Which is the whole basis of vertical drains: band drains at 1.5 m spacing cut a 5 m path to 0.75 m and the time by about forty.

questions.stem: Bernoulli's principle is based on the law of conservation of:
questions.solution:
**Energy.**

**What Bernoulli's equation states:**

> **p/γ + V²/2g + z = constant along a streamline**

> **Every term has the dimension of LENGTH, and each is an ENERGY PER UNIT WEIGHT of fluid — which is why they are called HEADS.**

| Term | Name | Energy it represents |
|---|---|---|
| **p/γ** | **PRESSURE head** | Energy per unit weight from pressure |
| **V²/2g** | **VELOCITY (kinetic) head** | Energy per unit weight from motion |
| **z** | **DATUM (potential) head** | Energy per unit weight from elevation |
| **Sum** | **TOTAL head** | **Constant for an ideal fluid** |

> **So the equation says the TOTAL ENERGY of a fluid particle does not change as it moves along a streamline** — energy is merely converted between the three forms.

> **The source confirms it: Bernoulli's principle is based on the law of conservation of energy, equating the total energy (pressure, potential and kinetic) at different points.**

**Why the distractors are wrong — and option (c) is the substantive one:**

| Option | Which principle it actually names |
|---|---|
| **POWER** | **Not a conserved quantity at all — power is a RATE of energy transfer** |
| **VOLUME** | **Conserved only for an INCOMPRESSIBLE fluid, and even then it is the continuity equation, not Bernoulli's** |
| **MASS** | **The CONTINUITY equation — A₁V₁ = A₂V₂, or ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 0** ← the real trap |
| **ENERGY** | ✓ **Bernoulli** |

> **Option (c) MASS is the designed trap, because conservation of mass IS a fundamental fluid-mechanics principle — it is just a different equation.**

> **The pair must be held apart:**

| Principle | Equation | What it says |
|---|---|---|
| **Conservation of MASS** | **CONTINUITY: A₁V₁ = A₂V₂** | **What goes in must come out** |
| **Conservation of ENERGY** | **BERNOULLI: p/γ + V²/2g + z = const** | **Total head is constant** ← |
| **Conservation of MOMENTUM** | **IMPULSE-MOMENTUM: ΣF = ρQ(V₂ − V₁)** | **Force equals rate of change of momentum** |

> **Those three are the whole toolkit of fluid mechanics, and almost every problem is solved by choosing which one to apply.**

> **A venturi meter needs continuity AND Bernoulli together: continuity gives the velocity ratio from the areas, and Bernoulli converts it into a pressure difference.** Neither alone is enough — which is a good illustration that the two are separate principles rather than versions of one.

**When to use MOMENTUM instead of ENERGY — a genuinely important choice:**

> **Bernoulli's equation assumes NO ENERGY LOSS. Where losses are large and UNKNOWN, it cannot be used.**

| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| **Losses small or known** | **ENERGY (Bernoulli, with an h_L term)** |
| **Losses LARGE and UNKNOWN** | **MOMENTUM** ← |

> **The classic case is the HYDRAULIC JUMP: a large, irreversible energy loss occurs in the turbulence of the roller, and its magnitude is not known in advance.**

> **So the jump is analysed by MOMENTUM — which needs only the forces and the flow, not the losses — and the energy loss is then computed as the DIFFERENCE between the upstream and downstream energies.**

> **The same applies to a sudden expansion in a pipe, and to the force on a bend or a nozzle.**

> **Knowing WHICH conservation law to apply is a large part of the subject**, and it is a more useful skill than manipulating any one of them.

**The assumptions Bernoulli's equation rests on, since the question concerns its basis:**

| Assumption | Why needed |
|---|---|
| **STEADY flow** | The derivation integrates along a streamline at one instant |
| **INCOMPRESSIBLE** | ρ must be constant to integrate dp/ρ |
| **NON-VISCOUS (inviscid)** | **Viscosity dissipates energy, so the total head would not be constant** ← |
| **ALONG A STREAMLINE** | Two points on different streamlines need irrotational flow too |
| **No energy added or removed** | No pump or turbine between the sections |

> **Each assumption can be relaxed by adding a term, and the extended form is the one actually used:**

> **p₁/γ + V₁²/2g + z₁ + h_pump = p₂/γ + V₂²/2g + z₂ + h_turbine + h_L**

> **That is the ENERGY EQUATION, and it is Bernoulli with the real-world terms restored** — the friction loss h_L, and any energy added or extracted by machinery.

> **Which makes the point clearly: Bernoulli's equation is the IDEAL case of an energy balance, and every practical application is that balance with the losses written back in.**

**And the role of the discharge coefficient, which quantifies the departure:**

> **A venturi's C_d of 0.97-0.98 says the ideal Bernoulli prediction is 97-98 per cent right for that geometry.**

> **An orifice plate's 0.60-0.65 says it is much further off, because the jet contracts and the losses are large.**

> **So the coefficient is not a fudge factor but a MEASURE OF HOW WELL THE ASSUMPTIONS HOLD** in that particular device — which is why a well-shaped venturi has a coefficient near unity and a sharp-edged orifice does not.

examTip.trick: **Every term in p/γ + V²/2g + z has the dimension of LENGTH and is an energy PER UNIT WEIGHT** — so the equation is an energy balance, and the constant is the total head.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) MASS names the CONTINUITY equation** — a genuine principle, a different equation. A venturi meter needs BOTH: continuity for the velocity ratio, Bernoulli for the pressure difference.
examTip.mnemonic: **Use ENERGY where losses are small or known; use MOMENTUM where they are large and UNKNOWN** — which is why a hydraulic jump is analysed by momentum and its energy loss computed afterwards as a difference.

questions.stem: The relative magnitude of the tractive force and the resistance to motion of a uniform sediment grain is expressed by:
questions.solution:
**τ₀ / [(γs − γw) d] = Cc.**

**What the expression is:**

> **This is the SHIELDS PARAMETER (also called the entrainment function), the dimensionless ratio that compares the flow's tractive force with the grain's resistance to being moved.**

| Term | Represents |
|---|---|
| **τ₀ (numerator)** | **The TRACTIVE FORCE — the bed shear stress the flow exerts on the grain** |
| **(γs − γw) d (denominator)** | **The grain's RESISTANCE — its SUBMERGED weight per unit area** |

> **The source states the form: τ₀/[(γs − γw)d] = Cc, termed the entrainment function, with γs and γw the specific weights of the sediment and water and d the grain diameter.**

**Why the denominator must be a DIFFERENCE — and this is the whole question:**

> **A grain lying on a river bed is SUBMERGED, so it is supported partly by BUOYANCY.**

> **Its effective weight — the weight that must be overcome to lift it — is its own weight MINUS the buoyant upthrust:**

> **Submerged weight ∝ (γs − γw) × volume**

> **So the resistance depends on the DIFFERENCE of the two specific weights, never on their sum.**

> **Option (a), which ADDS them, is therefore physically impossible: it would say that a grain becomes HARDER to move as the water gets denser**, when in fact denser water lifts it more easily.

> **That check needs no recall at all — Archimedes settles it.**

> **And there is a decisive limiting case: for a grain of the SAME density as water (γs = γw), the submerged weight is ZERO and the grain moves under any shear whatever.**

> **Option (b) gives an infinite parameter in that case, which correctly says "moves at any shear". Option (a) gives a finite one, which would say a neutrally buoyant grain still resists motion — plainly wrong.**

**The DIMENSIONAL check, which disposes of the other two:**

> **A dimensionless parameter must have matching units above and below.**

| Quantity | Dimensions |
|---|---|
| **τ₀ (shear stress)** | **F/L²** |
| **(γs − γw) (specific weight)** | **F/L³** |
| **d (diameter)** | **L** |
| **(γs − γw)·d** | **F/L³ × L = F/L²** ✓ |

> **So τ₀/[(γs − γw)d] is (F/L²)/(F/L²) = DIMENSIONLESS.** ✓

| Option | Dimensions | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **(a) τ₀/[(γs+γw)d]** | **Dimensionless** ✓ | **Fails on PHYSICS (sum, not difference)** |
| **(b) τ₀/[(γs−γw)d]** | **Dimensionless** ✓ | **CORRECT** |
| **(c) [τ₀/(γs−γw)] × Cc** | **(F/L²)/(F/L³) = LENGTH — and Cc is on the WRONG SIDE** | **Fails: not an equation for Cc, and not dimensionless** |
| **(d) [2τ₀/(γs−γw)]d = Cc** | **L × L = LENGTH², not dimensionless** | **Fails on dimensions** |

> **Option (c) fails twice: the d is missing from the denominator, and Cc has been moved to the wrong side of the relation** — it is written as a multiplier rather than as the quantity being defined.

> **Option (d) has a spurious factor of 2 and multiplies by d instead of dividing**, giving length squared.

> **So dimensions eliminate (c) and (d), and Archimedes eliminates (a).** Three independent checks, and none requires the formula to be remembered.

**What the parameter is FOR — the threshold of motion:**

> **The Shields parameter is compared against a CRITICAL value to decide whether the bed moves:**

| Condition | Result |
|---|---|
| **θ < θ_critical** | **The bed is STABLE — no motion** |
| **θ = θ_critical** | **INCIPIENT MOTION — the threshold** |
| **θ > θ_critical** | **The bed MOVES — sediment transport begins** |

> **For coarse sediment at high grain Reynolds number, θ_critical ≈ 0.06** — the value most often quoted and used.

> **The SHIELDS DIAGRAM plots θ against the grain Reynolds number R* = u*d/ν, and the curve flattens to 0.06 at high R*.**

> **Note that the diagram is IMPLICIT — τ₀ appears on both axes, through u* = √(τ₀/ρ) — so it must be entered iteratively or through one of the explicit modified forms.** That awkwardness is a known feature of the method.

**Where it is used in design — and the most common use is INVERSE:**

| Application | The question asked |
|---|---|
| **Unlined canal design (tractive force method)** | **Will the bed and banks scour? Keep τ₀ below the critical value** |
| **RIPRAP and stone protection sizing** | **How large must a stone be to stay put? SOLVE for d** ← |
| **Launching apron stone size** | Same |
| **Gravel-bed river stability** | Is the bed mobile at this discharge? |
| Ecological flow studies | Will spawning gravel be disturbed? |

> **The riprap use is the inverse of the threshold question and the commonest in practice: instead of asking whether a given grain moves, you SPECIFY that it must not and solve for the size.**

> **Rearranging with θ_critical ≈ 0.06:  d ≈ τ₀ / [0.06 (γs − γw)]**

> **For stone of relative density 2.65 in water, (γs − γw) ≈ 16,200 N/m³, so:**

> **d ≈ τ₀ / (0.06 × 16,200) ≈ τ₀ / 970**, with τ₀ in N/m² and d in metres.

> **So a bed shear of 100 N/m² needs roughly a 100 mm stone** — a figure worth carrying as a feel for the scale, and a useful check on any pitching or apron specification.

**And the honest limitations, since the parameter is often applied beyond them:**

| Complication | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Bed SLOPE** | **A grain on a slope is easier to move — hence the side-slope correction τ_c√(1 − sin²θ/sin²φ)** |
| **Grain SHAPE and packing** | Angular interlocked grains resist more than rounded loose ones |
| **ARMOURING** | **A mixed bed loses its fines, leaving a coarse protective surface layer** |
| **COHESION** | **Shields does NOT apply to CLAY — cohesive resistance can be an order of magnitude greater** ← |
| Turbulence bursts | Motion begins intermittently, not at a sharp threshold |

> **The cohesion limit must be stated plainly: the parameter is derived for NON-COHESIVE sediment, and applying it to a clay bed gives an answer that is wrong by a large and unpredictable factor.**

> **And ARMOURING is the one with the largest practical consequence: a gravel-bed river degrades until its surface layer is coarse enough to resist the flow, and then stops** — so a Shields calculation using the mean grain size of the whole bed will OVERPREDICT the scour.

examTip.trick: **The denominator is the grain's SUBMERGED weight, so the specific weights must be SUBTRACTED** — Archimedes settles it. A sum would say denser water makes a grain harder to move.
examTip.trap: **Three independent checks eliminate three options with no recall.** Dimensions kill (c) (missing d, Cc on the wrong side) and (d) (length², spurious 2); physics kills (a) (sum instead of difference).
examTip.mnemonic: **θ_critical ≈ 0.06 for coarse sediment**, and the practical use is INVERSE: solve for the stone size. Roughly **d(m) ≈ τ₀/970** — so 100 N/m² of bed shear needs about a 100 mm stone. And Shields does NOT apply to clay.

questions.stem: The tie bars in a concrete pavement are provided across:
questions.solution:
**Longitudinal joints.**

**What a tie bar does:**

> **A TIE BAR is a DEFORMED bar placed across a LONGITUDINAL joint to HOLD THE TWO SLABS TOGETHER — to prevent them separating and to keep the joint tight.**

> **It is NOT a load transfer device.**

> **The source states both points: the tie bars in concrete pavement are provided across the longitudinal joint, and tie bars are not load transfer devices but serve as a means to tie two slabs — hence they must be deformed or hooked and finally anchored into the concrete to function properly.**

**The contrast with a DOWEL BAR, which is the discrimination the question exists for:**

| | **TIE BAR** | **DOWEL BAR** |
|---|---|---|
| **Placed across** | **LONGITUDINAL joints** ← | **TRANSVERSE joints** |
| **Bar runs in the direction** | **TRANSVERSE (across the road)** | **LONGITUDINAL (along the road)** |
| **Purpose** | **HOLD the slabs together — prevent separation** | **TRANSFER LOAD between slabs** |
| **Bar type** | **DEFORMED (or hooked), and ANCHORED — must GRIP** | **PLAIN and GREASED — must SLIDE** |
| **Is it a load transfer device?** | **NO** | **YES** |
| **Size and spacing** | **SMALLER diameter, at LARGER intervals** | Larger diameter, closer spacing |

> **Every row is opposite, and the pair is easy to remember once the logic is seen:**

> **A TIE must GRIP the concrete on both sides — so it is DEFORMED and anchored.**

> **A DOWEL must SLIDE — so it is PLAIN and greased over half its length, letting the transverse joint open and close with temperature.**

> **Their purposes demand OPPOSITE bond behaviour, which is why using the wrong bar type is a genuine and consequential site error.**

> **A deformed bar used as a dowel LOCKS the transverse joint, and the slab then cracks somewhere the designer did not choose. A plain bar used as a tie does not hold the longitudinal joint at all.**

**Why longitudinal joints exist in the first place:**

> **A concrete pavement wider than about 4.5 m WILL crack longitudinally, whether a joint is provided or not.**

> **The causes are WARPING (the top and bottom of the slab at different temperatures and moisture contents) and UNEVEN SETTLEMENT of the subgrade across the width.**

> **So the longitudinal joint is provided to CHOOSE WHERE that crack occurs — and the tie bar keeps the chosen crack tight and the two slabs acting together.**

> **That is the general principle of jointing, and it is worth stating plainly: CONCRETE WILL CRACK, and a joint is a crack whose location the engineer decided.**

> **Contraction joints exist for exactly the same reason, in the other direction.**

**Why the joint must be kept TIGHT — the reason tie bars matter:**

| Consequence of a joint opening | Note |
|---|---|
| **Loss of AGGREGATE INTERLOCK across the crack** | **The two slabs stop sharing load, so each edge carries more** ← |
| **Water and grit enter the joint** | Leads to pumping of the subgrade fines |
| **The joint sealant fails** | It can only accommodate limited movement |
| **Faulting develops** | One slab steps relative to the other |

> **Aggregate interlock is the mechanism that makes a tied longitudinal joint work: the crack faces are rough, and while they are held tightly together the interlocking aggregate transfers shear across them.**

> **So the tie bar delivers load transfer INDIRECTLY — not by acting as a dowel, but by keeping the crack closed so that the concrete itself can transfer the load.**

> **That is a subtle and important distinction, and it resolves an apparent contradiction: a tie bar is not a load transfer device, and a properly tied joint does transfer load.**

**The joints of a concrete pavement, gathered:**

| Joint | Direction | Purpose | Bar |
|---|---|---|---|
| **EXPANSION joint** | Transverse | **Allow the slab to EXPAND — a gap with a compressible filler** | **DOWEL** |
| **CONTRACTION joint** | Transverse | **Control where shrinkage cracks form** | **DOWEL** |
| **CONSTRUCTION joint** | Transverse | Where a day's paving ends | Dowel |
| **LONGITUDINAL joint** | Longitudinal | **Control longitudinal cracking; relieve warping and uneven settlement** | **TIE BAR** ← |
| **WARPING joint** | Either | Relieve warping stresses | — |

> **Option (d) EXPANSION JOINT is the designed trap, because it is a real and important joint — and it carries DOWELS, not tie bars.**

> **Options (b) "vertical joints" and (c) "gap joint" are not standard terms in concrete pavement practice at all**, which is worth recognising: an option using non-standard terminology is usually a manufactured distractor rather than a real alternative.

**And the tie bar details, since they follow from its function:**

| Detail | Typical |
|---|---|
| **Bar type** | **DEFORMED, 10-16 mm diameter** |
| **Length** | **Long enough for full bond development on BOTH sides — commonly 500-1000 mm** |
| **Spacing** | **300-750 mm — much wider than dowels** |
| **Position** | **At mid-depth of the slab** |
| Coating | Sometimes epoxy-coated against corrosion |

> **The LENGTH requirement is the one that follows directly from the function: since the bar must GRIP, it needs a full development length in each slab** — unlike a dowel, whose length is set by the shear it must carry rather than by bond.

> **So the tie bar is longer and thinner than a dowel, and the dowel is shorter and thicker** — which is a useful physical check when the two are seen on site.

examTip.trick: **TIE bar across LONGITUDINAL joints; DOWEL across TRANSVERSE joints.** A tie must GRIP (deformed, anchored); a dowel must SLIDE (plain, greased). Their purposes demand opposite bond behaviour.
