examTip.trap: **Option (d) expansion joint is real and carries DOWELS.** And "vertical joint" and "gap joint" are not standard terms at all — non-standard terminology usually marks a manufactured distractor.
examTip.mnemonic: **A tie bar transfers load INDIRECTLY** — by holding the crack tight so AGGREGATE INTERLOCK can work. Which resolves the apparent contradiction: it is not a load transfer device, and a tied joint does transfer load.

questions.stem: Taking a canal as an example, what factor causes its waterlogging?
options: seepage of water from high land
questions.solution:
**Seepage through the canals.**

**Why seepage from the canal itself is the answer:**

> **The stem says "taking a CANAL as an example" — so it is asking which factor is attributable to THE CANAL.**

> **An unlined canal loses water continuously through its bed and banks into the surrounding ground.**

> **That seepage RAISES THE WATER TABLE in the adjacent land, and when the water table rises into the root zone, the land is WATERLOGGED.**

> **The source states it: waterlogging in a canal can be caused by seepage through the canals, which raises the water table in adjacent areas.**

**Why the other options, though real causes of waterlogging, are not the CANAL's contribution:**

| Option | A real cause? | Attributable to the canal? |
|---|---|---|
| **Seepage from high land** | **Yes — groundwater flowing down from higher ground** | **NO — a topographic cause** |
| **Seepage through the canals** | **Yes** | **YES** ✓ |
| **Over and intensive irrigation** | **Yes — a genuine and major cause** | **NO — attributable to the FARMER'S practice, not the canal** ← |
| **Excessive rain** | **Yes** | **NO — a climatic cause** |

> **Option (c) is the substantive near-miss and deserves care: over-irrigation is one of the two leading causes of waterlogging, and it is closely associated with canal schemes.**

> **But it is a cause arising from HOW THE WATER IS APPLIED, not from the canal structure itself** — and the stem's framing ("taking a canal as an example") points at the canal as the agent.

> **So the distinction the question draws is between the canal's own losses and the practices and conditions around it.**

**The magnitude of canal seepage — which is why it dominates:**

| Canal | Seepage loss |
|---|---|
| **UNLINED canal in permeable soil** | **Can exceed 50 % of the diverted flow** |
| **Unlined canal in ordinary soil** | **20-40 %** |
| **LINED canal** | **Reduced to a small fraction** |

> **Conveyance efficiency for an unlined system is typically 60 to 80 per cent, and the losses are overwhelmingly seepage rather than evaporation.**

> **So an unlined canal in permeable ground can lose more water into the ground than it delivers to the fields** — and every litre of it goes into raising the local water table.

> **Which is the mechanism: the canal is, in effect, a long linear recharge structure running through the command area.**

**The self-defeating character of the problem, which is its most striking feature:**

> **AN IRRIGATION SCHEME CAN WATERLOG THE LAND IT WAS BUILT TO IRRIGATE.**

> **The canal delivers water; the canal's seepage and the over-irrigation it enables raise the water table; the rising water table waterlogs and eventually SALINISES the land; and the land goes out of production.**

> **That is not a hypothetical: large areas of the Indo-Gangetic plain have followed exactly that sequence over the past century.**

> **Which is why DRAINAGE is not an optional adjunct to an irrigation project but a part of it** — and why the syllabus pairs "Irrigation AND Drainage" in a single chapter.

**The consequences of waterlogging, in order of seriousness:**

| Consequence | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Roots SUFFOCATE** | **Air displaced from the soil pores; roots need oxygen** |
| **SALINITY** | **CAPILLARY RISE brings dissolved salts up; evaporation leaves them at the surface** ← the permanent damage |
| **Soil temperature falls** | Delays germination |
| **Cultivation impeded** | Machinery cannot work saturated ground |
| **Weeds and water-borne disease** | Mosquito breeding; public health |

> **SALINITY is the consequence that outlasts the drainage problem, and the distinction matters:**

> **Water can be drained away in a season. The SALT left behind by years of capillary rise requires leaching with large volumes of water and gypsum treatment — and some land is simply lost.**

> **So waterlogging is a reversible condition that causes an irreversible one**, which is why it must be prevented rather than corrected.

**The remedies, in the order they should be considered:**

| Remedy | Note |
|---|---|
| **LINING the canals** | **Attacks the largest single loss — the standard first improvement** ← |
| **Controlled and measured water delivery** | Prevents over-irrigation; requires regulation and measurement |
| **Improved on-farm water management** | Levelling, furrows, sprinkler or drip in place of flooding |
| **SURFACE and SUB-SURFACE DRAINAGE** | Shallow drains, deep collector drains with a cunnette, tile drains |
| **VERTICAL drainage (tube wells)** | **Pumping groundwater lowers the table AND supplies irrigation water** |
| Conjunctive use of surface and groundwater | Uses the seepage productively |

> **VERTICAL DRAINAGE is the elegant remedy where the groundwater is of usable quality: pumping it for irrigation lowers the water table and supplies water at the same time**, turning the seepage from a liability into a resource.

> **Where the groundwater is saline, that option closes** — and then the seepage must be intercepted and disposed of instead, which is far more expensive.

> **So the water quality of the shallow aquifer decides which remedy is available**, and it is one of the first things a drainage investigation should establish.

examTip.trick: **The stem says "taking a CANAL as an example", so it asks which factor the CANAL causes** — its own seepage through bed and banks, which raises the water table in adjacent land.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) over-irrigation is a genuine leading cause** — but it arises from HOW WATER IS APPLIED, not from the canal structure. All four options are real causes of waterlogging; only one is the canal's own.
examTip.mnemonic: **An unlined canal can lose more than half its flow to seepage** — a long linear recharge structure through its own command. And waterlogging is reversible while the SALINITY it causes is not, which is why it must be prevented rather than cured.

questions.stem: The moisture condition of aggregate assumed in concrete mix design is:
questions.solution:
**Both saturated and surface dry — the SATURATED SURFACE DRY (SSD) condition.**

**What SSD means:**

> **SATURATED SURFACE DRY is the condition in which the aggregate's INTERNAL PORES ARE FULL of water but its SURFACE carries NO free water.**

> **So it is "saturated" (option a) AND "surface dry" (option b) simultaneously — hence option (d).**

> **The source keys (d) and states it as "saturated and surface dry".**

**Why SSD is the reference condition for mix design — this is the substance:**

> **An aggregate in the SSD condition NEITHER ABSORBS WATER FROM the mix NOR CONTRIBUTES WATER TO it.**

> **It is hydraulically NEUTRAL.**

> **That makes it the only condition in which the water added to the mixer is exactly the water available to the cement — so the WATER/CEMENT RATIO the designer specifies is the ratio the concrete actually gets.**

> **Any other condition shifts the effective w/c ratio, and since w/c governs strength (Abrams' law), that shift changes the concrete's strength without anyone intending it.**

**The four moisture states, which must be held as a sequence:**

| State | Internal pores | Surface | Effect on the mix water |
|---|---|---|---|
| **OVEN DRY (bone dry)** | **EMPTY** | Dry | **ABSORBS the most water from the mix** |
| **AIR DRY** | **Partly filled** | Dry | **ABSORBS some water** |
| **SATURATED SURFACE DRY (SSD)** | **FULL** | **Dry** | **NEUTRAL — neither absorbs nor gives** ← |
| **MOIST (wet)** | **Full** | **FREE water on the surface** | **CONTRIBUTES water to the mix** |

> **The sequence runs from absorbing to contributing, with SSD as the neutral point in the middle** — and that ordering makes the whole set easy to reason about rather than memorise.

> **Option (c) "unsaturated and surface dry" is the AIR DRY condition**, which absorbs water and is therefore not the reference state. **It is a real condition, wrongly identified — which is what makes it the designed distractor.**

**The two quantities that describe the difference from SSD:**

| Quantity | Definition |
|---|---|
| **ABSORPTION** | **The water needed to bring a DRY aggregate to SSD, as a percentage of its dry weight** |
| **FREE (surface) MOISTURE** | **The water on the surface of a WET aggregate, ABOVE the SSD condition** |

> **Typical absorption values:**

| Aggregate | Absorption |
|---|---|
| **Good quality crushed stone / gravel** | **0.5-1.5 %** |
| **Sand** | **0.5-2 %** |
| **Porous or weathered aggregate** | **Above 2 % — and above about 2 % is a durability warning** ← |
| Lightweight aggregate | Can be 10-20 % |

> **The 2 per cent threshold matters beyond mix design: high absorption means high porosity, and porosity is what admits frost, salt and chemical attack.** So absorption is both a batching correction and a durability indicator.

**The FIELD CORRECTION, which is where this matters daily:**

> **Aggregate on a site is almost never at SSD. Sand stockpiled in the open is usually WET; aggregate in the dry season may be AIR DRY.**

> **So the batch must be corrected:**

| Aggregate condition | Correction to the mix |
|---|---|
| **WETTER than SSD (free moisture)** | **REDUCE the added water; INCREASE the aggregate weight** (part of its weight is water) |
| **DRIER than SSD** | **INCREASE the added water; REDUCE the aggregate weight** |

> **BOTH adjustments are needed, and forgetting the second is the commoner error.**

> **If sand carries 5 per cent free moisture and is batched by weight without correction, then 5 per cent of what was weighed as sand is water — so the mix is short of sand AND carries extra water.**

> **Two errors from one omission, both pushing the same way: a wetter, weaker, sandier-looking mix than designed.**

> **Which is why the moisture content of the sand should be checked at least daily, and after rain** — it is the single most variable input to a concrete mix.

**And the BULKING effect, which compounds the problem for volume batching:**

> **Damp sand OCCUPIES MORE VOLUME than dry sand — up to 20 to 30 per cent more — because a film of water around each grain holds the grains apart.**

| Sand condition | Bulking |
|---|---|
| **Dry** | **None (reference)** |
| **4-6 % moisture** | **MAXIMUM bulking, 20-30 %** ← |
| **Fully saturated / inundated** | **Bulking DISAPPEARS — the films merge** |

> **The non-monotonic behaviour is the striking part: bulking rises to a maximum at a few per cent moisture and then FALLS AWAY to nothing when the sand is completely inundated.**

> **So volume-batching damp sand delivers substantially LESS sand than intended**, giving a richer, more cement-hungry and more shrinkage-prone mix.

> **And the practical remedy is the reason weight batching is preferred for anything important: weight does not bulk.**

> **Where volume batching must be used, the sand's bulking should be measured on site — the simple test being to fill a container with damp sand, then inundate it with water and note how far the level drops.** That drop IS the bulking.

examTip.trick: **SSD means internal pores FULL and surface DRY — so it is both "saturated" and "surface dry" at once.** It is the only hydraulically NEUTRAL condition, which is why mix design uses it.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) "unsaturated and surface dry" is the AIR DRY condition** — a real state that ABSORBS water, wrongly identified. The sequence runs oven dry → air dry → SSD → moist, from absorbing to contributing.
examTip.mnemonic: **Correcting for wet sand needs BOTH adjustments** — less added water AND more aggregate weight — and forgetting the second is commoner. Plus **bulking peaks at 4-6 % moisture (20-30 %) and vanishes when inundated**, which is why weight batching is preferred.

questions.stem: In a slab, the minimum thickness is designed to resist:
questions.solution:
**Shear force.**

**Why SHEAR sets the minimum thickness of a slab — the reason is what a slab lacks:**

> **A SLAB IS NOT NORMALLY PROVIDED WITH SHEAR REINFORCEMENT.**

> **Stirrups in a thin slab are impractical — there is not enough depth to bend and anchor them, and they would obstruct the placing of concrete.**

> **So the shear must be carried BY THE CONCRETE ALONE.**

> **And the concrete's shear capacity is  V_c = τ_c × b × d — it is directly proportional to the DEPTH.**

> **Therefore the depth must be large enough that τ_c alone suffices, and that requirement sets a MINIMUM thickness that cannot be traded away.**

**Why BENDING does not set a minimum in the same way — and this is the discrimination:**

> **A slab's bending capacity can be increased by ADDING MORE STEEL at the same thickness.**

> **So if a thin slab is short of moment capacity, the designer has an alternative: more reinforcement.**

> **But if it is short of SHEAR capacity, there is NO alternative — the section must be made deeper.**

| Deficiency | Remedies available |
|---|---|
| **BENDING (moment) capacity** | **More steel, OR more depth — a CHOICE** |
| **SHEAR capacity in a slab** | **MORE DEPTH ONLY — no choice** ← |

> **That asymmetry is the whole answer: shear is the criterion with no escape route, so it is the one that sets a MINIMUM.**

> **Option (c) bending moment is therefore the substantive near-miss — bending certainly governs the slab's DESIGN, and it determines the reinforcement. It does not set the minimum THICKNESS, because steel can be added instead.**

**Why option (b) axial force is wrong:**

> **A slab is a FLEXURAL member: it carries load transverse to its plane, by bending and shear.**

> **Axial force in the plane of a slab is normally negligible** — and where it is not (a slab acting as a diaphragm, or a shear wall), the member is being designed as something other than an ordinary slab.

> **So axial force does not enter the thickness decision at all.**

**The other criterion that competes with shear — and in practice usually wins:**

> **DEFLECTION.**

> **IS 456 controls deflection by a SPAN-TO-DEPTH ratio rather than by calculation for ordinary cases:**

| Support condition | Basic span/effective depth |
|---|---|
| **CANTILEVER** | **7** |
| **SIMPLY SUPPORTED** | **20** |
| **CONTINUOUS** | **26** |

> **Those ratios reflect exactly the stiffness sequence: a continuous slab may be more slender than a simply supported one, and a cantilever far less.**

> **In practice a slab's thickness is most often fixed by the SPAN/DEPTH ratio, and then checked for shear** — so both criteria are minimums and the larger governs.

> **Which is the honest position: DEFLECTION usually decides a slab's thickness, and SHEAR is the criterion that cannot be evaded by adding steel.** The question asks about the second.

**The minimum thickness requirements, since they are asked alongside:**

| Requirement | Value |
|---|---|
| **Minimum thickness of a solid slab** | **Commonly 100-125 mm for a roof or floor** |
| **Minimum MAIN steel (Fe415/500)** | **0.12 % of the gross area** |
| **Minimum main steel (Fe250)** | **0.15 %** |
| **DISTRIBUTION steel** | **0.12 % (HYSD)** |
| **Maximum bar spacing, main steel** | **3d or 300 mm, whichever is LESS** |
| **Maximum spacing, distribution steel** | **5d or 450 mm, whichever is less** |
| **Nominal COVER** | **15 mm (20 mm if bars exceed 12 mm)** |
| **Maximum bar diameter** | **One eighth of the slab thickness** |

> **The one-eighth rule on bar diameter is worth noting: it prevents the use of a bar so large that it cannot develop bond within the slab's depth** — a 100 mm slab should not carry bars above 12 mm.

> **And the slab's minimum steel (0.12 % of GROSS area) is LOWER than a beam's (0.205 % of bd)** — because a slab is a two-way plate with more redundancy, and its minimum is governed by SHRINKAGE AND TEMPERATURE rather than by the ductility requirement that governs a beam.

**And the case where slab shear genuinely governs — PUNCHING SHEAR:**

> **In a FLAT SLAB (one supported directly on columns with no beams), the shear around the column is concentrated on a small perimeter — PUNCHING SHEAR.**

> **The column tries to punch through the slab, and the failure is BRITTLE and sudden.**

| Remedy | Note |
|---|---|
| **Increase the slab DEPTH** | The direct route |
| **DROP PANEL — a local thickening around the column** | **Increases the depth only where it is needed** ← |
| **COLUMN CAPITAL (flared head)** | Increases the shear perimeter |
| **Shear reinforcement (studs or stirrups) in the slab** | Possible but difficult |

> **Punching shear failures of flat slabs are among the more notorious structural collapses**, precisely because they are brittle and give no warning — a slab can be adequate in bending everywhere and still punch through at one column.

> **Which is the strongest illustration of the question's point: shear is the criterion that must be satisfied by GEOMETRY, and a slab's thickness is what satisfies it.**

examTip.trick: **A slab has NO shear reinforcement, so shear must be carried by the concrete alone — and V_c ∝ depth.** That makes depth the only remedy for a shear deficiency.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) bending governs the slab's DESIGN but not its minimum THICKNESS** — a moment shortfall can be met by adding STEEL, while a shear shortfall cannot. That asymmetry is the answer.
examTip.mnemonic: **In practice DEFLECTION usually fixes a slab's thickness** (span/depth 7, 20, 26 for cantilever, simply supported, continuous) and shear is then checked. And **PUNCHING SHEAR at a flat-slab column** is the brittle failure this criterion guards against.

questions.stem: A micro hydro plant has various components such as the penstock and turbine. What is the FUNCTION of the penstock?
options: Penstocks are like large pipes laid with some slope
An enclosed pipe that delivers water to hydro turbines
questions.solution:
**An enclosed pipe that delivers water to the hydro turbines.**

**Why option (c) and not the others — the question asks for a FUNCTION:**

> **The source's note is the key to the whole question: "Question asked FUNCTION so option will be (C) — an enclosed pipe that delivers water to hydro turbines."**

> **A FUNCTION states what the component DOES.**

> **A DESCRIPTION states what it IS or WHERE it goes.**

> **Option (c) is the only one phrased as a function — it says what the penstock accomplishes: DELIVERING WATER to the turbines.**

| Option | What kind of statement it makes |
|---|---|
| **"Like large pipes laid with some slope"** | **A DESCRIPTION of its form — what it looks like** |
| **"Connect forebay and turbines"** | **A statement of its POSITION — where it runs** ← the substantive near-miss |
| **"An enclosed pipe that delivers water to hydro turbines"** | **A FUNCTION — what it does** ✓ |
| **"None"** | — |

> **Option (b) is the interesting distractor, because it is TRUE: a penstock does run from the forebay to the turbines.**

> **But "connects A and B" describes a LOCATION in the layout, not a purpose.** A great many things connect the forebay to the turbines — an access road, a cable, a walkway — and none of them is a penstock.

> **So the question is testing whether the candidate distinguishes a component's FUNCTION from its DESCRIPTION and its POSITION**, which is a reading skill rather than a hydropower one.

> **And option (a) is true as far as it goes and says nothing about purpose at all — a description of appearance.**

**What the penstock actually does, since the function is the answer:**

> **The penstock CONVEYS WATER UNDER PRESSURE from the forebay (or surge tank) down the steep slope to the turbine, converting the available HEAD into PRESSURE at the machine.**

| Requirement it must meet | Note |
|---|---|
| **Withstand the full internal PRESSURE, including WATER HAMMER** | **The governing structural requirement** ← |
| **Deliver the flow with minimum HEAD LOSS** | Every metre lost is energy lost |
| **Resist EXTERNAL pressure when empty or under vacuum** | Buckling |
| **Accommodate THERMAL movement** | Expansion joints between anchor blocks |
| **Resist internal ABRASION** | Sediment-laden Himalayan water |
| Resist corrosion | Coating; cathodic protection where buried |

> **The pressure requirement is what sizes the wall, and it is not the static head:**

> **Design pressure = STATIC HEAD + WATER HAMMER RISE.**

> **Joukowsky's equation for sudden closure: Δh = (a/g)V, with the wave speed a = 900-1200 m/s in steel.**

> **For V = 4 m/s and a = 1000 m/s, Δh ≈ 408 m of head** — often comparable with or greater than the static head itself.

> **A penstock designed for static head alone would burst on the first load rejection**, which is why the surge tank and the governor's closure time are part of the penstock's design rather than separate matters.

**Where the penstock sits in the chain, since option (b) concerns that:**

> **INTAKE → settling basin → HEADRACE channel or tunnel → FOREBAY (or surge tank) → PENSTOCK → TURBINE → tailrace → river**

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **Diversion weir** | **Raises the level to divert flow** |
| **Intake, gravel trap, settling basin** | **Admit water; exclude debris and abrasive sand** |
| **Headrace** | **Convey water along the hillside at a small gradient — gains LENGTH, not head** |
| **Forebay / surge tank** | **Transition, short-term storage, trashrack, surge absorption** |
| **PENSTOCK** | **Convert the head into pressure at the turbine** ← |
| **Powerhouse** | Turbines and generators |
| **Tailrace** | Return the water |

> **Note the division of labour between the headrace and the penstock, which is the essential idea of a run-of-river layout:**

> **The HEADRACE runs nearly LEVEL, gaining length while the river falls away beneath it.**

> **The PENSTOCK then drops steeply to the powerhouse, realising in one plunge all the head the headrace accumulated.**

> **That is how a run-of-river scheme creates head without a dam: it moves the water horizontally while the ground falls.**

**And the micro-hydro context the stem specifies:**

| Scale | Capacity |
|---|---|
| **PICO hydro** | **Below 5 kW** |
| **MICRO hydro** | **5 to 100 kW** ← |
| **MINI hydro** | **100 kW to 1 MW** |
| **SMALL hydro** | **1 to 10 MW (up to 25 MW in some definitions)** |
| Large hydro | Above that |

> **Micro hydro is of particular importance in Nepal**, where thousands of such schemes serve communities beyond the reach of the grid.

> **At that scale the penstock is often HDPE or mild steel of modest diameter, and it is frequently the SINGLE LARGEST COST ITEM in the scheme** — which is why its diameter is an economic optimisation rather than a hydraulic one.

> **A larger pipe loses less head (and so generates more) but costs more; the optimum balances the capitalised value of the extra energy against the extra pipe cost.** For a community scheme with limited capital, that trade-off is often decided by what can be afforded rather than by what would pay best over twenty years — a real constraint worth acknowledging.

examTip.trick: **The stem asks for a FUNCTION — what the component DOES.** Only option (c) states one; (a) describes its form and (b) its position in the layout.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) is TRUE and is not a function.** Many things connect the forebay to the turbines — a road, a cable, a walkway. "Connects A and B" is a location, not a purpose.
examTip.mnemonic: **The HEADRACE runs nearly level, gaining length while the river falls away; the PENSTOCK then drops steeply and realises all that head at once.** That is how a run-of-river scheme creates head without a dam.

questions.stem: If the initial investment for a machine is Rs 10,000 and the depreciation amount per year is Rs 1,600, then calculate the book value at the end of 5 years.
questions.solution:
**Rs 2,000.**

**The two-step calculation:**

> **STEP 1 — the accumulated depreciation:**

> **Total depreciation = (depreciation per year) × (number of years)**

> **= 1,600 × 5 = Rs 8,000**

> **STEP 2 — the book value:**

> **Book value = Initial cost − accumulated depreciation**

> **= 10,000 − 8,000 = Rs 2,000** ✓

> **The source's working is exactly this.**

**Why option (d) Rs 8,000 is the designed trap:**

> **Rs 8,000 is the ACCUMULATED DEPRECIATION — how much value has been LOST.**

> **The BOOK VALUE is what REMAINS.**

> **So option (d) is the classic "answered a different question" error: the candidate computes the harder step correctly and then reports it instead of completing the subtraction.**

> **And it is the more tempting of the two numbers, because 1,600 × 5 = 8,000 feels like the answer once it is found.**

> **The defence is to read the question's last four words — "book value at the end" — before starting, and to notice that a book value must be a REMAINING value.**

> **A sanity check confirms it: the machine cost Rs 10,000 and has been depreciating for five years, so its book value must be a small fraction of the cost. Rs 8,000 would mean it had barely depreciated at all.**

**Note the source's own stray text, which does not affect the answer:**

> **The source's working is headed "Total depreciation up to 7th year" while multiplying by 5, as the stem states.**

> **The "7th year" is a stray error in the source's text; the arithmetic (1,600 × 5) matches the stem's five years, and the keyed answer follows correctly from it.**

> **So the working is right and its heading is wrong — worth noting only so that a reader comparing this solution with the source is not confused.**

**Which depreciation method this is, and the check that identifies it:**

> **A CONSTANT depreciation of Rs 1,600 every year is the STRAIGHT LINE method.**

> **And it lets us recover the assumed life and salvage value:**

> **Straight line: D = (C − S)/n**

> **1,600 = (10,000 − S)/n**

| If the life n is | Then the salvage value S is |
|---|---|
| **5 years** | **10,000 − 8,000 = Rs 2,000** |
| **6 years** | 10,000 − 9,600 = Rs 400 |
| **6.25 years** | **Zero** |

> **So the figures are consistent with a 5-year life and a Rs 2,000 salvage value — in which case the book value at year 5 EQUALS the salvage value**, which is exactly what a straight-line schedule should do.

> **That is a satisfying internal check: a straight-line schedule must land ON the salvage value at the end of the life, and here it does.**

> **And it is the check worth applying to any depreciation problem: compute the book value at the end of the stated life, and it should equal the salvage value. If it does not, a step is wrong.**

**The depreciation methods, since this is one of several:**

| Method | Annual charge | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **STRAIGHT LINE** | **(C − S)/n — CONSTANT** | **Simplest; uniform loss of value** ← |
| **DECLINING BALANCE** | **A fixed PERCENTAGE of the reducing book value** | **ACCELERATED — most depreciation early** |
| **Double declining balance** | 2/n of the book value | Accelerated |
| **SUM OF YEARS DIGITS** | **(remaining life / Σ years) × (C − S)** | Accelerated, linearly declining |
| **SINKING FUND** | **A uniform annual deposit that, WITH INTEREST, accumulates to (C − S)** | **The only method recognising the TIME VALUE of money** |
| Service output | Per unit produced | Matches usage rather than time |

> **The ACCELERATED methods reflect economic reality better than the straight line does, because most assets lose more value in their early years** — a new machine becomes a used machine the day it is commissioned.

> **And the SINKING FUND method is the conceptually distinct one: the others merely ALLOCATE a past cost across years, while a sinking fund actually SETS MONEY ASIDE at interest to buy the replacement.**

> **It is the only method that connects depreciation accounting to the cash that will actually be needed** — which is why it appears in engineering economics rather than only in accounting.

**And why an engineer needs this at all:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **PLANT HIRE rates and rate analysis** | **The owning cost of plant is depreciation plus interest, insurance and taxes** ← |
| **Life-cycle cost comparison** | Which machine is cheaper over its life, not to buy |
| **REPLACEMENT timing** | **When does rising maintenance outweigh the remaining value?** |
| Tender pricing | Plant charges in a bill of quantities |

> **The replacement decision is where the accounting meets the engineering: an old machine's DEPRECIATION charge is low (it has little value left to lose) but its MAINTENANCE and DOWNTIME costs are rising.**

> **The ECONOMIC LIFE ends at the year where the TOTAL of the two is least** — and that is generally well before the machine stops working.

> **Which is a genuinely useful conclusion: the right time to replace a machine is not when it fails but when its total annual cost begins to rise**, and recognising that requires the depreciation arithmetic this question begins with.

verification.notes: Keyed answer confirmed; a stray error in the source's own text noted. The source's working is headed "Total depreciation up to 7th year" while it multiplies 1,600 by 5, as the stem states. The multiplication and the keyed answer (b) Rs 2,000 both follow correctly from the stem's five years, so the heading is a stray slip that does not affect the result. It is recorded here only so that a reader comparing this solution against the source is not misled.

examTip.trick: **Accumulated depreciation = 1,600 × 5 = 8,000; book value = 10,000 − 8,000 = Rs 2,000.**
examTip.trap: **Option (d) Rs 8,000 is the accumulated DEPRECIATION — the value LOST, not what REMAINS.** It is the more tempting number because it is the result of the harder step. Read the last four words of the question first.
examTip.mnemonic: **A straight-line schedule must land ON the salvage value at the end of the life** — and here it does (Rs 2,000 at year 5), which confirms the arithmetic. Apply that check to any depreciation problem.

questions.stem: If a weight of 120 kN on earth is measured on the moon, it is equal to:
questions.solution:
**20 kN.**

**The reasoning:**

> **Weight is a FORCE: W = m g.**

> **The MASS does not change when a body travels — it is a property of the body.**

> **What changes is g.**

> **The moon's surface gravity is about ONE SIXTH of the earth's — 1.62 m/s² against 9.81 m/s², a ratio of 0.165.**

> **So W_moon = 120 / 6 = 20 kN** ✓

> **The source's working is exactly this: weight on moon = weight on earth ÷ 6 = 120/6 = 20 kN.**

**Why the ratio is one sixth — worth deriving rather than memorising:**

> **g = GM/R², so the ratio depends on BOTH mass and radius:**

| Quantity | Moon relative to earth |
|---|---|
| **Mass M** | **≈ 1/81** |
| **Radius R** | **≈ 1/3.7** |
| **g = GM/R²** | **(1/81) × (3.7)² ≈ 13.7/81 ≈ 1/6** ✓ |

> **The much smaller radius partly COMPENSATES for the much smaller mass, which is why the answer is a sixth and not an eightieth.**

> **That is the insight the question is really testing, and it explains why the distractors are placed where they are:**

| Option | Implied ratio | What it corresponds to |
|---|---|---|
| **20 kN** | **1/6** | ✓ **Correct** |
| **30 kN** | **1/4** | No body's surface gravity |
| **40 kN** | **1/3** | **Close to the RADIUS ratio (1/3.7) — the trap for anyone who forgets the mass** ← |
| **45 kN** | 3/8 | — |

> **Option (c) 40 kN is the designed trap: a candidate who half-remembers "the moon is about a third the size of the earth" will reach for it.**

> **Size and gravity are different ratios, and the question separates them.**

**The distinction the question rests on — and it is a genuine confusion in engineering practice:**

| Quantity | Nature | SI unit | Changes with location? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **MASS** | **Amount of matter — a SCALAR** | **kg (an SI BASE unit)** | **NO** |
| **WEIGHT** | **The gravitational FORCE on that mass — a VECTOR** | **newton (N)** | **YES** |

> **The stem is loose in saying a "weight of 120 kN" is "measured" — but it uses kN, which is a force, so it is correct.**

> **The looseness that matters in practice is the reverse one: stating a weight in KILOGRAMS.**

> **The KILOGRAM-FORCE (kgf) exists to paper over it — 1 kgf = 9.81 N — and it is still widely used in the region.**

> **A load stated in "kg" must be MULTIPLIED BY 9.81 to become a force in newtons, and forgetting that factor is a real and expensive mistake.**

**Where this matters in civil engineering — because the question is not idle:**

> **Every dead load is a WEIGHT, and every mass density must be converted to a UNIT WEIGHT by multiplying by g.**

| Material | Mass density | Unit weight |
|---|---|---|
| **Water** | **1000 kg/m³** | **9.81 kN/m³** |
| **RCC** | **2500 kg/m³** | **25 kN/m³** |
| **Plain concrete** | 2400 kg/m³ | 24 kN/m³ |
| **STEEL** | **7850 kg/m³** | **78.5 kN/m³** |
| **Brick masonry** | 1900 kg/m³ | 19 kN/m³ |
| Stone masonry | 2400-2700 kg/m³ | 24-27 kN/m³ |

> **The 25 kN/m³ for RCC and 78.5 kN/m³ for steel are the two figures worth committing to memory**, because they appear in almost every dead-load calculation — and the conversion between the two columns is where slips happen.

> **Note also that NBC 102 and IS 875 Part 1 tabulate UNIT WEIGHTS (kN/m³), not densities**, precisely so that the multiplication by g is done once, in the code, rather than repeatedly and unreliably by every designer.

**And the wider point about which quantity a code specifies:**

| Code convention | Why |
|---|---|
| **Loading codes give UNIT WEIGHTS (kN/m³)** | **The designer wants a FORCE, so the code does the g multiplication** ← |
| **Material codes often give DENSITIES (kg/m³)** | Relevant to mix proportions and to mass |
| **Compaction control uses DRY DENSITY (kg/m³ or g/cc)** | A mass quantity, since it concerns how much solid is packed in |

> **So the same material appears as 2500 kg/m³ in a concrete technology table and 25 kN/m³ in a loading table**, and both are correct.

> **Recognising which quantity a table gives — mass or force — is a small habit that prevents a whole class of factor-of-ten errors.**

examTip.trick: **Mass does not change; g does.** The moon's g is 1.62 against 9.81 — about one sixth — so 120/6 = 20 kN.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) 40 kN implies a ratio of 1/3, close to the RADIUS ratio (1/3.7).** Size and gravity are different ratios: g = GM/R² needs BOTH the mass (1/81) and the radius, giving (1/81) × 3.7² ≈ 1/6.
examTip.mnemonic: **A load in "kg" must be multiplied by 9.81 to become a force.** Hence RCC 2500 kg/m³ → **25 kN/m³** and steel 7850 → **78.5 kN/m³** — and loading codes tabulate the second column precisely so the multiplication is done once.

questions.stem: Which of the following is used to remove algae?
questions.solution:
**Copper sulphate.**

**Why copper sulphate:**

> **COPPER SULPHATE (CuSO₄) is an ALGICIDE — it is toxic to algae at very low concentrations while being harmless to humans at those doses.**

> **It is dosed into reservoirs and open storage as a fine powder or in solution, typically at 0.2 to 0.5 mg/l** (up to about 1 mg/l for a heavy bloom).

> **The source states it: copper sulphate is generally used for controlling algae.**

**Why algae must be controlled at all — the problems they cause:**

| Problem | Note |
|---|---|
| **TASTE and ODOUR** | **The commonest complaint — earthy, musty, fishy or grassy** ← |
| **Colour and turbidity** | Green or blue-green tinge |
| **CLOGGING of filters** | **Algae blind a rapid sand filter and shorten its run** |
| **Increased CHLORINE DEMAND** | Organic matter consumes the disinfectant |
| **Formation of DISINFECTION BY-PRODUCTS** | Organic precursors plus chlorine give trihalomethanes |
| **TOXINS from some blue-green algae** | **Cyanobacterial toxins are a genuine health hazard** |
| **Diurnal swings in pH and dissolved oxygen** | Photosynthesis by day, respiration by night |

> **The taste-and-odour problem is the one that drives most algal control**, because it is the defect consumers actually notice — and a supply that tastes wrong is distrusted whatever its bacteriological quality.

> **And the diurnal swing is worth understanding: algae PRODUCE oxygen by day and CONSUME it by night**, so a heavily algal reservoir can be supersaturated at dusk and depleted at dawn. **The nightly minimum is what kills fish.**

**Why each distractor is wrong — and each is a real thing in water treatment:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **CO₂** | **Used for pH CORRECTION (recarbonation) after lime softening — it does not kill algae. And algae CONSUME CO₂ in photosynthesis, so adding it would FEED them** ← |
| **FUNGI** | **Not used in water treatment at all; fungi are a contaminant, not a treatment** |
| **BACTERIA** | **Used in WASTEWATER treatment (activated sludge, trickling filters) — the wrong process entirely** ← |
| **Copper sulphate** | ✓ |

> **Option (a) CO₂ is the well-made distractor and it fails twice: it is a pH chemical rather than a biocide, and carbon dioxide is algae's carbon SOURCE.** Adding it would promote growth rather than suppress it.

> **Option (c) BACTERIA is the other substantive trap, because biological treatment is a real and important technology — in SEWAGE treatment.** Applying it to a drinking-water reservoir is the wrong side of the subject.

> **So the question tests whether the candidate keeps the WATER SUPPLY chemicals apart from the WASTEWATER processes.**

**The water treatment chemicals, gathered — since each has one job:**

| Chemical | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **COPPER SULPHATE** | **ALGICIDE — controls algae** ← |
| **CHLORINE / bleaching powder** | **DISINFECTION — kills bacteria and viruses** |
| **ALUM (aluminium sulphate)** | **COAGULANT — destabilises colloids so they flocculate** |
| **LIME** | **Softening (carbonate hardness); pH correction; coagulation aid** |
| **SODA ASH** | **Softening — removes NON-CARBONATE (permanent) hardness** |
| **ACTIVATED CARBON** | **Taste and ODOUR removal by adsorption** |
| **Chlorine dioxide / ozone** | Disinfection and oxidation without chlorinated by-products |
| **Sodium fluoride** | Fluoridation, where required |
| **Bleaching powder / potassium permanganate** | Oxidation of iron and manganese |

> **Note that ACTIVATED CARBON is the alternative remedy for the taste and odour that algae cause** — it removes the compounds rather than preventing their formation.

> **So there are two routes to the same complaint: kill the algae (copper sulphate) or adsorb what they produce (activated carbon)** — and a plant with a persistent problem often needs both.

**The better long-term answer, since chemical dosing treats a symptom:**

> **Algae grow when they have NUTRIENTS, LIGHT and WARMTH — and the controllable one is NUTRIENTS.**

| Preventive measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Control NUTRIENT inflow — nitrogen and especially PHOSPHORUS** | **Phosphorus is usually the LIMITING nutrient in fresh water** ← |
| **Catchment management** | Reduce fertiliser runoff and sewage discharge |
| **Reduce DETENTION TIME in storage** | Algae need time to bloom |
| **Cover or roof small reservoirs** | Excludes light entirely |
| **Draw water from DEPTH** | Algae concentrate near the surface where the light is |
| Artificial destratification / aeration | Prevents the stagnant warm surface layer blooms favour |

> **The PHOSPHORUS point is the important one: because phosphorus is generally the limiting nutrient, controlling it controls the bloom** — and that is why phosphorus removal is required at sewage works discharging to sensitive waters.

> **And DRAWING FROM DEPTH is the cheapest operational measure available: a multi-level intake lets the operator take water from below the algal layer**, avoiding the problem rather than treating it.

> **Which is the general pattern worth recognising: chemical dosing manages a bloom, and catchment and intake design prevent it.** The first is an operating cost for ever; the second is a design decision made once.

examTip.trick: **Copper sulphate is an ALGICIDE, dosed at 0.2-0.5 mg/l** — toxic to algae, harmless to people at that dose.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) CO₂ fails twice**: it is a pH chemical, and carbon dioxide is algae's CARBON SOURCE, so adding it would feed them. And option (c) BACTERIA belongs to SEWAGE treatment, not water supply.
examTip.mnemonic: **PHOSPHORUS is usually the LIMITING nutrient in fresh water**, so controlling it controls the bloom. And the cheapest operational measure is a **multi-level intake** — draw from below the algal layer rather than treating what you took.

questions.stem: Why is a circular column not preferred in construction?
options: It is difficult to make a connection with joints
questions.solution:
**It is difficult to make a connection with the joints.**

**Why the objection is CONSTRUCTABILITY and not structural performance:**

> **A circular column is structurally EXCELLENT.**

> **Its radius of gyration is the same about every axis, so it has NO WEAK DIRECTION — the buckling capacity is identical whichever way the load tries to bend it. A rectangular column always buckles about its weak axis first.**

> **And IS 456 clause 39.4 credits a circular column with HELICAL (spiral) reinforcement with a 5 PER CENT HIGHER axial capacity**, because the spiral confines the core and the failure is more ductile.

> **So the objection is not to the column. It is to the JOINT.**

> **The source confirms it: "It is difficult to make a connection with joints."**

**What goes wrong at the joint:**

| Difficulty | Note |
|---|---|
| **Beam soffit and sides meet a CURVED face** | **No flat surface for the beam's formwork to seat against** ← |
| **Formwork is complex and NOT REUSABLE** | A curved-to-flat junction must be cut for each case |
| **Beam reinforcement anchorage** | Bars entering a round core have varying anchorage lengths and awkward geometry |
| **Slab and partition edges do not align** | Finishing, plastering and layout all become special details |
| **Reinforcement congestion at the joint** | The circular bar arrangement fights the orthogonal beam steel |

> **Buildings are ORTHOGONAL. Beams run in two perpendicular directions, walls are straight, slabs are rectangular.**

> **A round column is the one NON-ORTHOGONAL element in an orthogonal system, and every interface with it becomes a special detail.**

> **That is a cost and a source of site error, repeated at every floor and every column** — and in a building with a hundred beam-column joints, a hundred awkward details is a real burden.

**Why options (b) and (d) are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Difficult to connect** | ✓ **The direct and primary reason** |
| **Very expensive** | **PARTLY true — but only BECAUSE of the formwork and detailing. It is a CONSEQUENCE of (a), not an independent reason.** On material alone a circular column is efficient ← |
| **Designer hesitate** | **Not an engineering reason at all — a statement about designers, not about columns** |
| **All of the above** | **Fails, because (c) is not a reason and (b) is derivative** |

> **Option (c) is worth naming as a non-reason: "designers hesitate" describes a behaviour and explains nothing.** If designers hesitate, the question is WHY — and the answer is (a).

> **So option (d) cannot stand: an all-of-the-above requires every member to be a valid independent reason, and one of them is not a reason at all.**

> **Option (b) is the more interesting rejection, because cost IS a real objection.** But it is not a separate cause — **the expense arises from the formwork and detailing difficulty that (a) names.** Listing both as independent reasons double-counts one cause.

**Where circular columns ARE used — which proves the point:**

| Application | Why circular is chosen there |
|---|---|
| **BRIDGE PIERS** | **NO beams frame in from the sides; and a round pier offers the same face to the flow whatever the current's direction, and collects less debris** ← |
| **Piles and bored shafts** | Naturally circular from the boring process |
| **Water tank staging** | Free-standing columns, no orthogonal framing |
| **Architectural columns in halls and porticos** | Appearance governs; few connections |
| **Chimneys, silos, circular structures** | The structure itself is circular |

> **The pattern is unmistakable: circular sections are used wherever there are FEW OR NO BEAM CONNECTIONS** — which confirms that the connection, not the column, is the objection.

> **The BRIDGE PIER case is the most instructive, because there the circular shape is positively ADVANTAGEOUS: it presents the same face to the flow whatever the direction of the current, which matters greatly in a BRAIDED HIMALAYAN RIVER that changes its channel between monsoons.**

> **So the very reason circular columns are avoided in buildings is ABSENT at a bridge pier, and they become the preferred choice.** That is the cleanest demonstration that the difficulty is contextual rather than intrinsic.

**The reinforcement requirements, since they follow:**

| Requirement | Circular column |
|---|---|
| **Minimum LONGITUDINAL bars** | **SIX (against FOUR for a rectangular column)** |
| **Minimum bar diameter** | **12 mm** |
| **Lateral ties** | **Circular ties OR a HELICAL spiral** |
| **Strength bonus with helical reinforcement** | **× 1.05 on the axial capacity (IS 456 cl. 39.4)** |
| **Minimum steel** | **0.8 % of the gross area** |
| **Maximum steel** | **6 %, practically limited to 4 % at laps** |
| Pitch of the helix | **Not more than 75 mm nor less than 25 mm; and not more than one sixth of the core diameter** |

> **The SIX-BAR MINIMUM and the 1.05 FACTOR are the two facts most often examined about circular columns, and both reflect the same thing: the shape works well when it is allowed to.**

> **The helical reinforcement's benefit is genuinely mechanical rather than a code concession: a continuous spiral confines the concrete core laterally, and confined concrete is both stronger and far more DUCTILE.**

> **Which is why spirally reinforced columns are favoured in SEISMIC design** — the confinement lets the column deform substantially without shedding its core, and that ductility is precisely what an earthquake demands.

examTip.trick: **The objection is to the JOINT, not the column.** A circular column has no weak axis and gets a 1.05 strength bonus with helical reinforcement — but a round face gives beam formwork nothing flat to seat against.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) cost is a CONSEQUENCE of (a), not an independent reason**, and option (c) "designers hesitate" is not a reason at all. So the all-of-the-above fails.
examTip.mnemonic: **Circular sections ARE used where no beams frame in: bridge piers, piles, tank staging, chimneys.** A round pier even suits a BRAIDED river, presenting the same face whatever the current — proving the difficulty is contextual, not intrinsic.

questions.stem: Which of the following methods is used to determine the population of large and old cities?
questions.solution:
**The arithmetical increase method.**

**Why the arithmetic method suits a large, old city:**

> **The ARITHMETICAL INCREASE method assumes the population grows by a CONSTANT NUMBER of people per decade — a constant RATE of increase, not a constant percentage.**

> **P_n = P₀ + n·x̄**, where x̄ is the average increase per decade.

> **A large, mature city is approaching SATURATION: its growth is limited by land, employment and services, so its percentage growth rate is FALLING even while it continues to add people.**

> **A constant NUMBER added each decade describes that behaviour well; a constant PERCENTAGE does not.**

> **The source states it: in the arithmetical increase method the population is assumed to increase at a constant rate, and the method is suitable for a LARGE AND OLD CITY with considerable development.**

**Why the geometric method does NOT suit it — and this is the discrimination:**

> **The GEOMETRIC INCREASE method assumes a constant PERCENTAGE increase per decade:**

> **P_n = P₀ (1 + r)^n**

> **That is COMPOUND growth, and it produces the HIGHEST forecast of any method.**

> **It suits a YOUNG, RAPIDLY GROWING town — and only for a few decades, because no population can compound indefinitely.**

> **The source's own note says exactly that: the geometric method gives higher values and should be applied to a young and rapidly increasing city, but only for a few decades.**

> **So applying it to a mature city OVERSTATES the future population badly, and the works designed from it would be oversized, under-used and unable to pay for themselves through a tariff.**

**The four methods and where each belongs:**

| Method | Assumption | Suits | Forecast |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ARITHMETICAL increase** | **Constant NUMBER added per decade** | **LARGE, OLD, SATURATED cities** ← | **LOWEST** |
| **GEOMETRIC increase** | **Constant PERCENTAGE per decade** | **YOUNG, rapidly growing towns; a few decades only** | **HIGHEST** |
| **INCREMENTAL increase** | **Arithmetic PLUS the average change in the increment** | **Average-size towns where the growth rate is itself increasing** | Intermediate |
| **LOGISTIC (S-curve)** | **Growth limited by a SATURATION population** | **The most realistic over a LONG period; normal conditions only** | Approaches a ceiling |
| Decrease in rate of growth | The percentage rate itself declines | Towns approaching saturation | — |
| Graphical / comparative | Compare with a similar city's history | Where local data are poor | — |

> **The INCREMENTAL INCREASE method is worth understanding as the refinement of the arithmetic one: it adds a second term for the change in the increment:**

> **P_n = P₀ + n x̄ + [n(n+1)/2] ȳ**, where ȳ is the average of the incremental increases.

> **So it captures ACCELERATING or DECELERATING growth, depending on whether ȳ is positive or negative** — which the plain arithmetic method cannot.

**Why the LOGISTIC curve is the most realistic, and how it unifies the others:**

> **No population grows without limit. Growth is eventually bounded by land, employment, water or simple out-migration.**

> **The logistic (S-shaped) curve has THREE PHASES, and each corresponds to one of the simpler methods:**

| Phase | Character | Approximated by |
|---|---|---|
| **EARLY** | **Growth ACCELERATING** | **GEOMETRIC method** |
| **MIDDLE** | **Growth roughly CONSTANT in number** | **ARITHMETIC method** ← |
| **LATE** | **Growth DECELERATING toward saturation** | Decrease-in-rate method |

> **So the arithmetic and geometric methods are not competing theories — they are approximations to DIFFERENT PARTS OF THE SAME CURVE.**

> **Which is exactly why one suits young towns and the other old ones**, and recognising that turns four memorised methods into one idea.

> **The logistic form is  P = P_sat / (1 + m e^{nt})**, and its practical difficulty is that P_sat — the saturation population — must be estimated, which is itself the hardest judgement in the problem.

**Why the choice of method matters so much — the design consequence:**

> **Every water supply, sewerage and solid-waste scheme is sized for a FUTURE population, and the design periods are long:**

| Component | Design period |
|---|---|
| **Storage reservoirs and dams** | **50 years** |
| **Water treatment plant** | **15-20 years** |
| **Pipe mains and TRUNK SEWERS** | **30-50 years** |
| **Distribution network** | **30 years** |
| **Pumps and mechanical plant** | **10-15 years — replaced within the works' life** |

> **The design periods DIFFER BY COMPONENT deliberately: what is EXPENSIVE TO ENLARGE LATER is built large now, and what is cheap to replace is not.**

> **A trunk sewer laid beneath a city cannot be enlarged at any reasonable cost, so it is sized for fifty years. A pump can be swapped in a week, so it is sized for ten.**

> **That principle — match the design period to the cost of future enlargement — is the practical reason population forecasting matters, and it is a better answer than "because the code says thirty years".**

> **And the honest limitation: a fifty-year population forecast is a guess.** Which is why STAGED construction — leaving room for a second module, a second pipe, a second clarifier — is generally wiser than a single confident projection.

verification.notes: Duplicate option replaced. The source printed option (a) as "Arithmetic" and option (c) as "Arithmetical increase method" - the same method under two names, so the question had two correct answers. Option (a) has been replaced with "Logistic curve method", which is a genuine fourth forecasting method and makes the four options the four standard ones. The keyed answer is unchanged at (c).

examTip.trick: **ARITHMETIC (constant NUMBER per decade) suits a large, OLD, saturating city; GEOMETRIC (constant PERCENTAGE) suits a YOUNG, fast-growing one and gives the HIGHEST forecast.**
examTip.trap: **Applying the geometric method to a mature city badly overstates the future population** — and the works designed from it are oversized, under-used and unable to pay for themselves.
examTip.mnemonic: **Arithmetic and geometric are approximations to DIFFERENT PARTS of the same LOGISTIC curve** — geometric for the accelerating start, arithmetic for the straight middle. That turns four methods into one idea.

questions.stem: The topmost part of a pavement is called:
questions.solution:
**The surface course.**

**The layers of a flexible pavement, from the top down:**

| Layer | Typical thickness | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **SURFACE (wearing) course** | **25-50 mm** | **Resists ABRASION and weather; provides SKID RESISTANCE; WATERPROOFS the pavement** ← |
| **BINDER course** | **50-100 mm** | Distributes load; bonds the surface to the base |
| **BASE course** | **100-300 mm** | **The principal LOAD-SPREADING layer** |
| **SUB-BASE course** | **100-300 mm** | Further load spreading; drainage; separation |
| **COMPACTED SUBGRADE** | **150-300 mm** | The prepared natural ground |

> **The source reproduces exactly this table, and it also names the three bituminous applications between the layers:**

| Coat | Where | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **PRIME coat** | **On a GRANULAR base, before the bituminous layers** | **PENETRATES and seals the granular surface; provides a bond** |
| **TACK coat** | **BETWEEN two bituminous layers** | **BONDS them together** |
| **SEAL coat** | **ON TOP of the surface course** | **Seals an open-textured surface; improves skid resistance** |

> **The prime/tack distinction is the one examined: PRIME goes on a GRANULAR surface and soaks in; TACK goes BETWEEN BITUMINOUS layers and merely bonds.**

> **Using the wrong one leaves an unbonded interface — and an unbonded pavement is a stack of independent thin layers rather than a single thick one, which is a large loss of structural capacity.**

**Why the surface course has the most demanding specification despite being the thinnest:**

> **It is the only layer exposed to the tyre and the weather, so it must do several things no other layer does:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **SKID RESISTANCE** | **A safety requirement — the aggregate must resist POLISHING under traffic** ← |
| **Resistance to ABRASION** | Direct tyre contact |
| **WATERPROOFING** | **Keeps water out of the layers below, whose strength depends on staying dry** |
| **Resistance to RUTTING** | It carries the highest stresses |
| **Riding quality and low noise** | Serviceability |
| Resistance to ageing and cracking | Directly exposed to sun and air |

> **The WATERPROOFING function is the one most often overlooked and the most consequential structurally: the base and sub-base are GRANULAR, and a saturated granular layer loses much of its strength.**

> **So a 40 mm surface course protects 400 mm of pavement beneath it** — which is why a cracked or ravelled surface is a structural emergency rather than a cosmetic one, and why surface maintenance is the highest-return maintenance there is.

> **And SKID RESISTANCE depends on the aggregate's POLISHED STONE VALUE: some aggregates polish smooth under traffic and become slippery when wet, however sound they are otherwise.** That is a property tested for separately and specified for surface courses only.

**Why each distractor is wrong — and each is a real geometric element:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **Surface course** | ✓ **A LAYER of the pavement** |
| **CAMBER** | **The transverse SLOPE from the crown to the edges — a geometric rate, not a layer** ← |
| **SUPER ELEVATION** | **The transverse slope on a CURVE, banked toward the inside — again a rate** |
| **EXTRA WIDENING** | **Additional carriageway width provided on a curve — a plan dimension** |

> **So the question mixes two entirely different classifications: pavement LAYERS (a vertical, structural sequence) and geometric ELEMENTS (slopes and widths).**

> **Recognising that only one option names a LAYER answers the question with no knowledge of pavement composition at all** — and the stem's word "part" points at a physical component rather than a geometric property.

**And the contrast with a RIGID pavement, since the layer names differ:**

| | **FLEXIBLE pavement** | **RIGID pavement** |
|---|---|---|
| **Top layer** | **Bituminous SURFACE course** | **The concrete SLAB itself** |
| **Load spreading** | **Through SUCCESSIVE LAYERS, in a widening cone** | **By the SLAB'S OWN FLEXURAL STRENGTH, acting as a plate** |
| **Subgrade stress** | **Reduced layer by layer** | **Low and widely spread** |
| **Governing design property** | **Layer thicknesses and moduli; subgrade CBR** | **Concrete's FLEXURAL strength; modulus of subgrade reaction k** |
| **Failure criteria** | **FATIGUE cracking and RUTTING** | **Cracking from load and from WARPING** |

> **The essential difference is the mechanism: a FLEXIBLE pavement spreads load by depth, so its layers must each be strong enough for the stress reaching them; a RIGID pavement spreads load by BENDING, so the slab carries it almost regardless of what lies beneath.**

> **Which is why a rigid pavement tolerates a weak subgrade far better, and why it is far less forgiving of a differential settlement — the slab cannot follow the ground without cracking.**

examTip.trick: **Only one option names a LAYER.** Camber, superelevation and extra widening are GEOMETRIC elements — slopes and widths. The stem's word "part" points at a physical component.
examTip.trap: **PRIME coat goes on a GRANULAR base and soaks in; TACK coat goes BETWEEN BITUMINOUS layers and bonds.** Using the wrong one leaves an unbonded interface — a stack of thin layers instead of one thick one.
examTip.mnemonic: **A 40 mm surface course WATERPROOFS the 400 mm beneath it**, and granular layers lose strength when saturated. Which is why a cracked surface is a structural emergency, not a cosmetic one.

questions.stem: If the speed of the overtaken vehicle is 80 km/h, then the design speed is:
questions.solution:
**96 km/h.**

**The relation used in overtaking sight distance:**

> **V_b = V − 16**, where V is the DESIGN speed and V_b the speed of the OVERTAKEN (slower) vehicle, both in km/h.

> **Rearranged:  V = V_b + 16 = 80 + 16 = 96 km/h** ✓

> **The source's working is exactly this: V_b = V − 16, so V = V_b + 16 = 80 + 16 = 96 km/h.**

**Where the 16 comes from — it is a SPEED DIFFERENCE, not an arbitrary constant:**

> **The relation embodies an assumption about the overtaking manoeuvre: the OVERTAKING vehicle travels 16 km/h FASTER than the vehicle it passes.**

> **16 km/h is about 4.5 m/s, which is the speed differential IRC assumes for a normal overtaking manoeuvre.**

> **In some formulations it is written as 4.5 m/s directly**, and the two forms are the same assumption in different units — which is worth knowing, because a question may state either.

> **The logic: a driver overtakes by accelerating past, and the manoeuvre's duration depends on how much faster they travel.** A larger differential shortens the time and the distance; a smaller one lengthens both.

> **So the 16 km/h is a modelling assumption about driver behaviour, and it is the reason the design speed and the overtaken vehicle's speed are linked at all.**

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **80 kmph** | **The OVERTAKEN vehicle's speed, repeated — no relation applied** ← |
| **96 kmph** | ✓ |
| **100 kmph** | A plausible round design speed, but not what the relation gives |
| **106 kmph** | 80 + 26; wrong differential |

> **Option (a) is the designed trap for anyone who does not notice that a relation is being asked for**, and option (c) 100 is tempting because it is a standard design speed from the road-class table — **a real number in the wrong role.**

**Where the answer is used — the OVERTAKING SIGHT DISTANCE:**

> **OSD = d₁ + d₂ + d₃**

| Component | Meaning | Expression |
|---|---|---|
| **d₁** | **Distance travelled during the REACTION time, at the overtaken vehicle's speed** | **0.278 V_b t**, with t ≈ 2 s |
| **d₂** | **Distance covered during the ACTUAL overtaking manoeuvre** | **0.278 V_b T + 2s**, with T the manoeuvre time |
| **d₃** | **Distance travelled by the ONCOMING vehicle** | **0.278 V T** |

> **where s is the spacing between vehicles, s = 0.7 V_b + 6, and T = √(14.4 s / a)** with a the acceleration.

> **The essential structure is worth seeing even without the algebra: OSD must cover THREE movements — the overtaker's hesitation, the overtaking itself, and the approach of a vehicle coming the other way.**

> **The third component is why OSD is so much larger than stopping sight distance: it accounts for a vehicle travelling TOWARD you at the full design speed while you are in the wrong lane.**

**The three sight distances compared, since OSD is the largest:**

| Sight distance | Definition | At 96 km/h, roughly |
|---|---|---|
| **SSD — stopping** | **Distance to stop safely** | **~150 m** |
| **ISD — intermediate** | **TWICE the SSD** | **~300 m** |
| **OSD — overtaking** | **Distance to complete an overtaking manoeuvre** | **~600-640 m** |

> **So OSD is roughly FOUR TIMES the SSD**, and that ratio explains a great deal about road design:

> **Providing full OSD requires very long straight or gently curved lengths with clear visibility, which is expensive and often impossible in hilly terrain.**

> **Hence the INTERMEDIATE sight distance (2 × SSD) exists as a compromise: where full OSD cannot be economically provided, ISD is provided instead — enough to see and avoid, though not enough to overtake safely.**

> **And where even ISD cannot be achieved, overtaking must be PROHIBITED by marking and signing** — a solid centre line, which is the geometric admission that the sight distance is inadequate.

> **So a solid centre line on a hill road is not a caution; it is a design conclusion.**

**And the provision of OVERTAKING ZONES, since full OSD everywhere is impractical:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Overtaking zones provided at intervals** | **On a two-lane road, wherever the alignment allows** |
| **Minimum length of an overtaking zone** | **Three times the OSD (desirably five times)** |
| **Marked by signs at the start and end** | So drivers know where the opportunity is |
| Frequency | As often as the terrain permits |

> **The three-to-five times OSD requirement is worth noting, and the reason is behavioural: a zone barely long enough for one manoeuvre gives a driver no margin to decide, commit and complete.**

> **A zone must be long enough that a driver arriving anywhere within its first part can still complete the manoeuvre safely** — which is why it must be a multiple of the OSD rather than equal to it.

examTip.trick: **V_b = V − 16, so V = 80 + 16 = 96 km/h.** The 16 km/h (≈ 4.5 m/s) is the assumed SPEED DIFFERENTIAL of an overtaking manoeuvre, not an arbitrary constant.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) 80 repeats the overtaken vehicle's speed** — no relation applied. And option (c) 100 is a real design speed from the road-class table, in the wrong role.
examTip.mnemonic: **OSD ≈ 4 × SSD**, because it must also cover a vehicle approaching at full speed while you are in the wrong lane. Hence ISD (2 × SSD) as a compromise — and a SOLID CENTRE LINE is a design conclusion, not a caution.

questions.stem: The expected time for a PERT event will be ..... if the pessimistic time, optimistic time and most likely time are 10 days, 2 days and 3 days respectively.
questions.solution:
**4 days.**

**The PERT expected time formula:**

> **t_E = (t_o + 4 t_m + t_p) / 6**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **t_o** | **OPTIMISTIC time — the minimum, if everything goes to plan** | **2 days** |
| **t_m** | **MOST LIKELY time — under normal conditions** | **3 days** |
| **t_p** | **PESSIMISTIC time — the maximum, if everything goes against the plan** | **10 days** |

**The computation:**

> **t_E = (2 + 4×3 + 10) / 6 = (2 + 12 + 10) / 6 = 24 / 6 = 4 days** ✓

> **The source's working gives exactly this.**

**Reading the stem carefully — the values are given OUT OF ORDER:**

> **The stem lists them as "pessimistic, optimistic and most likely" — that is, 10, 2 and 3.**

> **The formula's natural order is optimistic, most likely, pessimistic — 2, 3, 10.**

> **So the values must be MATCHED TO THEIR NAMES rather than substituted in the order given**, and that is the trap the question sets.

> **A candidate who substitutes 10, 2, 3 in the formula's positions gets (10 + 8 + 3)/6 = 3.5 days** — which is not an option, so the error announces itself. **But a different mis-ordering could land on one.**

> **The defence is to write out the three named values before touching the formula**, which takes five seconds and removes the risk entirely.

**Why the weighting is (1, 4, 1)/6 — the reason is the assumed distribution:**

> **PERT assumes the activity duration follows a BETA DISTRIBUTION, and the formula is the mean of that distribution.**

> **The MOST LIKELY value is given FOUR TIMES the weight of either extreme**, because it is the modal value and by far the most probable.

> **The two extremes get equal weight of 1 each, and the divisor 6 is simply 1 + 4 + 1.**

> **So the formula is a WEIGHTED AVERAGE, and recognising that makes it memorable rather than arbitrary.**

> **Note the consequence in this problem: the most likely time is 3 days, and the expected time comes out at 4** — HIGHER than the most likely value.

> **That happens because the distribution is SKEWED: the pessimistic tail (10 days) is much further from the mode than the optimistic one (2 days).**

> **A long pessimistic tail pulls the mean upward, and that asymmetry is realistic — activities can overrun badly far more easily than they can finish early.**

> **Which is a genuinely useful observation: the expected duration of a risky activity EXCEEDS its most likely duration, and a plan built on most-likely times is systematically optimistic.**

**The variance and standard deviation, which are the other half of PERT:**

> **σ = (t_p − t_o) / 6**

> **σ² = [(t_p − t_o)/6]²**

> **Here: σ = (10 − 2)/6 = 8/6 = 1.33 days, so σ² = 1.78 days².**

> **The SPREAD between the extremes is the measure of UNCERTAINTY**, which is intuitive: a well-understood activity has a narrow range and a novel one a wide one.

> **And the rule that is most often got wrong:**

> **ALONG A PATH, VARIANCES ADD — NEVER STANDARD DEVIATIONS.**

> **σ_path = √(Σσ²)**

> **Adding standard deviations overstates the spread badly.** For three activities each with σ = 1.33, adding the standard deviations gives 4.0 while the correct value is √(3 × 1.78) = 2.31.

> **That is a substantial difference, and it goes in the unsafe direction if the error is made the other way.**

**What the statistics are FOR — the probability of completion:**

> **The project duration is treated as normally distributed about the sum of the critical path's expected times, with the path standard deviation above.**

> **The probability of finishing by a target date T is read from the standard normal table with:**

> **z = (T − T_E) / σ_path**

| z | Approximate probability |
|---|---|
| **−1** | **16 %** |
| **0** | **50 %** ← finishing by the expected date |
| **+1** | **84 %** |
| **+2** | **98 %** |

> **The z = 0 row carries the most important management message: THE PROBABILITY OF FINISHING BY THE EXPECTED DATE IS ONLY 50 PER CENT.**

> **The expected time is a MEAN, not a promise** — and a project committed to its expected duration is as likely to be late as early.

> **So a date that must be met requires a CONTINGENCY: to reach 84 per cent confidence, add one path standard deviation; for 98 per cent, add two.**

> **That is the whole practical value of PERT over CPM, and it is why the method exists at all: CPM gives a single date, and PERT gives a date with a stated confidence.**

**And the comparison, since the two are always examined together:**

| | **CPM** | **PERT** |
|---|---|---|
| **Time estimate** | **ONE per activity** | **THREE — optimistic, most likely, pessimistic** |
| **Nature** | **DETERMINISTIC** | **PROBABILISTIC** |
| **Orientation** | **ACTIVITY-oriented** | **EVENT-oriented** |
| **Suits** | **REPETITIVE work of known duration — construction** | **NOVEL work of uncertain duration — R&D, defence** |
| **Handles cost** | **YES — time-cost trade-off, crashing** | Not originally |
| **Developed** | **1957, DuPont** | **1958, US Navy (Polaris)** |

> **Each matches its information rather than being better: applying PERT's three estimates to routine concreting adds arithmetic and no knowledge, while applying CPM's single estimate to genuine research understates the risk.**

examTip.trick: **t_E = (t_o + 4t_m + t_p)/6 = (2 + 12 + 10)/6 = 4 days.** The most likely value carries FOUR times the weight of either extreme, and the divisor 6 is 1 + 4 + 1.
examTip.trap: **The stem lists the values OUT OF ORDER — pessimistic, optimistic, most likely.** Write out the three named values before touching the formula, or the substitution goes wrong.
examTip.mnemonic: **Note t_E = 4 exceeds the most likely 3**, because the pessimistic tail is longer — so a plan built on most-likely times is systematically optimistic. And **the probability of finishing by the EXPECTED date is only 50 %.**

questions.stem: A vehicle with a wheelbase of 6.5 m negotiates a 35 m radius curve. Find the off-tracking.
questions.solution:
**0.6 m (computed 0.604 m).**

**The off-tracking formula:**

> **OT = L² / (2R)**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **L** | **WHEELBASE — the distance between front and rear axles** | **6.5 m** |
| **R** | **RADIUS of the curve (to the front wheel path)** | **35 m** |

**The computation:**

> **OT = 6.5² / (2 × 35) = 42.25 / 70 = 0.6036 m ≈ 0.6 m** ✓

> **The source's working gives exactly this.**

**Why option (c) 0.62 m is the designed trap:**

> **0.6036 rounds to 0.60, not to 0.62** — and the two options differ by less than the rounding.

> **So the arithmetic must be carried properly: 42.25/70 = 0.60357, which is unambiguously nearer 0.6 than 0.62.**

> **A candidate who estimates 6.5²/70 as "about 0.62" will choose wrongly, and the option exists to punish exactly that.**

> **The clean route: 42.25/70 — note that 42/70 = 0.6 exactly, and the remaining 0.25/70 = 0.0036 barely moves it.** That decomposition settles the rounding in one step.

**What off-tracking IS — the physical picture:**

> **When a vehicle turns, its REAR wheels do NOT follow the path of its front wheels.**

> **The rear axle cuts INSIDE the curve, tracking a smaller radius than the front.**

> **OFF-TRACKING is the radial difference between the two paths** — how far inside the front wheel's path the rear wheel runs.

> **The longer the wheelbase and the sharper the curve, the greater the difference.**

> **Note the dependence: OT goes as L² and as 1/R.**

| Change | Effect on off-tracking |
|---|---|
| **DOUBLE the wheelbase** | **× 4** |
| **HALVE the radius** | **× 2** |
| **A long truck-trailer on a tight bend** | **Very large — which is why such vehicles need wide turning areas** ← |

> **The L² dependence is why articulated and multi-axle vehicles govern the design of turning geometry: a 12 m wheelbase on the same 35 m curve gives OT = 144/70 = 2.06 m**, more than three times the answer here.

**Where off-tracking is used — EXTRA WIDENING on curves:**

> **A carriageway must be WIDER on a curve than on a straight, and the extra width has TWO components:**

> **W_e = W_m + W_ps**

| Component | Cause | Expression |
|---|---|---|
| **MECHANICAL widening, W_m** | **OFF-TRACKING — the rear wheels cutting in** | **n L² / (2R)**, with n the number of lanes ← |
| **PSYCHOLOGICAL widening, W_ps** | **Drivers keep further from the edge and from each other on a curve** | **V / (9.5 √R)** |

> **So the off-tracking computed here IS the mechanical widening per lane**, and for a two-lane road it is doubled.

> **The PSYCHOLOGICAL component is the interesting one: it exists because drivers behave differently on a curve, not because the vehicle needs the space.**

> **A driver on a curve has less confidence about the path and about oncoming traffic, so they position the vehicle further from the edge line and further from the centre line.**

> **Codes recognise that and provide for it explicitly** — which is a rare and sensible instance of a design standard accounting for behaviour rather than only for mechanics.

> **And note that the psychological term depends on the SPEED V while the mechanical one does not.** Off-tracking is pure geometry and happens at any speed; driver hesitation grows with speed.

**A worked example, to show the two components together:**

> **For a two-lane road, V = 50 km/h, R = 35 m, L = 6.5 m:**

> **W_m = 2 × 6.5²/(2 × 35) = 2 × 0.604 = 1.21 m**

> **W_ps = 50/(9.5 × √35) = 50/(9.5 × 5.92) = 50/56.2 = 0.89 m**

> **Total extra widening = 1.21 + 0.89 = 2.10 m**

> **So a 7.0 m two-lane carriageway becomes about 9.1 m on that curve** — a substantial addition, and one that must be tapered in over the transition curve rather than appearing abruptly.

**Where the widening is applied, since the detail matters:**

| Practice | Note |
|---|---|
| **Applied on the INSIDE of the curve** | **Because that is where the rear wheels cut in** ← |
| **Sometimes split between inside and outside** | Where the alignment or the drainage requires it |
| **Attained progressively over the TRANSITION curve** | **The same length over which superelevation is attained** |
| **Fully developed at the start of the circular curve** | And removed over the exit transition |

> **Applying the widening over the transition length, together with the superelevation, is what makes a curve comfortable to drive: the width, the banking and the curvature all develop together and in step.**

> **A curve where the widening appears abruptly at the circular arc gives the driver a sudden change of available width just where the steering demand is greatest** — which defeats the purpose of providing it.

> **So the transition curve is doing three jobs at once: introducing the curvature, attaining the superelevation, and developing the extra widening.** That is why it is the element whose absence is most felt, and why a curve without one is uncomfortable even when its radius is adequate.

examTip.trick: **OT = L²/(2R) = 42.25/70 = 0.604 m.** Decompose it: 42/70 = 0.6 exactly, and the remaining 0.25/70 barely moves it — which settles the rounding at once.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) 0.62 differs from the answer by less than the rounding**, and exists to punish an estimate. Carry the arithmetic: 0.6036 is unambiguously nearer 0.6.
examTip.mnemonic: **OT goes as L² and 1/R**, so a 12 m wheelbase on the same curve gives 2.06 m — three times as much. And extra widening = MECHANICAL (this off-tracking) + PSYCHOLOGICAL V/(9.5√R), the second existing because drivers behave differently on curves.

questions.stem: The area of a channel section is 8 m² and the wetted perimeter is 8 m. Calculate the bed slope of the channel if the discharge is 33.33 m³/s and Manning's coefficient is 0.012.
questions.solution:
**1 in 400.**

**Step 1 — the hydraulic radius:**

> **R = A / P = 8 / 8 = 1 m**

> **The numbers are chosen so that R = 1 exactly, which simplifies everything that follows — R^{2/3} = 1.**

**Step 2 — Manning's equation in discharge form:**

> **Q = (1/n) A R^{2/3} S^{1/2}**

> **33.33 = (1/0.012) × 8 × 1^{2/3} × S^{1/2}**

> **33.33 = 83.33 × 8 × S^{1/2}**

> **33.33 = 666.67 × S^{1/2}**

**Step 3 — solve for S:**

> **S^{1/2} = 33.33 / 666.67 = 0.05**

> **S = 0.05² = 0.0025 = 1/400** ✓

> **So the bed slope is 1 in 400.**

> **The source's working follows this route exactly.**

**Why the numbers are so convenient — and it is worth noticing:**

> **R = 1 makes R^{2/3} = 1, removing the awkward exponent entirely.**

> **And 1/0.012 = 83.33, times 8, gives 666.67 — so S^{1/2} = 33.33/666.67 = 0.05, a clean two-figure result.**

> **When a problem's numbers collapse this neatly, it is a sign the arithmetic is on the intended path** — and conversely, an awkward intermediate suggests a wrong step.

> **The step most likely to go wrong is FORGETTING THE SQUARE ROOT: solving 33.33 = 666.67 × S would give S = 0.05 = 1 in 20, which is a mountain torrent rather than a canal.**

> **That magnitude check catches it: canal slopes are of the order of 1 in a few hundred to 1 in a few thousand, never 1 in 20.**

**Manning's equation and its two forms:**

| Form | Expression |
|---|---|
| **VELOCITY** | **V = (1/n) R^{2/3} S^{1/2}** |
| **DISCHARGE** | **Q = A V = (1/n) A R^{2/3} S^{1/2}** ← used here |

> **The discharge form is simply the velocity form multiplied by the area, and using it directly avoids computing V as a separate step.**

> **Here V = Q/A = 33.33/8 = 4.17 m/s — which is worth computing as a check, because it is high.**

| Velocity | Assessment |
|---|---|
| **Below ~0.3 m/s** | **Silting risk** |
| **0.6-2.0 m/s** | **The normal design range for a lined canal** |
| **4.17 m/s** | **HIGH — acceptable only in a well-lined channel; would scour an earth channel badly** ← |

> **And n = 0.012 confirms the picture: that is a SMOOTH CEMENT-PLASTERED or well-finished concrete surface**, consistent with a velocity of 4 m/s.

> **So the problem's data are internally consistent — a smooth lined channel on a moderate slope carrying a fast flow — and noticing that consistency is a check on the answer rather than a decoration.**

**The Manning roughness values, since n = 0.012 is one of them:**

| Surface | Manning's n |
|---|---|
| **Smooth cement plaster** | **0.010-0.013** ← |
| **Concrete lining** | **0.013-0.017** |
| **Brick lining** | **0.015** |
| **Earth channel, clean and straight** | **0.018-0.025** |
| **Earth channel, weedy or winding** | **0.025-0.040** |
| Natural stream with boulders | 0.040-0.070 |

> **0.013 for concrete and 0.025 for a clean earth channel are the two values worth having automatically** — most canal problems use one or the other.

**And a note on the exponent, since it is where Manning differs from Chezy:**

> **Manning:  V = (1/n) R^{2/3} S^{1/2}**

> **Chezy:  V = C √(RS) = C R^{1/2} S^{1/2}**

> **Equating them gives  C = R^{1/6}/n**, the exponent being simply 2/3 − 1/2 = 1/6.
