> **And that relation explains why Manning displaced Chezy: since C depends on R, a value of C measured in one channel cannot be carried to a channel of different size.**

> **Manning's n can be, which is why every textbook tabulates n and not C.**

> **Note also that Manning's equation is NOT dimensionally homogeneous — n carries dimensions of s/m^{1/3} in SI** — which is why its numerical value differs between SI and FPS units, and why using an SI n in an FPS formula is a factor-of-1.5 error.

**A final observation on the slope itself:**

> **S = 1 in 400 = 0.0025 is a steep gradient for a large canal and a normal one for a lined power channel or a steep hillside conveyance.**

> **Main irrigation canals typically run at 1 in 4,000 to 1 in 10,000** — far flatter — because a canal must lose as little height as possible in order to command the land it serves.

> **Every metre of head given up to friction is a metre of command lost**, and that is the constraint that makes canal alignment such a careful business: the channel must be steep enough to be self-cleansing and flat enough to keep its head.

examTip.trap: **Forgetting the SQUARE ROOT gives S = 0.05 = 1 in 20** — a mountain torrent, not a canal. The magnitude check catches it: canal slopes run from a few hundred to a few thousand.
examTip.mnemonic: **Check the velocity too: V = Q/A = 4.17 m/s, which suits n = 0.012 (smooth plaster) and would scour an earth channel.** Internal consistency is a check on the answer, not a decoration.

questions.stem: Calculate the Froude number for a channel having a discharge of 261.03 m³/s, a cross-sectional area of 42 m² and a top width of 6 m.
questions.solution:
**0.75 — a subcritical flow.**

**Step 1 — the mean velocity:**

> **V = Q / A = 261.03 / 42 = 6.215 m/s**

**Step 2 — the HYDRAULIC DEPTH:**

> **D = A / T**, where T is the TOP WIDTH.

> **D = 42 / 6 = 7 m**

> **This is the step the question is really testing, and it is easy to get wrong — see below.**

**Step 3 — the Froude number:**

> **Fr = V / √(g D)**

> **= 6.215 / √(9.81 × 7)**

> **= 6.215 / √68.67**

> **= 6.215 / 8.287 = 0.75** ✓

> **The source's working follows exactly this route and notes the conclusion: SUBCRITICAL.**

**Why the length scale is the HYDRAULIC DEPTH, not the hydraulic radius:**

> **The two are different quantities, and confusing them is the trap this question sets:**

| Quantity | Definition | Uses |
|---|---|---|
| **HYDRAULIC RADIUS R** | **A / P (area ÷ WETTED PERIMETER)** | **RESISTANCE — Manning's and Chezy's equations** |
| **HYDRAULIC DEPTH D** | **A / T (area ÷ TOP WIDTH)** | **The FROUDE number and wave celerity** ← |

> **The reason they differ in role is physical: RESISTANCE depends on the boundary the water rubs against, so it needs the WETTED PERIMETER.**

> **WAVE SPEED depends on the free surface, so it needs the TOP WIDTH.**

> **The question gives the TOP WIDTH explicitly and does NOT give the wetted perimeter** — which is the clue that the hydraulic depth is wanted. **A well-set question supplies exactly the data its intended method needs.**

> **For a WIDE RECTANGULAR channel both R and D approach the flow depth y, so the distinction vanishes** — which is why it is often glossed over and why it matters here, where the section is deep and narrow (42 m² through a 6 m top width).

**What the answer MEANS — and this is the substance of the Froude number:**

> **Fr = V / √(gD) compares the FLOW velocity with the speed of a SHALLOW-WATER WAVE, which is √(gD).**

| Froude number | Regime | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **Fr < 1** | **SUBCRITICAL (tranquil)** | **Waves CAN travel upstream; the flow is controlled from DOWNSTREAM** ← Fr = 0.75 |
| **Fr = 1** | **CRITICAL** | **Minimum specific energy for the discharge** |
| **Fr > 1** | **SUPERCRITICAL (rapid)** | **Waves CANNOT travel upstream; the flow is controlled from UPSTREAM** |

> **So Fr = 0.75 means the flow is SUBCRITICAL: it is moving more slowly than a disturbance would travel, so a change made downstream is felt upstream.**

> **That has a direct practical consequence: the depth in this channel is determined by conditions DOWNSTREAM — a weir, a gate, a junction or the tailwater level.**

> **And it means the water-surface profile must be computed by working UPSTREAM from a downstream control**, which is the opposite direction to a supercritical reach.

> **Getting that direction wrong is the commonest error in gradually varied flow computation, and the Froude number is what determines it.**

**Why the CRITICAL condition matters so much:**

| Property of critical flow | Note |
|---|---|
| **Specific energy is MINIMUM for the given discharge** | **The defining property** |
| **Discharge is MAXIMUM for the given specific energy** | The dual statement |
| **Fr = 1 exactly** | — |
| **The flow can be CONTROLLED there** | **A critical section fixes a unique depth-discharge relation** ← |

> **The last row is why critical flow is engineered deliberately: a section forced to critical depth becomes a MEASURING DEVICE, because the depth then determines the discharge uniquely.**

> **That is the principle of a VENTURI FLUME, a broad-crested weir and a standing-wave flume** — force the flow through critical and one measurement gives the flow rate.

> **And it is why a critical section is a CONTROL: profiles are computed away from it in both directions, subcritical upstream and supercritical downstream.**

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Likely origin |
|---|---|
| **0.65** | A near value; no clean derivation |
| **0.72** | Rounding of an intermediate |
| **0.38** | **Roughly half the answer — possibly from using 2D or a mis-taken root** |
| **0.75** | ✓ |

> **The options are deliberately close, so an estimate will not discriminate** — the calculation must be carried through.

> **But the SIGN of the answer can be checked instantly: 6.215 m/s against a wave speed of 8.29 m/s is clearly LESS THAN ONE, so the flow is subcritical and any option above 1 could be rejected on sight.** None is offered, which is itself a hint that the intended answer is subcritical.

**And a caution about the velocity, worth noting:**

> **6.2 m/s is a very high velocity for an open channel — well above the scouring limit for any earth channel and high even for a lined one.**

> **So this is either a steep lined chute, a spillway channel, or a hypothetical set of numbers.** Recognising that the data describe an unusual channel is a legitimate observation, and it does not affect the arithmetic.

examTip.trap: **The Froude number uses the HYDRAULIC DEPTH D = A/T (top width), not the hydraulic radius R = A/P (wetted perimeter).** Resistance needs the boundary; wave speed needs the free surface. The question gives T and not P — the clue to which is wanted.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fr < 1 subcritical: waves travel upstream, so control is DOWNSTREAM and profiles are computed upstream from it.** Getting that direction wrong is the commonest error in gradually varied flow.

questions.stem: A beam of span L is fixed at end A and has a roller at end B. There is an INTERNAL HINGE at C, a distance L/3 from the fixed end. A load of 10 kN is applied AT the internal hinge. Find the reaction at end B.
questions.solution:
**Zero.**

**The reasoning — take moments about the internal hinge, for the RIGHT-HAND portion only:**

> **An INTERNAL HINGE cannot transmit a MOMENT. That is its defining property, and it supplies the extra equation that makes the beam solvable.**

> **So consider the segment CB — from the hinge to the roller — as a free body.**

| Force acting on segment CB | Note |
|---|---|
| **The hinge reaction at C** | **Acts THROUGH C, so it has no moment about C** |
| **The roller reaction R_B at B** | **At a distance 2L/3 from C** |
| **The 10 kN load** | **Applied AT the hinge — so it is at C, and has NO moment about C** ← |

> **Taking moments about C for the segment CB:**

> **ΣM_C = 0:  R_B × (2L/3) = 0**

> **Therefore R_B = 0** ✓

> **The source's working is exactly this: ΣM_right = 0, R_B × 2L/3 = 0, so R_B = 0.**

**Why the answer is zero — the physical explanation:**

> **The load sits EXACTLY AT the hinge.**

> **Everything to the right of the hinge — the segment CB — carries NO applied load at all.**

> **A weightless segment with a pin at one end and a roller at the other, and no load between them, carries nothing.** Its roller reaction must be zero.

> **So the entire 10 kN is carried by the FIXED END A, and the segment CB is merely along for the ride.**

> **That is worth stating plainly because it makes the result intuitive rather than a piece of algebra: the right-hand part of the beam is unloaded, so its support does nothing.**

**The critical detail — that the load is AT the hinge:**

> **This is what makes the answer exactly zero, and it is the whole point of the question.**

> **If the load were even slightly to the RIGHT of the hinge, R_B would not be zero:**

| Load position | R_B |
|---|---|
| **AT the hinge (distance 0 from C)** | **ZERO** ← as asked |
| **At the midpoint of CB (L/3 from C)** | **10 × (L/3)/(2L/3) = 5 kN** |
| **At B itself** | **10 kN** |
| **To the LEFT of the hinge** | **ZERO — again, since segment CB is unloaded** |

> **So R_B varies from 0 to 10 kN depending purely on where the load sits relative to the hinge**, and reading the position from the stem is the whole task.

> **Options (b) 2.5 kN and (c) 7.5 kN correspond to load positions at L/9 and L/2 along CB respectively** — plausible answers to a slightly different question.

> **And option (d) 10 kN is what you get if the load were at B.**

> **So all three distractors are correct answers to the same problem with the load somewhere else, which is a well-made option set.**

**Why the internal hinge matters — the determinacy count:**

> **Without the hinge, this beam would be INDETERMINATE:**

| Element | Count |
|---|---|
| **Reactions: fixed end (3) + roller (1)** | **4 unknowns** |
| **Equations of equilibrium** | **3** |
| **Degree of indeterminacy WITHOUT the hinge** | **4 − 3 = 1** |
| **The internal hinge supplies ONE extra equation (ΣM = 0 at the hinge)** | **−1** |
| **Net degree of indeterminacy** | **ZERO — the beam is JUST DETERMINATE** ← |

> **So the hinge is not an incidental feature: it is what makes the beam solvable by statics alone.**

> **The general rule: EACH INTERNAL HINGE REDUCES the degree of indeterminacy BY ONE**, because it removes the beam's ability to carry moment at that point and thereby supplies one additional condition.

> **That is why internal hinges are deliberately introduced into long continuous structures — a three-hinged arch is the classic case, made determinate by exactly this device.**

**The general procedure for a beam with an internal hinge, since it is worth having:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **CUT the beam at the hinge and treat the two segments separately** |
| **2** | **Write ΣM = 0 about the HINGE for the segment with FEWER unknowns** ← |
| **3** | **That gives one reaction directly** |
| **4** | **Then use overall equilibrium (ΣV = 0, ΣH = 0, ΣM = 0) for the rest** |

> **Step 2 is the key: choosing the segment with fewer unknowns.**

> **Here the right-hand segment has only R_B unknown (the hinge force passes through the moment centre), so one equation solves it immediately.**

> **Taking moments about the hinge for the LEFT segment would involve the fixed end's three unknowns and get nowhere** — so the choice of segment is what makes the problem a one-liner rather than a simultaneous solution.

> **That is the transferable technique: at an internal hinge, always take moments about the hinge for the simpler side.**

**And the completion of the analysis, for the record:**

> **With R_B = 0, overall vertical equilibrium gives the fixed end's vertical reaction:**

> **V_A = 10 kN**

> **And overall moment equilibrium about A gives the fixing moment:**

> **M_A = 10 × (L/3) = 10L/3 kNm**

> **So the fixed end carries the whole load and the whole moment**, which confirms the physical reading: the beam behaves as a cantilever of length L/3 with the segment CB hanging inertly off its end.

examTip.trick: **Take moments about the HINGE for the right-hand segment.** The load is AT the hinge and the hinge force acts THROUGH it, so both have zero moment — leaving R_B × 2L/3 = 0, hence R_B = 0.
examTip.trap: **All three distractors are correct answers with the load somewhere ELSE** — 2.5 kN, 7.5 kN and 10 kN correspond to other load positions. Reading that the load is AT the hinge is the whole task.
examTip.mnemonic: **Each internal hinge REDUCES indeterminacy by one**, which is what makes this beam determinate. And the technique: **at a hinge, take moments about it for the side with FEWER unknowns** — that turns the problem into one line.

questions.stem: How many members are nominated by the Nepal Engineering Council itself?
questions.solution:
**Two.**

**The provision:**

> **Under the Nepal Engineering Council Act, TWO members are nominated BY THE COUNCIL ITSELF — holders of a bachelor's degree with at least seven years' experience, of whom AT LEAST ONE MUST BE A WOMAN.**

> **The source's own list of the Council's composition gives it as item 9: "Members = 2 (Bachelor's degree + 7 years experience, at least one woman, NOMINATED BY COUNCIL)".**

> **Every other member is appointed, elected or nominated by someone else — the Government of Nepal, or the Nepal Engineers' Association.** These two are the Council's own nominations.

**The full composition of the Council, since this question is one of a family:**

| Position | Number | How appointed | Qualification |
|---|---|---|---|
| **CHAIRMAN (President)** | **1** | **Nominated by GoN** | **Bachelor's + 15 years** |
| **VICE CHAIRMAN** | **1** | **Nominated by GoN** | **Bachelor's + 10 years** |
| **Members, one from each province** | **7** | **Nominated by GoN** | **Bachelor's + 7 years; at least THREE women** |
| **President of the NEA** | **1** | Ex officio | — |
| **Members ELECTED from the NEA** | **5** | **Directly elected** | **Tenure 4 years** |
| **Campus chief of an engineering campus** | **1** | Nominated by GoN | — |
| **Representative, Institute of Engineering, TU** | **1** | Nominated by GoN | — |
| **Representative of universities teaching engineering** | **1** | Nominated by GoN | — |
| **Members nominated BY THE COUNCIL** | **2** | **By the Council itself** | **Bachelor's + 7 years; at least ONE woman** ← |
| **MEMBER SECRETARY (Registrar)** | **1** | — | **Bachelor's + 10 years** |

> **So the Council is a mixed body of about twenty-one members, drawn from government, the profession, the universities and its own nomination.**

**Why a regulator's board is deliberately mixed — the design principle:**

| Element | What it contributes |
|---|---|
| **GOVERNMENT nominees** | **Public accountability — the regulator serves the public, not the profession** |
| **ELECTED practitioners (from the NEA)** | **Technical judgement, and legitimacy with those being regulated** |
| **ACADEMIC representatives** | **Judgement on qualifications and on institutions** |
| **The COUNCIL'S OWN nominees** | **Flexibility to bring in expertise or representation the other routes have missed** ← |
| Registrar (executive) | Continuity and administration |

> **The Council's own nominations serve a specific purpose worth understanding: they let the Council fill GAPS.**

> **If the elected and nominated members between them happen to leave a discipline, a region or a perspective unrepresented, these two places can correct it.**

> **And the requirement that at least one be a woman is a deliberate provision applied at two points in the composition** — three of the seven provincial members and one of the Council's two nominees.

> **So the Act builds in representation rather than leaving it to the outcome of appointments**, which is a policy choice made explicit in the statute.

**Why the mixture is necessary rather than merely political:**

> **A regulator composed ENTIRELY of practitioners risks becoming a GUILD** — protecting its members' interests rather than the public's, and reluctant to discipline its own.

> **A regulator with NO practitioners lacks the technical judgement to regulate at all** — it cannot assess whether a piece of engineering was competent.

> **So the mixture is the only arrangement that can do the job**, and the proportions are the substance of the Act's design.

**The regulatory facts that recur across these papers, gathered:**

| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| **NEC Act** | **2055 BS (1998 AD)** |
| **NEC Regulation** | **2057 BS** |
| **Bachelor's programme recognition** | **2066/06/23** |
| **Master's programme recognition** | **2076/09/06** |
| **First amendment to the Act** | **2079/05/05** |
| **Nature of the Council** | **AUTONOMOUS body** |
| **Who approves its rules** | **Government of Nepal** |
| **Chairman** | **Bachelor's + 15 years** |
| **Vice chairman** | **Bachelor's + 10 years** |
| **Members from each province** | **7 (at least 3 women)** |
| **NEA-elected members** | **5, tenure 4 years** |
| **Members nominated by the COUNCIL** | **2 (at least 1 woman)** ← |
| **Registrar / Member Secretary** | **Bachelor's + 10 years** |
| **Minimum qualification to register** | **Bachelor's degree** |
| **NEA's own legal basis** | **Social Service Act** |

> **This is a small, closed body of facts, and it appears in almost every sitting** — several times in some papers, including this one.

> **It is therefore among the cheapest marks in the examination, and the practical advice is to learn the set AS A SET rather than meeting each fact separately.**

> **The internal logic helps: the seniority requirements rise with the office (7 years for a member, 10 for the vice chairman and registrar, 15 for the chairman), and every appointing route is represented.** Reasoning from that structure recovers most of the table.

examTip.trick: **TWO members are nominated by the Council itself** — bachelor's degree plus seven years, at least one a woman. Every other member comes from GoN, the NEA or ex officio.
examTip.trap: **Distinguish the appointing ROUTE, not just the count.** The Council has 7 provincial members (GoN), 5 elected (NEA) and 2 of its own — three different routes with three different numbers.
examTip.mnemonic: **Seniority rises with office: 7 years for a member, 10 for the vice chairman and registrar, 15 for the chairman.** And the Council's own two nominations exist to fill GAPS the other routes leave — a discipline, a region or a perspective.

questions.stem: A Los Angeles abrasion test was conducted in the standard manner on an aggregate sample of 8 kg, and the weight of aggregate retained on the 1.7 mm sieve was found to be 6.2 kg. The Los Angeles abrasion value of the aggregate is:
questions.solution:
**22.5 per cent.**

**The formula:**

> **Abrasion value = (W₁ − W₂) / W₁ × 100**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **W₁** | **Original weight of the sample** | **8 kg** |
| **W₂** | **Weight RETAINED on the 1.7 mm sieve after the test** | **6.2 kg** |
| **W₁ − W₂** | **Weight WORN AWAY (passing 1.7 mm)** | **1.8 kg** |

**The computation:**

> **Abrasion value = (8 − 6.2)/8 × 100 = 1.8/8 × 100 = 0.225 × 100 = 22.5 %** ✓

> **The source's working gives exactly this.**

**Why the numerator is the LOSS, not the retained weight — the trap the options exploit:**

> **The abrasion value measures how much of the aggregate WORE AWAY, so it is the LOSS expressed as a percentage of the original.**

> **A candidate who computes 6.2/8 = 77.5 per cent has found the RETAINED fraction, which is the complement.**

> **And note the relation: 22.5 + 77.5 = 100.** So the two figures are two ways of describing the same result — **but only the LOSS is the abrasion value.**

> **Option (c) 18.26 per cent is worth examining: it is 1.8/9.86, or roughly the loss divided by something other than 8** — a plausible-looking figure with no clean derivation, placed to catch a mis-set division.

> **The clean route is 1.8/8, and it is worth noting that 1.8/8 = 0.225 exactly, with no rounding** — which is a sign the arithmetic is on the intended path.

**The 1.7 mm sieve, since it defines what counts as "worn away":**

> **The test tumbles the aggregate in a steel drum with steel spheres (the ABRASIVE CHARGE) for a specified number of revolutions.**

> **The material is then sieved on a 1.7 mm sieve: whatever PASSES is deemed to have been abraded away; whatever is RETAINED survived.**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Sieve for separating the worn material** | **1.7 mm** |
| **Number of revolutions** | **500 (or 1000 for graded coarser samples)** |
| **Speed of the drum** | **30-33 rev/min** |
| **Abrasive charge** | **Steel spheres, about 48 mm diameter, 390-445 g each** |
| Number of spheres | **6 to 12, depending on the grading** |

> **The steel spheres are the feature that distinguishes the Los Angeles test from the older DEVAL abrasion test**, which tumbles the aggregate without them.

> **The spheres impose an IMPACT component as well as pure rubbing** — so the Los Angeles test is more severe and correlates better with real pavement wear, which is why it displaced Deval.

**The permissible limits, which is what the answer must be judged against:**

| Pavement layer | Maximum Los Angeles abrasion value |
|---|---|
| **WBM base course** | **60 %** |
| **Bituminous macadam / base** | **50 %** |
| **Bituminous surface dressing, carpet** | **35 %** |
| **Bituminous concrete (surface course)** | **30 %** |
| **Cement concrete pavement (wearing surface)** | **30-35 %** |

> **So 22.5 per cent is a GOOD aggregate, acceptable for every layer including a bituminous concrete surface course** — and interpreting the answer, rather than merely computing it, is worth doing.

> **Note the pattern in the limits: the HIGHER the layer in the pavement, the STRICTER the requirement.**

> **The reason is direct exposure: a surface-course aggregate is rubbed by every tyre, while a base-course aggregate is protected by everything above it.**

> **Which is why options (a) 35 and (b) 45 are well chosen as distractors — they are LIMIT VALUES from that table, offered as if they were results.**

**What the test measures, and how it sits among the aggregate tests:**

| Test | Measures | Property |
|---|---|---|
| **LOS ANGELES ABRASION** | **Resistance to WEAR by rubbing and impact** | **HARDNESS** ← |
| **CRUSHING value** | **Resistance to a gradually applied compressive load** | **STRENGTH** |
| **IMPACT value** | **Resistance to a SUDDEN shock** | **TOUGHNESS** |
| **SOUNDNESS** | **Resistance to accelerated WEATHERING cycles** | **DURABILITY** |
| **Water absorption** | Porosity | Durability indicator |
| **Shape (flakiness, elongation)** | Particle geometry | Workability, interlock |
| **Polished stone value** | **Resistance to POLISHING under traffic** | **SKID RESISTANCE** |

> **Four principal mechanical tests, four distinct properties — and the abrasion test is the hardness one.**

> **The POLISHED STONE VALUE deserves a note because it is the one most often overlooked and is specific to surface courses: some aggregates are hard and durable and still POLISH SMOOTH under traffic, becoming slippery when wet.**

> **So a surface aggregate must pass abrasion AND polishing requirements** — they measure different things, and an aggregate can be excellent at one and poor at the other.

> **Limestone is the classic example: durable enough, and it polishes badly, which is why it is avoided in wearing courses on high-speed roads even where it is locally abundant.**

examTip.trick: **Abrasion value = LOSS ÷ original × 100 = (8 − 6.2)/8 = 22.5 %.** The numerator is what WORE AWAY, not what survived.
examTip.trap: **Options (a) 35 % and (b) 45 % are LIMIT values from the specification table**, offered as results. And 6.2/8 = 77.5 % is the retained fraction — the complement, not the abrasion value.
examTip.mnemonic: **The higher the layer, the stricter the limit** — WBM 60 %, bituminous macadam 50 %, surface dressing 35 %, bituminous concrete 30 % — because a surface aggregate is rubbed by every tyre. So 22.5 % passes everywhere.

questions.stem: What is the net section area of a steel plate 40 cm wide and 10 mm thick with one bolt, if the diameter of the bolt hole is 18 mm?
questions.solution:
**38.2 cm².**

**Step 1 — the GROSS area:**

> **Convert to consistent units first. Thickness = 10 mm = 1 cm.**

> **A_gross = width × thickness = 40 × 1 = 40 cm²**

**Step 2 — the area removed by the hole:**

> **Hole diameter = 18 mm = 1.8 cm**

> **Area of the hole through the plate = 1.8 × 1 = 1.8 cm²**

**Step 3 — the NET area:**

> **A_net = A_gross − (area of the hole)**

> **= 40 − 1.8 = 38.2 cm²** ✓

> **The source's working gives exactly this.**

**Why the deduction is (diameter × thickness) — the physical picture:**

> **The NET SECTION is the cross-section on a plane THROUGH THE HOLE, where the plate is narrowest.**

> **On that plane the plate's width is reduced by the hole's diameter, and the deduction is therefore d × t.**

> **It is NOT the hole's circular area (πd²/4) — that is a different quantity altogether and answers no structural question.**

> **A candidate who deducts πd²/4 = π(1.8)²/4 = 2.54 cm² gets 37.46 cm², which is not offered — so the error announces itself here, but it is worth guarding against.**

**Why the net section matters — the two failure modes of a tension member:**

| Failure mode | Governed by | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **YIELDING of the GROSS section** | **A_gross × f_y / γ_m0** | **A DUCTILE failure — the whole length stretches** |
| **RUPTURE of the NET section** | **0.9 × A_net × f_u / γ_m1** | **A BRITTLE failure — fracture at the hole** ← |
| **BLOCK SHEAR** | Combination of shear and tension areas | Also brittle |

> **The design strength is the LEAST of the three, and the net section governs whenever the holes remove enough material.**

> **The important asymmetry: gross-section yielding is DUCTILE and net-section rupture is BRITTLE.**

> **So the code applies a LARGER partial safety factor to the rupture case (γ_m1 = 1.25 against γ_m0 = 1.10) and an additional 0.9 factor** — deliberately biasing the design toward the ductile mode.

> **That is capacity design applied to a connection: make the brittle mode stronger, so that if the member is ever overloaded it yields visibly rather than fracturing suddenly.**

**Why the hole is bigger than the bolt, since the question gives the HOLE diameter:**

> **The hole is made LARGER than the bolt to allow for fabrication and erection tolerance:**

| Bolt diameter | Hole diameter (standard clearance) |
|---|---|
| **Up to 14 mm** | **Bolt + 1 mm** |
| **16 to 24 mm** | **Bolt + 2 mm** |
| **Above 24 mm** | **Bolt + 3 mm** |

> **So an 18 mm hole normally carries a 16 mm bolt.**

> **And the deduction uses the HOLE size, not the bolt size** — because it is the hole that removes the material, whatever fills it.

> **Note also that for a hole formed by PUNCHING rather than drilling, some codes require an additional 2 mm deduction**, because punching damages the material around the hole.

**The STAGGERED hole case, since a single hole is the simplest one:**

> **Where holes are STAGGERED, the failure plane may run diagonally, and the net width is computed by the CHAIN rule:**

> **b_net = b − Σd + Σ(p_s²/4g)**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **b** | Gross width |
| **Σd** | **Sum of ALL hole diameters on the chosen failure path** |
| **p_s** | **STAGGER (the pitch measured along the member axis)** |
| **g** | **GAUGE (the transverse spacing between the hole lines)** |

> **The p_s²/4g term ADDS BACK area, because a diagonal path is LONGER than a straight one and so retains more material.**

> **And every possible failure path must be checked — the critical one is whichever gives the SMALLEST net width, and it is not always obvious which.**

> **That is why staggering holes is a real design device: it lengthens the failure path and recovers some of the area the holes removed**, letting a connection carry more load for the same number of bolts.

**And a note on the units, since three of the four options use different ones:**

| Option | Value | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **38.2 cm²** | ✓ | **= 3820 mm²** |
| **24 cm²** | — | No clean derivation |
| **578 mm²** | **= 5.78 cm²** | **Two orders of magnitude too small for a 40 cm plate** |
| **465 mm²** | **= 4.65 cm²** | **Likewise** |

> **Options (c) and (d) can be rejected on MAGNITUDE alone: a plate 40 cm wide and 1 cm thick has a gross area of 40 cm² = 4000 mm², so a net area of 578 mm² would mean 86 per cent of the plate had been removed by a single 18 mm hole.**

> **That impossibility check costs nothing and eliminates half the options** — and it is worth making a habit of, because option sets in this examination frequently mix cm² and mm² precisely to exploit unit carelessness.

examTip.trick: **Deduct diameter × thickness, not the hole's circular area.** A_net = 40 × 1 − 1.8 × 1 = 38.2 cm². Convert the thickness to cm first.
examTip.trap: **Options (c) and (d) are in mm² and are two orders of magnitude too small** — a 40 cm × 1 cm plate has 4000 mm² gross, so 578 mm² would mean one 18 mm hole removed 86 % of it. Reject on magnitude alone.
examTip.mnemonic: **Gross-section yielding is DUCTILE; net-section rupture is BRITTLE** — so the code applies a larger safety factor to the rupture case, biasing design toward the ductile mode. And **staggering holes lengthens the failure path** and recovers area.

questions.stem: A broad-crested weir (Cw = 1.5) having a length of 30 m and a height of 2.5 m is placed across a river having an RL of the upstream bed of 1080 m. If the discharge passing the weir is 90 m³/s, find the RL of the flood wall. Take the free board as 1.2 m.
questions.solution:
**RL 1085.28 m.**

**Step 1 — find the head over the weir crest.**

> **Broad-crested weir discharge:  Q = C_w L H^{3/2}**

> **90 = 1.5 × 30 × H^{3/2}**

> **90 = 45 H^{3/2}**

> **H^{3/2} = 2**

> **H = 2^{2/3} = 1.587 m**

> **The source's working gives exactly this: H = 1.587 m.**

**Step 2 — build up the levels from the bed.**

> **The flood wall must reach the highest water level PLUS the free board, so the levels stack:**

| Component | Value | Running RL |
|---|---|---|
| **RL of the upstream bed** | **1080.00** | **1080.00** |
| **+ HEIGHT of the weir (crest above bed)** | **+2.50** | **1082.50 — the CREST level** |
| **+ HEAD over the crest H** | **+1.587** | **1084.087 — the upstream WATER SURFACE (HFL)** |
| **+ FREE BOARD** | **+1.20** | **1085.287 — the FLOOD WALL level** ✓ |

> **RL of the flood wall = 1080 + 2.5 + 1.587 + 1.2 = 1085.287 ≈ 1085.28 m** ✓

> **The source's working is exactly this sum.**

**Why option (b) 1084.08 m is the designed trap:**

> **1084.087 is the HIGH FLOOD LEVEL — the water surface — with the FREE BOARD omitted.**

> **So a candidate who computes the water level correctly and stops has done all the hydraulics and missed the last addition.**

> **That is the classic error in this class of problem, and the option exists to catch it.**

> **And option (c) 1081.58 m is what you get by adding only H to the bed level, omitting the weir HEIGHT as well — two omissions.**

> **Option (a) 1085.82 m is the correct total with the digits transposed (1085.28 → 1085.82)** — a well-made distractor, since the two differ only in the last two digits.

> **So all three distractors are the answer with something omitted or transposed, and the defence is to write the four levels out in a column as above rather than adding them in one line.**

**Working the exponent, since H^{3/2} = 2 must be inverted:**

> **H^{3/2} = 2  ⟹  H = 2^{2/3}**

> **2^{2/3} = (2²)^{1/3} = 4^{1/3} = 1.5874**

> **The cube root of 4 is worth recognising: 1.587**, since 1.587³ = 3.997 ≈ 4. ✓

> **A quick check: 1.5^{1.5} = 1.837 and 1.6^{1.5} = 2.024, so H lies just below 1.6** — which confirms 1.587 without a calculator.

> **The inversion is where the arithmetic can go wrong: taking H = 2^{3/2} = 2.83 instead of 2^{2/3} = 1.587 inverts the exponent** and gives a flood wall at 1086.53 m, which is not offered.

**The weir formulae, since the coefficient identifies which one applies:**

| Weir | Discharge | Typical coefficient |
|---|---|---|
| **BROAD-CRESTED** | **Q = C_w L H^{3/2}** | **C_w ≈ 1.5-1.7** ← as given |
| **Sharp-crested (rectangular)** | **Q = (2/3) C_d L √(2g) H^{3/2}** | C_d ≈ 0.62 |
| **OGEE spillway** | **Q = C L H^{3/2}** | **C ≈ 2.2 (SI)** |
| **Cipolletti (trapezoidal)** | Q = 1.86 L H^{3/2} | — |
| **V-notch (triangular)** | **Q = (8/15) C_d √(2g) tan(θ/2) H^{5/2}** | **Note the 5/2 exponent** |

> **The 3/2 exponent is common to every rectangular-crest weir, and the coefficient is what distinguishes the types.**

> **C_w = 1.5 in the stem identifies it as a broad-crested weir, which is why the simple form applies** — and it is worth noting that the stem tells you which formula to use through the coefficient rather than only through the words.

> **The V-notch's 5/2 exponent is the exception worth remembering: its flow area shrinks in BOTH dimensions as the head falls, which is why it suits SMALL flows.**

**Why FREE BOARD is provided at all, since it is the omitted step:**

| Free board allows for | Note |
|---|---|
| **WAVE action and wind set-up** | **Waves ride above the still-water level** ← |
| **Uncertainty in the design flood** | The HFL is an estimate, not a measurement |
| **Settlement of the wall or embankment** | Over the structure's life |
| **Debris and floating material raising the level** | Blockage effects |
| **Surges and unsteady flow** | Passage of a flood wave |

> **The wave allowance is usually the largest component, and it depends on the FETCH — the open water length over which the wind blows.**

> **A wide, exposed reservoir needs far more free board than a narrow river channel**, which is why the figure is not universal and must be stated as the stem does.

> **Typical values are 1 to 1.5 m for a river flood wall and 1.5 to 3 m for a reservoir embankment**, and the 1.2 m given here sits sensibly in the first range.

> **And the general principle: free board is the margin against everything the hydraulic calculation does not model.** Omitting it does not make the design more accurate — it makes it wrong by exactly the amount of the risks it was meant to cover.

examTip.trap: **Option (b) 1084.08 is the HIGH FLOOD LEVEL with the FREE BOARD omitted** — all the hydraulics done and the last addition missed. And option (a) is the right answer with the last two digits transposed.
examTip.mnemonic: **Write the four levels in a COLUMN: bed, + weir height, + head, + free board.** Adding them in one line is what loses a term. And free board is the margin against everything the calculation does not model — chiefly WAVES.

questions.stem: Calculate Lane's weighted creep length for a hydraulic structure with an upstream cut-off of 5 m, a floor length of 54 m and a downstream cut-off of 8 m.
questions.solution:
**44 m.**

**Lane's weighted creep length:**

> **L_w = (1/3) × (HORIZONTAL creep) + 1 × (VERTICAL creep)**

> **L_w = L/3 + 2(d₁ + d₂)**

| Component | Value |
|---|---|
| **Horizontal creep — the floor length L** | **54 m, weighted by 1/3 → 18 m** |
| **Vertical creep — both faces of each cut-off** | **2(5 + 8) = 26 m, weighted by 1 → 26 m** |
| **TOTAL weighted creep** | **18 + 26 = 44 m** ✓ |

> **The source's working gives exactly this: L/3 + 2(d₁+d₂) = 54/3 + 2(5+8) = 18 + 26 = 44 m.**

**Why VERTICAL creep counts THREE TIMES as much as horizontal — the whole idea of Lane's method:**

> **BLIGH'S original creep theory treated horizontal and vertical creep as EQUALLY effective**, giving a total creep of L + 2(d₁+d₂) = 54 + 26 = 80 m.

> **That was found to be wrong: observations showed that VERTICAL cut-offs are FAR more effective at destroying the seepage head than an equal length of horizontal floor.**

> **LANE'S weighted creep theory recognises it by weighting the horizontal path at ONE THIRD** — equivalently, vertical creep is three times as valuable as horizontal.

| Theory | Creep length here | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| **BLIGH** | **80 m** | **Horizontal and vertical EQUAL** |
| **LANE (weighted)** | **44 m** ← | **Horizontal weighted 1/3** |
| **KHOSLA** | — | **Solves the actual potential flow field; abandons creep entirely** |

> **Note that option (a) 48 m and option (d) 54 m are close to values obtainable by mis-weighting**: 54 m is the FLOOR LENGTH unweighted, and 48 m is roughly what you get by weighting the vertical creep instead of the horizontal.

> **And option (b) 57 m is near 54/3 + 2(5+8) computed with an error in one term.**

> **So the option set punishes exactly the two errors available: weighting the wrong component, or forgetting the factor 2 on the cut-offs.**

**Why the factor of 2 appears on the cut-offs — easy to miss:**

> **Water creeping along the seepage path travels DOWN one face of a cut-off and UP the other.**

> **So a cut-off of depth d contributes 2d to the creep length, not d.**

> **Forgetting that halves the vertical contribution: 54/3 + (5+8) = 18 + 13 = 31 m, which is not offered.**

> **The physical picture is the check: trace the path with a finger from the upstream water, down the cut-off, along the floor, up the downstream cut-off, and out.** Each cut-off is traversed twice.

**Where the creep length is used — SAFETY AGAINST PIPING:**

> **The purpose of computing a creep length is to check it against the head:**

> **L_w ≥ C × H**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **L_w** | **Weighted creep length** |
| **H** | **Seepage head (upstream minus downstream water level)** |
| **C** | **Lane's weighted creep COEFFICIENT, depending on the soil** |

> **Lane's coefficients:**

| Soil | C |
|---|---|
| **Very fine sand or silt** | **8.5** |
| **Fine sand** | **7.0** |
| **Coarse sand** | **5.0** |
| **Gravel and sand** | **3.5-3.0** |
| **Boulders, gravel and sand** | **2.5-3.0** |
| Soft to hard clay | **3.0-1.6** |

> **The pattern is the same as everywhere in seepage: the FINER the soil, the LARGER the coefficient required** — because fine particles are lifted more easily and piping starts at a gentler gradient.

> **So a 44 m weighted creep length would be adequate for a head of about 44/7 = 6.3 m in fine sand, or 44/5 = 8.8 m in coarse sand.**

**Why the creep theories were superseded — stated honestly:**

> **Both Bligh's and Lane's methods are EMPIRICAL: they assume the head is lost along a path, at a rate fixed by a coefficient.**

> **KHOSLA'S THEORY replaced them by solving the actual two-dimensional potential flow beneath the floor, using the theory of complex variables.**

| | **CREEP theories (Bligh, Lane)** | **KHOSLA** |
|---|---|---|
| **Basis** | **Empirical — head lost along a path** | **MATHEMATICAL — the real flow field** |
| **Output** | **A creep length to compare with the head** | **UPLIFT PRESSURE at points, and the EXIT GRADIENT** |
| **Intermediate sheet piles** | Credited fully | **Shown to be nearly USELESS** |
| **Verdict** | Superseded | **Standard practice** |

> **Khosla's most consequential finding was that INTERMEDIATE sheet piles contribute very little — they lie in a region of low pressure gradient — while only the END cut-offs earn their cost.**

> **That single result changed weir design: modern structures use deep cut-offs at the ends rather than long floors with piles distributed along them.**

> **So the creep theories remain on the syllabus because they are simple, because they give a quick check, and because they are still cited in older designs** — but the design of a new weir would use Khosla's method for uplift and exit gradient.

> **Which is worth knowing as a matter of professional honesty: a candidate should be able to compute a weighted creep length AND know that it is not how a serious design is done.**

examTip.trick: **L_w = L/3 + 2(d₁+d₂) = 54/3 + 2(13) = 18 + 26 = 44 m.** Horizontal creep is weighted ONE THIRD; vertical creep counts fully.
examTip.trap: **Each cut-off contributes 2d, not d** — the water goes DOWN one face and UP the other. Trace the path with a finger and each cut-off is traversed twice. And weighting the wrong component gives the other options.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bligh treated horizontal and vertical creep as equal (80 m here); Lane weights horizontal at 1/3 (44 m); KHOSLA abandons creep entirely** and solves the real flow field — showing that only the END cut-offs matter.

questions.stem: A pycnometer containing 400 g of sand and water filled to the top weighs 2150 g. If the clear water plus pycnometer weight is 1950 g and the specific gravity of the soil sample is 2.5, the water content of the sample is:
questions.solution:
**20 per cent.**

**The pycnometer water-content formula:**

> **w = [(M₂ − M₁)/(M₃ − M₄)] × [(G − 1)/G] − 1**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **M₁** | **Mass of the EMPTY pycnometer** | **100 g (taken as standard when not given)** |
| **M₂** | **Pycnometer + WET SOIL** | **100 + 400 = 500 g** |
| **M₃** | **Pycnometer + soil + water, filled to the top** | **2150 g** |
| **M₄** | **Pycnometer + WATER ONLY, filled to the top** | **1950 g** |
| **G** | **Specific gravity of the solids** | **2.5** |

**The computation:**

> **w = [(500 − 100)/(2150 − 1950)] × [(2.5 − 1)/2.5] − 1**

> **= [400/200] × [1.5/2.5] − 1**

> **= 2 × 0.6 − 1**

> **= 1.2 − 1 = 0.2 = 20 %** ✓

> **The source's working follows exactly this, and it notes the assumption M₁ = 100 g "if not given".**

**The assumption that must be flagged:**

> **The stem does NOT give the empty pycnometer's mass, and the formula needs it.**

> **The source assumes M₁ = 100 g, which is a conventional value for a standard pycnometer, and the numbers then produce a clean 20 per cent.**

> **That the answer comes out exactly on an offered option is the confirmation that the intended assumption was 100 g** — with any other value the result would not land so neatly.

> **So the question is answerable only with that assumption, and it is worth stating openly rather than glossing over: the datum is missing and the standard value supplies it.**

**Where the formula comes from — worth seeing, because it makes the terms intelligible:**

> **The pycnometer method works by comparing two weighings of a full vessel:**

> **(M₃ − M₄) is the DIFFERENCE between the vessel full of soil-and-water and the vessel full of water alone.**

> **That difference equals the mass of the solids MINUS the mass of the water they displaced:**

> **M₃ − M₄ = M_s − M_s/G = M_s (1 − 1/G) = M_s (G−1)/G**

> **So the DRY MASS of solids follows directly:**

> **M_s = (M₃ − M₄) × G/(G−1) = 200 × 2.5/1.5 = 333.3 g**

> **And the WET soil mass is M₂ − M₁ = 400 g, so the water mass is 400 − 333.3 = 66.7 g.**

> **Water content = 66.7/333.3 = 0.20 = 20 %** ✓

> **That two-step route — find the dry mass, then take the ratio — is more transparent than the single formula and gives the same answer.** It is worth using when the formula's structure is uncertain.

**Why the method exists — its advantage over oven drying:**

| | **OVEN DRYING** | **PYCNOMETER** |
|---|---|---|
| **Time** | **24 hours at 105-110 °C** | **MINUTES** ← |
| **Equipment** | Oven, balance | Pycnometer, balance, water |
| **Suits** | **Any soil** | **COARSE-GRAINED soil (sand and gravel)** |
| **Needs the specific gravity?** | **NO** | **YES — G must be known or assumed** |
| **Accuracy** | **The REFERENCE method** | Adequate for coarse soil |

> **The speed is the whole point: a water content in minutes rather than a day is what a compaction-control operation needs**, because a decision about whether to roll again must be made while the plant is still there.

> **Its limitation is that it requires G to be known, and it is unsuitable for fine-grained soil** — clay does not disperse readily and air is difficult to expel from it, so the vessel cannot be reliably filled.

> **The requirement to EXPEL ALL AIR is the practical difficulty in any case: entrapped air makes M₃ too low and the computed water content wrong.** Hence the sample is stirred, tapped and sometimes evacuated before the final weighing.

**The other rapid methods, for context:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **OVEN drying** | **The reference; 24 h at 105-110 °C** |
| **PYCNOMETER** | **Minutes; coarse soil; needs G** ← |
| **Sand bath / stove drying** | Quick and crude; risks overheating organic soil |
| **Alcohol burning** | Rapid field method |
| **CALCIUM CARBIDE (Speedy) moisture meter** | **Minutes; reacts with the water to give acetylene, and the pressure indicates the moisture** |
| **Nuclear (neutron) gauge** | Fast, non-destructive; needs calibration and licensing |

> **The 105-110 °C oven temperature is worth knowing and worth understanding: it is chosen to drive off the FREE water without decomposing the soil.**

> **A higher temperature would burn off organic matter and drive out water bound within the clay minerals' structure, giving a water content that is too high and a soil that has been chemically altered.**

> **So for ORGANIC and GYPSUM-rich soils a lower temperature (about 60-80 °C) is specified** — which is a genuine refinement rather than a footnote, since a peat tested at 110 °C loses part of the soil itself.

verification.notes: Keyed answer confirmed, with one assumption flagged. The stem does not give the mass of the empty pycnometer, which the formula requires; the source assumes M1 = 100 g, stating "if not given", and with that value the computation yields exactly 20 per cent - one of the offered options. The assumption is stated openly in the solution rather than passed over, since the question is not answerable without it.

examTip.trick: **w = [(M₂−M₁)/(M₃−M₄)] × [(G−1)/G] − 1 = [400/200] × [1.5/2.5] − 1 = 1.2 − 1 = 20 %.** The stem omits the empty pycnometer mass; take the standard 100 g.
examTip.trap: **A clearer two-step route: M₃ − M₄ = M_s(G−1)/G, so M_s = 200 × 2.5/1.5 = 333.3 g**, water = 400 − 333.3 = 66.7 g, and w = 66.7/333.3 = 20 %. Use it when the single formula's structure is uncertain.
examTip.mnemonic: **The pycnometer gives a water content in MINUTES rather than 24 hours** — which is what compaction control needs — but it requires G and suits only COARSE soil. And the oven's 105-110 °C is chosen to drive off free water WITHOUT decomposing the soil.

questions.stem: A hydropower plant of installed capacity 40 MW generated 210.24 GWh of energy in a year. Its annual plant load factor is:
questions.solution:
**60 per cent.**

**The plant load factor:**

> **PLF = ENERGY ACTUALLY GENERATED / ENERGY THAT COULD HAVE BEEN GENERATED AT FULL CAPACITY**

**Step 1 — the energy possible at full capacity for a year:**

> **Hours in a year = 365 × 24 = 8760 h**

> **E_max = 40 MW × 8760 h = 350,400 MWh = 350.4 GWh**

**Step 2 — the ratio:**

> **PLF = 210.24 / 350.4 = 0.60 = 60 %** ✓

> **The arithmetic is clean: 350.4 × 0.6 = 210.24 exactly**, which confirms the intended path.

**The 8760 figure — worth having automatically:**

> **365 × 24 = 8760 hours in a normal year.**

> **A leap year gives 8784 h, and for a large plant the difference is not negligible: 24 extra hours at 40 MW is 960 MWh.**

> **But for a load-factor calculation 8760 is the conventional divisor, and using it is what makes the numbers here come out exactly.**

**The three related factors, which are constantly confused:**

| Factor | Definition | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **LOAD factor** | **Average load / PEAK load over the period** | **A property of the DEMAND** |
| **PLANT (capacity) factor** | **Average load / INSTALLED capacity** | **A property of the PLANT** ← computed here |
| **UTILISATION factor** | **Maximum load actually reached / installed capacity** | **How fully the plant is ever used** |

> **The distinction between the first two is the one that matters and is the trap in this family of questions:**

> **LOAD factor divides by the PEAK LOAD; PLANT factor divides by the INSTALLED CAPACITY.**

> **They are equal ONLY when the peak load equals the installed capacity** — that is, when the plant is exactly sized to its peak demand.

> **And they are related by:  PLANT factor = LOAD factor × UTILISATION factor.**

> **The stem says "plant load factor" and gives the INSTALLED CAPACITY, so the installed capacity is the divisor** — the data supplied identify the intended definition.

**Why a load factor of 60 per cent is a meaningful number:**

| Plant type | Typical plant factor |
|---|---|
| **Run-of-river, no pondage** | **40-60 % — dictated by the river's flow** |
| **Peaking-run-of-river (with pondage)** | **50-65 %** ← this plant |
| **STORAGE (reservoir) plant** | **Can be high or deliberately low, depending on its role** |
| **Base-load thermal** | **70-90 %** |
| **Peaking plant (gas turbine)** | **5-20 % — it exists to run for a few hours** |
| **Solar PV** | **15-25 % — the sun sets** |

> **A HIGH plant factor is not automatically good, and this is the point most often missed.**

> **A plant with a high factor is being used near its capacity most of the time — which means it earns well from the capital invested, but it has NO SPARE CAPACITY to meet a peak.**

> **A PEAKING plant, by design, has a very LOW plant factor: it sits idle and exists to be available for a few hours a day.** Judging it by its plant factor would be a category error.

> **So the plant factor describes the ROLE a plant plays in a system, not its quality.** The right question is whether the factor matches the role intended.

**Why the plant factor of a hydropower plant in Nepal is what it is:**

> **Nepal's rivers are strongly SEASONAL: monsoon flows are many times the dry-season flows.**

> **A run-of-river plant therefore runs at full capacity through the monsoon and at a fraction of it through the dry months** — and the annual plant factor is the average of the two regimes.

> **That is the structural problem of Nepali hydropower: the country has a monsoon SURPLUS and a dry-season DEFICIT, from the same installed capacity.**

> **STORAGE projects address it by carrying monsoon water into the dry season**, which is why they are valued out of proportion to their installed capacity.

> **A 40 MW storage plant that can generate in April is worth more to the system than a 40 MW run-of-river plant that cannot** — even though their nameplates are equal, and even if the run-of-river plant has the higher annual energy.

> **Which is the deeper lesson behind this arithmetic: energy and capacity are different commodities, and WHEN the energy arrives matters as much as how much of it there is.**

**The energy computation in the other direction, since it is the commoner form of the question:**

> **Given a plant factor, the annual energy follows:**

> **E = installed capacity × 8760 × PLF**

> **For this plant: 40 × 8760 × 0.60 = 210,240 MWh = 210.24 GWh** ✓

> **That form is what a feasibility study uses**, since the plant factor is estimated from the hydrology before any energy has been generated.

examTip.trick: **PLF = actual energy / (installed capacity × 8760 h).** Here 210.24 GWh / (40 MW × 8760 h = 350.4 GWh) = **0.60.**
examTip.trap: **LOAD factor divides by the PEAK LOAD; PLANT factor divides by the INSTALLED CAPACITY.** They coincide only when the peak equals the capacity. The stem gives installed capacity, so that is the divisor.
examTip.mnemonic: **A high plant factor is not automatically good** — a peaking plant has a deliberately low one. The factor describes the plant's ROLE, not its quality. And 8760 hours in a year is worth knowing cold.

questions.stem: For a hydropower plant operating under a net head of 400 m with a discharge of 1.2 m³/s, the most suitable turbine is:
questions.solution:
**A PELTON turbine — a high head with a small discharge.**

**The selection is governed by HEAD above all:**

| Turbine | Head range | Discharge | Type |
|---|---|---|---|
| **PELTON** | **ABOVE ~250-300 m (up to 1800 m)** | **SMALL** | **IMPULSE** ← 400 m, 1.2 m³/s |
| **Turgo** | **50-250 m** | Small to medium | Impulse |
| **Cross-flow (Banki-Michell)** | **5-100 m** | Small | Impulse |
| **FRANCIS** | **~15-350 m** | **Medium to large** | **REACTION (mixed flow)** |
| **KAPLAN / propeller** | **BELOW ~30 m (up to ~70 m)** | **VERY LARGE** | **REACTION (axial flow)** |

> **At 400 m the head is decisively in Pelton territory, and the discharge of 1.2 m³/s — very small — confirms it.**

> **High head with small discharge IS the Pelton signature**, and low head with large discharge is the Kaplan signature. The two are opposite ends of the same trade.

**Why the two extremes exist — the physical reason, which makes the table unnecessary to memorise:**

> **Power = ρ g Q H η. A given power can be delivered by a large Q with a small H, or a small Q with a large H.**

> **A PELTON extracts energy from a high-velocity JET striking buckets in AIR. The jet velocity from a 400 m head is √(2gH) = √(2×9.81×400) = 88.6 m/s** — and a machine that converts that kinetic energy in open air is the natural device.

> **A KAPLAN works fully SUBMERGED, with water flowing through it like a propeller in reverse. It handles enormous volumes at gentle heads**, where there is no useful jet to be had.

> **A FRANCIS is the intermediate: water enters radially and leaves axially, submerged, over a very wide head range** — which is why it is the most widely used turbine in the world.

**The quantitative selector — SPECIFIC SPEED:**

> **N_s = N √P / H^{5/4}**  (in the metric form, with P in kW and H in m)

| Turbine | Specific speed range |
|---|---|
| **PELTON, single jet** | **8-30** |
| **Pelton, multi-jet** | **30-70** |
| **FRANCIS** | **60-400** |
| **KAPLAN** | **300-1000** |

> **The pattern is worth internalising: LOW specific speed = HIGH head = impulse; HIGH specific speed = LOW head = axial reaction.**

> **Let us check this plant. With η ≈ 0.88:**

> **P = 9.81 × 1.2 × 400 × 0.88 = 4144 kW ≈ 4.1 MW**

> **At N = 600 rpm:  N_s = 600 × √4144 / 400^{1.25} = 600 × 64.4 / 1789 = 21.6**

> **21.6 falls squarely in the SINGLE-JET PELTON range (8-30)** ✓ — so the specific speed confirms what the head suggested.

**Why option (a) Kaplan and (d) propeller are the same wrong answer:**

> **A PROPELLER turbine is a Kaplan with FIXED blades — a Kaplan has ADJUSTABLE runner blades, and that is the only essential difference.**

| | **Propeller** | **KAPLAN** |
|---|---|---|
| **Runner blades** | **FIXED** | **ADJUSTABLE** ← |
| **Guide vanes** | Adjustable | Adjustable |
| **Part-load efficiency** | **POOR** | **EXCELLENT — the flat efficiency curve** |
| **Cost and complexity** | Lower | Higher |

> **So offering both is offering the same family twice, and both are wrong by a factor of more than ten in head.**

> **The Kaplan's DOUBLE regulation — blades and guide vanes adjusted together — is what gives it a nearly FLAT efficiency curve from about 40 per cent load upward.** That is its great advantage and the reason it is preferred over a propeller machine wherever the flow varies.

**Why option (b) Francis is the serious distractor:**

> **Francis turbines DO operate up to about 350 m, and modern high-head Francis machines reach beyond it.**

> **So 400 m is near the upper boundary rather than absurd.**

> **But at only 1.2 m³/s the discharge is far too small for a Francis: a reaction turbine passing so little water at so great a head would be a tiny, inefficient runner** — the specific speed of 21.6 is well below the Francis range.

> **So the DISCHARGE, not the head, is what rules Francis out here**, and reading both figures together is the task the question sets.

**A practical note on Pelton machines in Nepal, since the case is common:**

> **Nepal's steep topography gives exactly this combination — a modest stream diverted with a high gross head — so Pelton and Turgo machines are the workhorses of small and micro hydropower there.**

> **A 4 MW Pelton on 400 m of head with 1.2 m³/s is a very typical Nepali run-of-river scheme**, and the numbers in this question are realistic rather than academic.

> **The engineering consequence: such a scheme's cost sits in the PENSTOCK and the headrace, not in the turbine.** Getting a small flow down 400 m of hillside is the expensive part, and the machine at the bottom is comparatively cheap.

examTip.trick: **High head + small discharge = PELTON.** 400 m is decisively above the Francis range for so small a flow, and the specific speed confirms it: N_s ≈ 21.6, inside the single-jet Pelton band 8-30.
examTip.trap: **Kaplan and propeller are the SAME family** — a propeller is a Kaplan with FIXED blades — so two options are one wrong answer. And Francis is the serious distractor: the head is arguable, but 1.2 m³/s is far too small.
examTip.mnemonic: **LOW specific speed = HIGH head = impulse; HIGH specific speed = LOW head = axial.** And the Kaplan's DOUBLE regulation (blades plus guide vanes) is what gives it a flat efficiency curve down to 40 % load.

questions.stem: The principal function of a surge tank in a hydropower conveyance system is to:
options: Increase the net head available to the turbine
Remove sediment from the water before it enters the penstock
Relieve water hammer pressures and supply water during load acceptance
questions.solution:
**To relieve water-hammer pressures and to supply water during load acceptance — a TWO-WAY function.**

**Why a surge tank is needed at all:**

> **A hydropower conveyance system runs water through a long, low-slope TUNNEL or HEADRACE, then down a steep PENSTOCK to the turbine.**

> **When the turbine's load changes SUDDENLY, the flow demand changes suddenly — and a long column of water cannot change its velocity suddenly.**

| Event | What happens without a surge tank |
|---|---|
| **LOAD REJECTION — the turbine gates SHUT** | **The moving water column is stopped abruptly → a pressure WAVE (water hammer) travels back up the conduit; pressures can far exceed the static head and BURST it** |
| **LOAD ACCEPTANCE — the gates OPEN** | **The turbine demands more water than the slow tunnel can immediately deliver → the pressure DROPS, possibly to below atmospheric, risking column separation and a collapsing conduit** |

> **A SURGE TANK — an open shaft or chamber at the junction of the tunnel and the penstock — solves both:**

> **On CLOSURE it gives the water somewhere to go: the surplus rises up the tank instead of compressing against a closed gate.**

> **On OPENING it gives the water somewhere to come from: the tank empties into the penstock while the tunnel flow accelerates to the new demand.**

> **So the correct answer must mention BOTH directions**, and option (d) is the only one that does.

**Why the other options are wrong — each is a real device, but a different one:**

| Option | The device that actually does this |
|---|---|
| **(a) Increase the net head** | **Nothing does — head comes from ELEVATION DIFFERENCE. A surge tank slightly REDUCES net head through its own losses** |
| **(b) Remove sediment** | **A SETTLING BASIN or desilting chamber, placed at the intake** |
| **(c) Store water for peaking** | **A PONDAGE or reservoir. A surge tank's volume is far too small — it is measured in minutes of flow at most** |

> **Option (c) is the most tempting because a surge tank DOES hold water and DOES release it.**

> **The distinction is one of TIME SCALE and PURPOSE: a surge tank's storage acts over SECONDS to a few MINUTES, to absorb a transient. A pondage acts over HOURS, to shift energy between times of day.**

> **Confusing the two conflates a safety device with an economic one.**

**The second function of a surge tank — REDUCING THE WATER-HAMMER LENGTH:**

> **This is the point worth understanding, because it explains WHERE the tank is placed.**

> **The water-hammer pressure rise depends on the LENGTH of conduit in which the column must be decelerated.**

> **A surge tank, being open to the atmosphere, REFLECTS the pressure wave.**

> **So water hammer is confined to the PENSTOCK — between the surge tank and the turbine — and does not travel up the long tunnel at all.**

> **That is why the tank is placed AS CLOSE TO THE TURBINE AS THE TOPOGRAPHY ALLOWS**, usually at the point where the gentle tunnel turns into the steep penstock.

> **The design consequence is large: a 5 km tunnel plus a 400 m penstock, with a surge tank at the junction, has its water hammer computed over 400 m rather than 5400 m** — reducing the pressure rise, and the required wall thickness, by more than an order of magnitude.

> **Without the tank, the whole 5.4 km would have to be designed for the transient pressure.** The tank is therefore an economic device as well as a safety one, but the economy comes from steel saved, not from energy stored.

**Types of surge tank, briefly, since the variants have purposes:**

| Type | Feature |
|---|---|
| **SIMPLE (cylindrical)** | **A plain vertical shaft; large surges, slow damping** |
| **RESTRICTED ORIFICE (throttled)** | **A constriction at the base DISSIPATES energy — smaller, better-damped surges** ← the common choice |
| **DIFFERENTIAL (Johnson)** | **An inner riser plus an outer tank — very rapid initial response** |
| **EXPANSION CHAMBER type** | Widened at top and bottom to limit extreme surge levels |
| **AIR CUSHION surge chamber** | **A SEALED chamber with compressed air — used where an open shaft to the surface is impossible** |

> **The restricted-orifice type is the workhorse: the throttle converts surge energy into turbulence, so the oscillation dies out in a few cycles rather than persisting.**

> **And the AIR CUSHION chamber is worth noting for deep-tunnel schemes: where the tunnel is 500 m below the surface, an open shaft would be prohibitively expensive, so a sealed chamber with a compressed-air volume performs the same function underground.** Several Norwegian and a few Himalayan schemes use it.

**Where a surge tank is NOT needed:**

> **If the conduit is SHORT and STEEP — the penstock running directly from the intake to the powerhouse — there is no long low-slope column to protect, and no tank is required.**

> **The usual criterion is the ratio L/H (conduit length to net head): a surge tank is generally needed when L/H exceeds about 5.**

> **So a small run-of-river plant with a 100 m penstock on 200 m of head needs none; a plant with a 5 km tunnel needs one absolutely.**

> **The alternative for smaller schemes is a PRESSURE RELIEF VALVE at the turbine, which dumps water rather than storing it** — cheaper, but wasteful and dependent on a moving part working at the moment it is needed. A surge tank has no moving parts, which is the deeper reason it is preferred wherever it can be built.

examTip.trick: **A surge tank works BOTH ways: it absorbs surplus water on load REJECTION and supplies water on load ACCEPTANCE.** Only option (d) states both, so it is the answer.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) peaking storage is the tempting one** — a surge tank does hold and release water. The difference is TIME SCALE: a surge tank acts over seconds to minutes to absorb a transient; a pondage acts over hours to shift energy.
examTip.mnemonic: **Being open to atmosphere, the tank REFLECTS the pressure wave** — so water hammer is confined to the penstock, not the whole tunnel. That is why it sits where the tunnel meets the penstock, and why it saves steel as well as lives.

questions.stem: A trench weir (bottom rack intake) is most appropriate for:
options: A wide alluvial river carrying a heavy suspended sediment load
A storage reservoir with a high and steady head
A steep mountain stream carrying boulders and a flashy flood flow
A canal offtake from an existing irrigation main canal
questions.solution:
**A steep mountain stream carrying boulders and a flashy flood flow.**

**What a trench weir is:**

> **A TRENCH WEIR — also called a BOTTOM RACK or Tyrolean intake — is a trench built ACROSS the bed of a stream, covered by a coarse inclined SCREEN (the rack).**

> **Water falls THROUGH the rack into the trench below and is carried away to the conveyance system.**

> **Boulders, cobbles and floating debris pass OVER the rack and continue down the stream.**

> **So the whole device is a horizontal sieve laid in the river bed, taking water from below while the coarse material rides over the top.**

**Why that suits a steep boulder stream specifically:**

| Feature of a mountain stream | How the trench weir answers it |
|---|---|
| **Carries BOULDERS that would wreck a conventional intake** | **Boulders pass OVER the rack and are never admitted** ← |
| **FLASHY floods — the discharge multiplies in hours** | **The structure is IN the bed, submerged and overtopped without damage** |
| **Very steep bed, high transport capacity** | **The stream's own energy carries the rejected material away — no flushing gate needed** |
| **Small dry-season flow that must be taken almost entirely** | **A rack across the full width can take nearly the whole low flow** |
| **A narrow gorge with no room for a settling basin at the bank** | **The intake occupies the bed, not the bank** |

> **The decisive advantage is that a trench weir has NO GATES, NO MOVING PARTS AND NOTHING TO BE DAMAGED BY A FLOOD.**

> **In a Himalayan stream where a flood may arrive in an hour, carry metre-sized boulders and no one can reach the site, that is worth more than efficiency.**

> **A structure that is simply overtopped and then resumes working is the right answer to a river that cannot be controlled.**

**Why the other options are wrong:**

| Option | Why not |
|---|---|
| **(a) Wide alluvial river, heavy SUSPENDED load** | **A trench weir excludes COARSE material but admits FINE SUSPENDED sediment freely — it would fill the trench and the conveyance with silt. A wide alluvial river needs a barrage with under-sluices and a proper silt-excluder** |
| **(b) Storage reservoir, high steady head** | **A reservoir intake is a submerged or tower intake in still water — there is no bed load to reject, and a bottom rack solves a problem that does not exist** |
| **(d) Canal offtake from a main canal** | **A canal offtake is a REGULATOR or a module (an APM, for instance) — the water is already clean and controlled** |

> **Option (a) is the trap, because it names a sediment problem and a trench weir is a sediment device.**

> **The distinction is the SIZE of the sediment: a trench weir rejects BED LOAD (boulders, gravel), and does nothing whatever about SUSPENDED load (silt, fine sand).**

> **So on a silt-laden alluvial river a trench weir addresses the wrong half of the problem, and the trench itself would silt up.**

> **A trench weir is therefore always followed by a SETTLING BASIN downstream, to remove the fines it cannot exclude.**

**The design features worth knowing:**

| Element | Practice |
|---|---|
| **Rack bars** | **Steel bars, typically 8-15 mm clear spacing, laid ALONG the flow direction** |
| **Rack slope** | **Sloped 10-20 % DOWNSTREAM, so material slides off rather than lodging** ← |
| **Trench** | **Sized to carry the full design flow with a free water surface, sloping toward the offtake** |
| **Intake capacity** | **Designed to take 20-40 % MORE than the required flow, to allow for partial rack blockage** |
| **Downstream** | **Always a SETTLING BASIN, because fines pass through the rack** |

> **The rack SLOPE and the bars running ALONG the flow are the two details that make the difference between a working intake and a blocked one.**

> **Bars laid across the flow would catch every twig; bars along it let debris slide over.**

> **And the excess capacity is not conservatism but necessity: leaves, grass and gravel WILL partially block the rack between visits, and a rack designed for exactly the required flow will deliver less than the required flow most of the year.**

**Why this matters in Nepal, since it is where the type is most used:**

> **Most Nepali run-of-river schemes divert from steep tributaries exactly of this character**, and the trench weir is the standard intake for small and medium hydropower there.

> **Its limitation is maintenance: the rack must be cleared, and in a monsoon it will be buried in gravel.**

> **So the practical design provides ACCESS to the rack and accepts that the intake will be dug out after large floods** — a maintenance burden traded against a structure that cannot be destroyed.

> **That trade is the essence of intake design on a mountain river: nothing survives untouched, so choose the structure whose damage is repairable with a shovel rather than a contract.**

examTip.trick: **A trench weir is a horizontal sieve in the river bed: water falls THROUGH the rack, boulders ride OVER it.** That suits a steep boulder stream with flashy floods — and it has no gates and nothing a flood can break.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) names a sediment problem, and a trench weir is a sediment device — but the WRONG sediment.** It rejects BED LOAD (boulders, gravel) and admits SUSPENDED silt freely, which is why a settling basin always follows it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rack bars ALONG the flow, sloped 10-20 % downstream, and sized for 20-40 % excess flow** — because leaves and gravel will block part of it between visits. Design for the blockage, not for the clean condition.

questions.stem: A hydropower plant that has a pond sufficient to store the day's flow and release it during peak demand hours, but cannot carry water from one season to another, is classified as:
questions.solution:
**A PEAKING RUN-OF-RIVER (PROR) plant.**

**The classification by STORAGE capability:**

| Type | Storage | What it can do |
|---|---|---|
| **RUN-OF-RIVER (ROR)** | **NONE (or only hours of pondage)** | **Generates whatever the river brings, when it brings it** |
| **PEAKING ROR (PROR)** | **A pond holding roughly a DAY'S flow** | **Shifts generation WITHIN the day — stores at night, generates at the evening peak** ← |
| **STORAGE** | **A reservoir holding WEEKS TO MONTHS of flow** | **Shifts generation BETWEEN SEASONS — monsoon water used in the dry season** |
| **PUMPED STORAGE** | **Two reservoirs; water PUMPED back up** | **Net energy CONSUMER; it stores ENERGY, not water** |

> **The stem's two clauses settle it exactly: "store the day's flow" and "cannot carry water from one season to another" — daily storage but not seasonal. That is the definition of PROR.**

**Why the distinction is not academic — what daily storage is worth:**

> **Electricity demand is not flat. In Nepal it peaks sharply in the EVENING, when lighting and cooking loads coincide.**

> **A pure run-of-river plant generates a flat output all day, most of it when demand is low.**

> **A PROR plant with the SAME annual energy can hold back the night's water and release it in the evening peak** — delivering the same energy at the hours when it is worth most.

| | **Pure ROR** | **PROR** |
|---|---|---|
| **Annual energy** | **The same** | **The same** |
| **Installed capacity for that energy** | Lower | **HIGHER — sized for the peak release** |
| **Value of the energy** | **Lower — delivered off-peak** | **HIGHER — delivered at the peak** ← |
| **Plant factor** | Higher | **Lower, deliberately** |

> **Note the paradox in the last row: the PROR plant has a LOWER plant factor and is MORE valuable.**

> **That is the clearest illustration of why the plant factor is not a measure of quality. The PROR plant runs at full output for a few hours and at reduced output otherwise, by design, because that is what the system needs.**

> **The cost is a larger turbine and generator for the same annual energy** — capacity is bought in order to place the energy at the right hour.

**Why PUMPED STORAGE is a different thing entirely — worth being clear about:**

> **A pumped storage scheme has an upper and a lower reservoir. It PUMPS water up when electricity is cheap and abundant, and generates by letting it down when electricity is scarce.**

> **Its round-trip efficiency is about 70-80 per cent, so it CONSUMES more energy than it produces.**

> **It is therefore NOT a generator at all — it is a BATTERY.** Its purpose is to store ENERGY, and the water is merely the medium.

> **That distinction is the reason pumped storage is being built worldwide as solar and wind grow: an intermittent supply needs storage, and pumped hydro remains the largest-scale storage technology in existence by a wide margin.**

> **A candidate should be able to say plainly that a pumped storage plant is an energy sink and still an economically sensible asset** — because the value of electricity differs between hours by more than the 20-30 per cent lost in the cycle.

**Nepal's situation, since the classification matters there more than most places:**

> **Nepal's installed hydropower is overwhelmingly RUN-OF-RIVER and PROR.**

> **The consequence is structural: a monsoon SURPLUS that must be exported or spilled, and a dry-season DEFICIT that must be imported.**

> **Only STORAGE projects can fix it, because only they can move water across seasons** — and they are the hardest to build, requiring large reservoirs, inundation, resettlement and very long payback.

> **So the classification in this question is, in Nepal, a description of the country's central energy problem.** A candidate who can explain why a 100 MW storage plant and a 100 MW run-of-river plant are not comparable assets understands something that matters well beyond the examination.

**The other classifications, for completeness, since papers ask by any of them:**

| Basis | Categories |
|---|---|
| **STORAGE** | **ROR, PROR, storage, pumped storage** ← this question |
| **HEAD** | **Low (<15 m), medium (15-70 m), high (>70 m)** |
| **CAPACITY (Nepal's own definitions)** | **Micro (<100 kW), mini (100-1000 kW), small (1-25 MW), medium (25-100 MW), large (>100 MW)** |
| **LOAD served** | **Base load, peak load** |
| **Interconnection** | Isolated / grid-connected |

> **The capacity bands are Nepal-specific and are worth knowing as stated, since the licensing and royalty regime depends on them** — a scheme below 1 MW, for instance, faces a materially lighter approval process than one above it.

examTip.trick: **Daily storage but not seasonal = PEAKING RUN-OF-RIVER.** The stem's two clauses — stores the day's flow, cannot cross seasons — define PROR exactly.
examTip.trap: **A PROR plant has a LOWER plant factor than a pure ROR plant and is MORE valuable** — it runs at full output for a few hours by design, placing the same energy at the hours worth most. The plant factor is not a measure of quality.
examTip.mnemonic: **Pumped storage is a BATTERY, not a generator** — round-trip efficiency 70-80 %, so it consumes more than it produces, and is still economic because hours differ in value by more than the loss. And in Nepal only STORAGE plants can move water across seasons.

questions.stem: The storage below the lowest outlet level of a reservoir, which cannot be drawn upon for generation and is reserved for sediment accumulation, is called:
questions.solution:
**DEAD storage.**

**The storage zones of a reservoir, from the bottom up:**

| Zone | Bounded by | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **DEAD storage** | **The river bed up to the MINIMUM DRAWDOWN LEVEL (the lowest outlet)** | **Sediment accumulation; cannot be drawn on** ← |
| **LIVE (useful) storage** | **MDDL up to the FULL RESERVOIR LEVEL** | **The working volume — this is what generates energy or irrigates** |
| **SURCHARGE storage** | **FRL up to the MAXIMUM WATER LEVEL during a flood** | **TEMPORARY — flood absorption only; cannot be retained** |
| **VALLEY storage** | The volume the river valley held naturally before the dam | A reference quantity, not a design zone |

> **The stem describes the lowest zone: below the lowest outlet, unusable, and reserved for silt. That is DEAD storage.**

**Why dead storage is provided — and it is a deliberate allowance, not waste:**

> **Every river carries sediment, and a reservoir traps almost all of it: the water slows, so its transporting capacity collapses and the load settles out.**

> **The reservoir therefore FILLS UP over its life, from the bottom.**

> **DEAD STORAGE is the volume deliberately provided BELOW the outlets so that decades of sediment can accumulate WITHOUT touching the live storage.**

> **It is sized from the estimated sediment inflow over the design life** — typically 50 to 100 years.

> **So the calculation is: annual sediment yield × design life ÷ the sediment's deposited density = the dead storage required.**

**Why this is the central problem of Himalayan reservoirs — stated plainly:**

> **Himalayan rivers carry among the HIGHEST sediment loads in the world: young, rapidly rising mountains, steep slopes, intense monsoon rainfall, and widespread landslides.**

> **Sediment yields of 1,000 to 5,000 tonnes per square kilometre per year are common — an order of magnitude above the world average.**

> **The consequence is that a Himalayan reservoir's economic life may be governed by SEDIMENTATION rather than by the structure's durability.**

> **A dam that will stand for 200 years may have lost its useful storage in 60.**

> **That is why sediment management is not a detail in Nepali reservoir design but a first-order concern**, and why storage projects there require far larger dead storage allowances than the textbook figures from temperate rivers.

**The sediment management measures, since dead storage alone is a passive answer:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **DEAD STORAGE allowance** | **The passive provision — accept the sediment, provide room for it** ← |
| **CATCHMENT treatment** | **Afforestation, check dams, gully control — reduce the yield at source; slow but permanent** |
| **SLUICING** | **Pass sediment-laden monsoon flows THROUGH low-level outlets while they are still in suspension** |
| **FLUSHING** | **DRAW THE RESERVOIR DOWN and let the river scour out deposited sediment** |
| **Density current venting** | Draw off the turbid underflow through low outlets before it settles |
| **Dredging** | Mechanically remove deposits; very expensive per cubic metre |

> **FLUSHING is the most effective and the most costly in a different currency: the reservoir must be EMPTIED, which means giving up the stored water and the generation it would have produced.**

> **It works only where the monsoon reliably refills the reservoir afterward** — which, in Nepal, it does. So drawdown flushing at the end of the dry season, just before the monsoon, is the classic strategy.

> **The low-level outlets required for flushing must be designed in from the start**, since retrofitting an outlet near the bed of an existing dam is close to impossible. That is a design decision made decades before it is used.

**A caution about the term "dead", since it is misleading:**

> **Dead storage is not entirely useless even in the meantime:**

> **It keeps the water surface at a level that keeps the intakes SUBMERGED, which the outlets require.**

> **It provides a minimum head for the plant.**

> **And it supports whatever fishery, recreation or navigation the reservoir carries at low levels.**

> **But it cannot be DRAWN UPON, and that is the operative definition.** A reservoir's yield calculation counts only the live storage.

**And a note on SURCHARGE storage, since option (b) names it:**

> **Surcharge storage lies ABOVE the full reservoir level and exists only while a flood is passing.**

> **It cannot be retained, because the spillway will discharge it: FRL is by definition the highest level the reservoir is allowed to hold.**
