> **Its purpose is FLOOD ROUTING — the reservoir absorbs part of the flood peak and releases it more slowly, which is why a dam attenuates a flood downstream.**

> **So surcharge storage is the top of the reservoir and dead storage the bottom, and confusing them is a confusion of the two extremes.** The stem's phrase "below the lowest outlet" removes any doubt.

examTip.trick: **Bottom to top: DEAD storage (below the lowest outlet), LIVE storage (MDDL to FRL), SURCHARGE storage (FRL to max flood level).** "Below the lowest outlet" fixes it as dead storage.
examTip.trap: **Dead storage and surcharge storage are the two EXTREMES** — the bottom and the top. Surcharge cannot be retained because FRL is by definition the highest permitted level; the spillway discharges it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Himalayan rivers carry 1,000-5,000 t/km²/yr — an order above the world average — so a Nepali reservoir's economic life is set by SEDIMENT, not by the dam.** Low-level flushing outlets must be designed in decades before they are used.

questions.stem: In Kennedy's theory of canal design, the critical velocity ratio (CVR or m) accounts for:
options: The bed slope of the canal
The side slope of the canal section
The grade of the silt carried by the canal
The roughness coefficient of the canal lining
questions.solution:
**The GRADE (coarseness) of the silt carried by the canal.**

**Kennedy's critical velocity:**

> **V₀ = 0.55 m y^{0.64}**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **V₀** | **CRITICAL VELOCITY — the velocity that will just keep the silt in suspension without scouring the bed** |
| **y** | **Depth of water** |
| **m** | **CRITICAL VELOCITY RATIO — a coefficient depending on the SILT GRADE** ← |
| 0.55, 0.64 | Empirical constants from Kennedy's observations on the Upper Bari Doab canal |

> **The values of m:**

| Silt grade | m |
|---|---|
| **Very fine silt** | **0.7** |
| **Fine silt** | **0.85** |
| **Fine, light sandy silt (Kennedy's own standard)** | **1.00** ← the reference case |
| **Coarser, sandy silt** | **1.1-1.2** |
| **Very coarse silt / debris** | **1.3** |

> **The pattern: the COARSER the silt, the HIGHER the value of m, and the HIGHER the velocity needed to keep it moving.**

> **Which is the physically obvious statement — a coarse grain needs more agitation to stay suspended than a fine one — expressed as a coefficient.**

**Why m = 1 is the datum, and what it means:**

> **Kennedy derived his equation from observations on the UPPER BARI DOAB CANAL in Punjab, whose silt was a fine light sandy grade.**

> **So m = 1 corresponds to THAT canal's silt, and every other value is a correction relative to it.**

> **That is a candid admission about the theory: it is EMPIRICAL and CALIBRATED TO ONE SYSTEM.** Applying it to a canal with markedly different silt means adjusting m by judgement, and the adjustment is where the uncertainty sits.

> **Recognising the empirical and local character of these regime theories is part of understanding them properly** — they are correlations that worked well on the canals they were derived from, not laws.

**What Kennedy's theory does and does NOT provide — its central limitation:**

| Kennedy provides | Kennedy does NOT provide |
|---|---|
| **A relation between VELOCITY and DEPTH** | **Any relation fixing the BED SLOPE** ← |
| **A silt correction through m** | **Any relation fixing the BED WIDTH or the B/y ratio** |

> **This is the theory's fundamental incompleteness, and it is why option (a) is wrong in an instructive way.**

> **Kennedy gives ONE equation with TWO unknowns (B and y for a given Q), so the design is INDETERMINATE.**

> **The slope must be brought in from OUTSIDE — from Kutter's or Manning's equation — and the B/y ratio must be ASSUMED by the designer from experience.**

> **So a Kennedy design proceeds by TRIAL AND ERROR: assume a depth, compute V₀, compute the area and hence the width, check the slope with Manning, and iterate.**

> **The answer therefore depends on the designer's assumed B/y ratio, which means two competent engineers can produce two different canals from the same data.** That is not a satisfactory state of affairs, and it is precisely what Lacey set out to remedy.

**Kennedy against LACEY — the comparison that every paper eventually asks:**

| | **KENNEDY (1895)** | **LACEY (1930)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Silt parameter** | **CVR, m — the critical velocity ratio** | **SILT FACTOR, f** |
| **Equations provided** | **ONE (V₀ vs y)** | **THREE — velocity, area, slope** |
| **Determinate design?** | **NO — B/y must be assumed** | **YES — a unique section results** ← |
| **Slope** | **From Kutter/Manning separately** | **Given by the theory: S = f^{5/3}/(3340 Q^{1/6})** |
| **Section shape** | Trapezoidal, assumed | **SEMI-ELLIPTICAL regime section** |
| **Silt kept in suspension by** | **The BED alone ("eddies rising from the bed")** | **The WHOLE PERIMETER, bed and sides** |
| **Distinguishes initial from final regime?** | **NO** | **YES — an important refinement** |

> **The last two rows are the conceptual advances.**

> **Kennedy attributed the suspension of silt to eddies generated by the BED only, and therefore used the DEPTH as his length scale.**

> **Lacey recognised that the SIDES generate eddies too, and used the HYDRAULIC RADIUS** — which is the more defensible physical picture and one reason his relations transfer better.

> **And Lacey's distinction between INITIAL and FINAL regime matters practically: a newly cut canal has an artificial slope and a bed not yet in equilibrium, and only after years of operation does it reach its true regime.** Designing for the initial condition gives a canal that then changes shape.

**Why the whole idea of a "regime" canal is worth understanding:**

> **A canal in alluvial soil is not a fixed channel — it can SCOUR its bed and DEPOSIT on it.**

> **So there is a velocity that is TOO LOW (silting: the canal fills up and loses capacity) and one that is TOO HIGH (scour: the canal deepens, the banks fail, and the offtakes are left stranded above the water).**

> **A REGIME channel is one in which neither happens — it carries its silt through without gaining or losing material.**

> **That is why the design velocity must be matched to the SILT GRADE, and hence why m exists.** The whole theory is an attempt to find the velocity at which the canal is in balance with what it carries.

> **And it is why LINED canals do not need these theories at all: a lined channel cannot scour or silt its boundary, so it is designed by Manning's equation for the required discharge, and the only velocity limits are those of the lining material.**

examTip.trick: **V₀ = 0.55 m y^{0.64}, and m is the SILT GRADE correction** — 0.7 for very fine silt up to 1.3 for very coarse, with m = 1 for Kennedy's own Upper Bari Doab canal.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) bed slope is wrong in an instructive way: Kennedy's theory gives NO slope relation at all.** It provides one equation with two unknowns, so the B/y ratio must be assumed and the slope brought in from Manning — which is exactly the incompleteness Lacey removed.
examTip.mnemonic: **Coarser silt → higher m → higher velocity needed.** And the Kennedy/Lacey split: Kennedy credits the BED alone with suspending silt (so uses DEPTH); Lacey credits the whole perimeter (so uses HYDRAULIC RADIUS) and gives three equations, hence a determinate section.

questions.stem: A cross-drainage work in which the drainage water is carried BENEATH the canal, with the canal flowing in a trough above it, is called:
questions.solution:
**An AQUEDUCT — the canal is carried OVER the drainage.**

**The naming rule, which is where every mark in this family is won or lost:**

> **The structure is named for WHAT GOES ON TOP — or more precisely, for what is carried across.**

> **In an AQUEDUCT, the CANAL is aqueducted — carried over — and the drain passes beneath.**

| Structure | CANAL | DRAIN | Flow condition |
|---|---|---|---|
| **AQUEDUCT** | **ABOVE, in a trough** | **BELOW, free surface** | **Drain flows freely under the canal** ← |
| **SYPHON AQUEDUCT** | **ABOVE, in a trough** | **BELOW, UNDER PRESSURE** | **The drain bed is depressed and the drain runs full** |
| **SUPER PASSAGE** | **BELOW** | **ABOVE, in a trough** | **Canal flows freely under the drain** |
| **CANAL SYPHON (syphon)** | **BELOW, UNDER PRESSURE** | **ABOVE** | **The canal bed is depressed and the canal runs full** |
| **LEVEL CROSSING** | **The two MIX** | **The two MIX** | **A common pool with regulators on each** |
| **Inlet and outlet** | The drain is admitted INTO the canal and let out downstream | — | For a small drain |

> **So the four principal types are two pairs, distinguished twice over: WHICH IS ON TOP, and WHETHER THE LOWER ONE RUNS FULL.**

**The memory device that makes the set reliable:**

> **An "AQUEDUCT" carries WATER (aqua) — and the water it carries is the CANAL. So in an aqueduct the CANAL IS ON TOP.**

> **A "SUPER passage" gives the DRAIN the SUPERIOR position. So in a super passage the DRAIN IS ON TOP.**

> **And "SYPHON" always means the lower channel is running UNDER PRESSURE, whichever it is:**

> **SYPHON AQUEDUCT → canal on top, DRAIN under pressure below.**

> **CANAL SYPHON → drain on top, CANAL under pressure below.**

> **Reading the compound name from the back tells you which channel is depressed: in a "syphon aqueduct" the aqueduct part says the canal is on top, so the syphoning must be the drain.**

**Which type is CHOSEN, and why — the decision that matters in practice:**

> **The choice is dictated almost entirely by the RELATIVE LEVELS of the canal bed and the drainage bed.**

| Condition | Structure |
|---|---|
| **Canal bed WELL ABOVE the drain's high flood level** | **AQUEDUCT — the cheapest and most desirable case** ← |
| **Canal bed above the drain bed but BELOW the drain's HFL** | **SYPHON AQUEDUCT — the drain must be forced under pressure** |
| **Drain bed well above the canal's water surface** | **SUPER PASSAGE** |
| **Drain bed above the canal bed but the canal cannot be carried under freely** | **CANAL SYPHON** |
| **Both at nearly the same level, and both large** | **LEVEL CROSSING — the last resort** |

> **An AQUEDUCT is always preferred where the levels permit, and the reason is worth stating: a free-flowing drain beneath a canal trough is a simple, self-cleaning arrangement with no pressure to contain.**

> **A SYPHON AQUEDUCT is more expensive and more troublesome, because the drain running under pressure through a depressed barrel will DEPOSIT SILT there, and the barrel must be designed for a self-cleansing velocity and provided with access for clearing.**

> **A CANAL SYPHON is worse still, because the canal itself — the thing whose flow must be preserved — is the one forced under pressure, and any silting there directly reduces the canal's capacity.**

> **So the hierarchy of preference follows the hierarchy of consequence: never depress the canal if the drain can be depressed instead.**

**Why a LEVEL CROSSING is a last resort:**

> **In a level crossing the canal water and the drainage water are allowed to MIX in a common pool, with a regulator on the canal downstream and a cross-regulator on the drain.**

> **The problems are obvious: the canal receives the drain's silt and whatever it carries; the operation requires two gated structures to be worked in coordination during floods; and a large flood can overwhelm the canal.**

> **It is adopted only where a large canal meets a large drain at nearly the same level, so that no crossing structure is practicable** — and it is then a permanent operational burden.

> **Which is a general lesson about cross-drainage: the structure is determined by levels fixed long before, at the alignment stage.**

> **A canal alignment that keeps the canal HIGH — on a ridge or watershed line, which is why ridge canals are preferred — avoids expensive cross-drainage works altogether, because every drain then passes beneath it as a simple aqueduct.**

> **So the money saved on cross-drainage works is saved during ALIGNMENT, not during design.** That is why the choice of a watershed alignment for a main canal is one of the most consequential decisions in an irrigation project, and why a contour or side-slope alignment brings a long train of costly crossings with it.

examTip.trick: **An AQUEDUCT carries WATER (aqua) — and the water it carries is the CANAL, so the canal is ON TOP** with the drain flowing freely beneath. A SUPER passage gives the DRAIN the superior position.
examTip.trap: **"SYPHON" always means the LOWER channel runs under PRESSURE.** So a syphon aqueduct has the canal on top and the DRAIN depressed; a canal syphon has the drain on top and the CANAL depressed. Read the compound name from the back.
examTip.mnemonic: **Never depress the canal if the drain can be depressed instead** — silt in a canal syphon reduces the canal's own capacity. And the money is saved at ALIGNMENT: a ridge canal stays high, so every drain crosses beneath as a simple aqueduct.

questions.stem: The most direct engineering consequence of a rising water table that reaches the root zone of crops is:
options: An increase in the crop yield due to abundant moisture
A reduction in the canal's seepage losses
Waterlogging, with reduced soil aeration and the accumulation of salts at the surface
An increase in the soil's shear strength
questions.solution:
**WATERLOGGING — reduced aeration and salt accumulation at the surface.**

**What waterlogging is:**

> **A soil is WATERLOGGED when its pores in the root zone are so saturated with water that the crop's roots cannot get the AIR they need.**

> **The usual definition in irrigation practice: the water table has risen to within about 1.5 to 2 m of the ground surface** — because CAPILLARY RISE then carries water into the root zone even where the water table itself is below it.

> **So the water table need not reach the surface to do the damage. It only needs to come close enough for capillarity to bridge the gap** — which in a fine-textured soil can be well over a metre.

**The TWO mechanisms of damage, and both matter:**

> **FIRST — LOSS OF AERATION.**

> **Roots RESPIRE: they consume oxygen and release carbon dioxide.**

> **A saturated soil has no air-filled pores, so oxygen cannot diffuse to the roots** — gaseous diffusion through water is some ten thousand times slower than through air.

> **The roots suffocate, and the soil turns ANAEROBIC, in which condition bacteria produce compounds toxic to plants and nitrogen is lost by denitrification.**

> **Note that this is why abundant moisture is NOT beneficial and why option (a) is wrong: a crop needs water AND air in its root zone, and saturation supplies the first by destroying the second.**

> **Rice is the exception that proves the rule — it has specialised tissue to carry air down to its roots, which is why it alone tolerates a flooded field.**

> **SECOND — SALINITY.**

> **This is the more insidious mechanism and the one that ruins land permanently.**

> **Capillary water rises to the surface and EVAPORATES there. The water leaves; the DISSOLVED SALTS DO NOT.**

> **So salt is delivered continuously to the surface and concentrated there, year after year.**

> **The result is a white crust — the SALINE or ALKALINE soil that has taken vast areas of irrigated land out of cultivation across the Indo-Gangetic plain.**

> **The cruel logic is that IRRIGATION ITSELF causes it: irrigation raises the water table, the raised water table brings salts up, and the salts destroy the land the irrigation was built to serve.**

**Why the other options are wrong, each for a reason worth knowing:**

| Option | Why wrong |
|---|---|
| **(a) Higher yield from abundant moisture** | **A crop needs AIR as well as water in the root zone. Saturation removes the air, and yields FALL sharply** |
| **(b) Reduced canal seepage** | **Partly TRUE physically — a high water table does reduce the seepage GRADIENT out of a canal — but that is a minor side effect, not the consequence asked about, and it is no consolation for the ruined land** |
| **(d) Increased shear strength** | **The OPPOSITE. Saturation raises pore water pressure, and effective stress σ' = σ − u FALLS, so shear strength FALLS** |

> **Option (b) deserves the note it gets, because it is not simply false.**

> **A canal whose surrounding water table has risen to meet it does lose less water by seepage.**

> **But naming that as "the most direct engineering consequence" mistakes a marginal hydraulic effect for the destruction of the command area.** The question asks for the consequence, and the consequence is the ruined soil.

**The CAUSES of waterlogging, since the remedy follows from them:**

| Cause | Note |
|---|---|
| **SEEPAGE from unlined canals and distributaries** | **Usually the largest single source** ← |
| **OVER-IRRIGATION — applying more water than the crop needs** | Farmer practice, and free or cheap water encourages it |
| **INADEQUATE natural DRAINAGE** | Flat land, or drainage lines obstructed by embankments and roads |
| **Impervious layer at shallow depth** | Perches the water table |
| **Excessive rainfall or flooding** | Seasonal contribution |
| **Obstruction of natural drainage by the project's own works** | **Canal embankments cut across drainage lines — which is what cross-drainage works exist to prevent** |

> **The last row connects this topic to cross-drainage: an irrigation project that blocks the country's natural drainage creates waterlogging on the upstream side of its own embankments.**

**The REMEDIES, in order of how fundamental they are:**

| Remedy | Note |
|---|---|
| **LINING the canals** | **Attacks the largest cause directly; also saves the water** ← |
| **Controlled, measured water delivery (and charging for it)** | **Removes the incentive to over-irrigate** |
| **SURFACE drains** | Remove excess surface water |
| **SUBSURFACE (tile) drainage** | **Lowers the water table itself — the definitive engineering answer** |
| **VERTICAL drainage — tube wells** | **Pump the groundwater down, and use the water for irrigation. Doubly useful where the groundwater is fresh** |
| **BIO-DRAINAGE — planting eucalyptus or similar high-transpiration trees** | Lowers the table by transpiration; slow, cheap, and needs no power |
| **CONJUNCTIVE USE of surface and groundwater** | **The strategic answer: use groundwater in the dry season, which keeps the table down, and canal water in the monsoon** |

> **CONJUNCTIVE USE is the most intelligent of these, because it turns the problem into the solution: the groundwater that is rising and causing waterlogging is itself pumped and used, which lowers the table and irrigates the crop at the same time.**

> **And it fits the seasonal pattern — canal water is plentiful in the monsoon and scarce in the dry season, exactly when the water table has recovered and can be drawn on.**

> **BIO-DRAINAGE deserves mention as the option that needs no energy and no maintenance: a belt of eucalyptus along a canal can transpire a remarkable volume, and where power is unreliable that reliability matters more than efficiency.**

examTip.trick: **Waterlogging damages a crop TWO ways: loss of AERATION (roots suffocate — diffusion through water is ~10,000 times slower than through air) and SALINITY (capillary water evaporates at the surface and leaves its salts behind).**
examTip.trap: **Option (b) is not simply false** — a high water table really does reduce a canal's seepage gradient. But that is a marginal hydraulic side effect, not the consequence; the consequence is the ruined command area.
examTip.mnemonic: **Irrigation causes the salinity that destroys the land irrigation was built to serve** — which is why CONJUNCTIVE USE is the intelligent answer: pump the rising groundwater in the dry season, lowering the table and watering the crop at once.

questions.stem: If the duty of a crop with a base period of 120 days is 1800 hectares per cumec, the delta of the crop is:
questions.solution:
**57.6 cm.**

**The duty-delta relation:**

> **Δ = 8.64 B / D**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Δ** | **DELTA — the total depth of water the crop needs, in METRES** | **to find** |
| **B** | **BASE PERIOD, in DAYS** | **120 days** |
| **D** | **DUTY, in hectares per cumec** | **1800 ha/cumec** |
| **8.64** | **The unit-conversion constant** | — |

**The computation:**

> **Δ = 8.64 × 120 / 1800 = 1036.8 / 1800 = 0.576 m = 57.6 cm** ✓

**Where the 8.64 comes from — worth deriving once, so it need never be memorised blindly:**

> **One cumec flowing for the whole base period delivers a volume:**

> **V = 1 m³/s × B days × 86,400 s/day = 86,400 B m³**

> **That volume is spread over D hectares = D × 10,000 m²:**

> **Depth = 86,400 B / (10,000 D) = 8.64 B / D metres** ✓

> **So 8.64 is simply 86,400 ÷ 10,000 — the seconds in a day divided by the square metres in a hectare.**

> **Knowing that means the formula can be rebuilt from first principles in ten seconds if it is misremembered**, which is worth more than the formula itself.

**The definitions, since they are constantly mixed up:**

| Term | Definition | Units |
|---|---|---|
| **DUTY** | **The AREA a unit discharge can irrigate over the base period** | **hectares per cumec** |
| **DELTA** | **The total DEPTH of water the crop needs over the base period** | **cm or m** |
| **BASE PERIOD** | **The period from the FIRST to the LAST watering** | days |
| **CROP PERIOD** | **From SOWING to HARVEST** | days |

> **Note the INVERSE relation between duty and delta, which is the conceptual point:**

> **A HIGH DUTY means one cumec irrigates a LARGE area — so each hectare gets LITTLE water — so the DELTA is SMALL.**

> **A crop with a high duty is an ECONOMICAL crop in water terms.**

> **So "high duty = good, low delta = good" — the two statements are the same statement.**

> **And that inversion is the check on the arithmetic here: 1800 ha/cumec is a fairly high duty, so the delta should be modest — 57.6 cm is a reasonable figure for a wheat or gram crop, not for rice.**

**Typical deltas, since the answer should be judged against them:**

| Crop | Delta (cm) | Base period (days) |
|---|---|---|
| **RICE (paddy)** | **100-150** | **120** |
| **Sugarcane** | **80-120** | **320-360** |
| **WHEAT** | **35-45** | **120** |
| **Cotton** | **40-50** | **200** |
| **Maize** | **45-50** | **100** |
| **Gram** | **25-30** | **120** |
| **Vegetables** | **45-60** | **90-120** |

> **A delta of 57.6 cm on a 120-day base period sits between wheat and a vegetable crop — entirely plausible.**

> **RICE is the outlier and the reason irrigation planning in South Asia is dominated by it: at 100-150 cm it needs three to four times the water of wheat**, because it is grown in standing water and loses enormously to percolation and evaporation.

> **Which is why a cropping pattern, not just a total area, determines a canal's capacity** — the same command area sown to rice rather than wheat needs a canal three times the size.

**BASE PERIOD versus CROP PERIOD, since the formula uses the base period:**

> **The CROP period runs from sowing to harvest. The BASE period runs from the first watering to the last.**

> **The base period is slightly SHORTER, because the crop is not watered right up to harvest — the final weeks are allowed to dry for ripening and reaping.**

> **In practice the two are taken as approximately equal for design, and papers use them interchangeably.**

> **But the distinction is real, and where a question gives both, the BASE period is the one the duty-delta formula requires** — because duty is defined over the period during which water is actually supplied.

**Why DUTY varies with more than the crop, which the formula hides:**

| Factor | Effect on duty |
|---|---|
| **Crop type** | **The principal factor** |
| **Climate and season** | **Hotter, drier → more evaporation → LOWER duty** |
| **Soil type** | **Sandy soil percolates more → LOWER duty** |
| **CANAL LINING and system efficiency** | **Less seepage loss → HIGHER duty** ← |
| **Method of application** | Drip and sprinkler give much higher duties than flooding |
| **Position in the system** | **Duty at the FIELD is higher than duty at the HEAD of the canal, because losses intervene** |

> **The last row is the one that matters most in practice and is easy to miss: DUTY MUST BE STATED WITH ITS LOCATION.**

> **DUTY AT THE FIELD (or nakka) counts only the water the crop receives.**

> **DUTY AT THE HEAD of the distributary or main canal must also carry all the conveyance and seepage losses, so the same crop shows a LOWER duty there — the canal must carry more water to deliver the same amount to the field.**

> **A canal designed with a field duty rather than a head duty will be undersized**, and the error is not small: with a 60 per cent conveyance efficiency, the head duty is only 60 per cent of the field duty.

> **So a duty figure without its point of reference is an incomplete piece of data**, and reading which is meant is part of interpreting these problems.

examTip.trap: **The 8.64 is just 86,400 s/day ÷ 10,000 m²/ha** — so the formula can be rebuilt from first principles in seconds rather than memorised. Derive it once and it cannot be misremembered.
examTip.mnemonic: **Duty and delta are INVERSE: high duty = one cumec covers a large area = little water each = small delta.** Check the answer against typical deltas — rice 100-150 cm, wheat 35-45 cm — and note that duty must always be stated WITH its location, at the head or at the field.

questions.stem: For a singly reinforced rectangular beam of Fe 500 steel designed by the limit state method as per IS 456:2000, the limiting value of xu/d is:
questions.solution:
**0.46 for Fe 500.**

**The limiting neutral axis depths:**

| Steel grade | **x_u,max / d** | **Limiting M_u / (b d² f_ck)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Fe 250** | **0.53** | **0.148** |
| **Fe 415** | **0.48** | **0.138** |
| **Fe 500** | **0.46** ← | **0.133** |

> **The three values 0.53, 0.48 and 0.46 are the whole answer to this family of questions, and all three appear as options here** — so the grade in the stem must be read carefully.

> **The pattern is worth noting: the HIGHER the steel grade, the SMALLER the limiting neutral axis depth.**

**Why the higher grade gives the SMALLER limit — the reason behind the numbers:**

> **The limiting depth is defined by the BALANCED condition: the concrete reaches its ultimate strain (0.0035) at exactly the moment the steel reaches its yield strain plus 0.002.**

> **Consider the strain diagram. From similar triangles:**

> **x_u,max / d = 0.0035 / (0.0035 + ε_st)**

> **where ε_st is the limiting strain in the steel — the yield strain plus 0.002.**

| Grade | **Design yield strain = 0.87 f_y / E_s** | **+0.002** | **x_u,max/d** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Fe 250** | **0.87 × 250 / 2×10⁵ = 0.00109** | **0.00309** | **0.0035/0.00659 = 0.531** ✓ |
| **Fe 415** | **0.87 × 415 / 2×10⁵ = 0.00180** | **0.00380** | **0.0035/0.00730 = 0.479** ✓ |
| **Fe 500** | **0.87 × 500 / 2×10⁵ = 0.00217** | **0.00417** | **0.0035/0.00767 = 0.456 ≈ 0.46** ✓ |

> **So the three code values are not arbitrary — each falls out of the strain compatibility condition for its grade.**

> **And the direction is now clear: a HIGHER grade steel yields at a LARGER strain, so the neutral axis must be HIGHER for the concrete's 0.0035 to coincide with it.**

> **Being able to reconstruct these numbers from the strain diagram means they need never be confused.**

**Where the extra 0.002 comes from — and it is not a fudge:**

> **IS 456's design stress-strain curve for reinforcement is BILINEAR up to 0.8 f_y and then a series of straight segments to the design yield stress 0.87 f_y at a strain of 0.87f_y/E_s + 0.002.**

> **That is, the code assumes that HIGH-YIELD steel does NOT have a sharp yield point — it yields gradually — and the design curve reaches full design stress only after an additional 0.002 of strain.**

> **Which is physically true: mild steel (Fe 250) has a definite yield plateau, while cold-worked and TMT high-yield bars do not.**

> **So the 0.002 addition represents the real behaviour of high-yield steel, and it applies to Fe 415 and Fe 500 — for Fe 250 the code also uses it in this derivation, which is why 0.53 rather than a larger value results.**

**What the limiting depth is FOR — the whole purpose:**

> **A beam whose neutral axis is DEEPER than x_u,max fails by CRUSHING OF THE CONCRETE BEFORE THE STEEL YIELDS — an OVER-REINFORCED section.**

| | **UNDER-reinforced (x_u < x_u,max)** | **OVER-reinforced (x_u > x_u,max)** |
|---|---|---|
| **What yields first** | **STEEL** | **Concrete crushes first** |
| **Failure mode** | **DUCTILE — large deflections, wide cracks, ample warning** | **BRITTLE, SUDDEN, no warning** ← |
| **Permitted by IS 456?** | **YES** | **NO — prohibited** |
| **Efficient use of steel?** | **Yes — the steel is worked to its full strength** | No — the steel never reaches yield |

> **IS 456 PROHIBITS over-reinforced sections, and x_u,max is how the prohibition is expressed numerically.**

> **The reason is entirely about WARNING. An under-reinforced beam sags visibly, cracks widely and deflects before it collapses — occupants can leave the building.**

> **An over-reinforced beam gives no warning at all: the concrete crushes and the beam drops.**

> **So the limit is not an efficiency rule but a safety-of-life rule**, and that is why it is mandatory rather than advisory.

> **It is the same principle as the net-section/gross-section factoring in steel design and the capacity design of seismic frames: wherever a structure can fail two ways, the code forces the DUCTILE one.**

**The limiting moment of resistance, since it follows immediately:**

> **M_u,lim = 0.36 f_ck b x_u,max (d − 0.42 x_u,max)**

> **For Fe 500, with x_u,max = 0.46 d:**

> **M_u,lim = 0.36 f_ck b (0.46d)(d − 0.42 × 0.46d) = 0.36 × 0.46 × (1 − 0.193) f_ck b d² = 0.133 f_ck b d²** ✓

| Constant | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **0.36 f_ck** | **The average stress in the equivalent rectangular compression block** |
| **0.42 x_u** | **The depth of the compression centroid below the extreme fibre** |
| **(d − 0.42 x_u)** | **The LEVER ARM** |

> **The 0.36 and 0.42 come from integrating the code's parabolic-plus-rectangular stress block** and are the same for every grade of steel — only x_u,max changes.

> **And if the applied moment exceeds M_u,lim the section cannot be singly reinforced: it must either be made deeper, or made DOUBLY reinforced with compression steel** — which is exactly the decision point this value governs in design.

examTip.trick: **x_u,max/d = 0.53 (Fe 250), 0.48 (Fe 415), 0.46 (Fe 500).** All three appear as options here, so read the grade in the stem.
examTip.trap: **Reconstruct them from the strain diagram rather than memorising: x_u,max/d = 0.0035/(0.0035 + 0.87f_y/E_s + 0.002).** For Fe 500 that gives 0.0035/0.00767 = 0.456. Then they cannot be confused.
examTip.mnemonic: **A HIGHER grade yields at a LARGER strain, so the neutral axis sits HIGHER.** And the limit exists for WARNING, not efficiency: an under-reinforced beam sags and cracks before it falls; an over-reinforced one crushes without notice.

questions.stem: A rectangular reinforced concrete slab is simply supported on all four edges with a longer span of 9 m and a shorter span of 4 m. It should be designed as:
options: A two-way slab, since it is supported on all four edges
A one-way slab, since the span ratio exceeds 2
questions.solution:
**A ONE-WAY slab, because the span ratio 9/4 = 2.25 exceeds 2.**

**The criterion:**

> **Ratio = longer span / shorter span = 9 / 4 = 2.25**

| Ratio L_y / L_x | Design as |
|---|---|
| **≤ 2** | **TWO-WAY slab** |
| **> 2** | **ONE-WAY slab** ← 2.25 |

> **So support on all four edges is NOT sufficient to make a slab two-way, and that is exactly the misconception option (a) is built on.**

**Why the ratio governs rather than the support arrangement — the physical reason:**

> **A slab carries load to its supports by bending. Given a choice of two directions, MOST OF THE LOAD TAKES THE STIFFER PATH.**

> **Bending stiffness varies as 1/L³, so the SHORTER span is very much stiffer.**

> **For a ratio of 2, the short direction is 2³ = 8 times as stiff as the long one, and so carries roughly eight-ninths — about 89 per cent — of the load.**

> **At a ratio of 2.25 it is 2.25³ = 11.4 times as stiff, taking about 92 per cent.**

> **So when the ratio exceeds 2, the long-span direction is carrying under about a tenth of the load, and treating it as carrying NONE is a small and safe simplification.**

> **That is the whole justification for the ratio-of-2 rule: it is the point beyond which the second direction has become negligible.**

> **The load then spans the SHORT direction and the slab behaves as a series of one-way strips**, even though its long edges are supported.

**What follows in the design, since the classification determines everything after it:**

| | **ONE-WAY slab** | **TWO-WAY slab** |
|---|---|---|
| **Main steel** | **Along the SHORT span only** | **BOTH directions, both designed** |
| **The other direction** | **DISTRIBUTION steel — a nominal minimum** | **Main steel** |
| **Moment coefficients** | Simple beam analysis of a unit strip | **IS 456 Annex D tables (Rankine-Grashoff or yield line)** |
| **CORNER reinforcement** | Not required | **REQUIRED at corners held down, in two layers, both directions** |
| **Deflection (span/depth)** | **Basic 20 for simply supported** | Same basic values, applied to the SHORT span |

> **The DISTRIBUTION steel in the long direction is not structural in the load-carrying sense but is essential nonetheless:**

| Why distribution steel is provided | Note |
|---|---|
| **Resists TEMPERATURE and SHRINKAGE stresses** | **The main reason** ← |
| **Distributes concentrated loads across adjacent strips** | Hence the name |
| **Holds the main bars in position during concreting** | Practical |
| **Resists the small moment that does exist in the long direction** | The neglected 8 per cent |

> **IS 456's minimum: 0.15 % of the gross area for mild steel and 0.12 % for high-yield deformed bars** — and that minimum applies to the total in each direction, not merely to the distribution steel.

**Why option (b) FLAT SLAB is a different thing entirely:**

> **A FLAT SLAB is supported DIRECTLY ON COLUMNS, with no beams at all.**

> **The stem says the slab is supported on all four EDGES, which means beams or walls** — so it is not a flat slab, whatever its span ratio.

| Slab type | Support |
|---|---|
| **One-way / two-way slab** | **Beams or walls along the edges** ← |
| **FLAT slab** | **Columns directly, often with drops and column heads** |
| **FLAT PLATE** | Columns directly, with no drops or capitals |
| **Waffle / ribbed slab** | Beams, with the slab lightened by voids |
| **Cantilever slab** | Supported on ONE edge only |

> **Flat slabs are chosen for a specific reason worth knowing: they give a FLAT SOFFIT, so the storey height can be reduced and services run freely beneath.**

> **Their weakness is PUNCHING SHEAR at the columns — the slab tries to punch through around the column perimeter — which is why drops and column capitals exist.**

**A caution about the ratio-of-2 rule, since real slabs are rarely simply supported:**

> **The rule as stated applies to a slab SIMPLY SUPPORTED on all four edges, which is the stem's case.**

> **Where edges are CONTINUOUS or RESTRAINED the behaviour changes, and IS 456 Annex D distinguishes nine cases of edge restraint for two-way slabs.**

> **But the ratio-of-2 boundary between one-way and two-way behaviour is applied generally, because it reflects the 1/L³ stiffness argument rather than the support conditions.**

> **And a practical note: even where a slab is designed one-way, providing somewhat more than the minimum distribution steel is cheap insurance**, because the long-span moment is small but not zero and cracking in that direction is unsightly and admits water.

> **A designer who provides the bare 0.12 per cent minimum has satisfied the code; one who provides a little more has satisfied the building.**

examTip.trick: **Ratio = 9/4 = 2.25 > 2, so it is a ONE-WAY slab** — regardless of being supported on all four edges.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) states the common misconception: four-edge support does NOT make a slab two-way.** The RATIO decides. At 2.25 the short direction is 2.25³ = 11.4 times as stiff and carries about 92 % of the load.
examTip.mnemonic: **Stiffness goes as 1/L³, so most of the load takes the SHORT path.** Beyond a ratio of 2 the long direction carries under a tenth, and neglecting it is safe — but still provide DISTRIBUTION steel (0.12 % HYSD) for shrinkage and temperature.

questions.stem: In the slump test on fresh concrete, a SHEAR slump — in which one half of the cone slides down an inclined plane — indicates that the mix:
options: Has the correct workability for a reinforced slab
Is too dry to be placed
Lacks cohesion and is liable to segregate
questions.solution:
**The mix LACKS COHESION and is liable to segregate.**

**The three forms a slump can take:**

| Slump form | Appearance | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **TRUE slump** | **The cone subsides EVENLY, keeping its shape** | **A satisfactory, cohesive mix — the only valid result** |
| **SHEAR slump** | **One HALF slides down an inclined plane; the mass is lopsided** | **LACK OF COHESION — the mix is harsh or lean and will SEGREGATE** ← |
| **COLLAPSE slump** | **The concrete collapses completely** | **The mix is FAR TOO WET — the test is meaningless** |

> **Only a TRUE slump gives a valid measurement.**

> **A SHEAR or COLLAPSE slump means the test must be REPEATED, and if the same form recurs the MIX is wrong, not the test.**

> **That is the practical instruction the codes give, and it is worth stating: a shear slump is not a low reading to be recorded but a defect to be reported.**

**Why a shear slump means poor cohesion:**

> **A cohesive mix behaves as a single plastic mass — when the mould is lifted it settles as a whole.**

> **A mix lacking cohesion has insufficient FINES or PASTE to bind the aggregate, so the mass has no internal shear resistance and one part simply slides off the other.**

> **The usual causes:**

| Cause | Remedy |
|---|---|
| **Too little CEMENT (a lean mix)** | Increase the cement content |
| **Too little FINE aggregate; a gap-graded sand** | **Improve the grading; add fines** |
| **Excess coarse aggregate, or an oversized maximum size** | Adjust the proportions |
| **Harsh, angular aggregate with no rounded fraction** | Blend the aggregate |
| **Deficient FINES generally** | **Add a mineral admixture — fly ash, slag or limestone filler** ← |

> **Note that option (c) — excessive cement — is the OPPOSITE of the usual cause.** A rich mix is generally MORE cohesive, not less; excess cement causes other problems (shrinkage, heat, cost) but not a shear slump.

> **And option (b) "too dry to be placed" is wrong for a distinct reason: a very dry mix gives a ZERO or very LOW TRUE slump, not a shear slump.** Dryness and lack of cohesion are different faults, and the slump test distinguishes them by the FORM of the slump rather than its magnitude.

**Why SEGREGATION is the consequence that matters:**

> **SEGREGATION is the separation of the constituents of concrete so that the mix is no longer uniform.**

| Type | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Coarse aggregate separating from the mortar** | **Typical of a DRY, harsh mix — the stones roll away and collect** |
| **Paste (cement and water) separating from the mix** | **Typical of a WET mix — the paste runs out** |
| **BLEEDING** | **A special case: water rising to the surface after placing** |

> **A segregated concrete is weak, porous and non-uniform: the top may be a laitance of paste and the bottom a honeycomb of stone.**

> **The steel is then embedded in whichever fraction happens to be around it, and the cover concrete — the part that protects the reinforcement — is the part most likely to be paste-rich and weak.**

> **So a mix that shows a shear slump on test will produce a structure whose durability is compromised in the very layer that matters most.**

> **The practices that provoke segregation:**

| Practice | Note |
|---|---|
| **Dropping concrete from a height** | **Use a tremie, chute or pipe; limit the free fall** |
| **OVER-vibration** | **Drives the coarse aggregate down and the paste up** ← the most common cause on site |
| **Long-distance conveyance in an open barrow over rough ground** | Continuous jolting separates the mix |
| **Discharging against an obstruction or shutter face** | The stones bounce away |
| **Placing a wet mix on a slope** | The paste runs |

> **OVER-VIBRATION is worth emphasising because it is the error made with good intentions: an operator who keeps the poker in until the surface looks perfectly smooth has usually vibrated until the paste has risen and the stone has sunk.**

> **The correct rule is to vibrate until air ceases to escape and the surface just glistens, then withdraw slowly** — a matter of perhaps 15 to 30 seconds per insertion, not minutes.

**The slump test's own limitations, stated honestly:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Insensitive for very DRY mixes** | **Slump near zero for a wide range of workabilities — use the COMPACTING FACTOR or VEE-BEE test instead** ← |
| **Meaningless for very WET mixes** | Collapse slump |
| **Not suitable for concrete with a maximum aggregate size above 40 mm** | The cone is too small |
| **Measures only one aspect of workability** | Says nothing directly about cohesion — except through the FORM of the slump |
| **Highly sensitive to operator technique** | Rodding, lifting speed, base condition |

> **Its virtues are why it survives regardless: it is cheap, it is quick, it needs no power, and it can be done at the point of discharge by the person placing the concrete.**

> **For SITE CONTROL — checking that today's concrete is the same as yesterday's — that is precisely the right instrument**, and detecting a change is more useful in practice than measuring an absolute value.

> **So the slump test is best understood as a CONSISTENCY-CONTROL test rather than a workability measurement**, and the shear slump is the one occasion on which it reports something about cohesion as well.

examTip.trick: **Three slump forms: TRUE (even subsidence — valid), SHEAR (one half slides off — LACKS COHESION, will segregate), COLLAPSE (far too wet — test meaningless).** Only a true slump is a valid measurement.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) confuses dryness with poor cohesion** — a dry mix gives a LOW TRUE slump, not a shear slump. And option (c) is backwards: a rich mix is MORE cohesive; a shear slump comes from too FEW fines, not too many.
examTip.mnemonic: **OVER-VIBRATION is the segregation error made with good intentions** — vibrating until the surface looks perfect drives stone down and paste up. Vibrate until air stops escaping and the surface just glistens: 15-30 seconds, not minutes.

questions.stem: As per IS 875 (Part 5) and IS 1893, in the load combination for the limit state of collapse involving dead load, live load and earthquake load, the factor applied to the imposed (live) load is:
questions.solution:
**1.2 — in the combination 1.2 (DL + LL + EL).**

**The limit state of collapse combinations:**

| Combination | Factors |
|---|---|
| **DL + LL** | **1.5 DL + 1.5 LL** |
| **DL + LL + EL (or WL)** | **1.2 DL + 1.2 LL ± 1.2 EL** ← |
| **DL + EL, no live load** | **1.5 DL ± 1.5 EL** |
| **DL alone opposing the lateral load (uplift, overturning)** | **0.9 DL ± 1.5 EL** ← the critical case for stability |

> **So when the earthquake acts TOGETHER with the live load, every load in the combination carries 1.2 — dead, live and seismic alike.**

**Why the factor DROPS from 1.5 to 1.2 when a third load joins:**

> **This is the substance of the question, and the reasoning is probabilistic.**

> **The factor 1.5 on dead plus live load allows for the possibility that both are at their characteristic values at the same time — which is credible, since a building's dead load is always present and its design live load is a plausible occupancy.**

> **But the probability that the FULL design live load and the FULL design earthquake occur SIMULTANEOUSLY is much lower.**

> **A design earthquake is a rare event — a return period of decades to centuries. The chance that it strikes at the precise moment the building is loaded to its full design occupancy is small.**

> **So the code reduces the factors on all three, recognising that requiring the structure to resist the simultaneous maximum of every load would be uneconomically conservative.**

> **That is the general principle behind every load combination in every code: THE MORE LOADS COMBINED, THE LOWER THE FACTORS**, because the joint probability of all reaching their maxima together falls.

**The separate and stricter reduction in IS 1893, which is worth knowing:**

> **IS 1893 goes further and reduces the LIVE LOAD ITSELF before the combination factor is even applied:**

| Live load on the floor | Percentage taken for SEISMIC WEIGHT |
|---|---|
| **Up to and including 3 kN/m²** | **25 %** |
| **Above 3 kN/m²** | **50 %** |
| **ROOF live load** | **ZERO — not included at all** |

> **So there are TWO distinct reductions operating, and they must not be confused:**

> **FIRST — the SEISMIC WEIGHT reduction (25 % or 50 %), which reduces the MASS used to compute the earthquake force.**

> **SECOND — the LOAD FACTOR of 1.2, applied in the combination to the loads acting on the member.**

> **Which explains option (c) 0.25: it is the SEISMIC WEIGHT percentage, offered as if it were a load factor.** A well-made distractor, because 25 per cent is a real and relevant number in the wrong role.

**Why the seismic weight uses so little of the live load:**

> **The earthquake force on a building is F = mass × acceleration. Only mass that MOVES WITH the building contributes.**

> **Furniture, stored goods and occupants are not rigidly attached to the floor** — they slide, shift and are only partly coupled to the structure's motion.

> **And the full design live load is present on all floors simultaneously only very rarely.**

> **ROOF live load is excluded entirely because it represents maintenance access — a person on the roof — which is neither massive nor likely.**

> **The DEAD load, by contrast, is taken at 100 per cent always: the structure's own weight and its finishes are rigidly part of it and move with it exactly.**

**Why the 0.9 DL combination matters, since it is the one most often forgotten:**

> **0.9 DL ± 1.5 EL applies where the DEAD LOAD IS STABILISING — that is, where it RESISTS the effect being checked.**

| Situation | Why 0.9 DL |
|---|---|
| **OVERTURNING of a wall or a frame** | **The weight resists; UNDERSTATE it to be safe** ← |
| **UPLIFT on a footing at the windward or leeward end** | Weight holds the footing down |
| **Sliding of a retaining structure** | Weight generates the friction that resists |
| **Tension in a column under lateral load reversal** | Gravity load offsets the tension |

> **The principle is general and worth stating clearly: a load factor is greater than 1 when the load's effect is ADVERSE, and LESS than 1 when its effect is BENEFICIAL.**

> **Applying 1.5 to a stabilising dead load would be UNSAFE, not conservative** — it would overstate the resistance.

> **That single insight resolves most confusion about load factors: ask what the load DOES to the effect being checked, then factor it up or down accordingly.**

**And a note on the ± sign, since it is not decoration:**

> **Seismic and wind loads must be applied in BOTH directions, because a frame's response is not symmetrical once gravity load is present.**

> **A column that is in compression under one direction of shaking may be in TENSION under the other, and a beam's end that requires top steel in one case requires bottom steel in the other.**

> **Which is why seismic detailing requires reinforcement continuous through joints and adequate at BOTH faces** — the code's ± is what makes that necessary, and it is the reason seismic beams are detailed so differently from gravity beams.

examTip.trick: **With three loads combined, every factor drops to 1.2: 1.2 (DL + LL ± EL).** The two-load case keeps 1.5.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) 0.25 is the SEISMIC WEIGHT percentage (25 % of a live load up to 3 kN/m²), offered as a load factor.** Two distinct reductions operate — one on the MASS for computing the force, one on the LOADS in the combination.
examTip.mnemonic: **A factor exceeds 1 when the load's effect is ADVERSE and falls below 1 when it is BENEFICIAL** — hence 0.9 DL ± 1.5 EL for overturning and uplift. Applying 1.5 to a stabilising dead load would be UNSAFE, not conservative.

questions.stem: A machine costs Rs 8,00,000, has a salvage value of Rs 80,000 and a useful life of 9 years. Using the straight line method, its book value at the end of the fifth year is:
questions.solution:
**Rs 4,00,000.**

**Step 1 — the annual depreciation by the straight line method:**

> **d = (First cost − Salvage value) / Useful life**

> **d = (8,00,000 − 80,000) / 9 = 7,20,000 / 9 = Rs 80,000 per year**

> **The numbers are chosen so that the annual charge happens to equal the salvage value — a coincidence, but a convenient one.**

**Step 2 — the accumulated depreciation after five years:**

> **D₅ = 5 × 80,000 = Rs 4,00,000**

**Step 3 — the book value:**

> **BV₅ = First cost − Accumulated depreciation = 8,00,000 − 4,00,000 = Rs 4,00,000** ✓

**The general formula, worth having:**

> **BV_n = C − n(C − S)/L**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **C** | First cost | 8,00,000 |
| **S** | Salvage value | 80,000 |
| **L** | Useful life | 9 years |
| **n** | Years elapsed | 5 |

> **BV_n = 8,00,000 − n × 80,000** — an arithmetic progression, which is exactly what "straight line" means: the book value plots as a straight line from C down to S.

**Why the salvage value MUST be deducted BEFORE dividing — the point of the question:**

> **DEPRECIATION represents the portion of an asset's value that is CONSUMED by use.**

> **The SALVAGE value is the portion that is NOT consumed — it is recovered when the asset is sold or scrapped.**

> **So depreciating the FULL first cost would write off value the owner will get back: it understates the book value throughout the life and overstates the annual expense.**

> **Option (b) Rs 3,55,600 is precisely that error made: d = 8,00,000/9 = 88,889 per year, giving BV₅ = 8,00,000 − 4,44,444 = 3,55,556.**

> **The error announces itself if the method is run to the end of the life:**

| Treatment | BV at year 9 | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **Deducting salvage first: 8,00,000 − 9 × 80,000** | **Rs 80,000 — exactly the salvage value** | **CORRECT** ✓ |
| **Depreciating the full cost: 8,00,000 − 9 × 88,889** | **ZERO — contradicting the stated salvage of 80,000** | **WRONG** |

> **That is the definitive check on the straight line method: RUN IT TO THE END OF THE LIFE AND IT MUST LAND EXACTLY ON THE SALVAGE VALUE.** If it does not, the depreciable base was wrong.

> **The check costs one multiplication and catches the only error this method admits.**

**The other distractors, for completeness:**

| Option | Origin |
|---|---|
| **(a) Rs 3,20,000** | **The book value at the end of year SIX** — right method, wrong year |
| **(b) Rs 3,55,600** | **The no-salvage-deduction error** |
| **(c) Rs 4,00,000** | ✓ |
| **(d) Rs 4,80,000** | **The book value at the end of year FOUR** |

> **So three of the four options come from the correct annual charge applied at the wrong year, or from the wrong depreciable base** — which is a well-formed option set, since each punishes one identifiable slip.

**The depreciation methods compared, since the choice changes the answer materially:**

| Method | Annual charge | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **STRAIGHT LINE** | **(C − S)/L — CONSTANT** | **Simplest; assumes uniform consumption** ← |
| **DECLINING BALANCE** | **A fixed RATE applied to the reducing book value** | **Accelerated — large early charges** |
| **DOUBLE declining balance** | **Rate = 2/L on the book value** | Most accelerated of the common methods |
| **SUM OF THE YEARS' DIGITS** | **(remaining life / Σ digits) × (C − S)** | Accelerated, and reaches S exactly |
| **SINKING FUND** | **A uniform deposit earning interest, accumulating to (C − S)** | **Lowest early charges; recognises the time value of money** |
| **SERVICE OUTPUT (units of production)** | **Per unit of output produced** | **Suits a machine whose wear tracks its USE, not its age** |

> **For this machine, the SUM OF THE YEARS' DIGITS would charge (9/45) × 7,20,000 = Rs 1,44,000 in the first year — nearly twice the straight-line figure — and only (1/45) × 7,20,000 = Rs 16,000 in the ninth.**

> **ACCELERATED methods are preferred by owners for a practical reason: a larger early charge reduces taxable income sooner, and money saved sooner is worth more.**

> **They are also more realistic for many assets — a machine loses more of its market value in its first year than in its last.**

> **The SINKING FUND method is the theoretically most interesting: it treats depreciation as a savings problem, asking what uniform annual deposit, earning interest, would accumulate to the replacement amount.** It gives the lowest early charges of all, because interest does part of the work.

> **SERVICE OUTPUT deserves a note for construction plant specifically: an excavator's wear depends on HOURS WORKED, not years owned, and a machine that stood idle for a year has not depreciated as one that ran two shifts.**

> **Charging depreciation per hour of operation is both fairer to the asset and far more useful for costing individual jobs** — which is why plant hire rates are quoted per hour and not per year.

examTip.trick: **Depreciate the DEPRECIABLE BASE (C − S), not the full cost: d = (8,00,000 − 80,000)/9 = Rs 80,000/yr, so BV₅ = 8,00,000 − 4,00,000 = Rs 4,00,000.**
examTip.trap: **Run the method to the END of the life and it MUST land exactly on the salvage value.** Here BV₉ = 8,00,000 − 7,20,000 = Rs 80,000 ✓. Depreciating the full cost gives BV₉ = 0, contradicting the stated salvage — which is option (b)'s error.
examTip.mnemonic: **BV_n = C − n(C−S)/L** — a straight line from C to S, which is what the name means. Options (a) and (d) are the right method at the wrong YEAR (six and four), so read n carefully.

questions.stem: In network analysis, the FREE FLOAT of an activity is the time by which the activity can be delayed:
options: Without affecting the project duration in any way
Without affecting the total float of any other activity
Beyond its own earliest finish time, using up the head event's slack
Without delaying the EARLIEST START of any following activity
questions.solution:
**Without delaying the EARLIEST START of any following activity.**

**The three floats, defined precisely:**

> **Let an activity run from event i (tail) to event j (head), with duration t, and let E and L be the earliest and latest event times.**

| Float | Formula | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **TOTAL float** | **L_j − E_i − t** | **Delay possible WITHOUT DELAYING THE PROJECT** |
| **FREE float** | **E_j − E_i − t** | **Delay possible without disturbing the EARLIEST START of the following activity** ← |
| **INDEPENDENT float** | **E_j − L_i − t** (taken as zero if negative) | **Delay possible with NO effect on either the preceding or the following activity** |

> **The ordering is always:  INDEPENDENT ≤ FREE ≤ TOTAL float.**

> **And the difference between them lies entirely in what is ASSUMED about the neighbours.**

**The distinction stated in words, which is what the question tests:**

> **TOTAL float uses the LATEST time of the head event — it assumes the following activities may be pushed as late as the project allows.**

> **FREE float uses the EARLIEST time of the head event — it assumes the following activities will start AS EARLY AS POSSIBLE, and asks how much delay is available without disturbing that.**

> **INDEPENDENT float assumes the WORST on both sides: the preceding activity finishes as late as it can, and the following one must still start as early as it can.**

> **So the three floats answer three different practical questions, and confusing them leads to real scheduling errors.**

**Why FREE float is the one a site manager actually uses:**

> **TOTAL float is often described as "the delay the project can absorb", and that is correct — but consuming it has a consequence the formula hides.**

> **When an activity uses up its TOTAL float, the float of every activity on the same chain behind it is REDUCED.**

> **So total float is SHARED along a chain: it is not the property of one activity, and two activities on the same path cannot both use it.**

> **FREE float, by contrast, belongs to the activity ALONE. Consuming it disturbs nothing** — the successors still start at their earliest times, and no other activity's float changes.

> **Which is why free float is the safe float: a manager who delays an activity within its free float has made a decision affecting nobody else.**

> **A manager who delays it within its total float but beyond its free float has silently borrowed time from activities further down the chain**, and may find later that a supposedly flexible activity has become critical.

> **Option (b) is a well-made distractor for exactly this reason: it describes something CLOSE to the truth about free float — consuming free float does not reduce another activity's total float — but it states the property rather than the definition, and the definition is what the question asks for.**

**Why option (c) is wrong, and instructively so:**

> **Option (c) describes float measured against the HEAD EVENT'S SLACK, which is a different quantity.**

> **HEAD EVENT SLACK = L_j − E_j.  TAIL EVENT SLACK = L_i − E_i.**

> **And the floats relate to them:**

> **FREE float = TOTAL float − HEAD EVENT SLACK**

> **INDEPENDENT float = FREE float − TAIL EVENT SLACK**

> **So the slacks are the amounts by which the floats differ, which is a neat way to remember the hierarchy:**

> **Start with TOTAL float, subtract the head slack to get FREE float, subtract the tail slack to get INDEPENDENT float.**

> **Which also shows why the three coincide on the CRITICAL PATH: there all slacks are zero and all floats are zero.**

**A worked illustration, since the formulae are abstract:**

> **Take an activity i-j with t = 4, E_i = 10, L_i = 12, E_j = 18, L_j = 22.**

| Float | Computation | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **TOTAL** | **22 − 10 − 4** | **8** |
| **FREE** | **18 − 10 − 4** | **4** |
| **INDEPENDENT** | **18 − 12 − 4** | **2** |
| Head event slack | 22 − 18 | 4 |
| Tail event slack | 12 − 10 | 2 |

> **Check: FREE = TOTAL − head slack = 8 − 4 = 4** ✓

> **Check: INDEPENDENT = FREE − tail slack = 4 − 2 = 2** ✓

> **And the interpretation: this activity can slip 4 days affecting nobody; 8 days without delaying the project but eating into the chain behind it; and 2 days even if its predecessor finishes as late as possible.**

**The two other floats sometimes met, for completeness:**

| Float | Formula | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **INTERFERING float** | **TOTAL − FREE = head event slack** | **The part of total float whose use INTERFERES with successors** |
| Safety float | **L_j − L_i − t** | Assumes a late start for the predecessor and a late finish for the successor |

> **INTERFERING float is a useful name for the dangerous part of total float: the days that can be used only by pushing successors later than their earliest start.**

> **So a complete float statement for the example above reads: 4 days free, 4 days interfering, 8 days total.** Presenting it that way makes the trade explicit, which a single total-float figure never does.

**Why this matters for the CRITICAL PATH itself:**

> **The CRITICAL PATH is the chain of activities with ZERO total float** — the longest path through the network, and the one that determines the project duration.

> **An activity with zero total float necessarily has zero free and independent float too, since free and independent floats cannot exceed the total.**

> **So a delay to ANY critical activity delays the whole project, day for day** — which is why critical activities receive the management attention, the resources and the contingency.

> **And the corollary that is often neglected: as float is consumed elsewhere, NEW critical paths appear.** A network's critical path is not a fixed feature of the project but a property of its current schedule, and it must be recomputed as work proceeds.

examTip.trick: **FREE float = E_j − E_i − t** — it uses the head event's EARLIEST time, so it is the delay available without disturbing the following activity's earliest start. Total float uses L_j instead.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) states a true PROPERTY of free float rather than its definition** — a good distractor. And option (c) describes measurement against the head event's SLACK, which is the DIFFERENCE between total and free float, not free float itself.
examTip.mnemonic: **TOTAL − head slack = FREE; FREE − tail slack = INDEPENDENT.** And free float is the SAFE float: it belongs to the activity alone, whereas total float is SHARED along a chain and borrowing it silently reduces everyone else's.

questions.stem: The whole circle bearing of a line is 208° 30'. Its reduced bearing is:
questions.solution:
**S 28° 30' W.**

**The conversion rule by quadrant:**

| WCB range | Quadrant | Reduced bearing |
|---|---|---|
| **0° to 90°** | **NE** | **N θ E** — RB = WCB |
| **90° to 180°** | **SE** | **S (180° − WCB) E** |
| **180° to 270°** | **SW** | **S (WCB − 180°) W** ← 208° 30' |
| **270° to 360°** | **NW** | **N (360° − WCB) W** |

**The computation:**

> **208° 30' lies between 180° and 270°, so the quadrant is SOUTH-WEST.**

> **RB = 208° 30' − 180° = 28° 30'**

> **So the reduced bearing is S 28° 30' W** ✓

**Why the quadrant must be identified FIRST:**

> **All four options carry the same angle, 28° 30'. Only the LETTERS differ.**

> **So the arithmetic is trivial and the quadrant is the entire question** — a deliberately constructed option set that gives no credit for the subtraction alone.

> **The reliable method is to picture the compass rather than recall the table:**

> **North is 0°, East 90°, South 180°, West 270°.**

> **208° 30' is a little PAST SOUTH, turning toward WEST. So the line points into the SOUTH-WEST quadrant, and the bearing is measured from SOUTH toward WEST: S 28° 30' W.**

> **Sketching the direction takes five seconds and cannot be misremembered, whereas the four-row table can.**

**The two systems, and why both exist:**

| System | Also called | Measured from | Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| **WHOLE CIRCLE BEARING (WCB)** | **AZIMUTH** | **NORTH only, clockwise** | **0° to 360°** |
| **REDUCED BEARING (RB)** | **QUADRANTAL bearing** | **The NEARER of North or South, toward East or West** | **0° to 90°, with two letters** |

> **The prismatic compass reads WHOLE CIRCLE bearings directly; the surveyor's compass reads QUADRANTAL bearings.**

> **That is the historical reason both systems survive — they correspond to two instruments** — and the conversion is needed whenever data from one are used with the other.

> **A further practical distinction worth knowing:**

| | **Prismatic compass** | **Surveyor's compass** |
|---|---|---|
| **Graduated ring** | **Attached to the NEEDLE (moves with it)** | **Attached to the BOX (moves with the sight)** |
| **Graduations** | **0-360°, WCB** | **0-90° in four quadrants, RB** |
| **Zero at** | **SOUTH end of the needle** | **North and South** |
| **Read through** | **A prism, while sighting** | **Directly from above, after sighting** |
| **E and W on the ring** | — | **INTERCHANGED, so that readings come out correct** |

> **The interchange of East and West on a surveyor's compass ring is the detail that surprises everyone and has a clean explanation: the ring is fixed to the BOX and the needle points north while the box turns**, so the graduations must be reversed for the needle to read the correct quadrant letter.

> **And the prismatic compass's zero at the SOUTH end of the needle exists so that the reading taken at the observer's eye — looking at the FAR side of the ring — is the bearing of the LINE OF SIGHT rather than its reverse.**

**FORE and BACK bearings, since bearing problems usually continue there:**

> **The BACK bearing of a line differs from its fore bearing by exactly 180°:**

> **BB = FB + 180° if FB < 180°;  BB = FB − 180° if FB > 180°**

> **For this line: BB = 208° 30' − 180° = 28° 30' — a whole circle bearing of 28° 30', or N 28° 30' E in reduced form.**

> **Note that the back bearing's reduced form is option (a)** — which is why that option is present, and it is a good distractor because it is the reduced bearing of the same line measured the other way.

> **In reduced-bearing form, the back bearing keeps the same ANGLE and REVERSES BOTH LETTERS: S 28° 30' W becomes N 28° 30' E.** That rule is simpler than the whole-circle one and is worth using.

**Why the fore-and-back check matters in practice:**

> **If FB and BB of a line do NOT differ by exactly 180°, something is wrong — and the discrepancy tells you what:**

| Finding | Diagnosis |
|---|---|
| **The difference is 180° at every station** | **The traverse is clean** |
| **The difference departs from 180° at ONE pair of stations only** | **LOCAL ATTRACTION at one of those two stations — iron, rails, a fence, a vehicle** ← |
| **The difference departs at MANY stations** | Instrument error, or an observational blunder |

> **LOCAL ATTRACTION is the classic compass-survey defect, and the fore-and-back comparison is how it is detected: a station affected by nearby iron gives readings deflected by a constant amount, so the lines radiating from it are all in error while the rest of the traverse is sound.**

> **The correction procedure is to find a station where the difference IS exactly 180° — an unaffected station — and correct outward from it**, adjusting each affected station's bearings by its own deflection.

> **Which is a good illustration of a general surveying principle: a redundant measurement is worth taking not because it improves precision but because it LOCATES the error.** A traverse with only fore bearings would contain the same local attraction and give no sign of it.

examTip.trick: **208° 30' lies between 180° and 270°, so the quadrant is SOUTH-WEST: RB = WCB − 180° = 28° 30', giving S 28° 30' W.**
examTip.trap: **All four options carry the SAME angle 28° 30' — only the letters differ**, so the quadrant is the whole question. Sketch the compass: 208° is just past SOUTH turning toward WEST. Option (a) is the BACK bearing's reduced form.
examTip.mnemonic: **In reduced form the back bearing keeps the angle and REVERSES BOTH LETTERS** — S 28° 30' W becomes N 28° 30' E. And if FB and BB fail to differ by 180° at just one pair of stations, suspect LOCAL ATTRACTION there.

questions.stem: In estimating the quantity of brickwork in the walls of a building, the CENTRE LINE METHOD is preferred over the long wall–short wall method because:
options: It gives a larger and therefore safer quantity
It is the only method permitted by IS 1200
It requires no deduction for openings such as doors and windows
A single continuous length serves for all walls of the same thickness, with a deduction only at each junction
questions.solution:
**A single continuous centre-line length serves for all walls of the same thickness, with a deduction only at each junction.**

**How the centre line method works:**

> **The total length of the CENTRE LINE of all the walls of one thickness is measured as a single continuous figure.**

> **Quantity = total centre-line length × thickness × height**

> **The elegance is that the centre line runs continuously around the building, so the projections and recesses at the corners cancel automatically** — the extra length on the outside of a corner exactly balances the shortfall on the inside.

> **No separate treatment of "long walls" and "short walls" is required, and the arithmetic is a single multiplication rather than two sets.**

**Why the JUNCTION deduction is nevertheless needed — the one complication:**

> **At a corner (an L-junction between two walls of the same thickness) the centre lines simply meet, and no correction arises.**

> **But at a T-JUNCTION or a CROSS-JUNCTION, where a partition meets a main wall, the centre line of the partition is measured right up to the centre line of the main wall — counting a length that the main wall already occupies.**

> **So a deduction is required:**

> **DEDUCT half the thickness of the main wall, at EACH junction, from the length of the wall that meets it.**

> **Equivalently, and the way it is usually applied: deduct (thickness/2) × the number of junctions.**

> **For a partition wall meeting main walls at both ends, that means deducting the full thickness once — half at each end.**

**A worked illustration, since the rule is easier seen than stated:**

> **Take a room 4 m × 3 m internally, with 230 mm walls, plus a central 115 mm partition running across the 3 m direction.**

| Step | Computation |
|---|---|
| **Centre-line length of the 230 mm external walls** | **Add half a wall thickness on each side: (4 + 0.23) and (3 + 0.23), so perimeter = 2(4.23 + 3.23) = 14.92 m** |
| **230 mm wall quantity (height 3 m)** | **14.92 × 0.23 × 3 = 10.29 m³** |
| **Centre-line length of the 115 mm partition** | **From centre line to centre line of the main walls = 3 + 0.23 = 3.23 m** |
| **Deduct at TWO T-junctions: 2 × (0.230/2)** | **− 0.23 m → 3.00 m** ← |
| **115 mm partition quantity** | **3.00 × 0.115 × 3 = 1.035 m³** |

> **Note that the deduction brought the partition length to exactly 3.00 m, which is its true clear length between the faces of the main walls plus their halves — the physically correct figure.**

> **Which is the check on the method: after the junction deduction, the length should equal what a tape laid along the wall would measure.**

**Why the other options are wrong — each is a real misconception:**

| Option | Why wrong |
|---|---|
| **(a) Gives a larger, safer quantity** | **Both methods give the SAME quantity when applied correctly.** An estimate is not made safe by being wrong upward — it is a price, and inflating it loses the tender |
| **(b) The only method permitted by IS 1200** | **IS 1200 governs the MODE OF MEASUREMENT — what is measured and what is deducted — NOT which arithmetic route is used to arrive at the length. Both methods are acceptable** |
| **(c) No deduction for openings** | **FALSE and important. Openings are deducted in EVERY method** — the centre line method changes how LENGTHS are computed, not what is deducted for doors and windows |

> **Option (a) deserves the emphasis it gets, because "safer" estimating is a genuine professional error.**

> **An estimate exists to predict a cost. An inflated estimate is not conservative — it is INACCURATE, and it costs the estimator the work.**

> **Contingency and risk are handled by an explicit CONTINGENCY ITEM, usually 3 to 5 per cent, not by quietly overstating quantities.** Burying a margin inside the measurements makes it invisible, unauditable and impossible to release when the risk does not materialise.

**When the LONG WALL–SHORT WALL method is still preferable:**

> **The centre line method's advantage disappears when the walls are of DIFFERENT THICKNESSES, because a separate centre-line length must then be computed for each thickness with its own junction deductions.**

| Situation | Preferred method |
|---|---|
| **All walls the same thickness, a simple rectangular plan** | **CENTRE LINE — fastest and least error-prone** ← |
| **Walls of several different thicknesses** | Either; centre line applied thickness by thickness |
| **An irregular plan with many recesses and projections** | **LONG WALL-SHORT WALL, or CROSSING (individual wall) method — easier to check** |
| **Circular or curved plan** | **CENTRE LINE — the only practical route, using the mean radius** |
| **A verification of someone else's estimate** | **The OTHER method — an independent route to the same figure** |

> **The last row is worth adopting as a habit: computing a quantity by BOTH methods and comparing is the cheapest possible check on an estimate**, since the two routes share no arithmetic and an error in one will not be reproduced in the other.

> **And for a CIRCULAR building the centre line method is not merely convenient but essentially the only sensible approach: the mean circumference at the wall's centre line, times thickness times height, gives the volume directly** — where a long wall–short wall treatment has no meaning at all.

**A note on what IS 1200 does govern, since option (b) invites the confusion:**

| IS 1200 rule for brickwork | Note |
|---|---|
| **Measured in m³ for walls above a nominal thickness** | Thin partitions measured in m² |
| **Openings DEDUCTED, measured over the opening size** | **No deduction for openings below a stated small area in some items** |
| **No deduction for bearings of joists, beams or lintels below a stated size** | The rule saves pointless arithmetic |
| **Measured NET as fixed in place** | Not as ordered or as delivered |

> **"Measured NET as fixed in place" is the governing principle of the whole standard**, and it is why wastage, breakage and over-ordering are priced into the RATE rather than measured in the QUANTITY — which is the same separation of concerns as keeping contingency out of the measurements.

examTip.trick: **One continuous centre-line length covers all walls of the same thickness** — corner projections and recesses cancel automatically — **with a deduction of half the main wall's thickness at each T- or cross-junction.**
examTip.trap: **Option (c) is false and important: openings are deducted in EVERY method.** The centre line method changes how LENGTHS are computed, not what is deducted for doors and windows.
examTip.mnemonic: **"Safer" estimating is a professional error** — an inflated estimate is inaccurate, and it loses the tender. Risk goes in an explicit CONTINGENCY item (3-5 %), never buried in the quantities. And computing by BOTH methods is the cheapest check there is.

questions.stem: The principal advantage of the TRIAXIAL compression test over the direct shear test is that:
options: It is quicker and requires simpler apparatus
The drainage conditions and the pore water pressure can be controlled and measured
It can be performed on a much smaller sample
The failure plane is predetermined by the apparatus
questions.solution:
**The drainage conditions and the pore water pressure can be CONTROLLED and MEASURED.**

**Why that matters more than anything else in a shear test:**

> **The shear strength of a soil is governed by the EFFECTIVE stress, not the total stress:**

> **τ = c' + σ' tan φ'  where  σ' = σ − u**

> **So a shear test tells you the soil's real strength parameters ONLY if you know the PORE WATER PRESSURE u.**

> **The triaxial apparatus can:**

| Capability | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **SEAL the specimen in a rubber membrane** | **Drainage happens ONLY through the valves the operator controls** ← |
| **Open or close the drainage valves at will** | **Unconsolidated-undrained, consolidated-undrained or consolidated-drained conditions can each be imposed** |
| **MEASURE the pore pressure through a transducer at the base** | **Effective stresses are known at every instant** |
| **Apply a BACK PRESSURE** | Saturates the specimen fully, so measured pore pressures are meaningful |
| **Measure VOLUME CHANGE during consolidation and drained shear** | Gives the volumetric behaviour, not just the strength |

> **The DIRECT SHEAR box can do NONE of this.** The specimen sits between porous stones in an open box, water can enter or leave freely at the top and bottom, and no pore pressure can be measured.

> **So a direct shear test on a clay gives a result whose drainage condition is uncertain — somewhere between drained and undrained, depending on the rate of shearing and nobody's control.**

> **That is the fundamental reason the triaxial test is the reference method for anything but free-draining sand.**

**Why option (a) is the reverse of the truth:**

> **The DIRECT SHEAR test is the quicker and simpler one — that is ITS advantage, not the triaxial's.**

| | **Direct shear** | **Triaxial** |
|---|---|---|
| **Apparatus** | **Simple shear box** | **Cell, pressure system, transducers, membrane** |
| **Time for a test** | **Minutes to hours** | **Hours to WEEKS for a consolidated drained test on clay** |
| **Skill required** | Modest | **High** |
| **Cost per test** | Low | **Several times higher** |
| **Drainage control** | **NONE** | **FULL** ← |
| **Pore pressure measurement** | **NOT possible** | **Possible** |
| **Stress distribution on the failure plane** | **NON-UNIFORM** | **Reasonably uniform** |
| **Failure plane** | **FORCED — the horizontal plane of the box** | **FREE — the specimen fails on its weakest plane** |
| **Suits** | **Sands, and routine work** | **Clays, research, and design parameters** |

> **So the two tests trade cost and speed against control**, and the direct shear box survives precisely because it is cheap and quick enough for routine sand testing where drainage is not an issue anyway.

**Why option (d) is wrong AND is an advantage of the OTHER test:**

> **A predetermined failure plane is a DISADVANTAGE, not an advantage — and it belongs to the direct shear test.**

> **In a shear box the soil is FORCED to fail along the horizontal plane where the two halves separate, whether or not that is the soil's weakest plane.**

> **The measured strength is therefore the strength ON THAT PLANE, which may exceed the true minimum.**

> **In a triaxial test the specimen fails wherever it is weakest, typically on a plane inclined at about (45° + φ/2) to the horizontal** — which is the theoretically correct orientation and gives the genuine minimum strength.

> **There IS one case where a forced failure plane is deliberately wanted: measuring the RESIDUAL strength along a pre-existing slip surface, or testing the interface between soil and a structure.** For that purpose the shear box — or better, the RING SHEAR apparatus — is the right instrument, because the plane is known and the displacement can be made large.

> **So the option is not merely wrong; it inverts which test it describes and whether the feature is a merit.**

**The three triaxial test types, since the drainage control is the point:**

| Test | Consolidation | Shearing | Gives | Represents |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **UU (unconsolidated undrained)** | **Drainage CLOSED** | **Drainage CLOSED** | **c_u, φ_u ≈ 0 for saturated clay** | **RAPID loading; short-term stability** |
| **CU (consolidated undrained)** | **Drainage OPEN — allowed to consolidate** | **Drainage CLOSED, pore pressure MEASURED** | **c', φ' (from measured u) and c_cu, φ_cu** | **A soil consolidated under its load then loaded rapidly** |
| **CD (consolidated drained)** | **Drainage OPEN** | **Drainage OPEN, very SLOW** | **c', φ' directly** | **LONG-TERM stability; slow loading** |
