> **The CU test with pore pressure measurement is the most useful single test in practice**, because it yields the effective stress parameters in a fraction of the time a CD test would take on a clay.

> **A CD test on a low-permeability clay may need WEEKS of shearing — the rate must be slow enough that no excess pore pressure develops anywhere in the specimen** — which is why it is uncommon in commercial testing.

> **And the UU test's result for saturated clay is the one that surprises: φ_u = 0, so the strength is a single number c_u independent of the confining pressure.**

> **The reason is that increasing the cell pressure on a sealed saturated specimen raises the PORE pressure by the same amount, leaving the effective stress unchanged** — so the strength cannot change either. That is a clean and complete explanation, and it is why the undrained strength of a clay is quoted as a single value.

**The other shear tests, for context:**

| Test | Note |
|---|---|
| **Unconfined compression** | **A triaxial test with zero cell pressure; quick, gives c_u = q_u/2** |
| **VANE SHEAR** | **IN SITU undrained strength of soft clay; no sample disturbance** |
| **RING SHEAR** | **Unlimited displacement — the only way to reach true RESIDUAL strength** |
| **Direct simple shear** | Uniform strain, no forced plane; used in research |

> **The VANE SHEAR test earns its place for a reason worth noting: soft sensitive clay is so disturbed by sampling that a laboratory test underestimates its strength badly.** Testing it in place, without ever removing it, avoids the whole problem — which is the general argument for in-situ testing.

examTip.trick: **The triaxial test's advantage is CONTROL and MEASUREMENT of drainage and pore pressure** — which is what lets effective stress parameters c' and φ' be determined. A shear box can do neither.
examTip.trap: **Options (a) and (d) both describe the DIRECT SHEAR test, and (d) describes a DISADVANTAGE as if it were a merit.** A forced failure plane may not be the soil's weakest, so it overstates the strength.
examTip.mnemonic: **UU: both closed (short-term). CU: consolidate open, shear closed with u measured (the most useful test). CD: both open, very slow (long-term).** And φ_u = 0 for saturated clay because raising the cell pressure raises u equally, leaving σ' unchanged.

questions.stem: A soap bubble of 50 mm diameter has an internal pressure in excess of the outside pressure of 20 N/m². The surface tension of the soap film is:
questions.solution:
**0.125 N/m.**

**The relation for a SOAP BUBBLE:**

> **Δp = 8σ / d**

> **The coefficient 8 — not 4 — is the entire content of this question, and the reason is that a soap bubble has TWO surfaces.**

**The computation:**

> **d = 50 mm = 0.05 m**

> **20 = 8σ / 0.05**

> **σ = 20 × 0.05 / 8 = 1.0 / 8 = 0.125 N/m** ✓

**The four cases, so the coefficient is never in doubt:**

| Body | Relation (diameter form) | σ from Δp = 20 N/m², d = 0.05 m |
|---|---|---|
| **Liquid JET (cylindrical)** | **Δp = 2σ/d** | **0.500 N/m** — option (a) |
| **DROPLET (one surface)** | **Δp = 4σ/d** | **0.250 N/m** — option (b) |
| **SOAP BUBBLE (TWO surfaces)** | **Δp = 8σ/d** | **0.125 N/m** ← ✓ |
| **The 8σ/d coefficient misapplied to the RADIUS** | Δp = 8σ/r | **0.0625 N/m** — option (c) |

> **Every distractor is therefore a specific, identifiable confusion: the jet formula, the droplet formula, or the diameter-form coefficient applied to the radius.**

> **Note the last one particularly, because it is the commonest slip: Δp = 8σ/d and Δp = 4σ/r are THE SAME relation, and using 8σ/r halves the answer.**

**Getting the coefficient right — the derivation, so it need not be memorised:**

> **Consider half a bubble, cut through its equator. Two forces balance:**

> **The PRESSURE force pushing the hemisphere outward: Δp × πd²/4**, acting on the projected circular area.

> **The SURFACE TENSION force holding it together, acting around the circumference of length πd.**

| Body | Tension force | Balance | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| **DROPLET — ONE surface** | **σ × πd** | **Δp πd²/4 = σπd** | **Δp = 4σ/d** |
| **SOAP BUBBLE — TWO surfaces (inner and outer)** | **2 × σ × πd** | **Δp πd²/4 = 2σπd** | **Δp = 8σ/d** ← |

> **So the 8 is simply the 4 doubled, because a soap film has an INNER surface and an OUTER surface, each pulling with σ per unit length.**

> **A DROPLET of water has only ONE surface — the interface between water and air — because its interior is liquid throughout.**

> **A SOAP BUBBLE is a thin FILM with air on both sides, hence two interfaces.**

> **That physical distinction is the whole meaning of the coefficient, and deriving it from the hemisphere balance takes twenty seconds and cannot be misremembered.**

**The LIQUID JET case, since it gives the third coefficient:**

> **For a cylindrical jet, take a length L and cut it lengthwise:**

> **Pressure force = Δp × d × L** (the projected rectangular area)

> **Tension force = 2 × σ × L** (two edges along the cut)

> **Δp × dL = 2σL, so Δp = 2σ/d**

> **The coefficient is 2 rather than 4 because a cylinder is curved in only ONE direction, while a sphere is curved in two.**

**All of them are one equation — YOUNG-LAPLACE:**

> **Δp = σ (1/R₁ + 1/R₂)**, with R₁ and R₂ the two principal radii of curvature.

| Body | R₁, R₂ | Δp |
|---|---|---|
| **Sphere (droplet)** | **Both = r** | **σ(1/r + 1/r) = 2σ/r = 4σ/d** ✓ |
| **Cylinder (jet)** | **r and ∞** | **σ(1/r + 0) = σ/r = 2σ/d** ✓ |
| **Soap bubble** | Both = r, TWO surfaces | **2 × 2σ/r = 4σ/r = 8σ/d** ✓ |

> **So the whole family is recoverable from one equation plus the count of surfaces**, rather than being four separate facts available to be confused.

> **And it explains a physical observation: since Δp goes as 1/r, a SMALL bubble has a HIGHER internal pressure than a large one.**

> **Which is why, when two soap bubbles of different size are joined by a tube, the SMALL one deflates into the LARGE one** — the opposite of what most people predict, and a direct consequence of the relation used here.

**Why surface tension matters in civil engineering, since it can seem a curiosity:**

| Phenomenon | Role of surface tension |
|---|---|
| **CAPILLARY RISE in soil** | **h = 4σ cos θ/(ρgd) — the mechanism that lifts groundwater into the root zone, causing WATERLOGGING and frost heave** ← |
| **Apparent cohesion in damp sand** | **Meniscus tension between grains — why a sandcastle stands** |
| **Frost heave in pavements** | Capillary water drawn to the freezing front forms ice lenses |
| **Menisci in manometers** | A reading correction |
| **Air entrainment in concrete** | Bubble stability depends on film tension |
| **Soil suction and unsaturated shear strength** | Negative pore pressure adds to the effective stress |

> **The APPARENT COHESION of damp sand is the most striking everyday demonstration: DRY sand has no cohesion, SATURATED sand has none, and DAMP sand has enough to be moulded.**

> **The reason is that the cohesion comes from the MENISCI between grains — and a meniscus requires BOTH water and air to be present.**

> **Remove the air (saturate it) or remove the water (dry it) and the menisci vanish, taking the strength with them.**

> **That is why a sandcastle collapses when the tide comes in AND when it dries in the sun** — the same failure from opposite causes, and a genuinely instructive piece of soil mechanics dressed as a seaside observation.

> **It also carries a design warning: the apparent cohesion of a damp silty sand can hold a temporary excavation face vertical, and it will disappear the moment the material dries or is wetted.** A trench that stood overnight is not evidence that it will stand tomorrow.

examTip.trick: **A soap bubble has TWO surfaces, so Δp = 8σ/d** (a droplet has one: 4σ/d). Here σ = 20 × 0.05/8 = **0.125 N/m.**
examTip.trap: **Δp = 8σ/d and Δp = 4σ/r are the SAME relation** — applying the diameter coefficient 8 to the radius halves the answer, which is exactly option (c). Options (a) and (b) are the jet and droplet formulae.
examTip.mnemonic: **Derive it from a cut hemisphere: pressure on πd²/4 against tension around πd, DOUBLED for two films.** Or use YOUNG-LAPLACE Δp = σ(1/R₁+1/R₂), from which jet 2σ/d, droplet 4σ/d and bubble 8σ/d all follow.
